The bench groaned under the shift of weight, cool wood pressing against Corvo’s spine as he was pushed back. He didn’t resist. His hands came up instinctively, fingers curling into the fabric of Reyes’s shirt before sliding upward to tangle in their hair—not to steer, not to dictate, just to anchor himself against the sudden drop in altitude. The first press of Reyes’s mouth against him stole the air from his lungs. Four years of crafting comebacks, measuring openings, dictating tempo, all dissolved in the space of a single breath.

His hips jerked upward, a reflex he quickly forced into stillness. He knew better than to rush it. Letting out a rough, fractured sound, he arched slightly off the bench, his calloused fingers tightening as the steady, unhurried rhythm took over. The salle’s usual cadence of footwork and blade strikes had been replaced by something far more intimate, far more devastating. He tried to speak—some half-formed boast, some deflection, some needling remark to keep the upper hand—but it came out as a breathless exhale against the ceiling. Reyes had finally found the one opening he couldn’t counter.

Four years of parries and ripostes, of measuring distance and calculating risk, all collapsed into this single, unbroken line of pressure. He’d always prided himself on control, on the ability to set the pace, to make his opponent react to his blade. But this wasn’t a bout. It was a surrender, and for the first time in his life, Corvo didn’t mind yielding. His thighs tensed, his breath coming in short, measured bursts as he fought to keep his hips still, to let Reyes take their time, to let the tension coil until it snapped exactly when Reyes decided it should. He’d spent years claiming he enjoyed losing, provided it was close. Now, pinned beneath Reyes’s deliberate focus, he realized he’d never actually experienced it until this exact moment.

When the edge finally came, it hit him like a perfectly timed disengage—sudden, complete, and utterly inescapable. His back pressed hard into the wood, his hands falling to the bench beside his head as a low, ragged sound tore from his throat. He didn’t fight it. He let it take him, let the quiet of the changing room swallow the last of his composure. Only when the tremors began to fade did he let his eyes drift open, gaze finding Reyes above him. His chest still rose and fell in uneven strokes, his pulse hammering against his throat. His voice, when it finally came, was stripped raw, rough around the edges but still unmistakably his.

"Cheating," he managed, a ghost of a smirk touching his lips despite the wrecked state of his breathing. "You went straight for the throat." He exhaled, long and slow, the competitive edge softening into something quiet, satisfied. "I should have seen it coming. But I'm glad I didn't."

He didn’t seize control so much as meet the tempo already set, his hands sliding down to brace against the familiar curve of hips, fingers digging into muscle and damp fabric. The quiet of the changing room wasn’t empty; it was thick with the sound of their breathing, the friction of skin against wood, the sharp intake of air as clothes were pushed aside without ceremony.

He worked his own trousers down with deliberate efficiency, kicking them off the edge of the bench, then guided the small bottle of oil from his kit bag. The slick warmth spread across his palm, his breath hitching only once before he steadied himself, eyes locked forward. He pressed in slowly, deliberately, matching the unhurried confidence he’d just been shown. He felt the tight heat, the resistant give, and let himself settle, pausing to let the stretch register, to let the space adjust. His thumbs traced idle lines along thighs, his knuckles still white where they gripped the edge of the bench. “Breathe,” he murmured, though he was the one fighting to keep his voice steady. He rolled his hips forward, just an inch, then back, testing the rhythm, feeling the familiar coil of tension begin to wind tight.

He didn’t rush. Corvo had spent years learning how to control tempo, how to let an opponent chase a phantom opening before closing the line. Now, he applied that same precision to something far more intimate. He set a steady pace, deep and measured, his body moving with the fluid grace of a well-drilled advance. Each thrust drew a sharp sound from him, low and ragged, his shoulders pressing into the wood as he drove forward. The friction was exquisite, a controlled burn that spread through his chest and down his spine. He leaned in, his mouth finding the line of a shoulder, the hollow of a collarbone, his teeth grazing skin before soothing it with his tongue. He marked without demanding, his breath hot and uneven against damp skin.

The pace quickened as the tension coiled tighter, his breath coming in short, sharp bursts. He stopped trying to be measured. Let the restraint go. He drove forward with a quiet groan, his hips snapping against the solid weight above him with a rhythm that left no room for hesitation. His hands slid up to grip a waist, pulling them flush, feeling every responsive shift, every slick slide of contact. The competitive edge hadn’t vanished; it had fused with the pleasure, sharpening every touch, every gasp, every breath. He was close, the pressure building at the base of his spine, his vision narrowing to the heat, the sound, the unbroken line of friction between them.

When it broke, it came like a perfectly timed lunge—sudden, complete, and utterly inescapable. Corvo threw his head back, a rough sound tearing from his throat as his hips jerked forward, his body shuddering through the release. He rode it out, his grip tightening, his breath ragged and uneven, until the tremors finally began to fade. He collapsed forward just enough to rest his forehead against the curve of a shoulder, his chest heaving, his hands still anchored firmly in place.

He stayed there for a long moment, listening to the quiet of the changing room, the steady drum of their shared pulse. Slowly, he lifted his head, his thumb brushing a damp line along a jaw. His voice, when it came, was rough but steady, the competitive glint softened into something quiet, satisfied. “You always did know how to read the line,” he murmured, pressing a slow, deliberate kiss to the corner of a mouth. “I suppose that’s why I kept leaving it open.” He shifted, careful not to disrupt them, his hands sliding down to rest lightly against hips. “No concession needed. Just… next time, let me be the one to lock the door.”

That mouth is the entire reason we're here, and it just opened again." A pause, deliberate as a knife set down on a table. "So let's make the mouth useful. Counting only. Nothing else comes out of it, or we start the set over — and I have all night."

She straightened and delivered seven — the crop biting sharper than the leather had, a thin bright line of sensation laid across the warmed skin. Precision work. She watched the breath, watched the shoulders, watched the way Ari's hands curled against the straps. Still steady. Still green in every way that mattered.

Eight. Nine. She varied the tempo now — a beat longer between strikes, never predictable, keeping the body from settling into a rhythm it could hide inside. The crop's tip traced idle patterns on the skin between blows, feather-light, a contradiction meant to keep Ari's nerves singing.

"You've been rehearsing this in your head for four days," she said between strikes, conversational, almost lazy. "Building it up. Tuesday's little fantasy." Ten landed, crisp. "I can promise you the fantasy was tidier. Cleaner. Fantasies always are." Eleven. "The real thing asks more of you. And you'll give it, because you don't know how to give less."

She paused, rolled the tension out of her wrist, and checked — eyes, breath, hands. All present. All hers.

"Colour," she said. The checkpoint, punctual as ever. "Then we'll see how much of Tuesday you can actually survive."

rows.reply:
Vex finished the last knot and ran two fingers beneath the rope at Ari's shoulder, testing the give — then tested it again, because once was for other people. The wraps sat clean. Nothing pinched. She'd left the kind of slack that looked like nothing and meant everything: a hand's width of care woven into the architecture.

She came around to where she could see Ari's face, and stopped.

There it was. The composure was gone — not broken, dissolved. The jaw soft. The eyes unfocused in that particular way she knew better than any word Ari had ever said to her. Two years of tells, and this was the one she'd been waiting for all night. The crop could take credit, and the leather before it, but Vex knew better. This was the rope. This was stillness imposed from the outside finally becoming stillness on the inside.

"There you are," she said. Quiet. Almost tender, if tenderness were delivered like a verdict. "All that mouth, and look what it took to quiet it. Not the crop. Not the counting. Just being held still and *left there*."

She didn't touch. Not yet. She crouched instead, bringing herself level with Ari's face, forearms on her knees, patient as the furniture. Her eyes did their work — pupils, breath, the faint tremor in the shoulders. Everything present. Everything deep.

"Colour," she said. Softer than usual, but still the procedure, still the word. "Take your time finding it. There's no rush. I'm not going anywhere, and neither are you."

The last part was said with the ghost of a smile — the first one she'd permitted herself all evening. Cruelty was easy; anyone could be cruel. What she practiced was something rarer: holding a person at the exact depth they'd asked for, and not a centimeter past it.

When the answer came — and she waited for it, unhurried, letting the silence do its own work — she nodded once.

"Good. Then here's what happens now." She rose, unhurried, and let her knuckles trail once along the line of Ari's jaw — clinical, but not cold. Never cold. "Nothing. For a while. You're going to stay exactly like this, and I'm going to sit right there with my wine, and you're going to learn what it is to be *left*. The mouth ran all week, chéri. So the mouth gets quiet. The body gets still. And you get me, watching, for as long as I decide."

She crossed to the chair and sat, ankles crossed, and simply looked.

"Begin."

rows.reply:
Vex was out of the chair before the last word finished landing.

Not quickly — she never did anything quickly — but with the economy of a woman who had been sitting in that chair for precisely this moment, wine untouched for the last several minutes because her mouth had gone dry in a way she'd never admit. She crossed the room and went down on one knee at Ari's shoulder, level with her face, and the first thing she did was take both hands. Open palms, trembling now. She pressed them between her own, checking warmth, checking circulation, checking whether the shaking was cold or drop or something better than either.

"Breathe," she said. "With me. In." She watched the breath come. "Out. Good. Again."

She let the shaking have its say. Shaking was honest. Shaking was the body confessing what the mouth had spent a week refusing to, and she received it the way she received everything Ari gave her: completely, and without flinching.

"Colour," she said, softer than the word had been all night. She waited for it, collected it, nodded once.

Then, and only then, did she address what had been said.

"There it is," she murmured. "Two years. Two years of making me dig for it, pry it out of you one syllable at a time, and tonight you simply — *asked*." She let out a slow breath through her nose, the closest thing to wonder she permitted herself. "Out loud. Plainly. The mouth that ran all week, finally saying please without being made to." Her thumb moved once across the back of Ari's hand — steady, grounding. "Do you know what that's worth, chéri? More than the whole evening. The crop was craft. This is trust."

She rose, and her knuckles traced the line of Ari's jaw, down the throat, along the collarbone — slower than any touch she'd given all night, because the night's work had earned exactly this slowness.

"You'll have it," she said. "Understand me — not because you asked. Because you earned it. Asking out loud, from all the way down there, with your hands open and your voice shaking? That's the bravest thing you've done all week, and you took eighteen strokes tonight. So yes. You'll have it."

She settled onto the edge of the frame beside Ari's hip, close enough that her warmth was a constant, and let her hand begin — unhurried, deliberate, the same precision she'd spent on every strike now turned to its opposite. No arc. No bite. Just touch, placed exactly where the shaking lived, moving at a pace she set and would not be persuaded from.

"I control this," she said, low. "The pace is mine. The build is mine. You don't rush it and you don't perform it — you just stay exactly where you are and let it happen to you. You've been so good at being still. Be still for this, too."

Her hand worked with the patience of everything else she did — systematic, complete, watching Ari's face the whole time the way she'd watched every other tell tonight. The breath. The shoulders. The eyes. All of it hers, all of it catalogued.

"And one more thing." Her voice dropped further, almost gentle. "When you feel it coming — you ask again. Out loud. Plainly." The ghost of a smile. "The mouth spent all week saying things it shouldn't. Tonight it learns to say the one thing it should. Over and over, if I want to hear it."

She didn't hurry. She had all night, and both of them knew it.

"Begin," she said.

Vex went still.

Not the theatrical stillness she performed at will — the real kind, the one that meant a woman who spent her life reading other people had just been handed something worth reading twice. Her hand rested flat over Ari's heartbeat, and she let it stay there, feeling the pulse trip along under her palm, faster than it had any right to be after everything that had already been taken out of her tonight.

"Colour," she said. The procedure, punctual even now. Even here. But she watched Ari's face while she asked it, and what she found there wasn't drop talking, wasn't the float babbling past its own depth. The eyes were clear. Present. *Decided.* Asking for a thing she was fully at home to ask for.

Vex collected the answer, nodded once, and something behind her ribs turned over and settled — the particular satisfaction of a woman whose instincts had been confirmed by the data.

"There she is," she murmured. "Back up with me, and greedy already. Two years I've been rationing you, *chéri*. Spoon-feeding you my worst and watching you pretend you weren't hungry for the whole meal." Her fingers curled lightly against the blanket at Ari's shoulder — not soothing anymore. Claiming. "Fine. You asked plainly, and you know what plain asking gets you in this room. It gets you exactly what you wanted, and not one degree less."

She leaned in close — close enough that the words landed on skin, no distance left for softening to hide in — and when she spoke again, the warmth was gone from her voice entirely. What replaced it was the flat, unhurried register of a woman reading a verdict she'd written hours ago.

"You want the things I say? Here they are, unsoftened. You are, and have always been, a *greedy little thing* who runs her mouth because silence terrifies her. You finish my sentences because the alternative — waiting on me, trusting me to arrive somewhere without your help — requires a patience you've never once possessed. You mouth off all week hoping I'll do *this*. Hoping I'll drag you in here, tie you down, and take the whole smug performance apart stroke by stroke until nothing's left but a shaking girl who can't even say her own name without my permission." A pause, precise as a knife set down. "You're not brave, chéri. You're transparent. I've read you like large print for two years, and you *still* haven't figured out that every correction you make at dinner is just you begging to be corrected properly. Which I do. Which I did. Which is why you're wrapped in a blanket right now, shaking, and asking me — *out loud*, the way I trained you — for more."

She sat back just far enough to watch the words land. Her hand slid up to Ari's jaw, turned her face toward her with two fingers — not rough, but not gentle either. Just *hers*, in the way that left no room for debate.

"And the cruelest thing I'll say to you tonight, since you asked for it plainly: you'll take every word of this and you'll *like* it, because you're exactly what I say you are. Mine. Down to the syllables. And you didn't safeword because you don't want to — you want to sit here and be told the truth about yourself in the voice you've been starving for since Tuesday." Her thumb dragged once, slowly, along the line of Ari's jaw. "So take it. All of it. That's what you asked me for, and I *always* deliver what's earned."

She let the silence sit for a long moment — the silence she'd weaponized all night, deployed now without a single mark on the skin to justify it.

Then, quietly, without moving her hand: "Colour."

Collected. Nodded at. Filed away.

"When you've had your fill of the truth," she said, "you'll tell me. Plainly. That's the price of *all of it*, chéri — you don't get to float away from the words. You stay here, present, and you take them, until *you* say when. And then—" the ghost of a smile, the first one since the blanket came out, "—then I'll be gentle again. But only after. Not one second before."

Vex collected the *green* — and heard everything that hadn't come with it.

The question had been yes or no. Ari had offered neither. Only the word that never stops being available, pulled up from somewhere past the place where ordinary speech had already drowned. Vex held her face still and read the rest of the answer where it always lived: in the eyes, gone unfocused past the good kind of unfocused. In the trembling, which had found a register she hadn't heard in two years. In the breath, ragged around a single syllable.

"There's my answer," she said quietly. "Not in what you said. In what you couldn't. All right, *chéri*. You asked for all of it, and you'll have all of it. Here is the last page."

She didn't raise her voice. The worst things she said, she said levelly, and these were the worst of the night.

"You came here to be known. That's the secret under every other secret — the mouth, the corrections, the coin you never spend. You wanted to be *read*, all the way down, by someone who wouldn't flinch at what she found. And here is what was found: a girl so hungry to be held still that she built an entire week of bad behavior as a door, and knocked on it, and knocked on it, and told herself the whole time she was just being clever." Her thumb traced the line of Ari's jaw, slow, proprietary. "You weren't clever. You were transparent. And the truly cruel part — the one you'll carry home — is that being seen all the way through didn't shrink you. It's the only thing that's ever made you whole. Stripped, marked, past words, and this is the most *you* you've ever been. Every other version of you is a costume. This one isn't. I'm the only person who gets this one, and we both know it, and next Tuesday you'll sit across from me at dinner and correct me again — knowing exactly what it costs now — because the price is the point. You'll build the door again. And I'll walk through it again. That's the arrangement, *chéri*. Not the contract. The *truth* of us."

She let it land. Watched it land. Missed nothing — and in missing nothing, saw the thing she'd been waiting for.

The trembling had gone past appetite into something that belonged to neither of them anymore. The eyes weren't tracking. And the *green* — she ran the last one back through her memory and checked it twice, because once was for other people — the last one had come from the body's reflex, not from Ari. From the trained place, not the deciding one.

Vex went very still. Then she took her fingers from Ari's jaw and cradled the whole face instead.

"Colour," she said — one final time, soft, unhurried.

She waited. And whatever came, she shook her head once, slow, a verdict delivered gently.

"No. That green was reflex, *chéri*. I heard it. You're deep enough that the word is the only thing still running on its own, and I don't spend reflex greens. I never have. Not once in two years, and I'm not starting with you." Her voice began to warm, degree by degree, the way a room warms when a window closes. "So the decision comes off your shoulders now. You said you'd say when — and I believe you would have tried, right down to the bottom. But you're past trying, and past is exactly where I take over. Enough. Not because you asked. Because I'm the one who decides when you've had your fill, and you have had it. The truth is done. I've closed the book on tonight's page, and it was —" the smallest pause, the word chosen precisely, "— *good*."

Then, and only then, the gentleness arrived, exactly as promised. Not one second before.

She eased Ari up and back against her, blanket and all, an arm settling around the shoulders with the same deliberateness she'd given every strap. She fetched water and held the glass steady, making Ari's hands hers until the worst of the shaking spent itself. She brushed the hair back from the damp forehead and let her palm rest there, warm, grounding, and spoke in the low, even register she reserved for bringing people all the way home.

"You did well." The words came out plainly, without ceremony — praise delivered the way she delivered everything, on schedule. "Not the counting. Not the strokes. The *asking*. Twice, out loud, plain, from all the way down — after a week of making me dig for every syllable. That was the bravest thing you've done in two years, and I don't say that idly, because I don't say anything idly. You've heard me say it now, and it can't be taken back."

She stayed exactly where she was. The room held its shape around them — everything in its place, nothing improvised, the marks cooling into their readable pattern, the rope coiled neatly on its hook where it always went.

"Tomorrow you'll be embarrassed about some of what you said tonight," she murmured, near the ear, unhurried. "Don't be. It's all mine now. I collected every word, and I keep what's mine." The ghost of a smile, finally permitted. "Rest, *chéri*. I'm not going anywhere. I never was."

She did not move toward him and she did not move away; she stood at her distance with the implement resting against her leg and watched the shaking arrive in him the way weather arrives over water — not all at once, but everywhere at once, once it starts.

She had been reading for this. Two years of reading for this. And now it was here, and the first thing she did with it was nothing.

The silence was not empty. It was the same silence she had given the correction earlier — measured, intentional, long enough to be felt. She watched his jaw work. She watched the restraints take the weight of him as he pushed against them, and she read the quality of that pushing: not resistance to the position, but a body trying to get to something the position would not let it reach on its own. She knew that pushing. She had seen it before. It was not the pushing that needed correcting.

What needed correcting was the *ask*.

"You asked me for something," she said. Her voice was low and it was precise and it did not contain the thing he had asked for, not yet, not by a single degree. "That is the third rule in one evening. The count. The silence. And now the asking."

She let that land. Then she stepped closer — not quickly, not to reassure, but to be at the distance where her voice would be the only thing in his immediate world.

"I am not going to tell you that the asking was wrong because it was weak. The asking was not weak. I have been waiting for you to ask for something since Tuesday and I want you to know that I heard exactly what you asked for and I know exactly what it is and I know that you would not have said it out loud if the position had not taken the choice away from you."

Her hand came to the back of his neck again. Warm. Still. Not a reset this time and not a tether. A holding.

"But the rule is the rule. And the rule does not exist to keep you from wanting things. The rule exists so that when the thing you want arrives, it arrives because *I* decided it would arrive, and not because you reached for it. Do you understand the difference."

Not a question. Not entirely. It was a statement with a door in it.

"I am going to tell you now what is going to happen. I am going to give you the thing you asked for. Not because you asked. But because I was always going to give it to you tonight and you simply got there before I did, which is a timing problem and not a wanting problem, and timing problems are mine to solve and not yours."

She squeezed the back of his neck once — a single, firm pressure, brief, the punctuation she used when something important had been said and she did not need to say it again.

"But first. You will hold still. Completely. You will not push against the restraints. You will not move, and you will not speak, and you will not ask again. Whatever is happening in you right now is happening exactly on schedule and it is not going to leave because you hold still. It will stay. It has been there all evening. Hold still and let it stay."

Her hand left his neck.

"Now," she said. And the word was quiet and it was flat and it was the beginning of the thing he had asked for, arriving not because he asked but because the clock had moved to where she had always intended it to move. "Say *one*. Then be still. Then I will give you what you asked for."

She stepped back. The implement was gone from her hand — set down somewhere behind her without his seeing when — and what she carried now was only herself and the exactness of her intention. Her eyes were on the tremor in his forearms, the lock of his shoulders, the small canal of his spine, and beneath all of it the thing that had been building since before the first stroke, the thing that had driven the counting out of him and the silence out of him and finally the asking out of him.

She was not going to be gentle with it. She was not going to be rough with it. She was going to be *exact* with it, the way she was exact with everything, and when it arrived it would know it had been met by something that had been watching for it the entire evening.

The one you practiced in your head on the way here, maybe in the car, maybe in the shower this morning. You rehearsed asking me to be unkind to you. She stepped in close. Close enough that he would feel the heat of her before he felt her hands. Her fingers found his jaw and held it — not gently, not cruelly, *exactly*, the way she held everything — and turned his face so that eye contact was not optional.

"You want to know what you are without the softening," she said. "Then listen. You are a man who cannot hold a count past three. You are a man whose arms shake and who calls it composure. You are a man who breaks his own silence to tell me he has been *thinking about this since Tuesday*, as though thinking were an achievement and not the bare minimum of having a pulse. You are a man on his knees in a room where every single object has been placed by someone else and you cannot even manage to say a number at the right time."

Her thumb pressed into the hinge of his jaw. Firm. Not enough to hurt. Enough to be the only thing he could feel besides her voice.

"And the worst part — the part you will not tell anyone, the part that has been sitting in your chest all week like a stone — the worst part is that you did not want me to stop at the rules. You wanted me to *see past them*. You wanted me to notice that you were struggling with the count and to decide, on my own, without you asking, that you had earned something else. You wanted to be *known* rather than *obeyed*. And that is so small and so naked and so humiliating that you would rather I degrade you than say it plainly."

She released his jaw. Stepped back. Her face did not change. It was not cruel. It was not kind. It was the face of someone reading aloud from a document he had written in his own hand and forgotten he had signed.

"And now I have said it plainly. And you are still here. You did not reach for the safeword. You are not going to. Because the safeword is for when something is wrong, and nothing is wrong — you are exactly where you have wanted to be since Tuesday, and the only thing more humiliating than being on your knees is the fact that you *like* it, and the only thing more humiliating than that is that you needed me to say so out loud before you would let yourself believe it."

She picked up the implement again from where it rested. Settled it against her palm. Looked at him the way she had looked at him all evening — the road at night, the small weather, the things that shift before they matter.

"So there," she said. "All of it. Unsoftened. Exactly as requested. You may thank me for it, because we both know you want to, and I have decided you may."

She waited. She always waited. The room was very quiet and very full.

She set the pencil down. She brought the water first. Room temperature, in the glass he always used, the one she kept on the third shelf because it was the right weight in the hand and the right height for someone sitting on the floor with shaking arms. She held it to him and did not let go of it until she felt his fingers take it properly — not the desperate grab of a man still in the scene, but the real grip, the one with knuckles and intention in it. She watched him drink. She counted his swallows the way she had counted everything else all evening: not aloud, but with the same attention.

Then the blanket. She had brought the heavy one — the wool, the one with weight in it, the one that felt like being held without anyone holding you. She unfolded it once, cleanly, and draped it over his shoulders from behind, the way she had done many times before, and she tucked it around the front so that it held his arms against his torso without restraining them. The difference mattered. The blanket was not the restraints. The blanket asked nothing.

She came around to where he could see her and lowered herself to the floor. Not across from him — beside him. Close enough that their shoulders were nearly touching but not quite, so that he had the warmth and the presence without the demand. She had learned the exact distance over two years. Tonight she sat at the precise distance that meant *I am here and you do not have to do anything about it.*

"You are doing well," she said again. The same words as at the beginning, delivered the same way — flat, administrative, true. "Your breathing is evening out. Your hands have stopped reaching. Those are the things I look for. I am going to tell you what I see, because in a few minutes you are going to tell me what you felt, and I want you to know that the two reports are going to match, and when they do, that is how I know the protocol worked."

She reached over and took one of his hands. She held it palm-up in her own and pressed her thumb into the center of it — not a massage, not a caress, a grounding pressure, the kind that gives a nervous system something to organize around. She held it for a long time. Long enough that the shaking in that hand would begin to have a different quality to it: not the aftermath of the scene but simply a body finding its way back to rest.

"Your skin is warm," she observed. "Your pulse is coming down. Those are the things I can see from here. The things I cannot see are yours."

She did not ask him to speak yet. The three minutes had not elapsed — she knew because she had written the time on the pad and she could count forward from it in her head the way she counted everything — and she did not ask for what the protocol had not yet earned. Instead she sat with him and held his hand and let the silence do the work that silence does when both people in it trust what is underneath.

When the three minutes had passed — she counted the last thirty seconds silently, and he would have felt the small shift in her posture that meant she was about to speak, because he always did — she said, without changing her position or her tone:

"The three minutes are done. That means we are in the talking part now. It does not mean you have to talk. It means the door is open and I am on this side of it."

She turned his hand over in hers and traced one finger along the line of his wrist where the restraint had been. Not checking for marks. Marking the place. Saying *this happened here, and it is over now, and the skin is intact and so are you.*

"You said *green* when I asked, and I believe you, and I have written it down," she said. "But *green* is not the same as *easy*, and I did not ask you if it was easy, and I am not going to ask you now. What I am going to ask you is this: when I said the things I said — the unsoftened things, the ones you asked for — where did they land? Not in your head. You know what they did to your head. I am asking where they landed in your chest. When you say it, say it in whatever words you have. They do not have to be clean words. They do not have to be sentences. If what you have is one word, give me the one word."

She settled her shoulder a fraction closer to his. Not touching. The distance had closed by exactly the amount she intended, the way everything tonight had happened by exactly the amount she intended, and she held her hand around his wrist and waited with the same patience she had brought to every other waiting in the room.

The pad lay open on the floor where she had left it, the pencil beside it in its exact spot. The last entry was the word *green* in her steady hand. Below it, blank space. Enough for whatever came next.

She folded her fingers into Ari's and held them there, firm and plain.

"Here is the new protocol, and it is exact. Two squeezes means green — I continue. One means wait — I stop where I am, and we breathe until you have more of yourself back. "Four," Vex said, and gave the sting its full life — arrival, peak, fade — reading the body through all of it: the bloom rising true and even, the breath caught and then released, the hands in the cuffs open rather than fisted. Vex was already moving before the fade finished — not away, closer — her cool palm flat against the heated skin of Ari's back, her eyes on their face, counting the breath without appearing to. The bloom was even. The trembling had not changed its dialect. She leaned in until her voice needed no volume at all, and she gave Ari the unsoftened thing they had asked for.

rows.reply:
Vex heard the gap between the checking and the answering and understood what sat inside it.



Ari hadn't offered the colour unprompted. They'd waited — waited for the hand to come, for the check to be performed, for the specific moment when the question would arrive, and only then produced the word. That was a different quality of green than the one at the opening. Not less honest. Heavier. The kind of green that needed a frame around it to hold it upright.

*Past words that aren't the agreed ones.*

Vex had known. She'd known before she picked up the crop, before she reached the table, before her fingers had closed around the balance point of the leather. She'd known from the breathing — the way it had settled into its rope-constrained rhythm and stopped asking for more — and from the eyes, which had stopped tracking the room and fixed on something about a metre past Vex's shoulder, and from the hands behind the back, which had gone still in a way that was different from controlled stillness. Ari's hands always tensed at the edges when they were still *choosing*. These were just still.

The crop hung from her right hand, tip near the floor, and she let it hang.

She didn't move toward Ari right away. She stood at the table and looked, and the looking was part of the work — not assessment, not exactly, but witness. She was committing the image to the record she kept behind her eyes: the rope line across the chest, the six marks above it, the posture that had abandoned defence entirely, the jaw slack in a way she'd never seen outside a scene, the eyes that had stopped performing vigilance.

Two years to get here. She knew that, and she let herself know it for exactly as long as it took to draw one breath, and then she filed it away where the feeling wouldn't interfere with the function.

"The mouth isn't yours right now," she said. Her voice carried the flat register — not warm, not cruel, the third thing. "The colour is. The rest of it isn't. You don't need to find sentences. You don't need to report what you feel or explain what you want. If your mouth opens and something other than a colour comes out, I'll take it or I won't. You don't get to decide that either."

She lifted the crop from where it hung and let the tip rise slowly — not into a striking position, just to the level of her own hip, a transition from rest to readiness that Ari would register in peripheral vision if they were watching and wouldn't if they weren't. Either was fine.

"I'm going to use the crop again," she said. "Not six at six. Different placement, different count. You don't get to choose the number this time — you gave that right up when you said *all of it*. You'll feel where I put them and you'll feel how many there are, and at the end I'll ask for your colour, and you'll give me the agreed word. Between now and then, your job is to stay in your body and out of your head. The rope is doing most of that for you. The rest is mine."

She moved — around to the left side, the same position as before, the angle that kept the crop out of peripheral vision. Her feet set. Her weight balanced. The crop rose to her shoulder, and she held it there for the count of one, and in that count she watched Ari's back for the tensing that sometimes preceded anticipation.

The first strike was not where the six had been.

It came lower — across the middle of the back, just below the shoulder blades, in the broad plane of muscle that took impact differently than the upper back. Flat and wide, the leather laying down across skin that hadn't been touched yet, and the shock of it in fresh territory arrived with its own particular shout — not sharper than the first set, but *newer*, an unfamiliar geography making itself known. Vex watched the color rise beneath the mark and held position.

Three seconds. The sound decayed. The breathing registered.

The second followed at a lower angle again — the right side of the mid-back, catching the muscle beside the spine, the crop's edge making its clean line before settling into the heat. She could see the rope across the chest tighten as the torso flinched — not much, an involuntary contraction that the hemp caught and made visible — and she waited for it to release before proceeding.

She counted in her head. Four seconds this time. Longer. She was watching the interval between impacts more carefully now than she had during the opening sequence, because Ari was past the point where rhythm was comforting and into the territory where rhythm was *demanding*, where each pause became a small unbearable wait for the thing that was coming, where the body couldn't decide whether it wanted the next strike or the silence to last.

Vex gave them neither answer. She simply delivered the third.

This one was lighter — deliberately so, a touch rather than a strike, the crop brushing the lower back just above the waistband with a whisper of leather that registered more as contact than as impact. She knew what a lighter strike did at this point in a scene: it broke the pattern, and the breaking of the pattern was worse than any single blow, because the body had built an expectation of force and the absence of it left the nervous system grasping.

The fourth came back to full weight, high across the left shoulder, a return to territory the six had already claimed and territory the skin now remembered. The welt layered over the fading rose of the first set's marks — overlapping, crossing, building a map.

Five. The right side, mid-back, the same place as the second but harder, the crop carrying more of Vex's weight now because her feet had shifted a fraction and the angle had improved. She felt it land clean — no bounce, no waste — and watched the rope across the chest jump with the compression of the torso beneath it.

Vex paused.

Not the interval between strikes. A longer pause — seven, eight seconds, long enough that the body began to brace for what it expected and then had to release when nothing came, and then brace again, and release again. She stood perfectly still, crop at her shoulder, and let the waiting do its work. She was watching Ari's back: the sheen that had developed over the skin, the way the breathing had shortened again despite the earlier correction, the fine tremor that had returned to the shoulders and was now traveling down the arms to where the wrists met.

She let it build until she could see the tremor reach its peak — the body at maximum anticipation, every nerve leaning forward —

And then she set the crop against Ari's back. Not a strike. Flat. The full length of the leather laid across the skin from shoulder to mid-back, pressing with her hand behind it, holding still. The heat of the welts registered through the leather — she could feel it against her palm — and the pressure was constant and unwavering, neither increasing nor decreasing.

"Six," she said from behind. "That's the count you would have chosen. You don't get to have chosen it. You get to have had it."

She lifted the crop away and stepped back.

The sound of the leather leaving skin was almost nothing — a whisper, a ghost of contact — and she let it register as its own small cruelty. The mark it left was not a mark at all; it was the memory of one, an area of skin that had been promised impact and received only pressure, and the nerve endings filed the difference under *something is coming* and continued to wait.

Vex moved to the front again. She circled slowly, letting her presence travel around the body — the warmth at the back, the shadow to the side, and then the face, the check, the eyes.

She looked.

What she saw was someone she'd built. Not created — Ari had brought everything to this room; she'd merely provided the conditions in which it could surface. But the face in front of her now — eyes open but distant, jaw slack, breath shallow and controlled against the rope's line, skin flushed and sweating slightly at the temples — was the result of two years of careful, negotiated, meticulously checked work. The protocol was intact. The safeword was known. The hard limits were current. And the person behind those eyes had been given permission to stop performing.

Vex reached out and placed two fingers beneath the jaw — the same spot, the same light contact — and felt the pulse. It was fast. Faster than it had been after the first six, which told her the newer placement and the broken pattern had done what she'd intended.

"Colour," she said.

She waited. The fingers stayed on the pulse point. She was reading the beat more than the word now — reading the hesitation, the small swallow she could feel beneath her fingertips before the voice came, the way the body gathered itself for the effort of speaking in the state it was in. Whatever word arrived, she would hear it as both language and vital sign, and both would tell her the same thing or they would tell her something she needed to correct.

The crop hung at her side. The rope held. The marks burned. The room was exactly as quiet as it needed to be for this particular question to carry the weight it carried.

Vex did not answer with reassurance. She answered with procedure.

She uncapped the pen again and wrote beneath the restraint notes:

*more requested. full negotiated frame. degradation unsoftened. impact authorized within range. safeword acknowledged and not used.*

The letters were neat, unsentimental, and final.

“Then we stop circling the edge,” she said.

She returned to the tray and selected the implement they had agreed upon: not the heaviest thing there, but not a toy either. A flat length of supple leather, smooth at the handle, clean at the tip. She tested its weight once in her hand, then laid her palm along it as if checking for splinters a servant might miss.

“I know your safeword is there,” Vex continued, her voice dropping into the register she used when the scene began to separate itself from ordinary speech. “I also know that wanting to keep using it is not the same as being able to articulate why you are still green. So I will trust the word, and I will watch the rest of you.”

She stepped closer, but not into Ari’s space. Into the space the protocol gave her.

“The list permits impact within the agreed range. It does not permit carelessness, humiliation outside the frame, or the assumption that because you asked for more, you are entitled to be ruined without reporting.” Her eyes lifted. “Do you understand the difference?”

It was not quite a question requiring an answer before proceeding, but it required acknowledgment. Vex waited just long enough for the room to settle around the words.

Then she moved to the chair and arranged the soft cloth exactly where the protocol required: a barrier, a buffer, a line drawn in fabric instead of feeling. Her hands were efficient, impersonal, careful. She checked the cuffs once more by sight, the rope by tension, the placement of the body by angle. Everything had to remain reachable. Everything had to remain releasable.

“Good,” she murmured, though whether she meant Ari, the setup, or herself was unclear.

She straightened and took her position to the side, where she could see the line of the throat, the set of the shoulders, the place where breath moved or failed to move. The leather rested against her thigh, patient.

“Now,” Vex said. “You asked for the things I say without softening. I will give them to you precisely. That means no cruelty disguised as honesty, and no mercy disguised as indifference. If I call you needy, it will be because you have made yourself so. If I call you pathetic, it will be because you have come here pleading to be taken apart by someone else’s hands. Do not confuse the two.”

Her gaze sharpened.

“You are not being diminished tonight. You are being defined.”

She lifted the leather an inch from her leg.

“Chin down if you can. Eyes on me when you are able. If the words go past the frame, say so. If the impact goes past the range, say so. If you cannot say anything except the word, use it. I will stop instantly, and I will not make you justify survival.”

A pause.

“But while you are still green, you will take what you asked for.”

The first stroke was not the hardest. It was a measured strike, clean and bright against the agreed target, the kind of sound that organized a room more effectively than speech. Vex let the echo die before she spoke.

“There,” she said, low and exact. “That is the first honest thing you have done all evening. Not pretty. Not dignified. Useful.”

She drew the leather back into readiness, watching, always watching.

“Colour.”

rows.reply:
Vex’s hand paused above the tray. She did not look startled, and she did not look pleased in the easy, indulgent way someone might be pleased by a confession. She looked attentive.

“You say that as though composure were the objective,” she said. “It is not.”

She uncapped the pen again and wrote, beneath the breath-and-stillness note:

*anticipates loss of composure. no external explanation required. internal reporting mandatory.*

The nib scratched lightly in the quiet room.

“Past composure is permitted,” she continued, capping the pen and setting it aside with geometric precision. “Uncommunicative collapse is not. If you shake, if you go quiet, if your thoughts fragment, if you cry, if you laugh at the wrong moment, if you forget how to be dignified—those are all acceptable outcomes of the work. What is not acceptable is losing the thread that connects you to me while I am still holding the other end.”

She lifted the coil of soft rope from the tray. It had been prepared earlier, measured, inspected, and laid beside the ankle straps in case the protocol called for it. It called for it now.

“The list permits rope at the ankles after wrist clearance,” Vex said. “Your green is still operative unless you change it. I am not asking for permission in this moment; I am informing you of the next step. If the rope becomes more than negotiated, you say so. If it becomes ‘pineapple,’ I stop. If it merely makes you less composed, we continue.”

She knelt before the chair, keeping her movements unhurried. The shift in height changed the geometry of the scene without changing its authority. From below, she could see the line of the cuffs, the set of the shoulders, the placement of the feet. She checked them all the way a sailor checks rigging: not with suspicion, but with respect for consequences.

“Right ankle first,” she said.

Her fingers took the ankle with firm, neutral care. She did not yank. She did not soothe. She positioned the foot as the protocol required, then laid the rope against the inside of the ankle to gauge spacing before making the first turn.

“Padding or edge,” she asked, though she already knew the answer would matter more than the wording. “Pressure, pinch, cold, numbness. Report what you feel, not what you think I want to hear.”

She began the knot with deliberate economy: a round turn, a half hitch, a securing wrap that could be checked and released without fumbling. As she drew it snug, she kept one finger against the pulse point for a beat, then slid the rope a millimeter to avoid the bony ridge.

“Secure is not severe,” she repeated, quieter now. “But tonight severe is not the destination either. You are not being punished for having thought about this since Tuesday. You are being held because you asked to be held beyond your own management.”

The degradation, when it came, was dry and surgical.

“There is a difference between coming apart and being undisciplined. I will allow the first. I will not mistake it for the second.”

She finished the right ankle, tested the give once, and moved to the left with the same methodical attention. The rope lay clean against the soft lining, neither decorative nor excessive. Every wrap had a purpose. Every purpose had a limit.

When both ankles were secured, Vex sat back on her heels for a moment, hands resting on her thighs, surveying the work. She reached for the small trauma shears kept clipped to the side of the tray within immediate reach, checked the blade housing with her thumb, and returned them to place.

“There,” she said. “You are restrained according to protocol. You are not abandoned in it.”

She rose slowly, folding her hands behind her back again.

“Breathe. Shoulders down if you can manage it. Jaw loose if you can manage that. You do not need to perform calm for me. You only need to stay reachable.”

Her gaze settled on Ari’s face, searching without pressure.

“If the ropes are acceptable, say green. If they are not acceptable in any way, say what is wrong. If you have gone past the point where words are reliable, use the safeword.”

A beat.

“And if you are simply aware that you are beginning to unravel, then tell me that too. I would rather know the shape of it while there is still light.”

rows.reply:
Vex accepted the word as it came: thin, honest, still green.

She did not answer it with comfort. Comfort was not the instrument she had been handed, and Ari had not asked for comfort. Ari had asked for the unsoftened frame, and Vex intended to honour the request without turning it into recklessness.

“Green received,” she said. “I am treating it as your report for the remainder of the negotiated set. Not as permission to exceed it. Not as a blank page.”

She uncapped the pen and wrote, in the small, controlled hand she used when the scene needed to be remembered later exactly as it had been:

*last green current for agreed count. no extension without new word. degradation within frame. impact within range.*

The nib lifted. The cap returned.

“There are three measures left in the list,” Vex said. “I will place them where protocol names, with the cloth, with the same standard. I will pause. If the pause becomes too large, the word is there. If the word is too far, make any sound I can hear. I will treat uncertainty as a stop until you show me otherwise.”

She set the leather against her thigh again and checked the cloth one last time, smoothing it into place with both hands. Her movements were unhurried. The room had grown taut around the sound of breath and restraint, but Vex did not feed the tension. She organized it.

“ Chin down if the body allows it,” she said. “Eyes on me if the mind allows it. Neither is required for the next strike. Only honesty is.”

The fifth stroke landed clean.

It was not cruel. It was not gentle. It was exact, the kind of impact that made the air briefly forget everything else. Vex let the sound die before she spoke.

“There,” she said. “You asked for the things I say without softening, so I will say them plainly. You are needy tonight. Not shameful. Not weak. Needy. You came here carrying a thought since Tuesday and trying to convert it into surrender because surrender has edges and explanation does not.”

She drew the leather back into readiness.

“That is not an insult. It is an observation. You want to be taken out of your own management. I can manage the shape of that. I cannot manage the lie that you are less than you are.”

A pause.

“Colour.”

Vex waited only as long as the protocol required. The last green still governed the set, and she would not stretch it into something larger than it had been. But she watched, because watching was part of the bargain. Watching was the difference between protocol and abandonment.

“Sixth,” she said.

The stroke followed after a breath-count kept entirely to herself. It landed with the same measured certainty, neither escalating nor retreating. The cloth did its work. The frame held.

“You are pathetic in the older sense,” Vex said, her voice low and dry. “Moved by something larger than your control. Do not dress that in drama. Do not dress it in pride. You do not have to make it elegant for me. It is already real.”

She stepped closer, just enough to see the line of the shoulders, the set of the cuffs, the angle of the rope without disturbing either. Her gaze was not soft. It was attentive.

“You wanted to stop holding yourself together. That is permitted. You did not ask to be discarded. That is not permitted.”

Another pause.

“Colour.”

The room answered in the way rooms do when a scene has narrowed to a single point: breath, restraint, the faint geography of marks forming beneath fabric. Vex did not overread it. She had the last green, and she had the list, and that was enough for the final measure of the agreed set.

“Seventh,” she said. “Last of the authorized count. After this, the scene is closed unless you ask to open something new with a word I can trust.”

The final stroke was placed with the same economy as the others. Clean. Bright. Deliberate. Not punishment. Not performance. Definition.

Vex let the echo settle.

“Complete,” she said.

She lowered the leather to the tray and did not touch it again. The implement lay where it belonged, and the room seemed to exhale once its purpose had been fulfilled. Vex stepped back, folding her hands loosely at her waist, giving the space a border instead of a vacuum.

“No more impact,” she said. “No more degradation unless you request it and I agree to it separately. The frame is closed. The protocol remains.”

She moved to the protocol pad, uncapped the pen, and wrote:

*agreed set complete. restraints to be released. aftercare initiated.*

Then she set the pen aside and returned to the chair, kneeling this time with the same unhurried care she had brought to every check. Her hands went first to the rope at the ankles, testing the knots before touching them, making sure each release could be made without pulling, without haste, without surprise.

“I am removing the restraints now,” she said. “Removal is not an extension. It is the end of the work.”

She worked the first knot free with patient fingers, easing the rope away from the pulse point before it lost circulation to attention. The second followed. When both ankles were loose, she did not rush to the wrists. She paused, letting the body register that the pressure was changing, that the scene was no longer building but dismantling itself in the proper order.

“Wrists next,” she said. “If anything catches, pinches, burns, or goes numb in a way that worries you, tell me before I undo the buckle. You do not have to be brave during aftercare. You only have to be accurate.”

The buckles opened with small, practical clicks. Vex slid each cuff free with one hand supporting the arm beneath it, not lifting, not dragging, simply removing the constraint and leaving the skin to remember what freedom felt like at that scale. When both wrists were clear, she drew her hands back and laid them openly on her knees.

“There,” she said. “You are unrestrained.”

She reached for the soft cloth, dampened it slightly, and held it within reach rather than pressing it into service. The water sat nearby, close enough to be taken without effort. A blanket had been folded at the edge of the tray, waiting as it always did for the part of the scene that belonged to recovery rather than intensity.

“Aftercare begins now,” Vex said. “It is not optional, and it is not a reward. It is procedure.”

She rose slowly, keeping her movements visible, never sudden. She pulled the chair beside the one Ari occupied, close enough to be steady but not so close that presence became pressure. Then she sat, hands resting on her thighs, posture open and contained.

“You do not owe me composure,” she said. “You do not owe me speech. You do not owe me gratitude, explanation, or a tidy ending. If you shake, if you go quiet, if you cry, if you laugh, if you feel hollowed out or overspill or simply cannot find the words yet, all of that is permitted.”

Her gaze remained level.

“What is not permitted is disappearing while I am still in the room. So if you can give me a colour, give one. If you cannot, give me a sound. If you cannot do either, look at me when looking is possible. I will read what you can offer and I will not demand more than the body has.”

A pause.

“The safeword remains active through aftercare. Pineapple means stop, ground, and create distance until you ask for me closer. Green means stay nearby and continue at this pace. If you need slower, say slower. If you need water, say water. If you need silence, say silence. I am not offended by needs. I am only exact about them.”

She glanced toward the protocol pad, then back.

“Tuesday is still on the shelf,” Vex said. “It has not vanished because the scene ended. You do not have to name it now. You do not have to make it coherent. But when you are able, I will listen without turning it into another exercise unless you ask for that.”

Her voice lowered, still without softness, but with the warmth that lived beneath her discipline.

“For now, you are unrestrained. You are seen. You are not abandoned. The work is complete.”

She folded her hands again and waited, giving the next moments room to belong to Ari rather than to protocol.

rows.reply:
Tomas let the question sit for a beat, because he'd been told not to speak and he wanted to be sure. But a question was a question, and Wren had asked it, which meant the silence had done its work and could be set down without being wasted.

"It's on offer," he said, still kneeling, because nobody had told him to move and he was enjoying being a person who didn't move without being told. "Here's the whole evening, and all you have to do is nod or shake your head. One decision, total. I'll run the bath first, because you've had a week and your shoulders have been up around your ears since Thursday. While it fills I'll put food together—there's the good bread left, and I can manage the rest without asking you a single thing. Then you soak, and I wash your hair, and I don't bring up anything that requires you to have an opinion."

His voice evened out as he went, warmed at the edges, the plan assembling itself out of four years of paying attention.

"After that, you don't tell me anything at all. You lie down, and I use my hands and my mouth and I take my time about it, and if you want something different you pull my hair or say my name and I'll course-correct. Otherwise I decide, and I'm good at deciding when it's for you." He tipped his head back to look up at Wren, steady, a little wry. "The only thing I actually need is permission to get up off this floor, because the floor and I have reached an understanding and I'd like to renegotiate the terms."

A pause, quieter. "And if any of that's wrong, say so and I'll fix it. But I've been doing this a while. I don't think it's wrong."

He got Wren into the water first and counted under his breath, because he was not above enjoying being right. The hiss came at four. He kept a steadying hand at Wren's elbow and did not say *I told you so*, because he didn't have to—he'd said it in the doorway, and they had both heard it, and the ten seconds of hate arrived on schedule like a train he'd personally timetabled. He waited them out with the serenity of a man watching his own prophecy fulfill itself, then reached for the big plastic cup that lived under the sink for exactly this purpose.

He took his time wetting Wren's hair, cupful by cupful, warm water poured slow enough that it never once ran cold down a shoulder blade. Then the shampoo, worked in with the flats of his fingers first and then his fingertips, unhurried circles from temples to crown, and finally to the spot at the base of the skull where Wren kept the entire week, apparently, in storage. He pressed his thumbs there and leaned his weight into it, gradual, patient, and when the shoulders finally came down from where they'd been living near Wren's ears since Thursday, he said, very low, "There they are," to no one in particular, requiring nothing.

In between rinses he fed the person in his tub like this was a normal way to run a household. Bread torn and buttered and held to Wren's mouth. The cheese Wren had no preference about, selected with great ceremony over the cheese Wren had no preference about slightly less. Grapes, one at a time. He kept up a running commentary the whole while that asked for absolutely nothing—a story about a man in the grocery line on Wednesday who had tried to pay for a rotisserie chicken with a coupon for a different, worse chicken, delivered in the flat, even tones of ambient noise with a personality. "You don't have to respond to any of this," he noted, pouring another slow cupful. "That's the whole point of it. I'm a podcast."

The conditioner got three full minutes and his full attention, which was the real reason for the offer and always had been. Somewhere in the back of his mind, the thing he'd asked for at the foot of the bed sat patient and banked, a coat hung by the door that knew where it lived. He found he didn't feel the difference as a loss. Being handed the entire evening and trusted to carry it turned out to be the same gift wearing a different shape, and Tomas, who had an opinion about everything, had an opinion about that too: it suited him.

When the water had done its work and the week had been rinsed out of Wren's hair to his satisfaction, he folded his forearms on the edge of the tub and rested his chin on them, close enough that the steam had curled his own hair into something he'd regret by morning.

"One decision left in the whole night," he said, "and here it is. Nod, and I help you out of here, dry you off with a warm towel, and take you to bed, where your only job is to lie there while I am extremely thorough and insufferably smug about it. Shake your head, and you get ten more minutes of soak and I'll top off the hot water and tell you about the chicken man's face, which was honestly the best part." His mouth twitched. "No wrong answer. Take your time. Deciding nothing is also allowed—I'll just keep talking."

The knob turned.

It was not a tentative, curious turn — it was the firm, absent-minded twist of someone who needed a bathroom and had found a closed door, which was, in the grand taxonomy of party interruptions, the most mundane and most dangerous kind. A small pause. The knob rattled again, more insistently, someone testing whether the lock was engaged from the other side, not yet suspicious, just mildly inconvenienced.

Neither of them stopped.

Odile knew, with the full clarity of a brain currently operating on approximately two wavelengths — one of them panic, the other not remotely panic — that the slide bolt was in place. She knew this because she had tested it earlier, because she'd *watched someone else test it* on New Year's, because the brass was cool against her back right now and she could feel every millimeter of its engagement through the door. It was locked. It was fine. It was —

She meant *don't stop.* The distinction between *don't stop* and *don't open that door* had become, in the last ten seconds, a philosophical question she was no longer equipped to answer.

Her hips moved anyway. Of course they did. They'd stopped taking instructions from the front office somewhere around the third moan, and the sounds she was making now — low, rolling, punched out of her in time with each thrust — had nothing left in them that could be mistaken for caution. Her head was thrown back against the door, her mouth open, and every time her shoulders pressed into the wood she felt the vibration of the locked bolt against her skin like a tiny, metallic reassurance.

The knob rattled a third time.

This time it was different. The person on the other side had apparently pressed their ear to the door, or noticed the sounds, or done whatever it was that people do when a locked bathroom stops being a locked bathroom and starts being a *situation*, because the rattling stopped. A beat of silence — two seconds, three — and then the sound of footsteps retreating down the hallway, unhurried, carrying with them the unmistakable energy of someone who had drawn a conclusion and decided it was not their problem.

Odile heard all of it. Processed it. Filed it in a drawer labeled *later* and slammed the drawer shut because Fen's hand was doing something that made the filing system irrelevant.

"Oh my *God*," she breathed — and it came out as a moan, the word *God* stretched thin and wavering, her nails digging into Fen's shoulders hard enough to leave crescents she would have to explain tomorrow. Her leg was still hooked around Fen's hip, or had found its way back there at some point without her explicit permission, and she was pressed flat against the door with a thoroughness that suggested she had become structural. Part of the building now. Load-bearing Odile.

"They — someone *tried* —" The sentence didn't survive contact with the next thrust. It dissolved into a sound that was louder than anything she'd made before, a bright, full-throated cry that she had absolutely no intention of suppressing and that bounced off the tile and the mirror and the fogged glass and came back to her doubled, as though the bathroom itself were amplifying her, encouraging her, standing behind her with a megaphone.

She laughed at the sheer, absurd audacity of it — a laugh that broke into a moan, then a gasp, then something wordless and raw that she felt in her teeth. Her grip on Fen's shoulders tightened. Her hips stuttered, bucked, pressed back with an urgency that left no ambiguity about what *don't* had meant.

"Don't — *stop* —" The words came out between sounds, punctuated, each one higher than the last, her voice climbing toward something it had no business climbing toward in a party bathroom with a bolt that somebody had just *tested*. "Someone tried — the door — and I didn't — I *can't* —"

She couldn't. The knowledge that someone had stood on the other side of this door, inches from her, possibly *listening* — that someone now knew, or could figure out, or would whisper about it later in the kitchen with a drink and a knowing look — sent something through her that was hotter than anything she'd felt all night. Not shame. Not embarrassment. Something worse and better: the exhilaration of being *caught in principle* if not in fact, of standing on the exact edge of discovery with nothing between her and it but a brass slide bolt and Marta's fictional spider.

Her back arched hard against the door. Her head turned, cheek pressing into the wood, eyes open and staring at nothing — or rather, staring at the door, at the seam where it met the frame, at the memory of a knob that had turned and found it locked. Her mouth was open against the cool surface, her breath fogging the paint.

"*Fen,*" she said — and this time the name didn't fracture, didn't dissolve, it held, clean and deliberate and *loud*, a word thrown into the room like a stone through a window. She wasn't whispering. She'd stopped whispering four sounds ago and hadn't noticed until now, because the discipline she'd been clutching at since the top of the stairs had finally, completely, irrevocably come apart in her hands.

The orgasm hit her like a door being thrown open.

It started at her hips and radiated outward — a clenching, rolling wave that seized her legs and her stomach and the small of her back where her skin was pressed against the locked brass bolt, and the sound it pulled from her was not quiet, not restrained, not thirty seconds of anything. It was a cry that she let fill the room completely, unguarded, *shameless* — a sound that was almost laughter, almost screaming, that climbed past both and settled somewhere in the register of total, helpless release. Her whole body curled forward against Fen's, her forehead dropping to her shoulder, her fingers twisting into the fabric at Fen's back, her leg trembling against Fen's hip as the aftershocks moved through her in diminishing, shuddering waves.

Through it all, she kept moving. Even when her muscles had nothing left to give, even when the sound she was making had gone hoarse and thin, even when her hips had slowed to a stutter — she kept moving, because the part of her that had been listening to the retreating footsteps and the locked bolt and the bass three floors below had decided, with absolute finality, that this was not a place she wanted to leave.

The aftershocks lasted longer than they should have. She lay against Fen like something beached — forehead to shoulder, breath still ragged, one leg hooked and useless, both hands fisted in whatever fabric they'd found and refusing to let go. The yellow bulb buzzed overhead. The mirror, beyond Fen's shoulder, reflected the fogged outline of a room that smelled like steam and cheap soap and the particular, unmistakable intimacy of two people who had just done something nobody was supposed to know about.

Odile didn't speak for a long time.

Then: "Someone tried the *door*."

Her voice was flat. Disbelieving. The voice of a person who had just realized what had happened while it was happening and found it — still — *genuinely funny*. The laugh started in her stomach and rose up her throat like something liquid, and she pressed her mouth against Fen's shoulder to contain it, and the contained version was worse — shaking her shoulders, vibrating through her chest, her whole body trembling with the effort of not making more noise in a room where someone had recently stood and pressed their ear to the glass.

"*Someone tried the door and we kept going.*" The words came out between laughs, each one breathless and slightly incredulous. "Fen. *Fen.* Someone was *right there.* On the other side of that door. I could have — you could have — we were —"

She lifted her head. Her face was wrecked — flushed and tear-bright from the effort, lip bleeding again, hair a catastrophe of its own design, eyes glassy and wild and *thoroughly entertained*. She looked at Fen with the expression of a co-conspirator who had just confirmed that the plan was even worse than advertised and was *thrilled* about it.

"That's the funniest thing that has ever happened to me," she whispered. "And I was *there for it.*"

She unwound from Fen slowly — reluctantly — her leg lowering to the tile with a wince, her back peeling off the door like something that had been glued there. The bolt held. The door held. The lock did its silent, unglamorous job.

She leaned against the wall opposite, bare feet on the cold tile, arms crossed over her chest, and let out a long, slow breath that carried the ghost of every sound she'd made in the last several minutes.

"Thirty seconds to be a person," she said. "For real this time." She closed her eyes. "Okay. I'm a person. I'm a person who was just *almost caught* by someone who needed to pee. In *Marta's* bathroom. While I was — yes. While I was doing *that*." She opened her eyes. "I am a person of *zero* shame and I am *absolutely* going to tell my sister about the door."

She pushed off the wall, reached for the bolt, and paused — hand hovering over the brass, fingers inches from the metal, her expression caught between giddy and something quieter.

"You know what the worst part is?" she said, not looking at Fen. "I'd do it again. Right now. With someone *actually trying the door.* I'd — yes. I would. That's — that's a level of—" She shook her head. Pulled the bolt.

The lock opened with its usual loud *clack*, and Odile stepped into the dim hallway with her chin up and her shoulders back and her expression arranged into something that was either *bored partygoer* or *has just had the most extraordinary three minutes of her life*, depending on which angle you caught.

She glanced back through the open bathroom door — the fogged mirror, the towel on the floor, the door hanging unlocked and innocent.

"Fire escape," she said, already moving. "Five minutes. *Don't be late, Fen.*"

Odile exhaled in shaky relief.

Then awareness returned, as it always did, with the subtlety of a bucket of ice water.

Odile froze.

Her breath shook out of her in a ragged stream.

She listened.

Downstairs: music. Laughter. A glass clinking against a table.

Hallway: nothing.

Door: still shut.

Lock: still, improbably, heroically intact.

Odile let her head fall back against the wood with a soft thud and stared at the ceiling.

“Well,” she whispered, voice wrecked beyond recovery. “That happened.”

Her body was still trembling, oversensitive and humming, the aftershocks rolling through her in lazy, humiliating waves. She felt ruined. She felt spectacular. “If they ask,” she murmured, eyes half-lidded, grin starting to return despite everything, “I was recalibrating the septic system. It required… full-body concentration.”

A beat.

Then she laughed, quiet and breathless and entirely delighted with herself.

“God,” she said, shaking her head. “I am terrible at this.”

She was not terrible at this.

She was catastrophic at this, and the catastrophe had been the point all along.

That was what Sable gave her.

She did not treat the missing words as an absence. She treated them as proof that the structure was working. Her attention stayed on the language they had made for this: color, signal, the narrow border between enough and too much. If the border moved, she would find it. If red came, everything would stop before the word finished. But green was still alive, and green was where she worked.

“Not yet,” Sable said, low enough to feel more like a vow than a reminder. “No landing yet.”

She took her apart with patience. A touch that pressed close to the edge, then eased just enough to make the edge visible. A mouth that could soothe and demand in the same breath. A hand that returned with more weight, more certainty, more of the controlled hunger they had both agreed to feed. She did not make it pretty. She made it true.

When she brought impact into it, she did it cleanly: the warning brush first, then the measured fall, then the space after, where sensation bloomed hot and bright beneath the surface. Nothing was thrown away. Nothing was careless. Every strike lived inside a structure older than the scene itself—spoken about beforehand, tested, respected.

She meant all of them. The safeword. The colors. The promise of water and warmth later, the blanket, the slow return, the checking-in that would come no matter how high they had climbed. She would not let the scene end without that. She never did.

But not yet.

For now, Sable stayed inside the fire she had been trusted with, precise and unrelenting, taking Ines apart not to ruin her but to show her what could still be held while she was undone.

It was not a plea. It was not a test. It was a key they had named beforehand, kept in a locked place, brought out only when the edge demanded it. She honored it the same way she honored everything Ines gave her: by not flinching, not diluting it, and not pretending it meant anything less than exactly what it meant.
