rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked at him for a long second — the knife in his hand, the boy under him, the request hanging in the air between them — and something in her face shifted and settled, the way a decision does when it's already been made before it's spoken.

"All right," she said. She came back and crouched on the boy's other side, forearms across her knees, close enough to reach and far enough to stay out of his way. "You asked for it straight. You'll get it straight, all of it. Go."

He went in wrong. She saw it before the blade touched skin.

"Stop. Your angle's flat." Her voice stayed level, the same voice she'd used for everything all day, the voice for work. "You're going in like you're stabbing a table. Tilt it — up, toward his far shoulder. Like you're trying to reach his heart from underneath the ribs. The angle does it. I told you that. The angle, not the arm."

The boy came alive under it the moment the steel found skin. His hand shot up and closed on Corvin's forearm — slick, gripping, impossibly strong for a dying man — and his eyes went wide, and the word came out again, water, mother, please, all the same word.

"He's got your arm. Let him keep it. He's not strong enough to matter and it gives him something to hold that isn't the knife." She didn't move. "Don't answer him. I told you that too. Answering makes it long."

The blade went in and Corvin stopped — halfway, the instinct of every first-timer, the body refusing what the mind had ordered — and Wrack's voice came in flat over the boy's noise.

"Push. All the way. Don't stop there — halfway is the cruelty, not the mercy. You've done the hurting, now finish the work." A beat. "Push like you mean it."

The sound came when the blade found its depth — a long wet exhale, air rushing out around the steel, and beneath it something smaller and worse, a bubbling in the throat.

"That sound's his lung, not his voice. The blade's let it off its leash. It's not pain, it's pressure leaving. Don't put that in your ledger as pain." Her eyes never left the work. "He's going to fight for about ten more of your breaths. Hold still. Hold the angle. Don't pull out early — you'll tear more coming than going and then you'll owe him another."

The boy's grip went from iron to something less, then to nothing. The hand slid off Corvin's arm and landed open in the dirt. The surprise stayed on his face — it hadn't left; it had been the last thing he wore.

Wrack counted the last of it in her head, the way she always did, and then let a silence sit over the three of them for exactly three breaths.

"Done," she said. "Count of about fifteen from first cut. Slow for the work, fast for the man — he was gone before he finished being surprised, whatever his face is telling you now. Faces lie. They stay at whatever scared them last."

She leaned in and looked at the wound, measuring, filing — a craftsman checking another man's joinery.

"You went in flat, corrected, went deep, stopped halfway once. That's three faults." She held up the accounting the way she'd hold up fingers. "None of them were cruelty. All of them were inexperience. There's a difference, and it matters later, so hold onto it: cruelty is a choice. You didn't make it once in there."

She straightened, knees cracking, and stood over them both for a moment.

"You wanted to know what you'd carry. Now you know. You'll get the sound — that air, the bubbling. You'll get the grip on your arm and the surprise. That's my first, what I told you about, and now it's yours too, and I'm sorry for that, and being sorry doesn't lift it off you." She said *sorry* the way she said everything — flat, unadorned, a fact about her and not a performance for him. "But you asked to see it true instead of walking away with a clean story, and I'll tell you the last straight thing I've got: the men who go strange aren't the ones who saw it. They're the ones who guessed at it afterward, alone, and let the guessing rot. You saw it. It's worse and it's better. Both. That's how most true things come."

She nudged his boot with hers — not unkind. An instruction with a foot.

"Close his eyes if you're going to — left hand, temple down, I told you the way of it. Then stand up and walk away straight, and don't look back, and that part's not for him and it's not for your conscience either. It's for me, because it's getting dark, and I'm not standing on this road when his friends come up it."

She was already turning toward the bodies, unhurried, voice dropping back into the register of work.

"You did it slow and you did it anyway. First time, with a man begging at you and his hand on your arm." She paused, half-turned, and the dry ghost of something moved through her voice that wasn't quite a smile and wasn't quite pride but lived in the same county. "There are men twenty years in who couldn't have finished that push. Write that down somewhere in yourself, next to the sound. You'll want both entries when the book gets long."

Wrack looked at him for a long moment — sitting back on his heels in the middle of the road with the dark coming down and the knife still in his hand, going cold on him the way knives do when a man stops remembering he's holding one. She'd seen men pay the toll standing, walking, over a bowl of stew three days late. She'd never once seen one sit down in the road and ask for the whole bill up front.

So she stopped working. That was the first thing. All day she'd talked with her hands moving — buckles, boots, pockets. Now she came over, lowered herself onto a flat rock across from him with the cracking of her knees, and let the silence stand for exactly as long as it needed to.

"All right," she said. "The rest."

She settled her forearms on her knees.

"The sound fades. I told you that. Here's what I didn't tell you: what comes after it fades. Nothing. That's what comes. First few years, the faces find you — his, others — and they cost you a minute here, a spoon set down there. Then they come less often. Then one night you notice you can't remember whether the face that came to you over dinner was this boy or a different boy, and that will scare you worse than the sound did." She let it sit a breath. "It shouldn't. Forgetting isn't the wound. Forgetting is the scar. It's what a healed thing looks like, and healed things are ugly and flat and don't hurt, and men spend years thinking they're rotting because the pain stopped. Pain stopping isn't rot. Rot is when the pain stops and you can't remember it was ever pain. Learn the difference now and you'll save yourself some bad nights."

She shifted her weight on the rock.

"I counted, my first four years. Kept it exact, like the number owed me something. Stopped at a hundred and something — not because I lost count. Because I noticed I'd stopped feeling the count, and a number you don't feel is just noise. That's the day I started keeping a different ledger. Not how many. How. Clean or not." Her eyes went to the boy behind him, then back. "The count belongs to the war. The how belongs to you. That's the only column in the book that's yours, and it's the only one you'll want to read when you're old and stupid like me."

The valley below had gone black. She talked on into it, flat and unhurried.

"You asked for the rest, so here's the rest of the rest. This war. Nobody you're bleeding for can tell you what it's over. Ten years on this border and I've heard three different reasons from men wearing the same colors, and the border's moved twice and moved back twice, and the only things that have changed are the price of bread and the names on the muster rolls. I don't fight for the border. I don't fight for the reasons. I fight because it's the trade, and I'm good at it, and the pay's honest, and because there's maybe four people left breathing I'd take a blade for, and every one of them is in the trade too. That's the whole of my patriotism." A small shrug. "It's small. Small things hold up. Big ones crack and drop you. Small ones you can carry in a kit."

She was quiet for a moment, and when she spoke again her voice hadn't changed at all, which was how he could tell she'd chosen these words a long time ago and never had anyone worth giving them to.

"Last thing, and this is the one to keep. The work stays work. That's not a description. That's a discipline. Killing is work, and work has details — the angle, the count, the closing of eyes — and you give it the details because details are how you keep a thing the right size. The day you let it be more than work — a craft you take pride in, a hunger, a story you tell — that's the day you start going strange. And you won't notice, because going strange feels like getting good. That's the trap of it. So you test yourself. Night before a fight, check. Tired, fine. Scared, fine. Hungry, fine. Eager — eager's the one to watch for. The day you catch yourself looking forward to it, that's the day you quit the trade, because past that line you won't want to come back, and wanting is the whole of the road back."

She looked at him the way she'd looked at the wound. Measuring. Filing.

"And the other half, because it's got two. You keep it work so the rest of you can stay whatever it is. Somewhere in there is a man who closed a stranger's eyes for no reason the stranger would ever know about. That part isn't work. That's the thing the work pays for. You do the killing clean because clean is the only thing the dead ever get off of you, and you do the living — the eating, the sleeping, the four people — because that's what the killing's *for*. Men who forget the second half go strange too. Different strange. They go quiet and careful and they die tidy deaths and nobody mourns them, because there wasn't anything left in them to mourn. Some hard night you'll want to be one of those, because it looks like peace." She shook her head once. "It isn't. It's just work with the pay stopped."

She let that be the end of it for a moment. Then she stood, knees cracking, and the working voice came back like a door closing.

"That's the rest. There's nothing under it — no secret beneath the secret. That's the whole of what twenty years teaches, and you got it in an afternoon, which some would call a shame and I call a bargain, because you paid for it in person." She nodded at the knife in his hand. "Clean it before we walk. On his cloak, same as I did. That's not a chore. That's your first entry in the how-column."

She took up the horse's lead and stood waiting, half a silhouette against the last iron light, and when she spoke again it was dry as the gravel.

"Now get up. Not because you're fine — you're not. Because the dark's here and his friends are on that road, and the dead don't mind waiting." She turned up the slope toward the treeline. "The living get killed by it. Walk."

rows.reply:
Wrack halted and turned back, her boots crunching on the gravel. She didn't soften her gaze. "Look at the arrows," she said, nodding toward the bodies near the cart. "Three in the first volley. One took a blade in the gut. That one over there by the wheel—throat, open. He bled out in seconds."

She gestured with her chin, sharp and dismissive. "They set the trap, we walked into it. That's all it is. No honor, no glory. Just geometry and blood." She turned on her heel again. "You've seen it. Now close your eyes if you need to, but don't stand here memorizing the view. Move."

rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack didn't slow her pace, but her voice carried back to him over the crunch of gravel. She didn't look at him; she kept her eyes on the ridge ahead.

"A spear doesn't slice," she said. "It drives. It takes the ribs and spreads them like a gate, then shoves the organs aside until they tear. You don't get a clean wound. You get a mess that keeps moving."

She paused, just for a breath, before continuing.

"The heat comes out first. Like steam off a butcher's table. Then the smell. Copper and sour milk. And he doesn't die quiet. He gags on his own air, makes a sound like a sack hitting mud. That's the geometry. That's the blood."

She stepped off the road into the tree line, checking the shadows.

"You wanted straight. Now keep it in your head and keep your legs moving. The wolves don't care about the details, and neither do the men who hunt us."

rows.reply:
Wrack halted. She turned back, her silhouette cutting the dim light. She didn't ask why. She just walked back to the cart, boots crunching on the gravel. She stopped a yard away, hands loose at her sides.

"Fine," she said. "You want the ledger, you get the ledger."

She watched him strike. She counted the breaths. She noted the change in the noise.

"Chest stops rising," she said, voice flat. "Lungs empty in three counts. Blood pools near the throat. He won't speak again."

She waited for the stillness to settle.

"Up," she said when the noise ended. "Wash your hands if you've got water. If not, use the dirt. We don't have time for ceremony."

Wrack walked back toward him. She didn't stop until she was standing just out of arm's reach, her shadow falling over his crouched form. She looked down at the raw hands, then past them to the body near the cart.

"You want the ledger in full?" she said. Her voice didn't rise. "Fine."

"The first blow drops him," she said. "The second makes him fight. He grabs at you. He claws for your throat, not because he wants to kill you, but because his hands remember what to do." She lifted her chin toward the dark shape by the wheels. "The third stops that. He doesn't go soft. He goes stiff. That's the spasm. He pushes out hard like he's trying to stand, then he locks."

"And the sound?" Corvin had asked once, before. She gave it to him now.

"Rattle," she said. "Like dry leaves in a tin box. Comes from the wet lung. He tries to breathe air that isn't there. Makes a wet click in his teeth. Then the eyes. They don't close. They turn up. They look past you."

She crouched down, bringing her face level with his, though her voice stayed flat.

"Then the smell changes. Copper fades. Sweat takes over. If his bowels open, you get the sour rot. That's the rest. He's meat after that. Meat doesn't think. Meat doesn't fear."

She stood up again.

"You need to know that so you know when it's over. Because the man you see is gone before the body stops twitching. The body is just a machine winding down. When you see the eyes roll up, you stop. You walk away."

She reached down and grabbed his shoulder, not gentle.

"You're still kneeling. The machine's wound down. Get up."

"Steel punches through the wall of the belly, usually just under the ribs if the spear's angled up," she said, flat as ever. rows.reply:
Wrack stayed by the ditch, one hand resting on her hip as the last of the light drained from the sky and the body near the cart kept its slow, uneven rhythm. She listened through another wet, bubbling exhale that turned into a low, involuntary groan, then the scrape of a heel dragging once through the dirt.

"Breath's getting shallower now," she said, voice unchanged. "That pink foam's turning thicker, darker—more blood than air. You can hear the rattle starting in the throat, like gravel shifting under water. He's not fighting the blade anymore, just twitching through the chest, small jerks that don't go anywhere. The legs are starting to kick a little, not hard, just the nerves catching up. Smell of it carries—iron and shit from the gut loosening. It'll keep on like that until the blood fills the space enough that the next breath doesn't come back out clean. Maybe another thirty heartbeats if the heart's still strong. Then the heels dig in once more, hard, and it stops. No last words. Just the quiet after the air leaks out." 

She rolled her shoulders, settling the mail, and added nothing else until the sounds had played through. "Horses now. Light's gone."

rows.ask: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.
rows.reply:
Sable nodded once, slow and absolute.

“Not yet is not yet.”

She drew her hands back from the buckles without ceremony and settled them on her knees, palms open and visible, as if to prove she was not going anywhere unless invited. The blanket remained draped over the cushion, warm from her hands. The water waited within reach, neither offered nor withheld.

“You can keep them on as long as they help,” she said, voice low enough to sit under the ringing silence. “But you’re coming down now, Ines. Scene or no scene, that part doesn’t wait for permission.”

There was no blame in it. Only the steady fact of her.

Sable tilted her head slightly, watching the lamp’s glow move across the floor. “So while you decide, I’m staying right here. Water when you want it. Blanket when you’re ready. Restraints off when you say so.” A pause, then the ghost of a smile. “And one more colour whenever you can manage it. No rush.”

rows.desc: explicit with specific anatomical and act language
rows.ask: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.
rows.reply:
Sable pulled back before a fourth near-miss could happen.

There was no performance in it, no lazy smile, no pretending she had not just taken the wheel. Her hands came up where the lamplight could find them, palms open, breath controlled even when the wanting was not. The wet warmth of her mouth left skin, and the room narrowed to the hum of the lamp and the sound of her own restraint.

“Okay,” she said. “Okay. I’m stopping.”

She shifted back onto her heels, giving space instead of filling it. One hand went to the water glass out of habit, testing the outside with her wrist before setting it on the low table within reach. She did not lift it to anyone’s lips. Not yet. Not without a word.

“That was me choosing for you,” Sable said, low and clear. “After I told myself I wouldn’t. So colour, Ines. Green, yellow, red. If your voice is gone, give me something. A blink. A nod. A finger tap. Anything that tells me you’re still with me.”

The blanket remained draped over the cushion, warm from her hands. Sable drew it a little closer, not covering, only making it easier to take. The heat lamp stayed angled low, softening the air without pressing against skin.

“If you’re yellow, we stop all touching and I bring you down: water, warmth, quiet, restraints when you say the word. If you’re green and you want more, we name it first—what kind, how long, where I stop, what happens after. If you’re red, it ends now and I don’t argue.”

A pause passed. Her thumb worried once at the edge of her sleeve, the only crack in the calm.

“And if you’re furious with me, that’s allowed too. You can save it for after. Right now I need to know where you are.”

She waited, open-palmed, the water and blanket and lamp arranged like small offers. No pressure. No pretending the last minutes had not tipped past the line she had promised to guard.

“Colour,” Sable said again, softer. “Then choose.”

rows.ask: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."
rows.reply:
Sable received the phrase like a blade handed hilt-first: precise, familiar, dangerous only if mishandled.

“Yes,” she said. “That’s the instruction. Finish it hard. All of it. No kindness during, every kindness after.”

She did not move toward Ines. Not yet. The correction from minutes before was still live in her bones, and she honoured it by staying where her hands could be seen.

“But I ask first,” Sable said, “because that is the rule now.”

Her voice dropped into the register they used at the edge of scenes: clear, unhurried, without decoration.

“Confirming terms: impact and restraint, the old shape, no soothing words while I’m working you. I stop at yellow or red. If you can’t speak, you tap, blink, or make a sound. I do not touch the hardware unless you say check, loosen, or off. Hard does not mean I get to ignore your body. If something numbs, burns wrong, or turns from heat into injury, you tell me and I respond.”

She glanced at the water glass, the blanket, the low lamp. Then she moved those things only: sliding the glass into easy reach, testing its temperature with her wrist, shaking the blanket once and laying it over the cushion nearest the heat. The warmth gathered in the room like a held breath.

“Last colour was green,” Sable said. “Your request is explicit. I am not reading beyond that. So: colour now. Green, yellow, red. If green, I begin. If yellow, we alter the terms before I touch you. If red, the scene ends and aftercare starts immediately.”

A pause opened between them. Sable let it remain empty of pressure.

“When I start,” she continued, “I won’t be kind in the way you mean. I’ll be exact. I’ll count, I’ll check, and I’ll bring you down when the piece is done. Afterward, water. Warmth. Blanket. Restraints off when you say. And if you want to bite my head off later, I deserve that too.”

Her hands rested palm-up on her thighs, the suede waiting within her reach but not lifted. The lamp made a small gold field across the floor. Sable watched Ines with the steady attention of someone who had made a promise and was determined not to spend it like a shortcut.

“Colour,” she said again, low and clean. “Then I’ll finish it hard.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack turned the question over the way she turned over most questions — like it had a real answer, and he might as well have it.

"Both. It's never one or the other, whatever the priests say." She sat back on her heels. "Gut's the slow one. Belly fills with what ought to stay inside it, and it poisons him by inches. Thirsty first, then fever, then he'll start talking to people who aren't there. He's young. Young ones hold on. Could be morning, could be longer."

She stripped the next body's belt knife, looked it over, kept it.

"So it's mercy for him and easier for us, and those two aren't enemies. People like to pretend they are, so they can feel dirty about doing the kind thing. I've never had the time for that." A shrug. "I took a pike through the side at Harrow's Ford, years back. Told the man next to me where to cut if it went bad. It didn't go bad. But I meant it, and he would've done it, and neither of us thought the worse of the other."

She nodded toward the cart.

"You've got till dark to decide what word you want to put on it. The work's the same either way."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack shifted to make room for him and walked him through it the way she'd walk him through any other job — top to bottom, nothing skipped.

"Start with the hands. He's holding his belly shut. The cut's under them, long as my hand, crosswise, deep enough that what's inside wants out. That's my work, that one — he came round the wheel at me, second man I put down." No apology in it. There wasn't one in her to give. "A hand's width higher and he'd be dead already. A hand's width lower and he'd be walking home. That's the whole difference between him and you, and it's luck, so don't make a religion out of it."

She moved the boy's chin with two fingers, showing her.

"Color next. Grey at the lips, sweat with no heat in it — that's blood going somewhere it shouldn't, slow. Eyes still find you when you move. See that. So he's not far gone yet. The fever, the talking to people who aren't there — that's later. You're looking at the best hour he's got left, and it's this."

She sat back on her heels.

"Rest of him's worth a look too. Cloak's mended at the hem, small stitches — someone careful did that. Sword's cheap steel but it's oiled, edge took a stone recent. He kept his kit. He was a careful soldier." She shrugged. "Didn't save him. It usually doesn't. But it's what there is to know about him, and now you know it."

The light had gone a shade thinner while they crouched there. Wrack glanced at the sky, then back.

"That's the whole of it. Nothing changes for looking longer. He doesn't get better, nobody rides over the hill, the wound doesn't close. What you see is what there is." She settled her grip on the boy's wrists again. "You've got an hour of light. He's got more than that, which is the problem."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack gave him a look that had something like approval in it, which from her was a rare coin.

"Knife, not spear. Mine. But the belly doesn't care what opens it." She shifted round on her heels. "Good that you ask. You should know the work. Most men do it for years and never look once, and they're the ones who go strange later."

She eased the boy's hands aside an inch, gentle as you'd move a sleeping man's, let him see, and settled them back.

"Under there's a cut a hand long, crosswise. Skin first — that parts easy. Then fat, yellow, like a goose. Then the muscle wall, then the bag that holds the works. I'm through all four, and what's underneath wants out. Grey-blue loops, shiny, thick as your wrist. That's bowel. It moves on its own, slow — still doing its job. It doesn't know."

She sat back.

"Blood's dark, not bright. Bright's a cut vessel and it kills fast, which is why he's unlucky. Dark means it's coming from deep and mixing with what's inside the pipe — the brown-green, the sour. You smell it already. Privy under the copper. A clean wound smells of the butcher's block; this smells wrong because it is wrong. What's meant to stay in the pipe is loose in the body, and the body can't fight it. Not the bleeding that kills him. The poisoning. Belly goes hard as a board by morning, fever cooks him, and he talks to his mother. They all talk to their mothers, at the end of that road."

A shrug, economical.

"Gut a deer and gut a man and your hands can't tell the difference. That's not a poem. It's just true."

She nodded at his knife-hand.

"So that's the whole of what steel does to a belly. What you're holding does the opposite. One push, and none of it matters anymore — the leak, the fever, the whole road. Closed. It's small and quick and it's the only thing on this field that is."

She resettled her grip on the boy's wrists.

"When you're ready. He's not going anywhere. Neither am I."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped, and came back, and knelt where she'd knelt before, and took the boy's wrists again without being asked.

"Alright. I'm here." She looked at the hilt, at the angle of it. "And since you want the whole of it, here it is: you went in shy. Blade's in the cord but not through it — you angled to the near eye instead of the far. A true cut is three heartbeats. This is the other kind. That's why he's still arguing."

The boy was arguing. His heels drummed the dirt in a slow, hard rhythm, his back bowed against her knee, and a sound came out of him on the exhale — low, through the nose, like a man snoring.

"That noise isn't pain. Pain's done — you took it with the first push, whatever else you missed. That's the body breathing wrong. The cord's half cut and it's sending the wrong letters down. Listen to it proper. That's the sound of a slip, and you'll want to know it, so you never make it twice."

She put her hand over his on the hilt.

"Mine's just the weight. Lean."

The give came — small, final, like a knot parting in wet rope — and the drumming stopped all at once, and the boy went loose from crown to heel.

"There. That's the rest of the cord. Now watch, because this is the part nobody tells you: he's not finished yet. The head's gone — him, the part that asks for water — that ended at the give. But the body keeps its own ledger, and it takes a minute to close the book."

She counted it for him, steady, the way she counted coin.

"Breath goes ragged first — hear it. Like a man pulled out of a river. That's called the fish breath, and it isn't him either; it's the lungs asking a question nobody's answering anymore. Three of those, maybe four. There. Feet go next. Then the hands — feel them slacken under mine. Color's going out of the lips now, grey to wax. And the eyes—" she turned his chin with two fingers, gentle as ever "—fixed. They were finding you a minute ago. Now they're not finding anything. That's the last of him leaving, and it goes out through the eyes, whatever the priests say about the heart."

One more breath went out, long, and didn't come back.

"Count it if you like. Sixty heartbeats, first push to last. A clean one is three. That's the whole price of a hand's width, and you've watched it paid in full, which is more than most men who pay it ever do."

She drew the knife out straight, the way it had gone, wiped it on the dead boy's cloak, and pressed it back into his hand, hilt first.

"Rest you already know. Bowels and bladder let go at the end — that's the smell changing under us, and it's why I told you the dry side. Nothing shameful in it. The body drops its pack when the march is done."

She stood, knees cracking, and looked down at him a moment.

"You asked for all of it and you watched all of it. Good. It's the men who look away that it comes back for, later, in the dark." She shouldered her kit. "Wood now. Dead and standing, twice what you think you need. Work's the thing for the next hour — I've had this evening more times than you've had hot dinners, and I know its shape."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at him a long moment, then unshouldered the kit she'd just put on, set it against the wheel, and sat down across from him with the boy between them under his cloak. She pulled the wine skin, drank, and passed it over.

"Alright. You're asking for the part after — what it does to you, now that it's done. That has an order too, like the rest of it. I'll give it to you in order." She glanced down the road out of habit, then back. "Nobody gave it to me. I learned it piecemeal, wrong end first, over years. You're getting it in one evening. That's the whole reason I'm talking."

"Tonight first. You'll be hungry and not want to eat, or want to eat and bring it back up — either's common. Eat anyway. Bread, not meat. The fire will seem better than any fire you've ever sat by, and that's not the wine talking, that's the body finding out it lived. Then you'll be tired down to the bone, lie down, and not sleep. Nobody believes that part until they're in it."

"The gap between waking and sleep is where it comes back. You'll close your eyes and feel the give of the blade, or see his hands, or nothing you can name — just the weight of it, wearing different clothes. That's not him. The dead don't come back; I've given them every chance over the years and not one has taken me up on it. It's the mind, filing what the day's work made. It takes nights. Sometimes weeks. Let it run. The men who fight it awake are the ones it keeps."

"Dreams, since you'll have them. You'll dream you did it wrong — that it took longer, that he spoke. You'll dream it's someone you love under your hand, and nobody warns you about that one, so I'm warning you: it means nothing. The mind shuffles the deck when it files. You'll wake with your heart going like a drum and the dark will feel full of things. It isn't. I'm the only thing in the dark, and I'll be awake anyway. First watch is mine."

She took the skin back, drank, held it a moment.

"Morning's the strange one. You'll expect the world to look different and it won't. Birds. Breakfast. The road. You'll look at your face in still water expecting a mark, and there isn't one, and the gap between the size of the thing and the size of the mark will feel like something's wrong with you. Nothing's wrong with you. The world doesn't keep our ledger. That's the whole of that."

"After that it comes at odd hours — never when you think about it, always when your hands are idle. Smells bring it back worst. Copper. The privy. The butcher's stall. You'll go off your food at some cookfire in some town and not know why, and then you'll know. It passes quicker each time. Keep your hands busy when it comes. Work's the thing. I keep saying it because it's true, not because I'm short of words."

She turned the skin in her hands, and her voice went a shade flatter, which for her was the sound of a door opening that she didn't open often.

"The second one is easier. That's its own trouble. The first sits heavy, the second sits less, and by the fifth you'll check whether it sits at all. I told you to come tell me the day it doesn't sit heavy. I meant it. That's not poetry, it's maintenance — a blade you don't check rusts. Count or don't count, but know which you're doing. I counted for eleven years, and then one winter I realised I'd lost the number, and I sat up a whole night trying to find it and couldn't. That sat heavier than any of them. Now I keep the ones I can name. This boy, I'd count. You did right by him. Some of mine I can't say that for."

"My first, I was nineteen, and it was nothing like this. Nobody knelt with me. Nobody told me where to cut. A man came at me in a breach and I put a knife in him by luck, high in the chest, and he took most of an hour, and I sat with him because there was nowhere else to be, and afterwards nobody told me one word of what I've just told you. So." A shrug, economical. "Somebody should have, once. Now somebody has."

The light had gone from ash to nothing while she talked. The crow had gone quiet. She didn't look at the sky; she knew where it was.

"The long view, and then I'm done. It doesn't go away — anyone who says it goes away is selling something. It gets smaller. It's a stone in your pocket. First year it's sharp and you cut your hand on it every time you reach in. Ten years on it's worn smooth, and you still know it's there, and it doesn't cut you anymore, and some days you reach in and turn it over on purpose, to remember the weight. That's the best it gets, and it's enough. I'm still here. Most of the ones who heard this talk from me are still here. The ones who wouldn't hear it — I buried three of those. Drink, mostly. Or they went strange and walked into a fight they didn't need. It's the looking away that kills, in the end. Not the work."

She corked the skin and set it down.

"And the last of it, because you asked me earlier whether it was mercy or easier: you gave him the best hour he had left, and you watched the whole price of it paid, and you didn't look away. If his mother could ask you — she won't, she'll never know your name — you could tell her he didn't die slow, and he didn't die alone, and the man who did it said sorry. That's more truth than most mothers get, in this war or any other."

She stood, knees cracking, and shouldered the kit again.

"That's the rest. All of it, in order, nothing left out. Ten years taught it to me and it didn't cost you ten years, so you're ahead on the deal." She nodded toward the treeline, black against black now. "Wood. Dead and standing, twice what you think, and keep the road in sight. Fire, food, sleep, in that order."

A pause, and then, for the first time all evening, his name.

"Corvin. When it comes back tonight, in the gap before sleep — it's just the filing. I'll be awake anyway."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack considered the question the way you'd consider a weather report. She'd seen the man go down — or heard it, anyway. There'd been a sound when the bolt took him, and then a different kind of sound after.

"Low belly," she said. "Got him under the ribs on the left and it came out the back. That's gut, and gut's slow. He's been trying to hold it in and he's got it mostly packed back up but it doesn't matter — it's the filth that kills you, not the hole. You can't clean a wound like that in a ditch."

She shifted the hatchet to her other hand, then back again. Getting the feel of it.

"So. Both. It's a mercy and it's easier and those aren't two different things, whatever the chaplain told you." She looked at him sideways. "If it helps, he's not thinking anything right now that's worth saving. That's the truth and it's all the truth there is."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack didn't look up. She had her fingers in a dead man's coat lining and found a seam that was too thick, which meant something sewn in, which meant it was worth the trouble of picking apart.

"You're looking at a man on his back with his knees up," she said. "That's how they go when it's gut — they draw up because it eases the pull on the belly muscles. His hands are probably on the wound. He's got his shirt stuffed in there, maybe his belt, and it's soaked through. The color of it — don't worry about the color. It looks worse than it is."

She got the seam open. A small leather packet inside. She put it in her own belt pouch without opening it.

"His face'll be grey and he's sweating even though it's cold. That's the shock. The eyes might look right at you and he might even say something, but he's not talking to you, he's talking to the pain. Don't take it personal if he says something ugly. Don't take it personal if he says something kind either."

She paused, thinking.

"Breathing's the thing to watch. You said it's bubbling. That means blood in the airway and he's drowning slow. Every breath's work now. He'll try to hold still because moving hurts, and then he'll gasp because he can't get air, and then he'll hold still again. That's the rhythm. You'll want to do it between the gasps — not during. During, he'll flinch and grab."

She pulled a boot knife off the third man. Decent blade. She kept that one.

"The hands. I told you. Look at the hands." A beat. "They'll be red to the elbow. That's his own insides. It's not as bad as it looks."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at him across the fire for a moment, the way you'd look at a man who'd asked a horse trader to explain the horse's teeth. Then she nodded. Fair enough.

She pulled the bread out and set it on a stone to cool. Talked while she worked, the same way she'd talk about a bad hinge or a lame mule — details, just details.

"All right. Straight, then. Bolt went in under the ribs on the left — you said spear, it's the same thing, just a different hole. Point's about this long." She held her thumb and forefinger apart. "And it went through everything in its way. Stomach, most likely. Maybe the spleen. Bowel, definitely — you can't hit that part of the belly and miss bowel, there's too much of it in there."

She picked up a stick and drew in the dirt beside the fire. Not a picture of a man. Just shapes. Tubes.

"Here's what happens. The gut's full of — food, waste, bile, all of it, and none of it belongs outside the gut. When you open it up, that stuff leaks into the belly cavity. The cavity's clean. It doesn't like being dirty. So it swells up trying to fight it and it can't, because there's too much and it's the wrong kind of filth."

She poked the stick into the dirt. "The swelling's what you'd have felt if you'd pressed on him. Hard as a drum. He'd have screamed. That's why he was on his back with his knees up — any movement pulls on the swollen parts and it's like being stabbed all over again from the inside."

"The bleeding's what people think kills you and sometimes it does, if they hit the big vessels. But gut wounds, it's usually the poison. Takes hours. First the fever, then the shaking, then the confusion — he stops knowing where he is. Then the body just... stops fighting. The heart keeps going a while after the mind's gone. You'll see that sometimes. The chest moves but there's nobody home."

She stopped drawing. Looked at the shapes in the dirt like they were a map of somewhere she didn't want to go back to.

"The smell gets bad toward the end. That's the gut contents coming up — he'd have vomited, near the last. Black stuff. You'd have smelled it from where you were standing in another half hour." She wiped the stick clean on her knee. "So. That's what a spear does. Takes a long time and it hurts the whole way and there's nothing at the end of it but more of the same until there isn't."

She tossed the stick into the fire.

"That's straight. I don't know what you'll do with it but you asked for it straight and that's the whole of it."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped with her hand half out for the bread. She looked at him over the fire — really looked, the way you look at a man who's just asked you to cut him open so he can see the inside of himself.

Then she got up. Slowly, because of the knee. She came around the fire and stood over the body with him, close enough to see what he was seeing.

"All right," she said. "I'll tell you."

She crouched down on her heels beside him. The dead man was on his back, knees still drawn up, hands still on the ruined wad of cloth at his belly. The hatchet had gone in at the temple, left side, and Wrack pointed to it without touching it.

"Here's what you did. You swung from the left and came down at an angle — see the way the wound runs? It's not straight down, it's about thirty degrees. That means your arm was coming across your body, not over your head. Over the head's stronger but it's slower and you were close. Close is good. Close is what you want."

She traced the air above the wound without making contact.

"The edge caught here," she tapped a spot on the dead man's temple, an inch from the wound, "and bit in here. Bone's thinnest at the temple — that's why I told you to aim for it. The hatchet went through the outer table of the skull, through the dura — that's the lining around the brain — and into the temporal lobe about two inches deep. Maybe less. Doesn't take much."

She sat back on her heels.

"The sound you heard. That crack. That wasn't the blade — that was the skull giving way. Bone sounds like that when it breaks fast. Kindling, like I said. The blade itself doesn't make much noise going in. It's the bone that talks."

She looked at the dead man's face. His eyes were open, still fixed on where Corvin had been standing.

"Now. What happened after. When the edge went through the dura and into the brain, it tore the middle meningeal artery — that's a blood vessel on the inside of the skull, and it's the one that bleeds fastest in head wounds. But it doesn't matter here, because the damage to the brain was instant. The temporal lobe controls — well, it controls a lot. Memory. Language. Awareness. You hit all of that at once."

She was quiet for a moment.

"He didn't feel it. That's the truth. The nerve signals from the wound site would have taken time to reach whatever was left of his awareness, and the awareness was already gone. What you saw — if you saw anything — was the body, not him. The body does things after the mind's gone. The eyes stay open because the muscles that close them are gone. The fingers twitch. Sometimes the mouth moves. It's not speech. It's just — the last of the electricity going through the wires."

She pointed to his hands again.

"See? The fingers are still curled. That's not him gripping. That's a contraction — the muscles locking up as they run out of what they need to keep going. It stops in about ten minutes. Then the body starts to go slack, and then the cold comes in, and by morning he'll be stiff as a board and you won't be able to move those legs at all."

She looked at the wound one more time.

"The blood. There's less than you'd think. Head wounds bleed a lot when they're alive because the heart's pumping. Here — he was already dying, heart was weak, pressure was low. So it's just... seeping. You see how it's pooling in the ear? That's gravity. It'll fill the ear canal first, then run down into whatever he's lying on."

She stopped. Looked at Corvin.

"That's all of it. The sound. The time — from the swing to the stop was less than a second. The body kept moving for maybe three seconds after. The twitching lasted about two minutes. Then it was just meat." She paused. "That's what you did. That's the whole of it. It's not more than that and it's not less."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped chewing. She sat there with the bread in her mouth and looked at him across the fire, and for a moment she looked every one of her forty-three years and then some.

She swallowed.

"The rest," she said.

She put the bread down. Picked up the brandy skin instead and pulled the stopper and had a drink that lasted longer than the other ones. She set it between her boots and pressed her palms flat against her thighs, like she was steadying herself for something that required steadying.

"All right. The rest."

She was quiet for a moment. Not the comfortable quiet from before — the other kind. The kind where a person is choosing which door to walk through.

"Here's the rest. Nobody tells you this part because there's no word for it and it doesn't bleed and you can't stitch it. The anatomy, that's easy. I can talk about the anatomy all night and it's just shapes and tubes and what happens when you open them. That part's *clean*. That's why I gave it to you first."

She looked at the dead man on the ground between them. Then she looked away from him.

"The rest is this. You're going to go home — not home, there's no home, but back to camp, back to wherever we set up tonight — and you're going to sit down and you're going to be fine. And then in about an hour you're going to realize you can still feel the handle. Not remember it — *feel* it. Like it's still in your hand. Like your palm's got the shape of it pressed into it. And you'll look at your hand and there'll be nothing there, but the feeling won't go."

She flexed her own right hand. Open and closed. She'd done it so many times it was almost invisible.

"That lasts about a week. Maybe two. Then it goes to the other thing."

She picked up a small stick — not the one she'd drawn with, a different one — and started peeling the bark off it. Slowly. Strip by strip.

"The other thing is the noise. Not the crack — you'll forget the crack, I told you that. I mean the before. The quiet. You're going to hear that quiet at three in the morning for the rest of your life. Not every night. Not even most nights. But some nights you'll wake up and the camp'll be still and the fire'll be low and you'll hear *that* quiet — the one right before — and your whole body'll go cold like someone poured water on you. And you'll lie there and you'll know exactly where you are and what you did and you'll wait for it to pass. And it does. It always does. But it takes about ten minutes and those ten minutes are yours and nobody else's."

She peeled another strip of bark. Let it fall.

"That's the rest. That's what's left over when the anatomy's done."

She looked at him then. Directly. Not the sideways look from before. Full on.

"And here's the other thing. The thing I should have said at the start but I didn't because you weren't ready for it and maybe you're not ready now but you asked for the rest and that's the rest."

She held the stick in both hands.

"It gets easier."

She let that sit.

"Not better. Easier. The tenth time, the handle doesn't stay in your hand as long. The fiftieth time, the quiet at night is just quiet. The hundredth time — " She stopped. Counted something in her head. "Well. I stopped counting somewhere in the second hundred. That was about six years ago. Now it's just work. Now it's cleaning a knife on a dead man's cloak and counting the coppers in their pockets and deciding whether the boots are worth carrying."

She looked at her hands. They were steady. They always were.

"That's the part that should scare you. Not the blood. Not the sound. The part where it stops scaring you. Because once it stops, you can't get it back. You can't un-know how easy it is. You can't go back to being the person who stood there with their throat tight and their hands shaking. That person's gone. And what's left is someone who can do it and eat bread after and sleep fine and do it again tomorrow. And that person is —"

She stopped again. Not for effect. Because she'd hit the end of what she knew how to say.

"That person is useful," she said finally. "That's what they are. Useful. And that's the rest of it. The rest is that you become something useful and you lose something that had another name for it but I've forgotten the name and I think that's the worst part, that I've forgotten the word for the thing I used to be."

She tossed the peeled stick into the fire. Watched it catch.

"You asked me to tell you straight. That's straight. That's all of it. The anatomy and the rest and the part after the rest." She picked up the brandy skin and held it out to him across the fire. "Now drink some of that. Properly. Not a sip. A drink. Because your hands are going to start in about five minutes and I'd rather you had something in you when they do."

She held the skin there. Waiting. Her arm didn't waver.

"And Corvin." His name. She didn't use it often. "The fact that you asked for the rest — that you wanted to know the whole of it and not just the pretty parts — that's the difference between you and most of the men I've served with. Most of them want the anatomy and not the other. They want to believe it's just shapes and tubes." She shook her head slowly. "It's never just shapes and tubes. The ones who think it is are the ones who break first. Usually at night. Usually alone."

She set the brandy skin down between them when he didn't take it, and she sat back and pulled her coat around her shoulders because the cold was coming in properly now and the fire was small and the dead men were getting cold too and it was all just — cold. Everything was cold. That was the rest of the rest, if there was any more of it: that the world gets cold and stays cold and you keep going anyway because there isn't a word for stopping.

Somewhere past the big rock, the stream ran over stones. The fire popped. Wrack sat with her hands on her knees and her back straight and her eyes on the middle distance and she waited, because waiting was also work, and she was good at that too.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack didn’t blink. She just watched him work the buckle, then gave a short, flat nod. "Straight it is."

She stepped closer, crouching just enough to gesture at the dead man’s midsection without touching him. "A spear doesn’t just pierce. It drags. The point’s usually rough-hewn or barbed. It tears through the abdominal wall, catches on the muscle, and rips straight through the mesentery. You’ll nick the liver on a right-side strike, or the spleen on the left. Either way, you’ve got internal bleeding that you can’t see until his face goes the colour of old ash and his pulse turns to a flutter."

She paused, voice even, eyes fixed on the corpse as if reading a ledger. "If it goes deeper, it shreds the intestines. Bowel contents spill into the belly. That’s not a wound that bleeds you out clean. That’s a wound that rots you from the inside while you’re still standing. Infection sets in within hours. Fever, rigors, delirium. If you’re lucky, you bleed out first. If you’re not, you spend two days on your back, shitting blood and vomiting bile, while your own gut bacteria eat you alive. The smell alone will clear a camp and sour your own water skin."

She stood, brushing grit from her knees. "Spears are just angry gardening tools. They make a mess. That’s why we use edges up close. Clean cut, fast bleed, less stink to wash out of your gear." She glanced at the darkening sky, then back to him. "Now finish his belt. We’re moving. And if you ever get skewered, you’ll know why we strip the dead fast. Rot doesn’t wait for dawn."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack stepped up beside him, boots sinking into the sodden earth. She didn’t flinch at the sight, just tilted her head and took in the details the way a cobbler inspected a split sole.

"You’re looking at a man who ran out of time," she said, voice flat. "That’s the wound. Clean through the sternum, nicked the aorta. See the dark pooling around his ribs? That’s not just blood. That’s what happens when a lung collapses and the chest can’t clear it. He’s been breathing his own fluid for twenty minutes."

She pointed a calloused finger at the face. "Jaw’s gone slack. Pupils blown wide. That’s not peace. That’s the nervous system clocking out. Muscles lose tone, veins empty, heat starts leaching into the ground. In an hour, rigor will set in. In two, he’ll be stiff as a board and twice as useless. I’ve field-dressed men with less blood in their veins and more sense in their heads. He’s done."

She crouched, brushing a thumb over the edge of his tunic where the knife had gone in. "Up close, it’s just meat and cloth. No grandeur. No drama. Just physics and bad luck. You’re wondering if it matters. It doesn’t. He’s not a tragedy. He’s just weight now."

She stood, wiping her thumb on her own trousers. "Strip him. Bootees, belt, water skin, anything with a buckle or a seam worth mending. Leave the rest. We don’t take what we can’t carry, and we don’t leave what’ll slow us down." She glanced toward the darkening treeline, then back to Corvin. "Fire next. Then watch. You’ve got the knife work down. Now learn the rest of it. The war doesn’t stop because you did your part for the night."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack didn’t smile. She just shifted her weight, boots squelching in the churned earth, and listened to the wet rattling past the timber. "Ribs cracked, lung taking on water, femoral nicked. He’s drowning in his own chest and trying to swallow air through a collapsed side. How bad is he? Bad enough that his own blood’s pooling in his ear."

She stepped closer, voice dropping to a flat, even register. "You’re trying to dress a field wound in philosophy. It doesn’t fit. Mercy and easier are just two words for the same clean cut. You put him down now, he doesn’t spend the night thrashing in his own filth. You don’t, you get up at dawn to a stiff corpse with a belly full of flies and a job you left half-done. The war’s been running on that arithmetic for ten years. Don’t pretend it’s a moral quandary."

She jerked her chin toward the cart, eyes tracking the shallow, uneven rise of his shoulders. "He’s lost half his blood. Shock’s keeping him quiet, but it’ll wear off. Then he’ll start begging. Or cursing. Either way, it’ll keep you awake and sour the next watch. Do it. Clean. Then we roll."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. She let the wind tug at the hem of her coat for a long moment before she turned back, boots pivoting in the mud. There was no sigh, no hesitation. Just a slow blink, then a nod.

"Fine," she said. "Watch and listen. I won't dress it up."

She stepped up beside him, keeping her hands loose at her sides, and fixed her gaze on the space between them. She didn't lean in. Didn't hover. Just tracked the mechanics.

"Feel that first resistance," she said, voice low and even. "That's the skin and subcutaneous fat giving way. You'll hear a wet tear, like damp canvas splitting. Don't fight it. Let the blade ride through."

She listened as the breath caught, then broke into a ragged, wet pull. "That's the diaphragm spasming. Lungs trying to draw air through a collapsed passage. It'll sound like a bellows choking on water. Takes about three seconds for the chest to stop rising. Then the jaw drops. Nerves fire one last time, muscles lose tone. You'll hear a soft click when the teeth lose tension. That's the end of it."

She kept her eyes on the work, voice matching the steady rhythm of the ditch. "If you hesitate, he thrashes. If you push clean, it's over before his brain registers the cut. You're doing it slow. That's fine. Just don't let your grip slip. Blood's slick. The blade follows the hand, not the thought."

When it ended, she didn't move for a beat. Just let the silence settle, then shifted her weight. "Done. Took you nine seconds. Longer than it should. But he's quiet. That's what matters." She crouched, not to check him, but to point at the ground. "See the pooling? That's arterial. It'll darken fast in the cold. Wipe your blade. Check the edge. Then stand up. You've got the sound now. You've got the time. Next time, it'll be faster. Not because you're cruel. Because you're efficient."

She stood, brushing grit from her thighs with a flat palm. "Fire's waiting. Move."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack didn’t move. She just set the broken twigs down on the flat stone, folded her hands in her lap, and let the cold air settle between them. Her eyes stayed fixed on the darkening slope, but her voice didn’t waver.

"You want the rest," she said. "Fine. I'll give it to you."

She began like she was inventorying a damaged cart. "First, the eyes. The corneas dry out. They'll cloud over, turn milky, then yellow. The eyelids won't stay shut. They'll stick half-open, catching the wind, until the skin shrinks around the sockets. You'll see the whites staring up at the sky like they're counting clouds."

She tapped a calloused finger against her knee, counting silently. "Next, the blood. It doesn't just stop. It settles. Gravity pulls it to the lowest points. You'll get purple bruising under the skin where he's lying. Livor mortis. Starts in ten minutes, fixes in four. After that, you can turn him over and the marks stay. The skin peels if you drag him across gravel."

Wrack's gaze didn't flicker. "Then the stiffening. Rigor. Starts at the jaw, moves down the arms, then the legs. Takes three to four hours to set, another six to peak. He'll be hard as iron. You can't fold the arms for burial. You can't strap him to a cart. You'll have to break the joints to move him, and the sound's like snapping dry branches. You'll feel it through the leather gloves."

She exhaled, a thin plume vanishing in the chill. "After rigor breaks, the softening starts. Bacteria in the gut and mouth get to work. They eat through the intestines first. Gas builds up. The belly swells. Skin blisters, splits. Green and black fluid seeps out of the mouth, the nose, the wound you just made. It smells like spoiled meat and copper. Then it smells like shit. Then it smells like rotting flowers. Flies come within an hour if it's warm. In this cold, they'll wait till dawn. Then they'll lay eggs in the open wounds, the eyes, the mouth. Maggots hatch in twelve hours. They'll strip the flesh to bone in two days if you leave him."

Wrack finally turned her head, meeting Corvin's line of sight without softening. "You'll hear him too. Not breathing. But the body doesn't stop making noise. Gas escaping through the throat sounds like wheezing. Fluid dripping from the nose hits the ground with a wet tap. The skin cracks as it dries. It sounds like paper tearing. At night, it sounds like he's still there. It'll keep you awake. It'll make you check the dark twice as often. Your ears will train to it, and you'll start hearing it in quiet rooms for weeks."

She shifted her weight, boots creaking. "And the gear. Blood soaks through leather, stiffens it, cracks it when it dries. Rust eats the buckles. Mud cakes the boots. By morning, his kit's ruined. You'll have to cut it off him with a knife. You'll get grease and grime under your nails that won't wash out for a week. You'll smell it on yourself for days. It'll sit in your clothes, your hair, your teeth. You'll taste it when you eat. You'll dream about it. Not the face. The smell. The weight. The sound of wet cloth tearing when you pull a shirt off a stiff shoulder."

Wrack leaned forward slightly, voice dropping but never losing its edge. "That's the rest. No glory. No quiet passing. Just meat cooling, fluids leaking, bacteria working, flies waiting, and the living having to walk through it to get to dawn. You wanted to know what a spear does to a gut. That's what a dead man does to a camp. It weighs you down. It stinks. It keeps you awake. It makes you hungry for a clean knife and a fresh ditch."

She sat back, picking up the twigs again, her movements economical, precise. "You've heard it. Now build the fire. And when you're on watch, if you hear wet dripping or soft cracking, you'll know it's just physics. Not ghosts. Not guilt. Just work."

She looked up at Corvin, her gaze steady. "You're right, it's a mercy. But it's also practical. We don't have the time or the supplies to tend to him, and leaving him here is a death sentence. So, it's a mercy for him, and a necessity for us. You understand that, right?"

She stood, her hand still on her sword. "I can do it, if you can't. But you should know, it's not a kindness to let him suffer. It's a curse. For him, and for us."

Corvin:
*I swallow hard, my grip on my sword tightening.* "Fine," *I say, my voice barely above a whisper.* "Do it. I... I can't."

Wrack:
Wrack nodded, her expression softening slightly. "It's not easy," she said. "But it's necessary. I've done it more times than I can count. It doesn't get easier, but you learn to live with it."

She drew her sword, the blade glinting in the fading light. "I'll make it quick," she promised. "And I'll make sure he doesn't suffer. That's all I can do for him now."

She knelt beside the man, her hand steady on his shoulder. "May the gods have mercy on your soul," she whispered, before driving her blade through his chest.

She took a deep breath, then nodded, her expression resolute. "So, what's it going to be, kid? You want to know, or you want to keep pretending? I can't make that choice for you. But I can tell you, it's a lot easier to face the truth, than to live a lie. And it's a lot easier to face the truth, than to face the consequences of pretending it's not there. So, what's it going to be? The truth, or the lie? Your choice, kid. Your future. Your life. What's it going to be?"

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
She didn’t stop the whetstone on steel. The rhythmic scrape filled the space between them, steady and indifferent. “You asked for straight,” she said, finally lifting her eyes from the blade. “A spear doesn’t ‘do’ anything to a gut. It punches a hole in the abdominal wall. The tip carries skin, fat, and muscle, and whatever’s sitting in the wrong place at the wrong time. The intestines spill. They don’t tumble out like a sack of grain. They fold. They stick to each other. They stick to the stone.”

She set the whetstone down and picked up her bow, thumb dragging along the string to check for tension. “You’ll feel the resistance give, then the heavy drag as the point catches on a loop of bowel. Pull it out clean, and you leave a wound that bleeds for ten minutes before the clotting takes hold. Twist it, and you tear the mesentery. He drops fast, because his blood pressure just met the dirt. The stomach acid mixes with the air. It burns. He’ll vomit before he passes out. It’s not pretty. It’s just pressure and anatomy.”

She slung the bow across her back and started walking back toward the ditch, boots finding the same churned path. “If you’re looking for poetry, you’re in the wrong trade. If you’re looking to know how to aim, aim low and drive it past the ribs. The liver’s right under the diaphragm. One clean pass and he’s down before he realizes he’s bleeding out. Now finish checking the pockets. We’re losing the light, and the dead don’t care about your education.”

rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
"What you're looking at," she said, dropping from the ridge with the quiet thud of a loaded pack, "is a man who spent eight minutes drowning in his own thoracic cavity." She stopped a pace away, gaze fixed on the corpse's face. "You're looking at the way the blood pools where gravity takes it. Left flank. Means he was rolled when the shaft went in. You're looking at the rigor starting to lock his fingers, and the way his mouth is still twitching because the diaphragm hasn't quite stopped spasming. It's not a person. It's a stopped clock."

She didn't wait for him to process it. "You're also looking at a beacon. The smell of copper and ruptured lung will pull every scavenger within two miles. You wanted a description? Here it is: you're looking at why we don't leave bodies in the open when we're trying to stay hidden. Wipe your blade on the inside of your tunic. Not the cloak. The cloak's already accounted for. Check his pockets for coin or papers, but don't spend more than a minute. Time spent looting is time spent breathing air that isn't yours."

She turned, already scanning the tree line again. "Lesson one of the border war: the dead don't matter. What matters is what they attract. Move."

rows.reply:
She didn’t move. She just shifted her weight, boots settling into the churned earth, and watched. The cold had already drawn the leather tight. “You’re working the left heel first,” she said, voice flat. “The stitching’s stiff. If you pull straight, it’ll hold. If you twist, the thread will snap. Dry snap. Like a dry twig. You’ll feel the ankle bone slip free. Then the sole’s going to resist. Packed with dirt and old mud. It’ll make a wet pull when it finally comes loose. Sucking sound. Followed by the smell—tanned leather, horse sweat, and the faint copper rot of a foot that’s been sweating in the dark for days. Takes thirty seconds. Maybe forty if the laces are frozen. Don’t rush it. Force it and you’ll tear the ligaments. They’ll stick together like wet paper. You’ll have to pick them apart with your knife. That’s just friction and cold.”

She adjusted her bow strap, eyes tracking the tree line before returning to him. “The right one’s heavier. The heel nail’s worked loose inside the sole. You’ll hear it click against the inner leather before it slips. When it clears the calf, it’ll catch on the dead weight. You’ll feel the drag give. That’s gravity. He’s already gone. You’re just moving what’s left. Wipe your hands on the grass. Don’t look at the foot. It’s just a thing that doesn’t work anymore.”

She let the silence stretch, counting the seconds in her head. “Forty seconds each. You’ve got two. Make them quick. Then we move.”
