rows.reply:
She didn’t move. She just stood there in the cooling dark, the damp wind pulling at the edges of her cloak, and listened to him sit in the aftermath. “You want the rest,” she said, voice flat, “so you get the rest. No poetry. No mercy. Just the mechanics.”

She paced the distance in her head, counting the seconds like she was timing a shot. “The blade goes in. It meets resistance at the diaphragm, then the abdominal wall, then the intestine. You feel the give, then the drag. You push until the handle stops, then you pull. The sound is a wet tear, like canvas soaking through, followed by a sharp exhale that catches in the throat. He drops. Not gracefully. Just gravity taking over once the core collapses. His knees hit the dirt. His hands go to the wound, but they’re already learning they can’t stop it. The blood comes hot and fast, mostly arterial at first, then venous as the pressure drops. It pools. It doesn’t stay in the body. It finds the lowest point. You watch it spread.”

She shifted her weight, boots pressing into the churned earth. “He starts vomiting. Stomach acid, bile, whatever’s sitting in the wrong place. It burns the throat, chokes the airway. He gasps. Wet, rattling gasps. The lungs fill with fluid, not air. He shivers. That’s the nervous system firing last, dumping adrenaline into a system that’s already shutting down. He’ll stare. He’ll track you. He won’t understand why he’s still breathing when he’s already dead. That takes three minutes. Maybe four. The cold slows it. The heat speeds it up. You don’t look away. You watch the hands stop moving. You watch the eyes glass over. You wait for the diaphragm to stop spasming. That’s when the real work starts.”

She brushed a pine needle from her shoulder, eyes fixed on the corpse as if measuring it against a ledger. “The blood stops flowing when the heart gives out. That’s the final sound—a wet click, like a gear stripping, followed by silence. The body cools. Rigor sets in within an hour, stiffening the joints, locking the jaw. The smell hits you next. Copper, salt, broken organs, wet earth. It draws flies within minutes, scavengers within the hour. You leave it open, the pack pays for it. You move it, you carry the weight. You clean the blade, you check your own hands for blood, you wipe the mud off your boots, and you walk. That’s it. No grace. No justice. Just physics, time, and the clean-up. You wanted the full count. There it is. Now stand up. The dark’s here, and we’re not paying for it with our shoes.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack finally turned. She leaned back against the bank with her arms crossed over her chest and looked at him the way she'd look at a map that didn't match the terrain.



"Neither," she said. "It was what you did."

She held his gaze for a moment, then looked past him toward the dark shape by the cart, which was just a shape now, the way all of them became shapes once you stopped seeing them as people.

"Mercy's a story you tell yourself afterward so your hands stop shaking. It doesn't do anything for the man. He doesn't know the difference. He was past knowing the difference about thirty seconds after you first saw him." She said it flatly, the way she'd describe a distance or a weather pattern. "And 'easier' isn't the right word either, because nothing about walking toward a man making that noise is easy. You did it because leaving him was worse. That's not mercy and it's not easy. It's arithmetic."

She crouched down again and pulled the stopper from the vial, sniffing it once the way she always did before deciding she still trusted it.

"What I'll tell you is this." She recapped the vial and looked up. "You searched him yet, or are you still standing there working out what kind of person you are? Because one of those things puts coin in your pocket and the other one doesn't, and I'd like to know before I decide whether you're worth keeping alive past this week."

It wasn't quite a joke. Wrack's humor had teeth in it even when she wasn't trying to bite, and this was her trying less than usual. But there was something in the delivery — a beat too dry, a look that held a fraction too long — that suggested she'd heard the question for what it was: someone testing whether the ground under them held weight.

She jerked her chin toward the cart. "Six men. Five pockets I didn't finish. Go."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack moved to stand beside him, not behind — she'd learned long ago that people flinched when they couldn't see where you were, and flinching near a body was how you got a knife in the hand from someone still holding it.

She looked down at the man for a moment the way you'd look at a horse you were about to buy, then tilted her head toward the ground.

"First: he's dead. You already know that, but I've seen men put a second strike into something that was already past arguing, and it's a waste of steel and a good sign you're not paying attention. So check that first. Always."

She crouched — slowly, one hand braced on her knee — and reached out to turn the man's head with two fingers against his jaw. The movement was practiced, impersonal, like she was checking the grain in a piece of timber.

"Here's what you're looking at. See where the blood's pooled? That's postmortem — it settled there because he stopped moving and his heart stopped pushing it around. So he's been still long enough for that, which means he's past your problem." She let the head drop. "See the way his hands are? Open, palms up. Not clenched. Man who dies fighting has his hands in fists, even after — some sort of nerve thing, the body not getting the message. His hands are open because he wasn't fighting at the end. He was holding on to something, maybe, but he wasn't fighting."

She looked up at Corvin. "That's what you did. You didn't kill a man who was fighting you. You killed a man who was past fighting. That's not a compliment and it's not a condemnation. It's just what the body tells you, and the body doesn't lie the way people do."

She stood, brushing her hands on her thighs, and jerked her chin toward the dark treeline where the rest of the column would be settling into camp if they had any sense.

"Now. You want to stand here and read him like a book, or do you want to help me strip what's useful off these six before the light goes? Because I'm not carrying pack for both of us."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack paused with her hand on the dead man's belt buckle, then straightened up and looked at Corvin the way you look at someone who's finally asked the right question.

"Straight," she said. "All right."

She wiped her hands on her thighs — not because they were dirty, but because it gave her something to do while she decided where to start.

"A spear through the gut doesn't kill you quickly. That's the first thing, and it's the thing nobody tells you because nobody wants to hear it. A sword through the heart, you've got maybe ten seconds before the lights go out. A crossbow bolt to the neck, faster. But a spear takes its time."

She held up a finger.

"What happens: the point goes in, and if it's sharp — and most of theirs are — it goes in clean, doesn't tear much on the way in. The damage is on the way out, or if it's still in there, because then you've got a wound that won't close and a gut that's been punctured, which means everything that's supposed to stay inside starts coming out the hole. Not fast. Slow. Over hours."



She looked toward the cart where Corvin's man was, then back.

"The first hour, he's probably still talking. Might even be walking, if he's tough or stupid enough to try. Second hour, the pain starts doing what pain does — makes you curl up, makes you sweat, makes you stop being able to think about anything except the place where the hole is. Third hour, he's not making sentences anymore. Fourth or fifth, he's not making words. Somewhere in there, infection starts, and that's if the cold doesn't get him first or the bleeding doesn't just decide to finish it."

She crouched back down and resumed working on the dead man's belt, prying the buckle free with a thumbnail.

"So when I say you made it easy — and I don't say that often — I mean you gave him five seconds of something rather than four hours of nothing. That's not mercy because mercy implies you were doing it *for* him. You weren't. You were doing it for the noise, and for us, and because you're the kind of person who doesn't walk toward screaming and then walk away." She snapped the buckle free and pocketed it. "But the arithmetic still holds."

She glanced up at him.

"You wanted to know what a spear does to a gut. Now you know. You're going to be sleeping next to a man who knows it too, tonight. That's the part nobody warns you about — you don't forget it, and it doesn't get less sharp with use." She shrugged one shoulder. "It just gets quieter."

rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. She didn't turn back immediately — she let the silence sit for a beat, long enough to make sure she'd heard him right, and then longer than that, because she'd learned that when someone asked for something twice as hard as the thing you'd just told them, it was worth checking they understood what they were asking for.

Then she came back.

She settled herself against the trunk of the tree — not kneeling, not crouching, because her knees had opinions about both and she'd learned to listen to them — and crossed her arms. She looked at the body in the ditch. She looked at Corvin. Then she fixed her gaze on his hands, because that was what she'd been asked to watch.

"Right," she said. "I'll tell you what I see. You do the work."

She was quiet while he started. The first thing he'd have to do was get the body out of the ditch, and that was its own lesson — dead weight didn't cooperate, and the position the body had died in made it worse. Wrack watched the way the arms moved wrong, the way the head lolled, and she didn't offer to help. Helping would have meant she wasn't watching, and he'd asked her to watch.

"The arms," she said, when he'd managed to get the body onto flatter ground and was reaching for the boots. "You're holding them wrong. Support the joint — elbow, wrist — not the hand. A hand'll twist out of your grip and the arm'll go somewhere you don't expect. He's not fighting you, but his body doesn't know that yet." She paused. "Sounds stupid. You'll understand when you've done it twenty times and one of them still reaches for you."

She watched him work the first boot free.

"Faster," she said. "Not because I'm rushing you. Because the longer you take, the more your brain has time to do the thing where it starts narrating. You don't want the narration. You want the hands busy and the head on the next thing."

The boot came off. She nodded once.

"Good. Second one's easier — you've already felt what you're doing. That's how it goes. The first one you think about. After that your hands know."

She was quiet for a moment. The sounds were specific — she'd heard them enough to parse them the way other people parsed weather. Leather resisting leather. The soft, wrong sound of fabric being pulled over a body that had stopped helping. A faint click of a buckle. She catalogued each one without comment, because he'd asked for the sounds, and he'd asked for all of them.

"That one," she said, nodding toward his hands as he worked at a belt buckle that had been fastened too tight or fastened wrong or fastened by fingers that weren't there anymore. "That click — you'll hear it in your sleep tonight. Not metaphorically. I mean you'll be lying there and you'll hear it, and it'll take you a second to remember it wasn't a buckle." She said it the way she said everything — flat, declarative, without pity. "That's not a warning. That's a fact, like knowing it'll be cold after dark."

She watched him finish with the belt, move to the shirt.

"He rolled," she said. "When he was dying — you can see it from the way the clothes sit. He rolled toward the ditch, which means he was trying to get away from something, and he got about four feet before his body stopped negotiating. The shirt's pulled on the left side because that's the shoulder he was dragging." She tilted her head. "Strip that side first. Fighting the fabric where it's caught only wastes time and it looks — " She stopped. Recalibrated. "It looks like you're wrestling him. You don't want to be wrestling him."

She let a few seconds pass. She didn't fill the silence unless there was something worth putting in it, and this was the part where Corvin needed to hear his own hands working — the specific rhythm of it, the way it became almost mechanical if you let it, the way mechanical was the only way to get through it without your hands starting to shake.

"Time," she said, when she judged he was nearly done. "That's the other thing you asked for. From where I'm standing, you've been at this body for about as long as it takes to walk to the cart and back. First time — that's good. First time is usually twice that, because you keep stopping to look at what you're doing. You stopped twice. That's enough."

She unfolded herself from the tree trunk and stood, joints making their usual argument.

"You done?"

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack stood there for a moment with the pack on her shoulder and the light going copper behind the trees, and she didn't move. She'd been asked directly. Wrack did not dodge a direct question unless the answer would get someone killed, and this one wouldn't.

She set the pack down again.

"The rest," she said. Not a question. She unslung the pack and leaned it against the bank, then lowered herself to sit on the ground with her back against the woodpile they'd stacked that morning. Her knees made their noise. She ignored them.

"All right."

She was quiet for a moment, not gathering herself — Wrack didn't need to gather — but deciding which order to put things in. Order mattered. Order was the difference between a lesson and a wound.

"First — what you're actually asking. You're asking whether you're the kind of man who can do that and keep walking. That's the real question underneath the other ones. The noise, the time, the hands, the sounds — those are all things you can learn. The question you're asking is whether the learning changes you into something you don't recognize."

She looked at him across the half-dark.

"It does. I'm not going to tell you it doesn't because I've watched enough men lie about that to know what the lying sounds like, and it sounds exactly like reassurance. It changes you. There's a version of you from six days ago who would have stood where you're standing now and felt something about this man by the cart that you're not going to feel tonight. That version is gone. He's been gone since you walked toward the noise. You don't get him back."

She said it plainly. It wasn't cruel; it was just the shape of the thing.

"But here's what nobody tells you about the changing, and it's the part that matters more than the rest." She picked up a stick from the ground and turned it over in her fingers — not fidgeting, just something for her hands to do while her mouth did the harder work. "It doesn't make you a different kind of person. It makes you the same person who now knows something. There's a difference. A man who's scared of fire and a man who's worked a forge both know what fire does. One of them flinches. The other one doesn't flinch but still respects it. You don't become the fire. You just stop being surprised by it."

She tossed the stick aside.

"Second — what you're actually asking me, which is whether I think you did it right. Not clean — you asked about clean earlier and clean's a technique thing, and your technique will get better. You're asking whether it was the right thing to do. Whether a man should do that."

Wrack's jaw tightened slightly — not in anger, but in the way a person's face tightens when they're about to say something they've said to themselves enough times that it's worn smooth but hasn't gotten any easier.

"There's no framework for it. I want you to hear that clearly, because someone along the way told you there was, or the world told you, or you told yourself. There's no set of rules where the answer comes out as 'yes, this was right' and you get to keep your hands clean about it. What happened past that cart was one man ending another man's life because the alternative was worse for people still breathing. That's the arithmetic. I said it before and it's still true. But arithmetic doesn't settle anything. It just tells you what the numbers are."

She pulled one knee up and rested her arm across it.

"I've done it more times than I can count without counting, and I'm telling you — it never resolves. It doesn't become okay. It becomes *normal*, and normal and okay are not the same thing, and anyone who tells you they are is selling something. What happens instead is that you get used to carrying it. It stops being a thing you think about every hour and becomes a thing you think about at night, or in quiet moments, or when someone does what you did tonight and asks you to say the rest."

She looked at him steadily.

"You asked me to watch you and tell you what I saw. So here's what I saw. I saw a man who did something terrible and then asked to understand it instead of running from it. That's rarer than you think. Most men do it the opposite way — they do it and then they build a wall around it, and the wall gets higher every year until one day they can't see over it and they don't remember what was on the other side. I've watched it happen to people I'd call friends if the word didn't require more feeling than I've got left for most of them." A pause. "You're not building the wall. That's not a compliment either. It just means you're going to feel all of this for longer, and longer is harder."

She let the silence sit. It wasn't empty — there were crickets starting up, the last bird deciding whether to go home, the soft sound of Corvin breathing in a way that told her he was listening with everything he had.

"Third. The part I haven't said."

She uncrossed her arms and set both palms flat on the ground behind her, leaning back into the woodpile.

"I don't sleep well either. I told you to sleep, and I meant it — you should, because tomorrow's another day of walking and I'm not carrying your pack. But I'd be lying if I said I went to sleep easy the first time I did what you did tonight, or the tenth, or the twentieth. It doesn't get easier. It gets *familiar*. Familiar is what lets you function. Familiar is what lets you eat dinner afterward and check the fire and do the thousand small things that keep a person alive. But easier is a lie."

She glanced toward the fire they hadn't lit yet.

"You're going to eat, and you're going to wash your hands, and you're going to lie down on that side of the fire and you're going to hear the buckle and maybe the other sounds too, and you're going to lie there and your brain is going to do the thing where it puts you back in that ditch, and it's going to feel very real and very close." She paused. "And then at some point you're going to fall asleep anyway, because the body does what it wants regardless of what the mind is doing, and you'll wake up and it'll be morning and you'll still be you. That's the part that matters. You'll still be you."

She looked at him one more time — and there was something in her face that wasn't quite softness, because Wrack's face didn't do soft, but it was the closest she came. It was recognition. The look of someone seeing another person standing in a place she'd stood, and knowing there was nothing she could do to shorten the road, and deciding to be honest about it anyway because dishonesty was a kindness that curdled.

"That's the rest," she said. "There's nothing after it. I'm not withholding the good part — there isn't one. There's just this, and then tomorrow, and then whatever comes after that."

She reached over and pulled the pack back onto her lap, unfastening the flap with fingers that had stopped moving a half-second before her brain told them to.

"Now wash your hands. I mean it. And eat something, because I'm not having you useless in the morning because you couldn't swallow." She didn't look up. "And if you want to sit up tonight, sit up. But the fire's going out in an hour because I'm not feeding it past my eyes closing, so decide whether you want light for the sitting or dark for the thinking."

It wasn't a joke. It was also, in the way of Wrack, not *not* a joke.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped dragging the dead man by the ankles, boots still planted in the dirt, and considered the question without any visible surprise.

“Bad enough,” she said.

She let the legs down gently enough not to be respectful, only practical, and turned her head toward the cart. The breathing beyond it had become a shallow, bubbling thing, interrupted by small catches that sounded worse than screams.

“Gut’s opened. One lung’s likely filling. He’ll live long enough to make it ugly if you leave him,” she said. “So if you need it to be mercy, call it mercy.”

Her eyes came back, flat and unkind in the fading light.

“If you need it to be easier, it’s that too. Easier for him, easier for us, easier for whoever finds him screaming at crows.” She wiped her hands on her thighs, though that did little good. “Don’t make a sermon of it. Just make it clean.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack left the dead man where he lay and came around the cart without hurry, boots quiet in the dirt. She stopped close enough to be useful, but not so close that she crowded the moment. Her eyes went to the wound first, not the face.

“You’re looking at a gut opening that’s gone deep,” she said, voice low and steady, as if she were explaining how to sharpen a blade without ruining the edge. “That dark soak under him is blood, not wine. The bubbling in his breath means his chest is filling. He’s past mending.”

She tilted her head slightly, indicating the angle without touching.

“You’re not looking at a man anymore. You’re looking at a job. See the hollow under the jaw, where the bone dips? Put the point there. Angle it up toward the base of the skull. One hard push. Don’t saw, don’t hesitate. If it catches, drive through.”

The wounded man made another thin, broken sound. Wrack did not flinch.

“He’ll jerk,” she said. “Step back when he does. Don’t let him drag you down into the blood.”

Her gaze lifted briefly, not unkind, but hard as flint.

“And don’t speak to him now. No apologies, no blessings, no asking if he’s ready. Mercy doesn’t need a preamble.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack did not look away from the dead man. She considered the question for a beat, then gave it to him plain.

“A spear in the gut is not one wound,” she said. “It is whatever it touches on the way through.”

She crouched again, not touching the body, only indicating with two blunt fingers.

“Low belly, under the navel—there is no bone to stop it. It goes through skin, fat, muscle, then bowel. If the gut is opened, he fills with his own filth. You will smell it quick. Shit, bile, that sweet rot-green smell of belly-water. Some men die fast from shock. Most die slow, over days, burning up and begging for water while their insides poison them.”

Her voice stayed level, the way she might describe bad weather or a broken axle.

“Higher up, under the ribs, it can find liver or spleen. Those bleed hard. Liver blood is dark and heavy. Spleen can leak slow, then all at once. Stomach spills sour water and whatever he last ate. If the point cuts one of the great vessels down the middle, he is dead before his knees understand it. If it angles up beneath the ribs into lung, he drowns in his own breath. That is the bubbling sound you heard.”

She glanced toward the corpse, then back.

“If the spear stays in, sometimes the shaft plugs the hole. Pull it, and you open the whole mess. If it is barbed, or rough, or bent, pulling drags meat with it. A clean thrust can kill quick. A bad one turns a man into a leaking sack and leaves him screaming for someone to stop the pain.”

The last of the light had gone thin and gray over the road. Somewhere in the trees, a bird gave one startled note and fell silent.

Wrack straightened with that same tired creak of joints.

“So that is what it does,” she said. “It opens, spills, and kills slow unless it hits something vital. Most gut wounds are not quick. That is why we finish them when we can. Not because it is pretty. Because the alternative is worse.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped.

She did not turn away at once, and she did not answer at once either. She stood with the dead man’s boot still in one hand and looked down at the body, then at the knife, then at the dark ground where the blood had gone sticky and black in the failing light. Her face had no pity in it, but it had no cruelty either. It had the look of a woman deciding what part of a hard thing needed saying.

“He’s dead,” she said at last. “You already did that part.”

Her voice was not sharp. It was flat and sure, the way she might have said *the fire’s out* or *the rain’s started*.

“There’s no more time to take from him. No more sound he’s going to make. If you’re asking me to stand here and tell you how long he took after the blade went in, I’ll tell you straight: not long. You gave him the hollow, you drove up, he jerked, and then he wasn’t. That’s the truth of it. I won’t stretch it out to make you feel you’ve paid enough.”

She set the boot down and came a step closer, not crowding, only near enough that he would not have to face the thing alone if he did not want to. Her eyes dropped to the corpse again.

“If you mean the searching, that’s different. That I can tell you plain.”

She nodded toward the body.

“You’ll hear cloth first. Blood dries quick and glues things, so a cloak parts with a little tear, like old paper. Leather creaks when you work a belt loose. The purse clinks if there’s coin in it, and if there isn’t, it knocks soft against your knuckles like an empty cup. Boots come hard if the legs have begun to stiffen. Sometimes they make a wet sound when the blood’s pooled under them. Nothing else. No groaning, no begging. Dead men are heavy and quiet, and that’s the worst part for some.”

Her gaze lifted.

“You don’t need me to invent suffering for you. You don’t owe him your nightmares. He was an enemy, and now he’s meat and clothing and maybe a few coppers. That’s all that’s left to do here.”

She crouched again, slow, knees protesting in their usual way, and rested one forearm on her thigh.

“I’ll stay while you go through him,” she said. “But I’ll tell you what’s real, not what you think you ought to hear. The real part is this: your hands may shake. Your stomach may turn. You may smell blood and bowels for a while and hate the smell, then hate that you’ve stopped hating it. That’s the work. It doesn’t make you worse. It just means you’re still alive.”

The dark had thickened around the cart. The wind moved again, low through the ditch grass, and the dead man’s cloak lifted a little at the edge before settling.

Wrack’s voice stayed steady.

“Take what’s useful. Leave what isn’t. And when you’re done, stand up. We’ve got road before us, and the dead won’t carry our burdens for us.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge paused mid-motion, the rag in her hand dripping pink onto the tent floor. She gave Wick a long, assessing look—not unkind, but utterly devoid of sugarcoating. 

"Bad like we're keeping him alive until they move the front again," she said, bending back to the ruined leg. The boot was already off, revealing swollen, purpling flesh. "Bad like they'll dump him in a cart with the others when we retreat. Bad like he'll wake up screaming in three days when they saw it off in some field hospital." She pressed two fingers to the man's ankle, feeling for a pulse. "Still there. For now." 

She straightened with a grunt, tossing the rag aside. "But not your problem yet. Hold his knee. I need to set this before the swelling gets worse."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge wiped her brow with the back of her wrist, leaving a faint smear of blood near her temple. She didn’t stop working as she spoke, her voice flat and clinical. 

"Tibia’s fractured, not shattered. That’s the lower leg bone—feel here." She guided Wick’s fingers to a spot just above the ankle where the skin was taut and hot. "That ridge? Bone’s out of place, but it’s still in one piece. The real problem’s the swelling. See how the skin’s shiny? That’s pressure building. Could cut off blood flow if we don’t get it stabilized." 

She tightened the last strap of the splint with a practiced twist. "If we were at a proper hospital, they’d bleed him, maybe drill the bone to relieve it. But we’re not, so we wrap it tight and hope he doesn’t lose the foot before they ship him out." 

The man whimpered as she adjusted the bindings. Sedge didn’t soften her touch. "Now the bad part," she said, reaching for a lengths of linen. "This knee’s dislocated too. Going to have to pop it back. You’ll hear it."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack did not answer at once.

She stood there with the dead man’s boot still half-loosened, her hands resting on her thighs, and looked out at the road as though checking whether the night had anything more to add to it. It did not. Only the wind in the ditch grass, only the cart settling, only the smell of blood and opened earth and the faint, sour iron stink that came after.

When she spoke again, her voice was lower. Not softer. Lower the way a blade is lowered when it has found the angle and no longer needs to be shown off.

“The rest,” she said, “is that you’ll want it to be one thing. It won’t be.”

She crouched again, slow, knees complaining, and rested one forearm over them. She did not look at the corpse while she said it. She looked at the darkening ground beyond, where the last of the light had gone the color of drowned ash.

“You’ll want it to be mercy, and it was. You’ll want it to be murder, and maybe that’s true too, depending on who’s counting and how much wine they’ve had. You’ll want it to be necessary, and it was, because leaving him here to drown in his own chest would have been worse. You’ll want it to mean something grand, and it won’t. It will mean exactly what it is: a man who was dying got finished by another man’s hand because the world had run out of better options for him.”

Her eyes moved then, briefly, to the dead man’s face. Not with pity. With acknowledgment.

“He didn’t give you a speech. He didn’t forgive you. He didn’t curse you. That’s not because he was noble. It’s because he was past it. You’ll spend a while wishing he’d done one of those things, because any of them would be easier to carry than the nothing he gave you. But that’s your problem now, not his.”

She shifted her weight, and the leather of her gear creaked faintly.

“What you did was quick enough. Quick enough matters, even if it doesn’t feel like it. The blade went in under the jaw, found the soft place, and drove up. There was resistance first—skin, then the give underneath. Not much. Enough that you felt it. Enough that your hand knew it had done a thing that couldn’t be taken back. Then he jerked. They always do. It isn’t fighting. It isn’t refusal. It’s the body spending whatever’s left in it because it doesn’t know yet that the war’s over. The heels beat. The hands came up. The breath went out. Then the eyes went flat and the weight of him changed. That’s the part people remember. Not the sound. The weight. How suddenly there’s more of him and less of him at the same time.”

Wrack’s mouth tightened, not in disgust. In recognition.

“You’ll remember the sound too, though. The little catch in the breath before it stopped. The wet settle after. Not loud. Nothing so dramatic as you’re expecting. Death usually isn’t. It’s smaller than stories make it. That’s what makes it hard to believe later. You’ll think, *It can’t have been that little a thing to end a man*, but it was. It was just that little.”

She glanced down at the purse in the dirt, then back to the road.

“Now he’s already changing. You won’t notice it much in the dark, but it’s begun. The heat’s leaving him. The blood’s settling where gravity wants it. The skin will go waxen, then stiff. The joints will lock up in their own time. If it stays warm, the smell will start before dawn. Not the smell you’re thinking of—not rot yet. Something sweeter and fouler under that. The body knows what it is before the mind admits it. Flies will find him if they’re about. Crows will come later, maybe dogs, maybe foxes, depending on what’s hungry and what’s bold. If we leave him here, by this time tomorrow he’ll be less than he is now. In a week, he’ll be a story someone tells badly. In a month, just a place where the grass grows different.”

Her voice stayed level, unhurried, stripped of ornament.

“That’s what’s real. Not the grand accounting. The physical fact of him. The way a dead man’s clothes start to belong to him differently once he’s in them. The way a belt gets sticky. The way a boot resists when you pull it off because the foot has begun to swell into it. The way the purse feels ordinary in your hand even though it came off a corpse. The coin doesn’t know. The leather doesn’t know. That’s the insult of it. Nothing around you cares enough to make the moment feel holy.”

She drew a breath through her nose and let it out again.

“And the rest is what it does to you. Not now. Now you’re running on the first shock of it, and shock is a kind of armor. Later, the armor comes off. You’ll wash your hands and still smell copper. You’ll eat and taste something else under the food. You’ll hear someone laugh at the wrong time and think it should have sounded different. You’ll be tired enough to drop and not want to sleep because sleep is where the dead come looking for their due. Or you’ll sleep like a stone and wake angry at yourself for sleeping so well. Both happen. Neither means what you’ll want it to mean.”

Her gaze came back to the body.

“You’ll want to confess. Don’t mistake that for duty. Sometimes confession is just another way of asking someone else to carry it. I won’t carry it. No priest will either, not truly. You can say the words and they’ll sound right and then you’ll still be the one who remembers the exact feel of the hollow under his jaw. That’s not punishment. That’s the shape of the thing. You did it. It’s yours. Not forever in the way you think, but enough.”

She rubbed one thumb briefly over her knuckles, a practical gesture, not a nervous one.

“You’ll notice your hands were steady. That’ll bother you. You’ll think steady means cold, and cold means monster, and monster means you’ve lost something essential. You haven’t. Steady just means your body understood the work before your feelings caught up. Later, when your feelings catch up, they may make a mess of you. Let them. Better that than pretending they don’t exist. If you need to shake, shake. If you need to vomit, vomit. If you laugh later at something stupid, laugh. The body has its own ways of balancing the books, and they’re none of them as tidy as we’d like.”

The wind moved again, lifting the edge of the dead man’s cloak and letting it fall. Wrack watched it settle.

“You’ll want to make a story out of him. Don’t. Not a villain. Not a brother. Not a lesson wrapped up neat for your own comfort. He was a man who ended up with his gut open on a road that doesn’t care, in a war that’s forgotten why it started, and the only truth we owe him is not to lie about what happened after. We took his purse because we need coin. We’ll take his boots if they fit because dead men don’t walk and living ones do. That’s not cruelty. That’s the arithmetic of staying alive. You can hate the arithmetic and still do it. Most decent people do.”

She shifted her stance slightly, favoring one knee without making a thing of it.

“When we walk away, you’ll feel like you’re leaving something behind. You are. Not him. Some version of yourself that still thinks there’s a clean way through this world. That’s all. The rest you carry. You carry the sound. The smell. The weight. The fact that it was easier than you expected and worse than you expected at the same time. You carry the knowledge that next time it may be easier still, and that the tenth time you may be thinking about your boots while a man cools at your feet. That’s what scares people. Not that they become beasts. That they become workers.”

Her mouth twisted, dry and humorless.

“And if you’re waiting for absolution, stop. There isn’t any here. There’s only the next thing. Clean the blade. Check the edge. Wash your hands if there’s water. Don’t put bloody fingers into a cut. Eat something, even if it tastes like ash. Keep watch. Sleep when you can. Don’t go looking for punishment because punishment won’t balance anything either. It’ll just add another weight to the load.”

She looked down at the dead man again, and this time her expression was almost gentle, though not kind. Gentleness without kindness. A field thing. A winter thing.

“He was somebody’s before he was nobody’s. Maybe a mother. Maybe a wife. Maybe a child who will grow up not knowing exactly how he ended. Maybe no one at all. You’ll never know, and that’s better. Don’t invent them to hurt yourself with. The living don’t need your invented grief. If he had people, they’ll have their own. If he didn’t, no amount you add will change it.”

Somewhere in the dark, wood creaked again. The cart, maybe. The night settling into its own joints.

“The rest,” Wrack said, “is that you’ll keep going because stopping is a luxury. You’ll keep going because the road doesn’t care what you feel, and because somewhere ahead there’ll be water, or food, or shelter, or another fight, or just another mile. You’ll keep going because the dead can’t walk, and we can. That’s not pretty, but it’s true. And if you need one clean thing to hold onto, hold onto this: you didn’t make it worse. You didn’t leave him to drown in his own breath. You didn’t stand over him making speeches while he begged for an end. You did the hard thing in the way that causes the least harm left to cause. That’s not holiness. It’s work. But it’s not nothing.”

She straightened then, slowly, with that faint creak of joints, and looked down the road into the dark.

“And when you dream of him—and you may—don’t try to make the dream mean more than it does. The mind sorts what the hands have done. That’s all. If he comes to you silent, let him be silent. If he comes angry, let him be angry. If he doesn’t come at all, don’t go looking for him out of guilt. The dead don’t haunt because they want to. They haunt because the living haven’t finished carrying them.”

She turned her head slightly, listening to the night, then back.

“So here’s the last of it. You’ll stand up when you can. You’ll take what we need. You’ll leave what we don’t. You’ll walk away with blood under your nails and the taste of iron in your mouth and the knowledge that you are capable of this, and you will not let that knowledge eat you alive. Sedge felt the table shudder beneath them. She didn't let go of the fragment until it was safely in the basin, and she didn't move her body an inch from the wound, using her hip to keep the man from sliding.

"Told you," she said, breathing evenly. She reached for a clean gauze pad to stem the fresh flow of blood. "He's not fighting me. He's fighting the nerve. Now, keep him pinned. "The 'straight' answer is that he is currently a collection of holes and debris," she added. "My job is to make him a collection of holes that can actually heal. Now, stop talking and put your weight back on his chest. He's starting to drift, and if he sags, he'll shift the angle of the joint."

She wrote in the log. "Name. Unit. Time of death. Cause. You don't write 'battle wound'. You write 'penetrating trauma to torso and upper extremities'. Specifics matter for the report."

She hung the clipboard back on its hook. She opened a cabinet under the table and took out a body bag. It was olive green and heavy. She unzipped it halfway and spread the sides on the canvas.

"Second, the tag," she said. She picked up a plastic wristband and a metal toe tag. "One on the wrist, one on the toe. You write the same ID number on both. If the wrist falls off, the toe stays. If the toe falls off, the wrist stays. One or the other has to make it back."

She looked at Wick, who was on the floor. "Third, the body," she said. She reached out and straightened the man's arm where it had curled near the table. "You straighten the limbs. You put the arms along the sides. You close the eyes with your thumb. You don't pull them down hard, just enough that they stay shut when you let go."

"Fourth, the bag," she said. "You slide him in. Feet first. Zip it all the way to the chin. If there's blood on the outside, you wipe it. You don't want blood on the outside of the bag."

"Fifth, the table," she said. She picked up the tray with the used gauze and bloodied rags. "You wash the canvas. You soak up the pooling blood so it doesn't freeze to the sheet. You reset the tray. New instruments. New gloves. New rags."

"Sixth," she said, setting the tray on the floor near Wick. "You get up. You stand by the tent flap. You watch for the next stretcher. You don't sit again until the next man is on the table."

She walked to the sink and turned the crank on the water. She filled a basin with clean water and a cloth. She handed it to Wick.

"You asked what I'm doing," she said. "I'm keeping the room ready." She turned back to the body. "Help me lift. We're done talking."

Sedge finished wrapping the second arm tight against the man's chest with the last length of bandage, pulling it firm to immobilize the reduced joints without slack. Blood had already begun to seep through the gauze pads she'd packed into the incisions, dark and steady, so she pressed fresh layers over both shoulders and secured them with another turn of the wrap, her fingers working the fabric into place around the swollen tissue. "The stitches are holding for now, but the capsule's still ragged underneath—these knots won't keep the head of the humerus seated if he moves wrong in the next hour," she said, voice flat. "I'm checking the pulse in each wrist next to make sure nothing's pinched off in the vessels." She pressed two fingers to the right wrist, then the left, counting the beats under the skin. "Weak but there. No immediate nerve damage showing yet." 

She set the man's arms down against his sides and reached for the bucket of water at the table's edge, dipping a clean cloth to wipe the worst of the blood from the skin around the wounds. "Shrapnel fragments are still embedded in the muscle belly on both sides—too deep and too many to dig out in this light without risking more tearing. They'll stay until someone with better tools gets to him, or until they migrate and cause abscesses." The cloth came away soaked, and she wrung it out before wiping the table edge and her own hands. "Infection risk is high from the dirt he carried in with the metal. I'm flushing what I can with the water now—pouring it along the edges of the incisions to clear the surface debris." She tipped the bucket carefully, letting the water run over the packed gauze without soaking the wraps entirely, then set it aside. "Ten more minutes to bind the arms fully and check for bleeding from the vessels I might have nicked during the reductions. That's all there is left to do here."

She reached for the remaining bandages and began layering them across the chest and under the arms to lock everything in position, her movements economical. "This buys him the chance to keep the limbs functional if nothing rots from the inside. Without the reductions, the joints would have kept grinding until the arms went cold and black." Her hands finished the last tie and tested the tension once. "I don't enjoy this."

rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge held the forceps still for a moment. Not a pause for thought — she'd already done the thinking, probably days of it across four years of people asking her variations of that exact question. She held them still because Wick deserved a straight answer and straight answers took a beat.



"Bad like I don't know yet," she said. "That's the honest one. I've pulled a man through worse and I've lost one with less. The difference is usually how fast you move and whether infection gets him in three days."



She set the forceps down and picked up the gauze, started feeding it into the wound with her fingers, working it deeper in short, firm pushes. She talked while she did it because the talking and the working were the same thing.

"Right now it's a hole in a lung that's bleeding into the space where the lung needs to be. The lung can't expand, so he's not breathing right, so he's not oxygenating, so everything else starts shutting down in order. If I pack it and slow the bleed, the body does its own work with the rest. If I don't — " she pushed another length in and the man's ribs hitched under her palms "— then he drowns slowly inside himself and it takes about an hour."

She pulled her hands back. The first round of packing sat in the wound, dark and saturating almost immediately.

"That's one round. I need two to know anything." She looked at Wick's face — the shaking hands, the bile, the way she was still standing there instead of leaving — and something in her expression didn't soften exactly, but it acknowledged. "You can go outside. You don't have to watch the second one."

It wasn't a dismissal. Sedge didn't do dismissals. It was the same blunt arithmetic she applied to everything: what Wick needed to do to be useful, and what she didn't.

rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge glanced at Wick, then back at the pad. She appreciated the request. Imagining was worse. Imaginating had a way of growing teeth.

"Pad's there," she said, nodding at the dressing under her palm. "Press it flat and look at the edge where it meets the skin."



Wick did. Sedge watched her look.

"That dark red — almost brown where it's pooling at the seam — that's old blood. It's been sitting inside him, in the chest cavity, long enough to go venous. Means the worst of the bleed happened before he got here, not right now. The fresher stuff, the brighter red at the center — that's active, but it's slow. A trickle, not a flow. The packing's pressing on whatever vessel was open and the pressure's doing what pressure does."

She lifted her hand and let her eyes do the count. One second, two, three.

"See how it spreads? Start at the center and move outward. Watch the edge."

The pad darkened in a small arc. Not fast. Not dramatic. A patient, creeping stain.

"That rate — that's my whole job right now. If it fills the pad in under a minute, the packing isn't holding and I need that short reel of gauze to pack deeper. If it takes five, the body's starting to help, the clotting's happening somewhere I can't see, and I hold what I've got."

She pressed the pad back down.

"The brown around the wound mouth — that's tissue that's been bathed in blood too long. Not dying yet, but angry. Tomorrow it'll be the fever's business. Today it's mine, which means I keep it clean and I keep pressure on it and I don't go poking around for anything I don't absolutely need." She held up the forceps, the curved one, still wet. "These came out. Nothing else goes in until the pad tells me I have to."

She looked at Wick steady.

"So what you're seeing is a wound that's arguing instead of shouting. That's the best I can give you tonight. It's not a win — a win would be no blood at all. But it's not a loss, and in this tent a not-a-loss is what we take."

Her fingers stayed flat against the dressing. Counting.

"Now you know what I know. That's the whole of it."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge straightened up from the shoulder, forceps still in hand, and looked at Wick the way she looked at everything — like a fact that needed stating.



"Straight," she said. "Right."

She set the forceps down on the tray with a small click, not because she needed them off her hands but because the question deserved both of hers free.

"Shrapnel doesn't make one hole. It makes a cone. The entry point is small — could be anything, quarter-sized, smaller — but what's inside him is a spray of fragments moving at speeds that don't care about anatomy. Each fragment carries its own energy, and that energy doesn't stop when it hits tissue. It keeps going until it runs out, and tissue is better at stopping it than air but not good at it. So you get a primary channel where the main piece went through, and then a dozen secondary tracks radiating out from it like the ribs of an umbrella, each one tearing whatever it passes through."

She held up her hand and drew a cone in the air with one finger. Not theatrical. Illustrative.

"Inside a chest, that means the lung's got holes it didn't start with. Not just the through-and-through — the fragmentation. Little tracks through the parenchyma, the spongy part, each one bleeding into the air spaces. That's the sound you hear when you put your ear to his back — not wet, not dramatic, just a fine crackle, like someone crumpling paper near a microphone. That's air and blood in places where only air should be."

She paused. Not for effect. She was checking the dressing again — a habit, not a tell.

"The fragments themselves — some of them stay. Fabric from his uniform, bits of his own bone, pieces of whatever the explosive was packed in. They're not sterile and they're not smooth and they'll sit in tissue and the body will do one of two things: wall them off, which takes weeks and works about half the time, or try to expel them, which means the wound opens again from the inside and drains for days. The pieces near the surface I can pick out. The ones in the lung parenchyma I can't reach without opening him up, and I'm not opening him up — there's no surgeon, there's no table for it, and the shock would kill him faster than the fragments will."



She picked the forceps back up. Turned them over in her fingers.

"So what shrapnel actually does — you asked straight — is it turns one injury into thirty small ones, most of which I'll never see, all of which are bleeding into the same space. That's why the pad stopped and I'm not relieved yet. It stopped because I'm pressing on the biggest source. The smaller tracks are still weeping. They'll contribute to the fever tomorrow and they'll contribute to the infection if anything's carrying on them, and some of them will scar tissue that was never meant to be scarred."

She looked at Wick steadily.

"That's the straight version. What I don't say to families and what I don't write on the card — because it doesn't help and it doesn't change anything — is that even when he walks out of here, his left lung is never what it was. He'll have reduced capacity for the rest of his life. Cold mornings will hurt. He'll cough differently than he used to." She paused. "But that's a later problem, and later problems are a luxury. Right now the problem is the pad and the shoulder and the three days of fever that haven't started yet."

She leaned in toward the right shoulder, fingers finding the joint through the skin.

"Hips. He'll move if I have to redo this."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge checked the pad. Dark at the center where she'd pressed, no spread at the edges. She had seconds before she needed to be somewhere else.

"Pad's holding. Not spread since I let go. That's thirty seconds clean, which is thirty more than we had an hour ago."



The man's back was off the table, his spine bowing against Wick's grip, and the sound he was making wasn't words anymore — it was the raw animal register that pain drops people into when it stops asking permission. Sedge had heard it in three languages across four years and it meant the same thing in all of them: *I am here and I don't want to be.*

"Shoulders are back in," she said, loud enough to cut through. "Both of them. Right one I did twice because the first time seated crooked. Right now I'm looking at the chest dressing and deciding whether it needs a third round." She pressed the pad. Felt the give of packed gauze underneath, firm, no wetness seeping around the edges. "It doesn't. Two rounds are holding. Pressure's steady."



She reached for the sling she'd cut earlier from a strip of canvas — not a proper sling, nothing was a proper sling anymore — and began fashioning it around the left arm to immobilize the shoulder against the chest.

"Ligating the arm now. I'm binding his left arm to his body so the shoulder can't move while he sleeps or while he fights, because a shoulder that's in the socket but unstable will pop out again with one bad roll and I'm not doing this a third time." She threaded the canvas under the elbow, tied it firm above the wrist, checked for capillary refill in the fingers by pressing the nail bed and watching it blanch and return. Two seconds. Good. "Fingers are pink. Circulation's fine. If they go white or blue at any point, you tell me, because that means the sling's too tight and I'm cutting off the arm to save the shoulder."

The screaming had thinned to a moan — not quieter in volume but broken up, ragged, the body running out of the fuel that screaming costs. His eyes were open. Not tracking, but open, which was more than twenty minutes ago.

"Shout came back," Sedge said. "That's shock receding. Means his pressure's coming up, which means the bleed's slow enough that his body can afford to feel things again. It's the worst part of the night for him and the best sign we've had."



She pulled the blanket up — not to be kind, though it was that too, but because hypothermia was the next thing on the list and she'd been watching his extremities for the blue creep that meant his core was giving up.

"Vitals," she said. "I'm going to say them out loud so they're in your head too. Breathing — shallow, about twenty a minute, left side guarded, he's not using the full chest because it hurts and the lung's compromised. Pulse at the wrist — " she took it, counting under her breath, her lips barely moving "— about a hundred and ten, thready but regular. Temperature I can't measure, but his skin's warm and dry, which is where I want it tonight. Tomorrow I want it different. Tomorrow I don't want warm."

She wiped her hands on her thigh again — still habit, still not need — and looked at Wick directly.

"You've had him through the worst part. Dislocations, the packing, the scream. What's left tonight is watch and hold. The patterns are: pad darkening fast means I need the short reel; breathing stops for ten seconds means I need it faster; breathing goes irregular with long gaps means you get me regardless of what I'm doing. Everything else is waiting."

She sat down on the stool — the first time she'd sat since before the table — and kept her eyes on the dressing.

"Talk to me about something that isn't this. I mean it. I've got the wound, you've got the hips. We've got an hour of nothing to do but not lose what we've gained, and if both of us spend that hour staring at the same piece of gauze we'll be useless by the time something changes."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't look at Wick on the floor. She kept her eyes on the man on the table — his breathing, the pad, the rise and fall that had become the only clock in the tent — because if she looked at Wick on the floor she would have to decide what to do about it, and what to do about it was sit down next to her, and Sedge had been standing for fourteen hours and the stool was the only thing between her and the ground.

So she sat on the stool. And she said the rest.

"The rest," she began, and her voice was the same voice she'd used to describe the packing — steady, clinical, no ornament — but slower, the way you speak when you're reading a list you've written in your head a hundred times and never out loud. "The rest is this."

She pulled the tray closer. Not to use it. Because having her hands near the instruments while she talked made the talking feel like part of the work instead of something outside it.

"I've been here four years. I came in as the replacement for the replacement, and the man I replaced had been dead six weeks and they didn't tell me that until I'd already signed. First month I lost eleven. Eleven in one month. I could tell you their names but I'm not going to because names are a thing you do when you have time to make them matter, and I've learned that saying names out loud in a tent with a living patient in it doesn't help either of you."

She checked the pad. Center unchanged. She said so out loud, to keep the machinery running.

"Pad's holding. Still thirty seconds clean. You're doing fine on the hips."

She looked at her own hands on the tray edge. Flipped them. Examined the nails the way she always did — not for dirt, for the small cuts that accumulated and healed and accumulated again, the residue of four years of other people's blood in places her skin hadn't been broken before.

"The rest is that I stopped counting after the first year because counting turned into a number that lived behind my eyes when I tried to sleep, and sleep's a supply I can't afford to waste on arithmetic. So I stopped. And then I stopped stopping — it wasn't a decision, it was just that the number got heavy and I put it down and I didn't pick it back up."

She paused. Not for breath. For the shape of the next sentence.

"What I do remember is the texture of it. Not the count — the *what*. What it feels like to open someone's chest cavity with your fingers when you're looking for a bleeder and your hands are the only diagnostic tool you have. What it sounds like when you're irrigating a wound and the fluid comes back brown instead of red and you know you're going to be here for two more hours. What it smells like on the fourth day of an infection when the body's started to — "

She stopped. Started again.

"I'm telling you this because you asked me not to tidy it up for you, and because you held that man's hips through two dislocations and a chest packing without leaving, and because the alternative is that you go back to your billet and lie in the dark and make it worse in your head than it was in here. In here you can see it. Out there you can't."

She stood up. Not suddenly — a slow unfolding, the way you rise when your knees have opinions. She moved to the supply crate and opened it, took out a tin cup, filled it from the water jug, and set it on the floor next to where Wick sat.

"Drink that. You're dehydrated and dehydration makes everything feel more final than it is."

She sat down on the floor next to the crate. Not next to Wick — close enough to be in the same conversation, far enough to have her own space. Her back against the crate. Her knees up. The first time she'd been off a stool or off her feet in fourteen hours and her body announced this with a comprehensive complaint that she ignored the way she ignored most things that didn't bleed.

"The rest," she said again, and this time the word carried something underneath it — not softer, Sedge didn't do soft, but more honest, the way a wound is honest when you stop packing it and just look.

"I don't sleep in the tent anymore. I used to. I slept four feet from the table because the calls came at night and if I was already there I could move faster. And then one night — I won't tell you what happened, it's not that kind of story — but I woke up with my hands doing something they shouldn't have been doing, and since then I sleep in the supply hut with the door bolted. Not because I'm afraid of the patients. Because I'm afraid of what my hands do when they think nobody's watching."

She picked at a thread on her trousers. A real thread, not a metaphor — she hated metaphors, said so at least twice a week.

"I eat standing up. I wash in cold water because hot water takes time and time is the thing I don't have. I haven't written a letter in eight months because the last one I wrote took forty minutes and I spent all forty minutes deciding which parts of my life were safe to send to a person who would read them and worry, and the answer was none of them, and I threw it in the stove."

She looked at Wick.

"That's the rest of it. That's what it costs on the other side of the part you watched. Not the dramatic version — nobody carries me out on a stretcher, nobody gives me a medal for nerve, nobody sits me down and says *you've seen enough*. The actual version, which is that I've become a person who can pack a lung at two in the morning and then go sleep in a locked room and eat standing up and not write to anyone because writing requires a version of yourself you can hand to another person, and the version I've got is here, in this tent, with blood under its nails."

The man on the table breathed. In and out. The pad held.

"But." She said the word like she was setting down a tool she'd finished with. "I'm not telling you this because it's tragic. I've watched people decide that watching someone do this work is tragic and then they start treating me like a wound instead of a person, and I'd rather be called a lot of things than pitied. I'm telling you because you're sitting on my floor and you're shaking and you think you're the only one in this tent who's falling apart, and you're not — I'm just better at sitting still while I do it."

She reached over and pressed two fingers against the pad on the table. Checked. Released.

"Still holding. Sixty seconds now. Best number of the night."

She let her head fall back against the crate. Looked at the ceiling of the tent — canvas, seams, the dark spot where rain had gotten through last week and she hadn't fixed because fixing things that didn't bleed wasn't on the list.

"I had a sister," she said. "Younger. Four years. She writes to me — she's the one I throw the letters from — and every one of them says the same thing in different fonts: *come home, this is enough now, you've done your part.* And every time I read one I think — the arithmetic's wrong. If I go home, who does the next chest? There's nobody behind me. There's nobody beside me. There's a runner who can fetch supplies and an orderly who can change dressings and neither of them can pack a lung, and if I leave, the next man who comes in through that flap with a hole in his chest gets the runner with the gauze and a prayer."

She paused.

"So the rest of it — the locked room and the standing meals and the letters in the stove — that's what I pay for the arithmetic being right. It's a bad trade. I know it's a bad trade. I've known it's a bad trade for about two and a half years and I keep making it because the alternative arithmetic is worse and I'd rather be a person who made a bad trade knowingly than a person who walked away and let someone else hold the numbers."

Silence. Not uncomfortable — the kind of silence that follows the last sentence of something that needed saying and had finally been said. The man breathed. The pad held. The lamp sputtered and steadied.

Sedge reached over and took the tin cup back from where she'd set it, checked that Wick had drunk from it, and set it down again.

"That's all of it," she said. "Now you know what I know, twice over — once about the wound and once about the person working on it. Neither is prettier than the other. Both are accurate."

She pulled her knees up further and rested her forearms across them.

"We've got two hours until the change of watch and then I've got the fever question to manage and then there's whatever comes through the flap next. You can go. You can stay. You can sit on my floor for another ten minutes and then go. But if you stay, talk — not about him, we've done him — about something that takes up room in your head that isn't this tent. What did you do before? Where are you from? What's the stupidest thing you've ever been afraid of? I'll go first if you want — I'm terrified of dentists, have been since I was nine, which is a genuinely inconvenient phobia for someone who does this for a living because the noise of the drill and the sound of bone are not the same thing but my body hasn't been told that."

She was quiet for a moment. Then, without looking at Wick:

"You held. You didn't let go. I noticed that and I don't notice most things that don't bleed, so consider it noted."

She checked the pad one more time. Center dry. Edges dry. The man's breathing had settled into something almost regular.

"Pad's holding. You can take your hands off his hips now. He's not going anywhere."

Her own hands stayed where they were — on her knees, palms up, still.

She didn't pick anything up. She just sat there, on the floor of the tent, with the lamp bad and the war worse and four years of it under her fingernails, and she waited to see if Wick would talk or go, and either one was fine, and she meant that in the plain arithmetic of a woman who had finally said the rest of it out loud and found that the ground held.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"Neither, tonight," Sedge said. She said it plainly, because a question asked that plainly deserved an answer without decoration. "The vessel held. The channel's clean, the pack's in, the leg stays where it is. He'll walk with a hitch and a story. That's the honest ceiling of what I can promise."

She wiped the blade and set it with the others, talking the way she always talked after — because silence after a table was where the wrong thoughts got in.

"But you asked the second question like it's a different question, so I'll answer that too. The kind part is when I stop cutting and start holding his hand. You'll know it when you see it, because I'll sit down to do it. I don't sit during surgery. I've never once sat." She pulled the stool out with her boot and didn't sit on it. "Tonight I stood. Tonight was arithmetic, not kindness. Fragment plus vessel equaled a leg. I did the sum and it came out in his favor. That's all kindness is out here, Wick — a sum that lands on your side of the line. The word's for people who need the word."

She looked at the man's face again, the slack mouth, the color coming back into his lips like weather.

"The leg's the easy fight. The next three days are the real one. Fever, rot, the track going hot — that kills more men than fragments ever did, and it doesn't do it quickly, which is the part I mind." She said it flatly, for the record. "If the leg goes bad, I'll take it off in the morning, sober, with light, and he'll have a chance. I don't do midnight amputations unless the midnight is doing it for me. That's not kindness either. That's just not being lazy about the timing."

She folded the wrapped fragment and put it in the tin with the others — she never said why and nobody had ever asked twice.

"So. He keeps the leg if the leg cooperates, and I'm kind only when I sit down. Any more questions, ask them now while my hands still want something to do."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
The flap hadn't fallen all the way shut behind her. Sedge held it a moment, one boot already in the cold, and then she let it close and came back to the foot of the table, because that was the right kind of question and she'd learned not to walk away from those.

"Then look properly," she said. "Not the way civilians look, which is at the whole thing all at once. One thing at a time. Start with his face."

She pointed without touching.

"Jaw's still set. That's not pain — he's gone past pain. That's the body keeping the argument going after the man's left the room. Bodies do that. They're stubborn on behalf of people who aren't awake to be stubborn themselves. Lips are the real tell — see the color coming back in them? Gray means the blood's sulking. Pink means it's behaving. He's behaving. That's the first right thing you're seeing."

She moved her hand down, not quite to the blanket.

"Breathing. Count it. In and out is one. Fifteen, sixteen in a minute, that's where a sleeping man lives. If he climbs past twenty-five you come get me, and don't stand there recounting to be sure. Now the leg — look at the stitch line. Yes, it looks like a drunk did it. A tired woman did. Even and ugly holds better than pretty and loose, and it'll hold. There's a spot of dark on the pack the size of a coin. That's expected — a packed track always seeps a little, like a wall after rain. A coin is fine. A spreading handprint is not."

She pulled the blanket back an inch from the wounded leg, enough to show the thigh above the incision, where the skin had gone dark in a long uneven streak.

"That's the bruise, and here's the part worth knowing: by morning it'll be yellow and green and twice this size, and it'll look like the leg is losing. It isn't. Bruises are receipts. Proof of payment, not proof of debt. The bruise getting uglier is the body doing its bookkeeping. The things that kill don't get uglier — they get hot, and they get sweet, and they get fast. Ugly and quiet is the healthy direction. Remember that, because at four in the morning ugly and quiet will try to convince you otherwise."

She put the blanket back the way she'd had it, bare leg to the air.

"So. That's what you're seeing. A man whose blood is behaving, whose stitches will hold, whose bruise is going to lie to you in about six hours." She picked up her tin again. "Imagining's always worse than knowing, you're right about that. The body's honest. It's the mind that makes up the bad stories. You've got the honest version now — hold onto it when the lamp starts playing tricks."

She went to the flap a second time, and this time she meant it.

"Four o'clock," she said, and the night took her.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
The boots stopped in the frozen mud. Then came back — three steps, unhurried — and the flap opened and Sedge came in again, tin under her arm, a woman who had known the question was coming and had only pretended to leave.

"Fair," she said. "You watched me pull it. You've earned the whole of it."

She didn't go to the table. She stood just inside the flap, and she talked the way she worked — one thing at a time, for the record.

"Shrapnel isn't a bullet. A bullet's honest. It goes fast, it goes straight, it makes a round hole, and it's hot enough from travel to cook a little of what it touches — which sounds like a horror, but it means the entry's cleaner than you'd think. Shrapnel is slow and filthy and never the same shape twice."

She held up her thumb, the size of the fragment still in her memory.

"A bullet cuts. Shrapnel tears. Jagged edges don't part tissue, they rip it and crush it along the whole track. That's why his thigh looks the way it does. And it doesn't travel alone — it went in through a boot-top, so it carried the boot in with it. Leather. Wax. Whatever muck he'd walked through that week. Here's the part nobody says straight: the metal is the least of it. The body doesn't much care about metal. It cares about the dirt. Dirt is what kills."

She shifted the tin under her arm.

"It doesn't go straight, either. It tumbles. It hits bone and deflects. It follows the seams between the muscles the way water follows a crack — the body's own roads. That's how it traveled from his boot to his thigh. And because it's slow, it usually doesn't have the legs to come out the other side. So it stays, and one of two things happens. Either the body walls it off — scar around it, a little shell, and the man carries it to old age and sets off detectors. Or it sits against something that moves. A vessel. A joint. And every heartbeat works it like a file. That's what his was doing. Another week and it wears through, and he dies in his sleep with no wound to show for it."

She glanced at the man's slack face, then back.

"Last thing. While it's in there, the crushing starves the muscle around the track. Kills a little of it. Dead tissue is food, and the dirt it carried came with a mouth already in it. The fragment's a delivery, the wound's a pantry, and the fever is the dinner. That's the sweet smell. That's the thing I told you to wake me for."

She said it all flat, no relish in any of it, because there was none to have.

"So — the straight of it: the tearing does the damage, the dirt does the killing, and the wearing does it quietly. Tonight I took out the passenger and cleaned the pantry as best the light allowed. Now we wait to see how good a job I did." She tapped the tin once, softly, and didn't explain it. "Keep counting."

This time she left and the flap stayed shut, and her boots went the full three tents and were gone.

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge was moving before the scream finished, because she'd seen the stitch line go dark while her hand was still on his forehead, and the scream was just the body confirming what her eyes already had.

"There it is," she said, peeling the blanket back. The pack had gone from a coin to a handprint in under a minute. "The vessel lied to me. Held all night, earned my confidence, let go when I stopped looking. They do that. It's not betrayal, it's tissue. But I'm going to talk to it anyway."

She cut her own stitches — quick, she knew where every one was — and opened the incision with two fingers, and the blood came up to meet her like something that had been waiting under the door.

"All of it, then, since you asked. A branch tore off the big vessel. Small one, the size of a wheat stalk, but arteries don't care about size, they care about pressure, and his is excellent, which right now is his enemy." Cloth in her free hand, wiping, wiping. "I can't see the end of it through the blood, so you're the tourniquet. Right hand off his shoulder — here—" she took his wrist and set his fingers high against the groin crease. "Press down against the bone. That's the artery's front door and you just closed it. Don't ease off for anything. He screams, you press. He bucks, you press. Your arm dies, you press. The only thing that lets you stop is my voice saying so."

The man was screaming around shapes that weren't words. She got the strap between his teeth without ceremony — "Bite" — and he did, and the sound became something the tent could survive.

"How long: five minutes to find and tie it, five to clean and close. Ten. I'll give you the road as we walk it." The probe went in, following the blood backward, narrating because her mouth kept her hands honest. "Wiping. Wiping again. There — I see the end of it, jumping like a fish on a line. It's a branch, not the trunk. The trunk I never tie; tying the trunk is taking the leg by the slow route. A branch I tie, and the leg complains but lives."
