She laid the thread. Loop, twice around, and she said so as she did it. Then the knot, pulled down slow, and the blood that had been a fountain became a trickle, and the trickle became nothing.

"There. Feel that under your fingers? The pulse just dropped. That's mine — that's the pressure coming off the house. Ease up now. Over five seconds, slow, because if I'm wrong I want to find out gently." She watched the wound, counting silently, and nothing came back. "Good. It held. You can let go. Your arm's going to shake for a while; that's the rent it charged, and it was worth it."

The man had gone from screaming to a low animal moaning, and she noted it for the record.

"So you have all of it, as asked: I put a thread around a vessel inside his leg and pulled it shut, and he screamed because that's what a body does when a stranger ties off its plumbing. Nothing about it is pleasant, and I'd be a horror if I pretended otherwise. But hear the useful part — screaming means the blood's still moving. Men who are bleeding out go quiet. The screaming is on our side of the ledger."

She cleaned the track again, thoroughly this time, packed it, and closed it with the same quick ugly stitches.

"Blood loss — a pint, maybe a little over. A man his size carries eight or ten. That's a rent payment, not the house. But it's why he'll be pale at breakfast and weak as a kitten, and why the arithmetic changed. Yesterday he was a leg that keeps. Today he's a leg that keeps if the remaining roads can carry the closed road's traffic. They usually widen to do it. Usually. And he won't remember any of this — the body doesn't store the middle parts. He'll wake up remembering the first surgery and hating me for it, and tonight will be blank. That's the one mercy in a bleeder. The mind's already out the door."

She straightened. Rolled her neck. Didn't sit.

"You held. Second time tonight. That's twice you were the difference between a surgery and a funeral, and I'm not saying it to make you feel anything. It's in the record." She pulled the blanket back over him, wounded leg bare to the air, same as before. "I'm staying till light now. Not kindness — arithmetic. A vessel that's lied once gets watched, and I don't farm out watching to someone who's never seen one lie. You've done a full watch. Go wake the next pair of hands and teach them the count. That's how a watch works."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't answer until she'd looked. That was the rule — you didn't grade a wound from across the tent, and you didn't grade it from the stretcher-bearer's face, either.

The man they carried in had a belt cinched high on his right thigh, and below it the leg was the wrong color — grey going bronze at the edges, swollen tight as a sausage skin. Whatever had done it had taken most of the calf and driven the dirt in after. She pressed two fingers into the skin above the wound and it crackled under her touch, faint and wrong, like snow giving under a boot.

"Gas," she said. "Feel that, if you want to learn it. You'll smell it in a minute — sweet, like apples gone over." She slid her hand up past the knee and pressed again. Warm. No crackling. "When did the belt go on?"

"Just past dark," one of the bearers said.

"Then the leg was dead before you tied it. The iron killed it, not the belt — don't let anybody tell you different." She straightened. "Bad like he loses the leg. The rot's below the knee and it hasn't climbed yet. Being kind is the other answer, and it isn't tonight's answer. Being kind is when the crackling's up in his hip and there's nothing left to cut to — then it's everything I have in the bottle and somebody's hand to hold. I've done that job. I'll tell you plain when that's the job. This isn't it."

She was already laying things out in their row — knife, saw, ligatures, the curved needle. "But hear the rest. That answer's good for maybe an hour. Gas doesn't wait, so we don't."

She set her hand on the man's shoulder until his eyes found her. "I'm taking the leg. It's already gone — I'm only making it official. Bite the strap. Hate me later."

Then, to Wick, flat and even: "Your job is the belt. When I say slack, you ease it a quarter turn so I can see what bleeds and tie it off. When I say tight, it goes back. He'll buck worse than the last one and the strap will do most of the holding. You do the belt. Nothing else is yours."

She tested the knife's edge with her thumb, once, and set her feet.

"Belt ready. On my word."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at him on the floor for a long moment. She didn't tell him to get up. Floors were where the body put people when it ran out of arguments, and she'd stopped arguing with the body on anyone's behalf years ago.

"Fair," she said instead. "You've earned the rest. Most people earn half of it and get a third. You closed an artery with your hand tonight, so you get all of it."

She went to the table first — the watch didn't stop for conversation, it never had — and did the round: lips pink, pack a coin, breath at fifteen on her first count, no sweetness anywhere in the air. She pulled the blanket up an inch, and then she took the tin down from the shelf, and instead of the stool she came and sat on the floor across from him, her back against the table leg, the tin balanced on her knees.

"You've now seen me refuse a stool twice," she said. "So I'll give you the distinction before you have to ask for it. There are three kinds of sitting in this tent. The first is during surgery — I don't, ever, because sitting is what you do when the cutting's over, and I have never once operated on a man I'd already given up on. The second is the kindness, the one I told you about — when the arithmetic lands on the other side of the line and you stay in the room anyway. The third is this. Two people, a night survived, the work holding steady on the table above them. Nobody teaches the third kind because nobody plans for it. It's the rarest one. I'm doing it now. Make a note."

She opened the tin.

Inside: small bundles in waxed cloth, each tied off with thread, packed tight as seeds. And apart from the rest, a single rolled strip of linen, darker than the others.

"The roll is the school one," she said. "The man who waited too long. You'll smell it when you're ready to learn it. Not tonight — tonight your nose is full of this man and your own adrenaline, and I need it accurate tomorrow, not raw. The bundles are what you already think they are. Every fragment I've pulled since my first table." She turned the tin slightly, not offering it, just letting it be seen. "There are eleven at the bottom that weren't mine."

She let that sit the way she let a pack sit before she judged it.

"Her name was March. She had this tent before me and the habit before me and the count before me. Everything I said to you tonight that sounded like it had weight — the talking while you work, the counting out loud, the relief at four whether anything's wrong or not — that was hers. I stole it the way you steal anything worth keeping. She said it to me once and I kept it, and now I say it to you, and if you keep it, that's three of us carrying the same load, which is how loads survive."

She picked up one bundle, the smallest, and held it in her palm without unwrapping it.

"My first table. A boy, shoulder, easy pull — I found the fragment in a minute and thought I was a natural. The dirt had been in him four days before he reached us. Fever took him on the second morning. March caught the smell at the end of the first day and knew, and she sat with him through the second night, and she told me afterward: watch the ones you save, because the pulling is the easy half. Then she held out this tin and said, put it in. I asked why. She said — receipts. That was her word. I stole that too."

She put it back. Her hands went on doing the work of the tin — settling, aligning — the way hands do when the mouth is carrying something heavier.

"Now the part I left out on purpose. I told you the kind part is when I stop cutting and start holding his hand, and that I'd never once sat during surgery. Both true. What I didn't give you was the number of times I've sat after. It's not small. The first was a gut-shot man my second month. Nothing to cut that would help — you learn that fast with a gut, there's no third choice there either — and I stood over him doing sums, and March put a hand on my shoulder and pushed me down onto the stool and said: sit, watch, this is also the work. So I sat. He took forty minutes. I counted out loud the whole way down, because she'd taught me hearing is the last thing to go, and a man should go down to a voice and not to silence. Fifteen, twelve, nine, six, four, two. Then I stopped saying numbers, because there wasn't a throat to hear them, and I sat a while longer anyway, because the sitting isn't for him at the end. It's for the one still upright. That's the part nobody says."

She looked at the table above them, at the blanket, the bare leg, the even lift of the chest. Checked nothing. Just looked.

"The hand rule — don't hold it unless he asks, he won't ask. That was hers too. She never asked either, all the years I knew her. People who spend their lives watching never ask, because asking is a kind of being watched, and they can't bear the reversal." Her voice didn't change at all, which was how he would know what was coming. "Except at the end. She asked at the end."

Sedge was quiet for exactly as long as the record required.

"Scratch on the back of her hand. Off a bone fragment, third year, a bad week — you know the kind, when the tables don't stop and neither does the mud. She didn't report it. She wrapped it herself and kept working, because that's what the last medic in a row does, and she was the last one in hers the same way I'm the last one in mine now. The rot got in. And here's the joke the war tells, the one I'd laugh at if I still did: you can't smell yourself. The one smell I've taught every pair of hands since to wake me for, and she couldn't smell it on her own arm, and I didn't check her, because she was the one who checked me. I was twenty-two and she told me to sleep and I was polite about it."

She said it flat, for the record, because describing was part of doing it properly, even this.

"I woke at dawn. She'd counted herself down sometime in the small hours — out loud, I'm certain of it, because that's what she taught and she was professional to the last number. Nobody heard it. Fifteen, twelve, nine. Into an empty tent." She looked at the tin in her hands. "So. Now you have the rest of the sentences I gave you tonight. Sleep light — that's not discipline, that's debt. Everyone gets relieved on time — because she never was. Politeness kills more men than fragments — I was the politeness. And don't hold his hand unless he asks — he won't ask, until he does, and you had better be in the room when it happens."

She closed the tin. Didn't put it back on the shelf. Set it on the floor between them instead, which she had not done in front of another living person in over a year.

"Last thing, and then you can be quiet as long as you want, I'm done needing your half of the conversation. I've done the sum on that morning a thousand times. My arithmetic says nobody's to blame — she hid it, the hour was cruel, I was young, there's no third choice, nobody's to blame. I built that arithmetic myself and I stand behind every piece of it, and it has never once come out balanced. That's how I know the arithmetic is a tool and not a truth. It works on tables and vessels and fever. It doesn't work on her. I keep doing the sums anyway, because the sums are the job, and the job is the only grief I've ever been able to afford. Grief with a job. That's the tin. That's all of it."

Above them, the man breathed — fifteen, and fifteen again — and the lamp hissed, and Sedge stayed where she was, on the floor, the third kind of sitting, keeping nobody's count for once, and finding she didn't mind it.

"He'll hate me at breakfast," she said. "That part's still true. Some things hold."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
"Then look in order," Sedge said. "Bleeding first, because bleeding kills fastest. Everything else waits its turn."

She pointed with a bloody finger at the stump. "That's the flap. Muscle over the bone end, skin over that, three stitches to keep it honest. See the color — red, wet, shining? That's living meat. It should look like a butcher's shop, and it should bother you that it does. Grey is dead. Bronze is worse than dead. Red and ugly is what you pray for."

"Now the weeping. Come closer. See how it seeps through the linen — slow, dark, no rhythm? That's ooze. Every raw surface in there weeping at once, and it's nothing. A bleeder is different. A bleeder *jumps*." She held two fingers a hair above the dressing. "Bright red, and it comes in pulses, with the heartbeat, because it is the heartbeat pushed out through a hole. You see that, you don't think and you don't fetch me — you put your thumb on it and shout. Thumb first, shout second. A man can empty himself in the time it takes to cross this tent."

She took the belt the last quarter turn herself, eyes on the stump. The linen darkened, slow and even. Nothing jumped.

"There. That's a tied vessel holding. Two knots in there the size of peas, and they're the difference between this man and a corpse. The belt did its work up here —" she tapped the thigh above the wound "— and now the knots do it down there. In a week the flesh grows over them and they rot away on their own, and that's the last anyone thinks of them."

Then she moved up the table, because the order went stump, then man. "Now him. Face first. Grey is fine — he's bled, and grey is what bled looks like. It's the lips you watch." She lifted his lip with a thumb. "Pink underneath. Blue is the bad color. Blue means the air isn't getting where it goes." Two fingers to his throat. "Pulse is fast and thin, and it should be — that's a body doing its work with less than it had this morning. What frightens me is a pulse I can't find, or one that gallops and won't be caught. This one's just working."

She laid her hand flat on his chest and felt it rise, counting nothing. "Breathing's shallow. He'll do that for a day. Deep breaths hurt when you've been cut on, even when the cut's nowhere near the breathing. The body doesn't reason. It guards."

She stepped back and wiped her hands again, out of habit more than hope.

"That's tonight. The week has its own signs, so learn them now. The stump will weep — good. It will stink a little by tomorrow — all wounds stink, that's just wound. What you watch for is the smell going sweet again, like it was under the belt. Sweet means the gas came back. And you watch the skin at the edges. If it goes bronze —" she pressed two fingers into her own forearm "— if it crackles when you press it, you come get me, and you don't tell him why. That's the other conversation. The kind one. I'll know it when I see it, and I won't dress it up for you either."

She looked at Wick a moment, flat and unreadable.

"You asked to know instead of imagine. That's near the whole of this trade. The wound is always worse in your head than on the table — on the table it's only meat, and meat has rules. Learn the rules and there's nothing left to imagine." She nodded once. "You looked. You didn't go grey and you didn't look away. Most men look once, and either they run or they stay. The ones who stay, I can use."

She turned to the basin, to the instruments, to the boil that was always going somewhere in the camp.

"Wash to the elbow, hot as you can stand it. Then come back — tomorrow I'll show you how to change that packing, because you'll be the one doing it."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't answer right away. She reached into the basin and fished out something that clinked against the tin, and set it on the table between them — a piece of metal the size of a thumb joint, dark, jagged, bent back on itself like a torn nail.

"That's out of the first man tonight. Not the leg — the shoulders. It was sitting in his back and he never knew it. Keep it or don't, but look at it, because that's the truth of it. It isn't a ball. It isn't a point. It's a tear in the world with weight behind it."

She turned it over with one finger.

"A bullet drills. It's made to — smooth, round, going one way, and if it misses the vessel and the bone you're left with a hole front and back and a man cursing his luck. That —" she tapped the fragment "— ploughs. It comes off the shell any shape it likes, spinning, and it doesn't care about going one way. It hits a rib and turns. It hits the soft parts and tears them wide instead of parting them. A bullet wound you can sometimes follow with a finger. This makes a track like a ploughed field, and everything along the track is bruised past living, even where it isn't cut."

"Second thing. It's hot. Comes off the burst burning, and it cooks the flesh it touches on the way in. That sounds like mercy — cooked flesh doesn't bleed, and you'll see men come in with terrible holes and hardly any blood, and the bearers say he's lucky. He isn't. Cooked edges are dead edges, and dead edges rot. The man who bleeds free is better off. Remember that when you're the one grading them at the flap — the quiet bloody one before the quiet dry one."

"Third. It doesn't come in alone." She held up her free hand and counted on her fingers, blunt as a shopping list. "Dirt. Cloth off the uniform. Leather off the boot, if it's low. Bits of the man standing next to him — bone, sometimes, driven in like shot itself. Whatever was on the ground when the shell found it. That's why the gas and the rot follow shell wounds worse than any other. It isn't the iron that kills them after. It's the field the iron carried in with it. Every fragment wound is a dirty wound even when it looks clean, and that's why I pack them open and let them weep, every one, no matter how pretty I could make them."

She picked the fragment up and held it to the lamp.

"Fourth — and this is the one that kills men who should have lived. The hole lies. The skin shows you a mouth this big and the track inside is this long, and it goes where it likes. I've taken a fragment out of a man's back that went in at his thigh. So you count the holes. Always count them. Even number, maybe it went through. Odd number, one of them's still inside, and you'd better know which direction it was travelling, because a fragment that stops against a vessel doesn't bleed — it just waits. It sits there a week, two weeks, with the pulse wearing at the wall it nicked, and then the wall gives and the man empties himself into his own leg before anyone gets a belt on. That's the one who dies smiling, telling you the wound's nearly healed. If a man with a shell wound says his leg aches deep, worse at night, you bring him to me. That's the ache I'm talking about."

She set the fragment down.

"The belly's its own country and I'll be short with it. A fragment through the gut lets the inside leak into the inside, and there's no belt for that and no flap for it either. Some of them I can open and wash and sew, and fever decides. Most of them, by the time they reach me, the leaking's been going on too long. Those are the kind conversations, more often than not. I'll teach you the signs, and then you'll know them too, and I'm sorry for that in advance."

She went back to the instruments, one at a time, out of the boil and onto the rag.

"Last thing, because you'll ask it eventually, so I'll save you the trouble. I don't chase every fragment. One sitting deep in the muscle, quiet, away from the vessels — the body walls it off and the man carries it the rest of his life and it rains on him in his joints when he's old. Chasing it does more harm than it does. The judgment isn't in the digging. It's in knowing which ones to leave, and you learn that by watching me be wrong about it, because I have been, and the man paid for my tuition."

She jerked her chin at the flap, at the noise outside.

"That's shrapnel, straight. It tears, it burns, it dirties, it hides, and it waits. The hole is the least of it — the hole is the lie it tells on the way in. Now you know, and you'll see every one of it true inside a week, because there's always more."

The lamp flared as she turned it.

"Go eat. That's an order, and I don't give them twice."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
"Talking's free," Sedge said. "Watch while I do it. And since you asked — the bad part's ten minutes. The whole of it, half an hour. I always lie on the long side. Hope's cheaper that way."

She ran her hands over him first, fast, head to heel, before she looked at any wound.

"First thing, always — count the holes. Not the blood. The holes." She lifted the man's arm. "One. Front of the arm." Turned it. "Two. Back of it. Even. That one went through, and through is the best news a fragment gives you — what's gone can't kill him twice. Missed the big vessel by luck and the bone by more of it. It's meat, and meat waits." She bound it tight, quick, not gentle, and the man screamed into the strap she'd given him. "Screaming's free too. Moving costs. That holds him. Now the one that matters."

She eased him onto his unhurt side, and he bucked, and the table creaked.

"Three. Here — back of the shoulder, under the blade. Three is odd. Odd means one of them's still inside, and this is the one he's screaming about. Through-holes don't scream like that. Deep ones do. The body knows."

She cleaned it enough to see, no more.

"Watch my hands, not his face. His face will lie to you — everything hurts him the same right now. The track tells the truth." The probe went in slow, a hair at a time, her eyes on nothing, on the feel. "Track goes in and up. It hit the blade bone and turned — like I told you they do. A bullet would have drilled straight. This one ploughed." Her hands went still. "There. Hard. That's not bone — bone's smooth. This has edges."

She didn't move the probe. She held it the way you'd hold a snake.

"And there's the rest of it. The probe's trembling, and I'm not trembling. That's the vessel's beat coming up the metal. The fragment's sitting on the big vessel under the arm. This is the one I told you about — the one that waits. Leave it, and in a week the pulse wears through the wall it nicked, and he empties himself smiling, telling somebody the wound's nearly healed. So it comes out. Tonight it comes out."

She laid ligatures and forceps out in their row, close, where her hand would fall on them blind.

"Hear the risk plain, because it's the whole of the next five minutes. It may be plugging the hole it made. When it comes out, the bleeding it's been stopping may start. So we don't pull until we're ready to be wrong. If it jumps, my finger goes in the hole and onto that vessel, and it stays there until I tie it or he dies of it. Your job doesn't change. He'll buck like the world ended. He can spend himself — you can't. If he comes off this table with my finger inside him, we both lose. Hold."

Then, to the man, not softer, just nearer: "There's iron in you and it's coming out. Bite down. Hate me later."

The forceps went down the track the way the probe had — slow, feeling.

"Slow here. Fast is for skin and bone. Down a track, slow is the only speed that doesn't tear." A pause. "Touching it. Opening. Got it by an edge. Now it comes out the way it went in, and it went in crooked, so it comes out crooked — I turn it as I pull. Feel for the give. Never force. The track made room on the way in. I'm asking it to give the room back."

The man came off the table against Wick's hold and the strap's, and something in the tent frame popped, and Sedge's hands never changed speed.

"Hold him. Almost — there."

The fragment came out dark and bent back on itself, thumb-sized, and she dropped it in the basin, where it clinked against the first one.

"Look at it after. That's the thing that was going to kill him in his sleep. Now we learn if it was plugging. Watch the hole with me. Watch it."

The track welled dark, slow, and kept to slow.

"Dark and even. That's ooze. No jump, no pulse in it. The wall holds — he keeps his luck." She packed the track with linen, firm, and left it open. "Open, same as the leg, same as every fragment wound I'll ever show you. It dirtied him on the way in and the cooked edges will slough, so it weeps and it drains and I don't make it pretty. You know why now."

She sewed the arm last, front and back, four stitches each, quick.

"Bad part's done. Eight minutes, not ten — I lied on the long side, like I said. He gets the same lecture the leg man got: fever decides the week, not me, and I'll give him the true odds when he wakes. And he gets the ache rule, same as every man who's been near a shell — a deep ache, worse at night, and he comes to me running. The count was clean. Three holes, one through, one out. Still. The rule stands."

She straightened, and the left shoulder clicked, and she ignored it.

"You asked for all of it. That's all of it. Count, probe, decide, pull, pack. There isn't any more to this trade than that, done fast, in the right order, on a man who's screaming. Learn the order and the screaming stops mattering. It doesn't stop hurting — it stops mattering. There's a difference, and you'll feel it by the end of the week."

She wiped her hands on the rag.

"And since you told me to keep talking — know why I do. The talking's part of the doing. It keeps my hands honest and it keeps you learning, and a medic who goes quiet is thinking, and thinking at the table means something's gone wrong. If I ever go quiet on you, hold tighter."

She nodded at the basin, at the two bent pieces of iron settling in the bloody water.

"You stayed to hold instead of eating. Eat double after. That's not an order, that's arithmetic."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at him on the floor for a long moment. Then she did something she had not done since the first stretcher came through the flap: she stopped. Dried her hands, took the jug and the bread off the shelf, set them within his reach, and sat down herself, back against the table leg, the rag across her knees.

"The floor's honest," she said. "I've done my best thinking on floors. Eat while I talk — chewing's free, like screaming. You wouldn't go to the food, so the food comes to you. That's triage."

She rolled the left shoulder. It clicked. For once she didn't ignore it; she looked at it, then back at him.

"The rest, then. In order, same as always — because there's an order to this part too, and nobody gave it to me, and I'm giving it to you, and that's the only inheritance this trade has.

"One. What you've got right now — the shake, the grey, tonight playing back in your head whether you want it or not. That's not ruin. That's the bill. The work ran you hot and now the fire's out and you're cold. It comes every night at first. Then bad nights only. Then it comes when it likes — years from now, in some peacetime bed, because you smelled apples gone over. You don't get to schedule it. You get to expect it. Expected is half of beaten.

"Two. The dreams. You'll dream the count. One, two, three — and the third hole won't stop bleeding no matter what you tie. Everyone who stays dreams the count. The woman who taught me dreamed it twenty years in, and told me so, and it's the only soft thing she ever said. The dreams aren't the work hurting you. The dreams are the boil. I told you everything goes in the same boil in the end — instruments, linen, the leg. The day goes in too. A head's like this tent: you don't sleep among the instruments. The dreams are the cleaning. And the night you dream the count and your hands in the dream know what to do — that's the night you're trained. Nobody will tell you that but me, so I'm telling you now.

"Three. And this is the one nobody told me, and I learned it late, and it cost the most, so listen. All night I've taught you the belt. High, tight, stays on till I say. Here's the rest of the belt: a belt that never comes off kills the limb. Slow. Grey, then bronze, then it crackles, and then you're cutting off something that was sound when you tied it. You understand me. The work is the belt and you're the limb. At the table you keep it tight — you have to; tight is how you hold a screaming man and tie a knot at the same time. But at night you ease it a quarter turn. On purpose. You let it hurt. You think of the man's face, or you say his name if you got it, or you sit on a floor and don't get up — and that's not you failing, that's the quarter turn, that's the limb staying alive. Off is the other failure, and off comes in three shapes. Off is the bottle — the bottle's for the table, and the day you dose yourself from it, you tell me, and I'll take it off you and you'll dig latrines for a week and thank me in a year. Off is walking into the treeline some night and not coming back. And off is the worst of the three — the ones who stop feeling anything and call it strong. Numb isn't strong. Numb is the limb dying under the belt. A numb medic will do anything at a table, because nothing costs him, and a man nothing costs is the most dangerous thing in this camp. More than the shelling. I'd rather work beside a man who weeps in his sleep than a man who feels nothing awake. Quarter turn, every night, or the work takes the limb. That's the rule I learned latest, and I'm handing it to you on your first night, and you don't even have to hate me for it.

"Four. The other count. You'll want to know if I keep one. I do, and I'll give you the shape of it so you don't invent worse. I don't count the dead. The war's dead are the war's — carry them and you drown, and that's arithmetic, not coldness. I count mine. The ones my being wrong bought. The number's eleven. Four years, eleven. I say the names once a year, on the night of the first one, and it takes less time than it should and longer than you'd think. When you have a name for that list, you'll know it — you won't have to ask me whether it goes on. And you don't share the list. It's not grief; grief's for the living to spend. The list is accounting, and accounting's private.

"Five. Why stay. You'll ask it some night, so here it is sober. It's not love of them — love burns out in the first year. It's not duty; duty's a word officers use to spend other people. It's smaller. There's a queue outside that flap, and I'm the one who knows the order. Count, probe, decide, pull, pack. Every night the queue's shorter because I know it, and some nights that's enough and some nights it isn't, and I stay on both kinds. Staying isn't a feeling. You don't feel your way into it. You just don't leave, daily, and it adds up. And I'll allow myself one pleasure in it, because I'm not a saint and saints are useless at a table: I take no pleasure in the work — none, and if I ever do, you take the knife off me — but I take pleasure in the knots holding. In the row being straight. In a man carried out breathing who came in dying. That's not the same thing as enjoying this. The difference is the whole job.

"Six. You." She said it flat, the way she graded everything. "You asked for the rest because what you want to know is whether you can carry it. So I'll grade you same as any man on my table, and I won't dress it up. Three men you held tonight. You shook after, not during. You sat down when the work was done, not while it was doing. You asked every question the runners never ask. You'll do. That's not comfort — comfort's a lie, and I don't tell lies, I tell odds. It's a diagnosis. You'll do, and in a month you'll be the one saying *hold* to some new pair of hands, flat, the way I taught you, and he'll believe you. That's how this trade outlives a war that's run out of medics. One holder at a time.

"Seven. And since you've been grading my shoulder across the tent all night, against my own rule, I'll save you the trouble. First year. A man came off a table and took me with him, and it went out, and there was nobody to put it back, so I put it back myself against a tent pole. It clicks. It'll click till I'm done. You heard my own lecture — once a joint's been out, it wants to go out again. That's true of more than shoulders. I work around it. And that's the last of the rest: everything I've told you tonight, I've told you with a joint that slips. Worn isn't broken. You'll get worn. Worn is the job."

She reached up and turned the lamp down — the first time all night it had gone down instead of up. Outside, for once, the noise stayed where it was. She didn't trust it. She used it.

"That's the whole estate. The wounds, the belt, the dead, the dreams, the list, and me — you've had all of it now. Sleep where you're sitting if it comes. I'll wake you at first light, and the packing's yours, and the man it's attached to will scream at you, and you'll do it anyway. Because now you know the order.

"The rest doesn't end, Wick. That's the last thing. It doesn't end — and you do it anyway. There's always more. But not in the next hour. And an hour's a thing too."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge stopped with her hand over the instruments and looked at Wick for a moment — not long, just long enough to see the question for what it was. He wanted to know how much of this he had to hold inside himself. She remembered the first years when she had wanted someone to tell her the same thing.

"Neither," she said. She put the probe back in its place and turned down the lamp. "Not yet anyway."

She went to the end of the table and pulled the blanket off the man's legs. The left one was swollen through the thigh and dark below the knee, the shin wound wrapped in a dressing that had bled through once and gone stiff. She pressed a thumb into the top of the foot and held it there, watching the white go and the color come back. It came back. Slow, but it came.

"Foot's warm," she said. "Color comes back when I press. That means the blood's getting down past the knee and it means the vessels are open. If that stops, then we're having a different conversation and I'll tell you straight when we are."

She pulled the blanket back up. Her knees cracked when she stood and she didn't bother to hide it.

"The wound's dirty," she said. "It was dirty when it was made and it's been dirty since. I cleaned what I could reach and I'll clean it again tomorrow and the day after that. Whether he keeps the leg comes down to whether the rot gets ahead of me, and I've got no way to tell you that tonight and neither has anyone else who tells you they can."

She began washing her hands in the basin. The water went pink and she kept going, working the fingers one at a time, the way she did — not because she was fastidious but because grit in a cut on her own hand would take her out of the tent for a week, and there was no one to replace her.

"This isn't the kind part," she said, not looking up. "Kind is a word for people who've got a choice of two things. We've got the one thing. I do it the best it can be done and that's the whole of it." She dried her hands on the cloth. "You want to help him, you hold him straight tomorrow when I redress it, and you don't flinch. That's what he needs from you. Not feeling."

She glanced at the man on the table. His breathing had gone deeper, more even — the slack, animal breathing of a body that had finally outrun the pain for a while.

"He'll sleep," she said. "Sit where he can hear someone and don't wake him. I'm going to look at the other two."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge opened her eyes. She looked at him for a moment with something that might have been approval or might have been the face she wore when she was about to say something she'd said before and it never did any good.

"Straight," she said. "All right."

She leaned forward with her elbows on her knees, the same way he was sitting, and held her hands out in front of her with the fingers spread.

"Shrapnel's not a bullet. A bullet goes through and makes a hole and the hole is what it is. Shrapnel is a piece of iron that's been blown into shape by an accident and it tumbles. So it doesn't go in neat. It goes in at an angle and it turns and it carries whatever it was next to when it broke — canvas, leather, mud, a piece of someone's kit, a piece of someone. It doesn't stop where it made the hole. It stops wherever it stops and you can't tell that from the outside, ever, no matter what anyone's told you."

She put one finger on her own forearm.

"First thing it does is crush. The track it makes isn't a clean cut — it's a channel of tissue that's been destroyed. Not torn. *Destroyed.* Crushed to the point where the tissue is dead even though it's still sitting there. That's the part people don't understand. They see a wound and they think the wound is the edges of it. It isn't. The wound is everything between the edges that's been killed and hasn't come out yet."

She held up the finger.

"Second thing is the pieces. It breaks into more of itself, or it drags fragments in with it. Bone gets shattered and the bone splinters become more shrapnel going the other direction. So you've got a hole and you've got a mess inside it and you've got pieces of iron and pieces of bone and pieces of the world sitting in a pocket of dead flesh that's now warm and wet and open to everything in the air."

She leaned back.

"Third thing is the dirt. You asked about the rot earlier and this is where the rot comes from. The dead tissue doesn't bleed anymore so it doesn't get cleaned by the body, and whatever went in with the metal is sitting in it. That's a garden. It grows. It grows fast and it grows up the tissue toward the belly or toward the heart and it doesn't care about you or him or whether we want it to."

She looked at the man on the table.

"What's in his leg right now is this: a channel of dead tissue from the shin up through the calf, with fragments somewhere in it that I cannot see and cannot reach and will not pretend I can. I've taken out what was at the surface. What's deeper, I leave, because going after it does more damage than leaving it, and I learned that the hard way before you got here."

She turned her hands over and looked at her own palms.

"What I do is this. I open the wound wide enough to see as far as I can see. I take out what I can take out without tearing him open further. I wash it — water, and whatever I've got that kills things, and today that's not much. Then I leave it open to drain, and I change it, and I look at the edges every day to see whether the flesh is going grey and whether it's spreading. That's the whole job. It's not fixing him. It's slowing the garden down enough that his own body can get ahead of it, and whether his body does that is not up to me."

She folded her hands.

"That's straight. It's a rotten job and the odds aren't good and I've seen men lose legs over less than he's got and I've seen men keep legs over worse. I don't tell you which he'll be because I don't know and I won't guess at you."

She looked at Wick's face in the low light.

"You wanted it straight. There it is. Now you know what's under the dressing and you'll sleep worse for it and so would I." She said that last part dry, without heat. "Watch the four things."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge was off the crate before the second scream finished. She didn't tell Wick to hold — he was already holding, and she could see his weight was right, and that was all there was time to see. She got the lamp up with one hand and had the other on the man's jaw before the third scream got its full breath.

"Look at me," she said, to the man, not to Wick. "Open your eyes. Look at me."

The eyes came open. They were wrong — too wide, too far in, seeing something that wasn't the tent — but they came.

"Keep talking," Wick said.

"I'm looking at his eyes first," Sedge said, and she said it the way she said everything, flat and as she did it. "Pupils wide. That's pain or that's fear and right now it's both and it doesn't matter which. I'm checking the shoulders — I'm putting my hands on the tops of them and I'm feeling for the shape of the joint under the shirt. The left one's still where I put it. The right one's still where I put it. He's not thrashing for the shoulders."

She moved down. The lamp went with her.

"I'm pulling the blanket back. I'm looking at the dressing before I touch it. Same as before — dry at the edge, damp at the center, but the damp is bigger than it was. Not much bigger. I'm not pulling it off. I'm looking at the leg above the bandage and I'm comparing the swelling to what it was an hour ago and I'm telling you it's up. Not a lot. Some."

She put the backs of her fingers against the skin above the knee, then lower, then lower still.

"The skin's hot. Not fever hot — local hot, around the wound. That's the body fighting what's in there. It's expected. It's not good and it's not the worst thing."

She looked at his face again. The screaming had gone down to a long ragged breathing with sounds in it that might have been words.

"His pain's outrun what I gave him. That's what's happening. The laudanum's worn off and the leg is waking up and it's telling him the truth about itself. This is the part I can't fix and I'm telling you that straight so you know there isn't something I'm not doing."

She reached for the table beside the bed and measured out what was left in the bottle into the cup. She held it up and looked at how much it was. It was not much.

"I'm giving him a half dose. Not a full one, because I've got what I've got until the next supply comes and I don't know when that is, and if I give him the bottle tonight I have nothing for tomorrow when it's worse. That's the decision and it's not a kind one and I've made it."

She got one hand behind the man's head and put the cup to his mouth. He coughed. She waited and gave it again. He swallowed.

"That'll take the edge off in about a quarter hour. Between now and then he's going to make noise and he's going to fight and you're going to hold him and you're not going to let the shoulders move. How much longer — he screams until the dose lands, that's how long, and then he goes down some and we get four or five hours if we're lucky."

She put the cup down and looked at Wick across the man's chest.

"Keep his head turned to the side. If he's sick he'll choke on it lying flat. And talk to him. Not to me. Say his name and say other things. Doesn't matter what. Your voice is one of the four things tonight, same as the dressing."

She put her hand on the man's forehead and left it there.

"I'm here," she said, to the man. "You're in the tent. You're on the table. I've got you."

The screaming went down to something like breathing again. She kept her hand where it was and looked at nothing in particular and kept it there for a long time.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge stopped at the tent flap. She stood there for a moment with her back to him, and then she came back — not all the way, just far enough to hold the lamp over the table again. The light caught the man's face and the blanket over his chest and the dark patch on the left leg where the dressing had soaked through.



"Look at the blanket first," she said. "Up and down, slow. That's his breathing. It's deep and it's even and it's not doing any work. That's what a body sounds like when it's stopped fighting you. Good. Now look at the collarbones — see how they're not pulling? When a man's having trouble breathing you see the muscles here working, the shoulders come up. He's not doing that. Means his chest is fine and his lungs are fine and nothing above the belly is giving him trouble tonight."

She moved the lamp down to his face and put two fingers under his jaw again, and held them there.

"I'm feeling his pulse. You can do this. Two fingers, not the thumb — the thumb's got its own pulse and you'll hear that instead. You feel for rate, and you feel for whether it's skipping. His is fast and it's thin and it's not skipping. Fast is all right. I'd rather fast and regular than slow and skipping."

She lifted the blanket at the edge and showed the dark dressing on the shin without unwrapping it.

"This is the one I want you to learn to look at. The dressing is wet here and dry here. Wet means it's still bleeding on the inside. Dry means it's stopped. Right now it's damp — not wet. That's stopped. If you come back in an hour and that whole dressing is soaked through and the wet is spreading, that's the bleeding starting again and you call me. Don't pull the dressing off. Don't press on it. Just come get me."

She let the blanket fall.

"The color of him. Look at his lips and the beds of his fingernails." She lifted his hand and turned it in the lamplight. The nail beds were pale but pink under the grime. "That's not the white of a man who's bled out. He's lost some — I can't tell you how much, I've got no way to measure it here. But he's not losing now and his body's holding what it has. If those nails go white or go blue, you call me. Blue is the one I'm afraid of."

She put his hand back under the blanket.

"That's the whole of it," she said. "Breathing, pulse, the dressing, and the color. Four things. You look at those four things and you don't look at anything else. You don't look at his face and think about who he is. You don't look at the swelling and imagine what's under it. You look at what I just told you to look at and you think about those four things and nothing else. That's how you'll be useful to me tonight and it's how you'll be useful to him."

She held the lamp out toward him so the light came up between them and she could see his face.

"If any one of those four changes, you come find me. If all four are the same when I come back, then this was a quiet night and you sit with it and you don't make it into something it isn't."

She went out through the flap then, and the tent settled around Wick and the breathing man and the dark.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"Bad like he'll be in pain for a while, and bad like he might not walk again. But not bad like we're doing him a favor. He's young, strong. He'll fight. And we'll do everything we can to help him."

She looked at Wick, her eyes serious. "But I won't lie to you. This is going to be a long road for him. And for us. We've got a lot of work ahead."

She took a deep breath and let it out slowly, her voice steady. "But we'll get through it. Together. And he'll get through it. We just have to keep going, one step at a time. One patient at a time."

She looked back at the man on the table, her eyes softening. "He's tough. He'll make it. We'll make sure of it."

With that, she turned and left the tent, her shoulders squared and her head held high, ready to face whatever came next.

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge stood there with the lamp in her hand and looked at him on the floor of the tent. He had slid down the canvas wall and he was sitting with his legs out in front of him and his hands open on his thighs and he looked the way men looked when the holding was done and the body caught up to what it had been doing. She had sat on floors herself. She had sat on worse than floors.

She set the lamp on the crate and she sat down on the ground across from him. Not on the crate. On the ground, which she did not usually do, because it was harder to get up from and there was always something to get up for. She sat with her back against the tent post and her knees up and her hands in her lap and she looked at him for a moment and then she looked at the man on the table and then she looked at the floor between them.

"The rest," she said. "All right."

She breathed in once through her nose and let it out slow. Not because she was gathering herself — she did not gather herself, gathering was for people who had time — but because the next stretch of talking was long and she wanted to get through it without stopping.

"The man on the table. His name is Colm. I know that because someone told me on the first day and I wrote it on the board because if he dies in this tent someone has to write it down and it might as well be me and it might as well have his name on it." She paused. "I'm telling you that because you've been sitting with him all night and you should know it. Colm. Twenty-three. Enlisted in the second year. His mother's address is in his jacket and I moved the jacket to the chest so it wouldn't get blood on it."

She shifted her weight. The ground was cold through her trousers and damp from the rain coming under the canvas.

"The leg. I told you about the garden and I told you about the rot and I told you I can't tell you which way it'll go and that's true. But there's a difference between not knowing and not saying what I've seen, and you asked for the rest, so here's what I've seen."

She held up one hand and began on the fingers, the way she had begun with the four things, because counting things on her fingers was how she kept herself from rounding the edges off.

"The swelling is above where it was this morning and the heat is up to the knee and not past. That's one. The wound edges are red and raised and angry and that's the body fighting, which is what I want, but the fact that it has to fight this hard on the third day tells me the garden is strong. That's two. The smell is sweet and thick and it's not the worst it can be but it's not getting better and smell is how I know what's happening inside more than anything else I've got. That's three."

She closed the hand and opened the other one.

"The dressing was damp an hour ago and spreading. I opened it and washed it and repacked it and it looked — " She stopped. She chose the word the way she chose instruments, one at a time. "It looked like a wound that is trying. Not winning. Trying. There's a difference and the difference is about a week and I can't tell you which side of the week he'll land on."

She put her hands flat on her knees.

"Here's the rest you're wanting. The odds. I've had nine men with wounds like this since the spring. Four kept the leg. Three lost it and lived. Two died." She said it flat. "Nine is not enough to make a rule out of and I know that and I'm telling you anyway because you asked. If I had to put a number on Colm — and I said I wouldn't and you've asked me twice now, so — I'd say it's worse than even that he keeps the leg and it's better than even that he lives. That's the most honest thing I can say and it's not very honest because a number is a way of pretending you know something you don't."

She stopped and looked at him on the floor.

"That's Colm. Now the rest of the rest."

She tilted her head back against the post and looked up at the canvas above her where the rain was making a sound like something being dragged.

"The third one. The fever one. His name is Aldous. He came in two days ago with a ball through the meat of his thigh and I took the ball out and it was clean — clean as anything I get here — and he should be doing well and he isn't. His fever started yesterday afternoon and it's been going up since and I've been sponging him and I've been giving him what I've got and it's not touching it."

She looked at the ceiling of the tent.

"When a fever comes up like that after a clean wound it means one of two things. It means the wound is infected deeper than I can see and the body is fighting something I can't reach, or it means the humors have gone wrong in a way I don't have a name for and don't have a treatment for. Either way, I'm watching a man burn up and I'm doing things to him — sponging, dosing, changing linen — that make me feel like I'm working and might not be doing anything at all."

She said that last part carefully. It was the closest she came to saying something about herself and she knew it and she let it stand.

"Aldous is the one I'm worried about. More than Colm. Colm's leg is a fight I can see. Aldous's fever is a fight I can't see and can't find and can't reach and it's been two days and the number on the thermometer — I don't have a thermometer, I've got my hand and a glass of water and forty-four years of knowing what skin is supposed to feel like — the number is going the wrong way and it hasn't stopped."

She folded her hands together.

"If Aldous goes, it'll be fast at the end. Fevers like this either break in the night or they don't and when they don't they take a man between one hour and the next and you'll be sitting here with Colm and you'll hear me in the other part of the tent and you won't know what's happening and I'm telling you now so that you do. I'm telling you because the not knowing is the part that gets into people and I've watched it get into people and I'd rather you heard it from me than figured it out from the sound."

She was quiet for a moment. The rain filled the quiet.

"The supplies. You should know this too. I've got laudanum enough for four days at the rate I'm using it and then I've got nothing and I've sent for more and I don't know if it's coming because I sent for more three weeks ago and what arrived was carbolic and lint and no laudanum at all and a note that said they were doing what they could. Carbolic and lint. That's what the war sent me. I've got enough carbolic to last and I've got enough lint to last and what I don't have is the thing that keeps men from screaming while I work on them, and when that runs out I'll be doing what I did to Colm tonight with nothing in him at all and he'll feel every bit of it and so will you."

She said it without heat. It was not a complaint. It was a fact about the world, like the rain.

"And then there's the rest of the rest, which is me."

She looked at her hands.

"I've been doing this four years. I was trained in eighteen months by a surgeon who was good and who is dead now — not in the war, a fever, the irony of which I've had enough time to appreciate. Since then I've been the only one in this section and sometimes the only one in two sections and I have not had a full night's sleep since I cannot remember when and I have lost count of the number of men I've worked on and I have not lost count of the number I've lost but I don't keep the number where I can see it."

She looked at him.

"I'm telling you this because you asked me how I stand it and I gave you an answer earlier and it was true but it wasn't the whole of it. The whole of it is that I don't always stand it. There are hours — usually around four in the morning, usually when I've been up since the day before — when I sit where you're sitting now and I can't remember why any of this matters and I can't feel anything about any of them and that scares me more than the blood ever did. Not because I think I've gone cold. Because I know I haven't and the not-feeling is just the body putting a wall up so I can keep working, and the wall comes down later, at the wrong time, over nothing. I dropped a cup last month and I sat on this crate and cried for ten minutes and then I went and redressed a man's arm. That's the rest."

She rubbed her hands together once.

"I don't say this so you'll feel something about me. I say it because you're sitting on the floor of my tent after holding a man through two rounds of the worst pain a body can make and you asked me to say the rest, and the rest includes me because I'm part of what's happening in this tent and if I lie to you about how I'm doing then I'm lying about the situation and you can't make good decisions on a lie."

She looked at the man on the table. Colm. His breathing was deep and even and the laudanum had landed and he was somewhere else for a while.

"Here's the whole of it, then. Colm may keep the leg or may not and I'll know more in three days and until then I'll do the work and you'll hold him and we'll watch the four things and the dressing and the line on the skin where the heat stops. Aldous may break his fever tonight or may not and if he doesn't he'll likely be gone by morning and I'll wash him and wrap him and write his name on the board and someone will come for him. The laudanum will run out in four days and after that this work gets worse in a way I can describe to you but won't because you'll find out and there's no use in both of us carrying it tonight. And I will keep doing this because there is no one else and because the alternative is those men lying there with no one, and no one is worse than me, and I know that because I've seen what no one looks like."

She stopped. She had been talking for a long time and her throat was dry and she didn't get up for water because getting up would mean the talking was over and she wasn't sure it was.

"That's the rest," she said. "All of it. What I know and what I don't and what I am and what's coming. You asked for straight and I've given you straight and now you know as much as I do about what's in this tent tonight."

She looked at him on the floor.

"You can sit there as long as you need to. I'm not going to tell you to get up and I'm not going to tell you it's all right because it isn't all right and we both know it. But the rain's coming in under the canvas and you're going to be wet through in about twenty minutes and I'd rather you moved to the crate before that happens because a wet man in a cold tent is the next patient and I've got enough of those."

She said it without smiling. But it was the closest she came.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge paused, her hands still as she looked at Wick. "Shrapnel does a lot of things. It tears. It shreds. It pulverizes. It doesn't just cut or slice. It doesn't care about neatness or symmetry. It's messy and brutal and bloody. It turns flesh into mincemeat and bone into splinters."

She looked back at the man on the table, her voice steady. "It does a lot of damage. But it doesn't mean it's the end. It just means we have a lot of work to do. A lot of cleaning. A lot of stitching. A lot of healing. But we can do it. We can give him back what he's lost. We can give him a chance."

She turned to Wick, her eyes meeting his. "But we have to be honest with each other. No sugarcoating. No lies. Just the truth. The ugly, brutal truth. Because that's what we're dealing with. That's what we're fighting. And we can only win if we face it head-on. Together."

She took a deep breath, her voice firm. "So, are you ready for the truth? The whole truth, no matter how ugly? Because that's what I'm going to give you. Every step of the way. No matter what it takes."

Wick:
I nod, my jaw tight. "Tell me everything. I can handle it."

Sedge:
Sedge nodded, her eyes never leaving Wick's. "Alright. Then let's get started. Let's see what we're really dealing with."

She turned back to the man on the table, her voice steady and sure. "Shrapnel causes a lot of internal damage. It can puncture organs, tear through muscles and tendons, shatter bone, and cause extensive bleeding. It can cause infection, sepsis, and gangrene. It can lead to amputation, paralysis, or even death. But it doesn't have to. Not if we work together. Not if we give it our all."

She looked at Wick, her eyes sharp. "This is going to be hard. Messy. Brutal. But it's necessary. It's what we signed up for. It's what we do. And we do it because we believe in giving people a chance. No matter what. No matter how hard. No matter how ugly."

She took a deep breath, her voice steady. "So, are you ready to do this? To really do this? To give him a chance, no matter what it takes? Because I am. And I need to know you are too."

Wick:
"I'm ready," I say, my voice rough. "Let's do this. Let's save his life."

Sedge:
Sedge nodded, a small, determined smile on her face. "Good. Then let's get to work."

She turned to the table, her eyes focused and her voice calm. "First, we need to assess the damage. We need to see what we're dealing with. We need to see the extent of the injuries. We need to see the truth. And then we need to act. Together. Side by side. No matter what it takes."

She looked at Wick, her eyes meeting his. "And we need to do it now. Because the longer we wait, the worse it gets. The more blood he loses, the more damage is done. The more pain he feels. The less of a chance he has. So, we need to be quick. We need to be efficient. We need to be relentless."

She took a deep breath, her voice steady. "And we need to be honest. With each other. With ourselves. With him. Because that's the only way we can win. That's the only way we can save his life. That's the only way we can make a difference."

She looked back at the man on the table, her eyes softening. "And that's what we're here for. That's what we do. That's who we are. So, let's get to work. Let's save a life. Let's make a difference. Let's do what we do best. Together."

Wick:
I move to his side, bracing myself. "Tell me where to start."

Sedge:
Sedge nodded, her eyes never leaving the man on the table. "Alright. First, we need to stop the bleeding. We need to apply pressure to the wounds. We need to use gauze and tourniquets. We need to be quick and efficient. We need to save his life. And we need to do it now."

She looked at Wick, her eyes meeting his. "So, let's get started. Let's save a life. Let's make a difference. Let's do what we do best. Together. No matter what it takes. No matter what it costs. No matter what it means. We're going to save this man. And we're going to do it together. Side by side. No matter what."

She took a deep breath, her voice steady. "And we're going to start now. Right now. With this first step. With this first cut. With this first stitch. This is where it begins. This is where we make a difference. This is where we save a life. Together. Now. Let's go."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge turned to face Wick, her expression serious. "You're seeing a man who's been through a lot. His body's broken, but it's not beyond repair. He's lost a lot of blood, and he's in a lot of pain. But he's alive, and that's a start."

She gestured to the wounds on his shoulders. "These are deep. The bone's shattered in several places. We'll have to set it, clean it, and stitch it. It'll take time, and it'll hurt like hell, but we can do it."

She looked at Wick, her eyes steady. "We can save him. But it won't be easy. It'll take everything we've got. And it'll take you holding him steady, just like before. Are you ready for that?"

She waited, her eyes searching Wick's face for any sign of hesitation or fear. "Because if you're not, I need to know now. I can't do this alone, and I won't risk his life on uncertainty."

Sedge took a deep breath, her voice firm. "So, are you ready to do this? To save his life, no matter what it takes?"

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack let him stand there a moment. The dead man’s chest had settled, and the quiet after was the ordinary kind, not holy.

“You’re looking at a man who ran out of arguments,” she said.

She crouched beside the body, keeping her boots clear of the widest darkening patch, and used the point of her knife to lift the torn cloak from the wound without pulling it free.

“Blade went in under the right ribs, angled up. You missed the heart. If you’d hit the heart, he’d have dropped before he could make a mess. Instead you opened liver edge and bowel, maybe the lower lung. That’s why the breath rattled. Blood backed up where it shouldn’t be.”

She let the cloth fall.

“The red on his chin came from the mouth. The black under his shoulder is pooling where he lay. His fingers are half-curled because he tried to grab something and found no one coming. The scrape on his cheek is from the ditch. The cloak is borrowed; it smells wrong for him. Boots are good, older than his trousers. He marched far and ate recently enough that his belly wasn’t empty.”

Wrack’s gaze moved over the body with the flat attention of a woman checking a wagon wheel for cracks.

“No prayer beads. No wife’s hair in his fist. No last letter sticking out. Just a soldier who was paid to wait for tomorrow and got today instead. Whether he was the sixth name or the hand meant to scratch it, I can’t tell from meat. For that, we need the box.”

She reached for the man’s belt with two fingers, testing the buckle.

“So look, then learn. Death isn’t a picture. It’s a change in material. The man is gone; the matter is still here, and it has details. If you can carry the details without carrying the story, you’ll live longer.”

A dry pause.

“If your stomach objects, let it object quietly. The flies will be here soon enough without help.”
