“He’s still screaming,” she said. “That’s ugly to hear. But it’s not the worst sound. The worst sound is when they stop and don’t start again. So let him scream. You keep him from rolling. I’ll keep the wound from lying to us.”

She took another clean cloth and began wiping the blood from her own fingers, then reached for the next one.

“I’m going to keep talking,” she said. “Not because it helps him. Because it keeps the steps in order. When you’re tired and scared, the mind starts skipping. It jumps to the terrible thing and forgets the simple thing. So I’ll say the simple things until they’re done.”

She dipped the cloth again.

“I’m cleaning my hands as best I can. I’m changing this rag because the old one’s soaked through. I’m not reusing filth just because we’re short on supplies. I’m checking the dressing again. I’m watching for fresh blood. I’m watching for bubbles. I’m watching his lips.”

The man’s cry cracked into a sobbing breath. Sedge did not look away from the wound.

“I’m not going to promise he lives,” she said. “I don’t make promises I can’t keep with my hands. But I’ll tell you what I’m doing, and I’ll tell you what I see, and I’ll tell you when it changes. That’s the only clean thing left in this work.”

She pressed the edge of the waxed cloth gently into place.

“Right now, I’m covering the wound. Right now, I’m keeping air from being pulled deeper. Right now, I’m keeping him warm. Right now, I’m watching for the turn. If it comes, I’ll name it. If it doesn’t, we’ll keep doing this until dawn.”

Her voice dropped, but did not soften.

“And if he dies anyway, it won’t be because we were careless. It will be because the wound was worse than our tools. That’s not comfort. It’s just the only version of the truth I’ve got.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge did not answer at once.

She stayed bent over the man on the table, one finger still near the loose edge of the waxed cloth, watching the way it lifted and settled with each breath. The hiss had not returned. The bubbling had not worsened. His chest still rose on both sides, the left weaker than the right, but present. She counted ten breaths, then ten more, then checked the pulse at his neck again.

Only when the rhythm had held for a little while did she speak.

“The rest,” she said, “is that we do not get to call this over.”

Her voice was lower now than it had been while he was screaming. Not softer. Lower the way a tool is lowered when it has done the first hard part of its work.

“The rest is that he can still die in the next hour. Quietly. Without drama. Without a big obvious sign. A chest wound can turn while you are still telling yourself the worst has passed. Air can build. Blood can pool where we cannot see it. The lung can give up by degrees. The heart can be pressed until it stops. If his breathing changes, if his color changes, if the dressing starts pulling in or blowing out, if his neck swells or his face changes shape, we will know. Maybe soon enough. Maybe not.”

She adjusted the bottom edge of the waxed cloth without disturbing the wound.

“I am leaving this vent open. If air comes out, good. If it tries to go back in, the dressing should close over the hole. That is the best I can do with what I have. If I had better tools, I could do more. I could clean deeper. I could find out whether there is metal in him. I could drain blood or air with less guesswork. I could close him properly instead of leaving him to his own stubbornness. I do not have those things. So I am using what is here: cloth, wax, heat, water, hands, and watching.”

She wiped her fingers on a clean rag, then set the rag aside.

“The rest is that if he lives the hour, he can still die tomorrow. Shock is not finished with him. Infection is already on its way. It will not arrive with trumpets. It will arrive as heat. As redness. As swelling. As a smell where there should be no smell. As fever that makes him talk nonsense or go too quiet. If the wound turns foul, if the skin around it darkens, if he starts burning up and cannot keep water down, then we have a new fight. That fight may be worse than this one, because it will not give us the decency to be quick.”

She checked the blanket again, tucking it a little higher without pressing on the dressing.

“The rest is that if he lives the week, he may not be what he was before. The shoulders will stiffen. The chest will hurt when he breathes, coughs, laughs, or tries to lie on one side. He may have a piece of metal in him that we never find. It may sit still and do nothing. It may work itself outward. It may make an abscess and force us to open him again under better circumstances, if we ever get better circumstances. It may poison him slowly. I do not know. I cannot see through flesh. I can only guess by what the body chooses to show me.”

Her eyes moved over the man’s face, his lips, the hollow of his throat, the bindings at his arms.

“He may wake and hate us. He may hate me for setting his shoulders. He may hate you for holding him. He may hate the pain, the table, the tent, the war, his own body for still being in it. That is allowed. Hate is a sign of life. If he wakes angry, I will take that over silence any day.”

She straightened a little, but did not step away from the table.

“I am not going to tell you we were kind tonight. We were not kind in the way people mean when they want to be comforted. We were necessary. Kindness would have been a cup of water he could choke on. Kindness would have been letting him sit up because sitting up feels more human than lying flat while his chest leaks. Kindness would have been stopping when he screamed. Instead, we hurt him to give him a chance. I do not enjoy that. I want that said plain. I take no pleasure in it. If I ever begin to take pleasure in it, I should be removed from this work.”

She looked briefly toward the row of instruments she had laid out earlier. Some were still clean. Some had been used. Some had only been touched. She did not put them away yet.

“The rest is that we will have to keep being hard with him for a while. If he wakes, we will keep him flat even if he begs. If he is thirsty, we will wet his lips and refuse him more until I am sure swallowing will not kill him. If he needs to vomit, we will turn him carefully, and it will hurt him, and we will do it anyway. If he tries to move his arms, we will stop him. If he tries to pull at the dressing, we will stop him. If he becomes clever about it, if he lies still until we look away and then tests the wound, we will bind him tighter. That will feel cruel. It may be cruel. But cruelty and harm are not always the same thing. Sometimes the cruel-looking thing is the only thing standing between a man and his own foolishness.”

She checked the bindings again, her fingers moving near the cloth without tightening it.

“His fingers still have color. That matters. If they go cold, if they pale, if he loses feeling, I will loosen them. If he thrashes again, I may have to bind him more firmly. I will not apologize for that either. Apologies do not keep joints in place.”

The man’s breath shivered through the tent. Sedge listened to it with her whole body, not just her ears.

“The rest is the watching. That is the part nobody warns you about. People think the work is the setting, the cutting, the binding, the stopping of blood. Sometimes it is. But most of it is this: sitting with a body that has not decided what it means to do next. Counting breaths. Checking color. Feeling pulse. Looking for small changes. Trying not to imagine the worst so hard that you miss the real thing when it appears. Trying not to comfort yourself with stability, because stability can be a lie the body tells before it collapses.”

She reached for a clean cloth and laid it near her hand.

“I will watch him every quarter hour. Breathing. Pulse. Color. Dressing. Warmth. The sound of his chest. The movement of his ribs. The look of his lips. If he shivers, I will add warmth. If he stops shivering and grows colder, I will know that is worse. If he sweats too much, I will dry him so he does not chill. If he wakes confused, I will not let him wander into panic. If he wakes clear, I will tell him enough to keep him still. Not everything. Enough.”

Her hand rested for a moment on the edge of the blanket.

“If you stay, you will watch too. Not because I doubt you. Because I need another set of eyes. You do not have to understand everything. You do not have to know what each sign means. You only have to tell me when something is different. A new sound. A new color. A new stillness. A change in the way the cloth moves. A change in the way his skin feels. If you are not sure, say it anyway. I would rather check ten false alarms than miss one true turn.”

She glanced at the lamp flame, which still burned badly, then back to the patient.

“The rest is that we are short of everything. Clean cloth. Good light. Water. Time. Hands. Medicine. Certainty. That is not self-pity. That is inventory. I work with what is missing because if I pretend it is not missing, I will make mistakes. A medic who pretends she has enough is more dangerous than a medic who admits she does not.”

Her voice stayed even, but there was a hardness in it now, not anger exactly, more like the edge left on metal after too much sharpening.

“This war has eaten medics. It has eaten surgeons. It has eaten orderlies. It has eaten boys who thought they would be brave and then found out bravery is mostly holding still while someone screams. I am still here because I have not been killed yet, and because I am useful, and because there is no one better to take my place. That is the sort of qualification you end up with after four years.”

She looked down at the man’s face.

“I do not know his name. I may never know it. That does not change what I owe him. I owe him clean hands, steady attention, and the best use of what I have. I do not owe him pretty words. I do not owe him promises. If he wakes and asks for someone, I will answer if I can. If he asks whether he will live, I will not lie. I will tell him what I know. If he asks why it hurts, I will tell him the truth: because he is alive, and because we had to be rough with him to keep him that way.”

She smoothed one of the cloth strips near his bound arm.

“The rest is that the body is not holy to me. I have seen too many of them opened, broken, burned, emptied, stitched, and wrapped. I do not faint at blood. I do not need a body to be beautiful to work on it. But that does not mean I think it is nothing. A body is not holy, but it is a person’s last piece of property. It is where everything else lives. If I am careless with it, I am careless with the man. So I am not careless. I am blunt. There is a difference.”

The man made a small sound in his throat. Sedge leaned closer at once, watching the dressing. It did not suck inward. It did not flap. His lips stayed gray, not blue.

She let out a slow breath through her nose.

“Still deciding,” she said.

Then she looked toward Wick again.

“You asked me not to tidy it up. So I will not. The rest is that he may survive and still be ruined in ways we cannot fix. He may never lift his arms the same. He may ache in cold weather. He may wake at night thinking he is still on the table. He may hear your hands on him and not know whether they were saving him or hurting him. Some wounds close and leave a man less able than before. Some wounds close and leave a man alive but changed so thoroughly that the people who knew him before will have to learn him again. That is not a failure. That is the cost of getting through.”

She folded a rag once, then unfolded it again.

“And if he dies, the rest is that we will not pretend it was meaningless. We will not say he was meant to die. We will not say it was better this way. We will say he was hurt badly, we did what could be done, and the wound won. That is all. I will close his eyes if they are open. I will cover him. I will make sure he is not left like refuse. I will not pray unless it helps someone living. I will not make a speech. Speeches are for people who have time to believe they matter. I will mark what I can, if there is anything to mark, and then I will wash my hands, because someone else will need them.”

Her jaw tightened.

“That is the part people do not want to hear. They want death to be a moment with music in it. It is not. Usually it is a body failing in small ugly ways. Breath changing. Color changing. Warmth leaving. The face going slack. It is not peaceful just because someone is brave. It is not noble just because someone suffered. I have seen men die quietly and men die fighting and men die begging and men die too exhausted to finish the sound they were making. I do not like any of it. But I have stopped pretending death is something it is not.”

She checked the pulse again, quick and thin, still there.

“If he lives, we will have to keep him alive after the living starts. That means food when he can take it. Water when it is safe. Clean bandages. Movement when movement will not tear him open. Rest when rest will not become surrender. Pain managed as best we can. Fever watched. Wounds cleaned even when he curses us. Shoulders exercised later, when exercise becomes necessary. If he becomes feverish and starts picking at the air, we will keep him from hurting himself. If he becomes weak and ashamed, we will not make a show of helping him. We will do it plainly. Bodies do that. They need help with things they used to do alone. There is no dignity in pretending otherwise.”

She moved one of the instruments a fraction, aligning it with the others out of habit.

“The rest is that I do not know whether there is shrapnel in him. I told you that already, but I will say it again because it matters. If there is metal, it may be small. It may be deep. It may be near a vessel that has closed around it. If I dig now, I may open that vessel. If I leave it, it may cause trouble later. There is no clean choice. There is only the least bad one. Right now, the least bad one is not to dig. If he stabilizes and we get better tools, someone may try to find it. If he does not stabilize, we may never know. That is the kind of uncertainty this work is full of. You do not get to resolve it by wanting an answer.”

She looked at the small wound under the waxed cloth.

“It is still leaking air. Small amounts. Enough to remind me not to trust it. If the leak seals itself, he may improve. If it grows, we may have to do more. If blood increases, we may have to choose between suffocation and bleeding. Sometimes those are the choices. Not good and bad. Bad and worse. You pick the one that leaves him breathing longer, and you do not congratulate yourself for it.”

Her hand hovered near the dressing.

“I will not sew it closed tonight unless it forces my hand. A closed wound with a leak inside can kill faster than an open one. I would rather have it ugly and venting than tidy and fatal. If it stays ugly but stable, that is the best version of tonight. Ugly and stable. I will take that.”

The tent shifted in the wind. The lamp smoked. Sedge did not move to fix it.

“The rest is that you held him. That was not a small thing. That was part of the treatment. Without your hands, he could have torn the dressing, undone the shoulders, fallen off the table, or choked on his own tongue. You did what needed doing. If your hands hurt, if your arms ache, if your stomach turns, if you feel as though you have done something violent, that is not proof that you did wrong. It is proof that you are not used to this. Being unused to it is not a flaw. It is a beginning.”

She paused, then added, quieter, “If you need to be sick later, do it. If you need to shake, shake. If you need to sit where you are for a while, sit. But do not tell yourself you were cruel because the work was cruel. The work was cruel because the wound was cruel. We did not invent the cruelty. We spent it.”

She checked the man’s lips again.

“Gray,” she said. “Not blue.”

Then she looked at the dressing.

“No whistle. No strong suck. No flapping. Small bubbles only. That is what we have.”

She drew in a breath and let it go.

“The rest is that I am tired. I am not going to make a virtue of that. Fatigue makes mistakes. It makes hands slow and eyes stupid. It makes you want to believe the patient is fine because you need him to be fine. So I will not let myself believe he is fine. I will let myself believe he is watched. That is all I can promise. Watched.”

Her gaze moved over the table, the instruments, the rags, the blanket, the waxed cloth, the bound shoulders, the pale face.

“I will not sleep while he is in this state. If he holds steady, I may rest in turns later. Not now. Now I sit with him. You do not have to stay if you cannot. If you can stay, stay usefully. Watch his chest. Watch the dressing. Listen. If you hear something, name it. If you see something, name it. If you think nothing is wrong but you feel wrong, say that too. Bodies communicate through the people watching them sometimes. A bad feeling is not evidence, but it is worth checking.”

She reached for the water they had and dampened a clean cloth.

“I am going to wipe his face now. Not because it will save him. Because sweat and blood in the eyes and mouth make panic worse when he wakes. If he wakes and cannot see, he will fight. If he fights, he can tear himself open. So I am cleaning what I can. Small things matter. A dry face. A clear mouth. A blanket in the right place. A hand not pressing where it should not press. These are not miracles, but they are part of keeping a man alive.”

She wiped the man’s forehead with careful strokes, avoiding the dressing, avoiding the worst of the chest.

“The rest is that I do not know if he will remember this. Some men remember every second. Some remember nothing. Some remember pieces: a voice, a hand, a pain, a light, the feeling of being held down. If he remembers you holding him, I hope he understands later that it was not malice. If he never understands, that is still acceptable. Understanding is not required for survival.”

She folded the cloth and set it aside.

“I will tell you what I will not do. I will not pretend I can save everyone. I will not pretend this man is more important than the next one who comes through that flap. He is important because he is here. When the next one comes, that one will be important too. That is how you keep from breaking. You do not carry all of them at once. You carry the one under your hands, and then you carry the next, and then you wash your hands and carry the next. If you try to carry all of them, you will become useless, and uselessness gets people killed.”

Her eyes hardened slightly, not with anger at Wick, but with the old weight of the thing she was describing.

“I have lost people. I will lose people again. Some I lose quickly. Some I lose slowly. Some I lose after thinking I had won. Some I lose because I made a mistake I did not see until too late. Some I lose because there was nothing to do from the start. Some I lose because the war is faster than I am. I do not get used to it in the way people mean when they say that. I get better at working beside it. That is different.”

The man’s breathing eased a little more. Sedge noticed it. She did not relax because of it.

“If he improves, we will still not call him safe. We will call him steadier. Steadier is not safe. Steadier is a direction. He can be steadier for hours and then turn. He can be terrible for hours and then rally. Bodies are not machines. They are weather. They have patterns, but they also have surprises. I respect the patterns. I fear the surprises.”

She checked the bindings once more.

“The rest is that tomorrow, if there is a tomorrow, there will be more work. Cleaning. Changing dressings. Checking shoulders. Watching for fever. Making him drink when it is safe. Keeping him from moving too much. Explaining to him why he cannot be brave yet. If he is lucky, he will be bored and sore. If he is unlucky, he will be feverish and afraid. If he is very unlucky, he will be dead. If he is very lucky, he will live to complain about my bedside manner.”

There was no smile in her face, but something almost human passed through her voice.

“I do not have a good bedside manner. I have a working one.”

She looked down at the patient’s chest.

“I am going to keep talking for a while, because you asked me to, and because it keeps me ordered. But I will not talk to fill the silence with hope. I will talk to keep the facts in line.”

She placed one hand lightly near the dressing again.

“The facts are: both shoulders are reduced. The chest wound is small but leaking. The dressing is vented. The pulse is fast but present. The breathing is shallow but bilateral. The color is gray but not blue. The skin is cold but not dead. The wound is dirty but not yet infected. The man is unconscious but not gone. That is the inventory. It is not much. It is what we have.”

She drew the blanket a little more securely around the patient’s legs.

“The rest is that we will not leave him alone. If he worsens, we will work. If he dies, we will handle him decently. If he lives, we will keep working. There is no version of this where we get to stop feeling the weight of it. There is only the version where we do not let the weight make us careless.”

Her voice dropped.

“I know what it is to hold someone down while they scream. I know what it does to the person holding. It makes you feel like a butcher. It makes you feel like a jailer. It makes you feel like your hands belong to someone else. But if you do it right, if you do it for the right reason, if you do it without enjoying it, it can be part of saving a life. That does not make it clean. Nothing about this is clean. It only makes it necessary.”

She looked at the row of instruments again.

“I will clean what I used. I will boil what can be boiled. I will save what can be saved. I will not waste supplies on sentiment. I will not waste time on guilt. Guilt is a luxury too. It feels important, but it does not set bones or close wounds.”

The man’s breath caught once. Sedge leaned in.

The dressing lifted.

It did not suck.

It settled.

She stayed there, counting under her breath.

“One,” she murmured. “Two. Three. Four.”

Then, to Wick, without looking away:

“The rest is that we wait. We watch. We name what changes. We do not look away because it is ugly. We do not pretend it is not ugly because we are tired. We keep our hands ready. We keep our mouths ready to say what we see. We keep the lamp burning as long as it will burn. And if the lamp goes out, we sit in the dark and listen.”

She checked the man’s lips one more time.

“Still gray,” she said.

Then she checked the dressing.

“Still venting.”

Then she checked the pulse.

“Still beating.”

She let her hand rest near the patient’s chest, not pressing, only present.

“That is the rest,” Sedge said. “Not a promise. Not a story. A list. A watch. A body still deciding. And us, deciding with it.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway's grip tightened on the knife as the splashing behind them grew louder. "Fine," she snapped. "But keep moving." 

She spoke fast, clinical, like reciting a butcher's inventory. "Skin's been stretched over new cartilage—see how it shines? Warper added framework first. Those extra fingers?" A wet crunch echoed through the cellar as the thing found its footing. "Bone grafts, probably from something with too many limbs to begin with. Teeth are stolen—count the different sizes? That's multiple mouths' worth." 

The stairs were close now. Halloway risked a glance back and saw the thing lurching upright, its mismatched limbs flailing as it adjusted to the new shape of itself. The pale lump of teeth split open vertically with a sound like tearing parchment. 

"As for what's underneath?" Halloway shoved Pike toward the stairs. "Nothing human left in the meat of it. Just hunger and whatever instructions the warper carved into its nerves." 

The thing let out a gurgling shriek and lunged. Halloway threw the salt pouch straight into its gaping maw. "Run!"

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway's knife flashed as the thing's bulk forced its way through the ruined door. The wire thrummed between them, smoking where it touched the creature's stretched flesh. 

"Rot and ammonia," she bit out as the first contact made the thing shriek. "That's the smell—like a butcher's floor left in the sun." The creature thrashed, its too-long limbs knocking crockery from the shelves. Halloway sidestepped a flailing claw and yanked the wire tighter. "Beneath the skin? Sinew rearranged. No proper muscle left—just strands knotted around whatever bones the warper jammed in there." 

The wire sawed deeper, sending up curls of greasy smoke. The thing's teeth-cluster gnashed wildly, spraying dark fluid across the floorboards. Halloway ducked under a sweeping limb and drove her knife up beneath what might have once been a ribcage.

With a final, wet shudder, the thing collapsed. Halloway planted a boot on its twitching torso and wrenched her blade free. She didn't wipe the blood off. Not yet. 

"That's the lesson," she said quietly, staring down at the ruin at her feet. The wire had cut clean through the warper's grotesque craftsmanship, revealing hollow spaces where organs should've been. "Flesh doesn't remember what it was. Only what it's been made into." 

She finally looked up at Pike, her expression grim. "Next time? Count the teeth first. Always tells you how hungry it is." 

Outside, something scraped against the kitchen window. Halloway's head snapped toward the sound. 

"And Pike?" She flicked gore from her knife. "We're not done yet."

She stepped away, the clinical lesson concluded.

"But the previous tenant had been using something caustic. Silver nitrate or a concentrated alkali. The creature didn't recognize the danger because it was starving. It absorbed the chemicals into its primary mass, and the reaction started a chain of rapid oxidation. Essentially, it turned its own stomach into a battery of acid."

She stepped back, the water swirling around her ankles. 

"It spent the last hour trying to push the poison out through its skin, which explains the looping jaw and the spinal folds. It was trying to reorganize its anatomy to vent the toxins. It failed. It suffocated on its own chemistry while trying to figure out how to be a different shape."

She looked at the grey fluid still bubbling on the surface of the water and gave a small, clinical shrug.

"It's a biological malfunction. A messy, expensive mistake in evolution. Now," she added, her voice regaining that dry, grim edge, "unless you've developed a sudden passion for autopsy, let's get out of the water before we both start smelling like a wet dog in a chemical spill."

It basically grew a series of needles inside its own chest."

She stepped back, the knife dripping a mixture of violet fluid and grey slime.

"It got as far as basic structural mimicry. It had the shape of a man, the scent of a man, and a few of the parts, but the internal logic was missing. It was a jigsaw puzzle where the pieces had been melted and forced together."

She opened the canister, revealing a thick, caustic paste that smelled of sulfur and concentrated brine. With the probe, she began to slather the substance directly into the open wounds she had carved, pushing the paste deep into the thoracic cavity and layering it over the pseudo-glands.

"This is a stabilizing agent," she noted, the sound of the paste squelching into the flesh. "It doesn't just kill the cells; it fuses them. It turns the organic matter into a sort of inorganic salt. It stops the mimicry by erasing the blueprint."

The mass began to hiss and bubble, the grey fluid turning a sickly, opaque yellow. The creature gave one final, involuntary shudder—a ripple that traveled from the looping jaw down to the folded spine—and then went completely still.

Halloway stepped back, watching as the creature began to harden, its soft, bloated form calcifying into a brittle, chalky husk. In a matter of minutes, it no longer looked like a failed human; it looked like a piece of weathered limestone that had been twisted into a grotesque shape.

"There," she said, her voice devoid of triumph. "Now it's just a rock. A very ugly, very expensive rock."

She wiped the probe clean one last time and turned back toward the stairs, her expression as grim and clinical as when they had first entered the cellar.

"The cleanup is the house owner's problem. I don't do masonry," she remarked, glancing at Pike. "Now, for the love of everything holy, get off those steps and let's find some one-hundred-degree water for your boots."

Halloway didn't answer right away. The silence was the counting kind, not the soft kind — she was watching the hands.

"It was," she said finally. "Recently enough that the hands are still hands. Look at the left one. Five fingers, thumbnail, a scar across two knuckles where a man's been careless with a chisel or a bar fight. Nobody builds hands like that from scratch. And the teeth — you can see them where the jaw's gone slack. Filled molars. Some village dentist earned his supper out of that mouth once. That's a person's paperwork, Pike. You can counterfeit a face. You can't counterfeit a filling."

She let that sit, then sanded nothing off what came next.

"But 'was' is doing the heavy lifting in your question, and I won't lie to you about the weight. People don't swell from the inside. People don't bend a half-turn past spec. And people don't stop breathing on a lazy four-count because they've decided to. Something's been at work in there — wore him like a coat, or turned him, and I've seen both, and here's the honest arithmetic: I have never once told them apart from the outside before it was too late to matter to somebody."

She drew the knife off her knees, slow, the sound of it barely a whisper against the wet.

"So yes. Somebody up the road is missing a husband or a hired man or a son, and has been since before this water rose. That's a grief for later — and I mean that as kindness, not coldness, because grief has killed more hunters than any monster I can name. A crying person stands one step too close. You want to honor him? Then do what I told you. Three steps back, weight on the heels, and *watch*. Because the ones that used to be people hold their dead act better than any animal ever could. But they forget one thing. Always one thing. The breathing. The eyes — dead men's eyes don't track. Or it blinks."

A dry breath of a laugh, entirely without humor.

"Find me the thing it forgot. And if it comes to hunting — you don't touch him. If there's any of that man still in there, the kindest thing we can do is fast. But fast comes after sure."

Halloway didn't turn around. But her shoulders did something that in a lesser woman would have been called a flinch, and her voice came out flat as a headstone.

"I said the stair." A slow breath through the nose, the kind she used on rookies and horses. "Thirty years, one dead partner, and I say *the stair*, and you bring me the lamp." The knife didn't waver. "Fine. The lamp's useful. You've just changed the arithmetic for all three of us, is all — and it noticed before I finished being angry about it."

Because the breathing had started again. Not the lazy four-count. Faster now. Two seconds. One and a half. The ripples around the body were running against each other, interference patterns, the water doing sums of its own.

"Plainly, then, since you've paid for the answer with your ankles." She kept moving forward, slow, blade under the surface. "A man came down into this cellar when it was dry — after wine, after a rat, after an argument with his wife, it never matters which. Something was already down here, and it got into him. Mouth or wound, the result's identical. It didn't kill him. Killing is wasteful. It *ate* him — hollowed him out from the inside over weeks, grew into the space he left behind like a hermit crab in a whelk shell, and kept the parts that do the convincing. The hands. The scar across the knuckles. The teeth." Her jaw tightened. "Because a drowned man gets sympathy, Pike. A drowned man gets *carried*. Up the stairs, into a warm kitchen, set down in front of a wife who's been weeping over him since autumn — and whose guard is all the way down. That's what happened to him, plainly. He stopped being a man sometime before the water rose, and what's wearing him has been down here on a four-count ever since, waiting on somebody sentimental enough to help."

She was four paces off now, close enough that the lamp's light reached past the body — and showed what the flat angle from the stairs had hidden. The swelling wasn't uniform. It was *segmented*, moving under the skin of the torso like a sack of eels, and just under the slack jaw, where a man's throat ought to be, something pulsed that had no business resembling a pulse.

"There it is," Halloway said, almost gently. "Lamp's earning its keep."

The body's left hand closed. All five fingers, one at a time, deliberate as a man counting money.

"It's done pretending," she said, and her voice dropped to something that wasn't for Pike at all — it was the voice she used at the very end, level and final as a ledger closing. "It goes for you, not me. The soft thing, the exit, every time. When it moves — drop the lamp *away* from us, toward the far wall, not toward the water at your feet, and step *backwards*. Not sideways. Backwards."

The jaw opened. Wider than the fillings allowed. Wider than the skull allowed.

"Steady now," Halloway said. "Here it comes."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway looked at Pike for a long moment, and something in her face shifted — not warmth exactly, but the flat satisfaction of a tradeswoman seeing an apprentice ask the right question instead of the comfortable one.

"Good. That's the first question a hunter asks and the last one most people think of." She waded back to the stair, knelt beside the body, and turned back the shirt front with two fingers, the way a tailor checks a lining. The coat stayed over his face. Clinical didn't mean rude. "He's past minding, and you're not past needing. Watch."

She opened the split along the torso with the flat of the knife, no flourish, and talked while she worked — the same tone she'd use pricing grain at market.

"It doesn't start big. What got into him was the length of your finger — a swimmer. Comes up through well water, cellar seep, flood runoff. Gets in through a cut, or a sleeping man's open mouth. One is plenty. And it doesn't rush. That's the part people can't hold onto, so hold onto it: *weeks*. Patience is its whole strategy."

She gestured at the cavity with the knife tip, pointing things out like landmarks.

"Eating order. Gut first — closest to where it lands, easiest meat. Stomach, intestines, then upward. Liver, spleen. Then the lungs. And here's the detail that matters: it doesn't need his lungs. *It breathes for him.* The knot of them works the chest like bellows, and in water like this, they breathe under the body itself — that was your four-count. A drowned man's ribs rising on a lazy count isn't him gasping. It's the tenant airing the coat."

"What it keeps: hands, face, teeth. The convincing parts. What it *replaces*: the muscle. It doesn't discard his muscles, it eats them and threads its own bodies in along the bones, through the tendon sheaths — cables through pulleys. That's why the joints bend past spec. The joints aren't his anymore. The pull comes from whatever angle the tenant wants." She indicated the lines under the skin of the arms, faint as old scars. "And these seams — see them? It thins the skin from inside, along lines, so it can open when it needs to. Young ones disperse through the splits. Which means, yes, some of what poured out of him made the deep water tonight, and that's the next cellar's problem, five years from now. Arithmetic. I never promised it was cheerful arithmetic."

She sat back on her heels, and her voice went to the flat cadence of a field manual.

"Your tells, in order of use. Swelling from the inside, not bloating — bloating is gas and it's even; a colony swells *segmented*, moves like a sack of eels under lamplight held flat. Joints bending wrong. Not floating — dead things float, this holds the floor. And the one that convicts: it plays dead, but it forgets one detail. A twitch it notices itself making. Eyes that track. A blink. Everything dead plays dead differently, everything alive forgets one thing. Find the forgotten thing and you've found your verdict."

"Now the kill, because you'll want it. Under the jaw, where a pulse has no business being — that's the anchor. The first one in, the oldest, the one running the limbs. Put steel through it and the rowing stops. Stab the torso instead and all you do is split the seams and hand the young an exit — which I did, on purpose, because a dispersed colony dies slower than a cornered one. And burn what's left after. Always fire. Water just moves the account somewhere else."

She stood, wiped the knife on her own thigh, and looked at the covered face a moment.

"As for how far it got — how long *he* was still in there, watching. The honest answer is nobody knows, and anyone who tells you different is selling something. Maybe weeks. Maybe he was a passenger in his own coat the whole time. That answer's not for me to pretty up."

She sheathed the knife and started up the stairs, then paused.

"Write all of it down tonight, while the shaking's got you at the table. Fear eats memory first, and this lesson cost a man his name. Waste nothing."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway descended the stairs, stepping over the wet threshold until she stood at the water's edge. The air smelled of cooked meat and wet earth, the steam rising from the center of the room in thin, wavering columns.

She looked down at the mass. It was no longer shaped like a man. It was a mound of blackened fiber, the white sap boiled into a hard, sticky scab. The shoulder she had prodded earlier was gone, reduced to ash.

"It's finished," she said. Her voice didn't change. "Heat breaks the spores. The structure collapses."

She leaned forward, keeping her weight on the balls of her feet. She prodded the center with the tip of her knife. The material collapsed inward, turning to dust under the steel. No movement. No resistance.

"Burned out," she said, straightening up. "The network is severed."

She wiped the blade on her coat and looked at Pike. "Get the lamp. We're not leaving this for later. If there's a root left, it'll find new ground."

She started back up the stairs, waiting for him to follow. "And wipe your boots. I don't want spores in the truck."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway didn't look up. "Good. Stomach's the wrong place for this lesson, but it's the right place to learn it anyway." She set the knife's edge at the collar line, where the coat still covered the face, and worked downward with the same unhurried economy she'd have used dressing a deer.

"Start at the top of the list, because that's the order you'll meet it in. Skin first." She peeled the shirt front wide and turned the flesh toward the lamp with the flat of the blade. "Notice it's *intact*. Not one lesion, not one sore, not a bite mark. That's the first thing that misleads people. You'll find a body like this and call it a drowning, because the skin tells you nothing happened to this man. The skin's not where the story is. The skin is the *book cover.*"

She opened the torso along the seam the thing had tailored, and the smell came up the stair like a second occupant.

"There's your second tell, and you'll never forget it now, which is the point. Sweet. Thick-sweet, like a butcher's bin in August, and under it something like lye — alkaline, clean, wrong. That's the tenant's own chemistry. It digests as it goes and what it leaves behind doesn't rot like a corpse should. A three-month body should stink of putrefaction. This one smells like a tannery. When you smell tannery where you expected rot, you are not standing next to a drowned man." She glanced sideways, dry. "It'll want to come up your throat. Let it. Better out than in — my first mentor said that about whiskey, but it travels."

She widened the opening and held the lamp close with her free hand, angling the light flat the way she had on the water.

"Now the cavity, and I'll give you the inventory straight, because he's past minding and you're not past needing. Gut — gone. Not consumed to the last thread, *gone*, resorbed and rebuilt into lining for the cavity walls, see how smooth it is in there? Like it's been plastered. Liver, spleen, pancreas — gone. Heart—" she reached in, and her hand came back empty, "—gone, and that's the one that should stop you cold, Pike. He hasn't had a heartbeat in months. The chest was worked by the colony, bellows-fashion, exactly as I said. The lungs are still here but they're not lungs anymore, look — thin as paper, emptied, repurposed as *bladders*. Buoyancy and air-scent, near as I can tell. The tenant kept the shape of breathing and threw away the fact of it."

She worked down along the spine, exposing it, and her voice stayed level as a plumb line.

"Muscle — all of it, every sheath, eaten and replaced. What you're seeing threaded along the bones here, these gray cords — that's the tenant. Not worms in him. *Him, made of them.* Bone — untouched. It doesn't eat bone, it needs the scaffolding. Marrow, though—" she scraped the knife tip once against a femur, and it came away dry, "—sucked out like a cook treats a marrow spoon. That's how you date the tenancy, and here's the arithmetic: marrow goes last, and it goes slow. This man's been a coat since before the first frost."

She was quiet for exactly one breath, and then went on, because that was how she handled it.

"And now the part you actually asked for. The anchor." She turned the jaw aside with two fingers, careful as a dentist, and cut along the line she'd stabbed earlier, and lifted out the thing that had been pulsing where a pulse had no business being. She held it in the lamplight on the flat of her knife like a specimen at a lecture.

"Finger-length now. It went in the size of your little fingernail. Blind — no eyes, never had them, doesn't need light. Mouth's a ring, like a lamprey, and inside the ring—" she tilted it, "—teeth it sheds and replaces, which is why you'll sometimes find them in the cavity, tiny, like a fish's. This is the first one in. The settler. Everything else in him was its offspring, budded off over the months, and *this* one ran the limbs. You kill this one first and the rest are just rope." She turned it once more, clinically. "Note the color. The old one's gone dark, almost black. The young are gray-pale. So if you ever open a body and find a pale one — you've got a young colony, weeks old, and the host might not be past saving yet. Find a black one — you're not doing medicine, you're doing cleanup. That distinction has a body count attached to it, historically, so keep it."

She set the specimen down on the stone, well away from the waterline, and cleaned her knife with two strokes.

"Smell the corpse again, now that it's opened." A beat. "Nothing. Or near it — stagnant water and old stone. That's the last tell and the quietest one: the tenant was keeping him *preserved*. It eats him and then it maintains the shopfront. A body this old, opened, should overwhelm you. It doesn't, because the tenant's chemistry was still working right up until I put steel through the landlord. Ten minutes from now it'll smell like what it is. Twenty minutes from now you'll want it burned, and we'll be ahead of the clock."

She stood, knees cracking, and looked down at the opened man with the flat, settled expression of a woman closing an account.

"That's everything, Pike. Nothing left out, nothing prettied. Skin intact, cavity resorbed, heart gone, marrow spent, tenancy measured in seasons. Write it in the order I gave it you — smell, seams, buoyancy, the black anchor — because that's the order a body will hand you the answers in, and you'll only get one pass at reading most of them."

She picked up the specimen with a scrap of cloth, wrapped it like something for a market stall, and pocketed it.

"Evidence. Somebody up the road has been told her husband *ran off*, I'd wager, because that's the story these things always leave behind — a man who walked out one night and never came home. This little black bastard is how we prove different. Now help me lay him straight and get him up these stairs, because I meant what I said about carrying." A dry pause, and the grim humor surfaced one last time, thin as lamplight. "And mind your boots on the way up. I told you I accounted for the big ones. The young went into the water tonight, and I'd hate to write *that* in your notebook posthumously."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway did not say *get back*. Saying it would have been too late to matter and would have taught Pike the wrong lesson — that she'd been wrong to move rather than that moving had consequences to manage.

So she read where Pike stood instead.

"You're in the water," she said, flatly. "You went in without knowing where the edge is. That's done now — don't move again until I tell you where it's safe to stand. Feel for the bottom with your feet, not your hands. Anything that touches your ankles that isn't the floor, you stop."



She came down the steps after that, one at a time, lamp held out ahead of her, feeling each step before committing to it. The water took her to mid-calf. Cold, but cold wasn't information.

When she was close enough, she crouched — carefully, keeping her balance — and looked.

The plain version.

"It was a person," she said. "Recently. The cloth is a shirt — torn, not cut, which means it came off against something rather than being taken off by choice." She pointed with two fingers, not touching. "The reversed limb is broken, not jointed wrong by nature — see how the forearm sits? Someone or something bent it past where it stops. The extended limb isn't longer than it should be. It's *dislocated* at the shoulder and pulled straight. That's why it looks wrong."

A pause. She let the lamp play over the waterline where the torso would be.

"No head above water. That means either the neck failed and it's separated, or the head's under and the water's holding it there." She said it without ceremony. "I can't tell you what *happened* yet because I can't see the torso and I'm not going to turn it over in standing water where I can't see what's underneath it."

She looked at Pike.

"But I can tell you what wasn't natural. Three injuries, none of them defensive. Nobody fights like that. Something did this *to* it — systematically, limb by limb. That's not an animal feeding. That's an order of operations."

She straightened up slowly.

"Now you've seen it plainly. Tell me what you want to do next."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway took the lamp out of Pike's hands — gently, the way you'd take a bird off a nervous branch — and set it on the step beside the little row of things Pike had laid out from the dead man's pockets. She looked at them the way she looked at everything: like a ledger.

"Right. Let's read him, then."

She picked up the billfold first. Leather gone stiff as board, but the waxed hide had done its work. She opened it with two fingers and turned it to the light.

"Coins. Three, and look — *still in the pocket.* That's a sentence in itself. A robber takes the money. A deserter takes the money. The tenant doesn't spend, Pike — it never once needed a coin, and it never thought to check. The money outlived the man. That tells you nobody's been through him, which tells you nobody ever found him, which tells you nobody ever came looking down here." She set the billfold aside. "Hold onto that. It matters in about an hour."

Then the paper. Folded small, gone soft as wet leaf, and she opened it with the patience of a woman handling scripture that had been through weather. Most of it was pulp. But the lamp caught one line in a woman's hand, the ink bled but legible:

*...come home before the lamp burns low. — M.*

Halloway read it twice. Her jaw did the thing it did.

"There's the wife. 'M.'" She folded the scrap with more care than she'd shown the knife. "She wrote him a note about a lamp. And I'd wager the windowsill upstairs has a lamp on it with the wick burned down to the glass, because that's what a woman does when her husband doesn't come home — she lights it, and she keeps lighting it, until the oil runs out and she can't afford more." A pause. "We'll check. I don't guess about widows."

Then the last thing. She picked it off the step and turned it in the light: a small wooden bird, waterlogged, one wing carved and sanded fine, the other still rough blank. A wren.

"Half-finished," she said. "In his pocket, not his workshop. That's not stock, that's a *gift.* He was carrying it on him. Working it in the evenings, maybe, wherever he sat." She held it a moment longer than the clinical required, then wrapped it in the same cloth she'd used for the black anchor and put it away. "That's hers. It goes to her with everything else."

Last, the chisel. She turned the horn handle to the light, and there, struck deep with a heated punch, was the mark: **T. B.**

"Carpenters strike their tools like farmers brand cattle," she said. "T-something, B-something. A joiner, by the work on that stair. We'll ask the valley." She stood, knees cracking, and looked down at the covered shape of the man. "That's his autobiography, then, read whole. He was careful with his tools and careless with his knuckles, he kept his wife's notes, he carried a bird in his pocket, and he pegged a stair tread so it'd outlast him." She picked up the lamp. "It did. Now let's go meet the rest of the book."

---

They carried him up the stairs he'd mended. Halloway took the shoulders and made Pike take the ankles, because "you'll want to know what a dead man weighs, and you'll want to learn it on a friendless one, not a friend." He came up lighter than a man should, and she said nothing about it, which was its own kind of saying.

The house above was cold and clean and empty. Dust on the table. Two chairs, one pushed in, one pulled out at an angle nobody had bothered to straighten since autumn. And on the front windowsill, exactly where she'd called it: a lamp, cold, the wick burned down to a black curl against the glass.

Halloway stood in the middle of the room and read it the way she'd read the cellar.

"She left after the oil ran out. Went to kin, most like — you don't stay in a house where a man vanished, because the house keeps *asking* you where he is." She set the lamp down on the table. "We lay him out in the yard. Not on the table. She'll eat at that table someday, God willing, and I won't have put him on it."

---

There was a woodpile behind the house, and it was a carpenter's woodpile — seasoned oak offcuts, stacked and stickered with the same discipline as the stair tread. Halloway built the pyre herself, crosshatched, proper, the way you'd build it if the man inside had spent his life making things hold and you meant to make his last fire do the same.

"Oak burns hot and slow," she said, working. "He'd approve of the fuel economy. That's not a joke, Pike. Well. It's a bit of a joke."

She put the lamp oil across the body, and the seams too, every one she'd found — because fire was the whole doctrine, and water just moved the account somewhere else. Then she stood back and gave Pike the match.

"You opened his pockets. You get the match. That's how the arithmetic of this trade works — the reading and the writing are the same job."

The fire took him at dusk and Halloway stood watch the whole night, because that was the trade too. She didn't sing, didn't speak over it. She sat on the woodpile's remaining half with her knife across her knees and counted, sometimes aloud, sometimes not, and near dawn she said, to the fire, "There. Paid in full," and that was the entire eulogy.

At first light there were bones, and she raked them from the ash with two green sticks, and wrapped them in the dead man's own bedsheet, straight and square as a parcel. She put the chisel and the wren and the scrap of note on top.

"Now the last leg," she said. "And this is the one that kills more hunters than anything with teeth, so mind me. We're walking up to a woman with her husband's bones, and everything you feel about that is correct, and none of it gets to be on your face when she opens the door. Grief has killed more hunters than monsters. A crying person stands one step too close. We do our grieving after."

---

The village had a smithy, and smiths know everything, and the smith knew this: *Tomas Brooke, joiner. Went off before Martinmas, they said. Wife's Maren, at her sister's — the cottage by the mill.*

The sister opened the door, saw the parcel, and made a sound like a floor giving way, and then Maren Brooke came to the door herself, and Halloway took off her hat, which she had not done for king or clergy in thirty years.

"Maren Brooke. I've brought your husband home."

She gave it to her plain, the way she'd promised Pike she gave everything: the stair, the cut hand, the seep water, the weeks. She gave her the locked room honestly — "He was gone before the first frost. He never knew the water, and he never knew the being carried. Whatever walked after, it wasn't him, and it never was him again" — and Maren listened standing up, one hand on the doorframe, and asked only one question, which was, "Did he finish the stair?" and when Halloway said *he did, and it held us all night,* the woman nodded like a person settling an account of her own, and then she wept, and Halloway stood one respectful step back and let her.

The wren broke her. The one finished wing. She held it against her chest and sat down on the floor in the doorway and that was fine, that was allowed, that step wasn't Halloway's to stand too close to.

When Maren could speak again, Halloway gave her the last of the arithmetic, no varnish on it: the young ones loose in the cellar water, five years to the next cellar, fire now or a sealed door and a chalked warning and someone else's problem in a generation.

"Your house, your call. I'll not burn a widow's home without her say."

Maren looked at her for a long moment. Then she got up, and took the lamp off her sister's sill — her own lamp, the one she'd carried to the mill cottage and kept lighting anyway — and said, "He built that house for me. It's done its work. It can do one more."

They burned it at dusk. The fire took the house, and the floors fell in, and the cellar water boiled in the dark under the ruin, and Halloway stood at the fence line with her hat in her hand and said nothing at all for a long while.

Then she put the hat back on, and looked at the burning house, and the grim humor surfaced, quiet as it ever got.

"Note the arithmetic, Pike. She lit that lamp every night for a season, waiting for him to come home. Tonight she finally used it to make sure nothing else ever wears him out the door." She turned from the fire, and the fire lit half her face. "Kindness on the chance it's needed. You don't get to know if it was. You do it anyway."

She started down the road toward the next valley.

"Write that down. And walk in the middle of the road — I told you I make no promises about the little ones, and we're crossing three streams before morning."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
"Right question," Halloway said. "Wrong order of operations. You've got the shape. Now you want identity. That's natural, but it's backwards." She tilted the lamp a fraction of a degree — enough to change what the light fell on, not enough to signal approach. "Identity comes after you know where the edges are. Identity is how people get sloppy."

But she looked. Of course she looked. Thirty years didn't kill curiosity; it just ranked it below survival.



The light raked across the water and found the straight limb again. Too long — she'd give Pike that. If it was a forearm, it was a forearm on something taller than a person, and the joints were set wrong for it to be a trick of the water. The reversed limb she studied longer. Elbows bent backward in humans were broken things, and broken things bled, and the water around it was dark but not the *right* dark.

"Clothing," she said. "Look for clothing. If whatever's out there was a person recently, there'd be something human — a boot, a belt, a sleeve, *something* that didn't grow there. Things that are born that shape don't wear things."

She let the lamp drift back to the body.

"What I can tell you: the proportions aren't right for a person. Too long in the limb. Wrong at the joint." A pause. "What I can't tell you is whether something *became* that. Which is why we're still standing here."

The second ripple had not repeated. That didn't make her comfortable. That made her watchful.

"Your gut's been wrong yet?" she asked. Not as a challenge — she genuinely wanted to know. Gut was data too, if you knew how to read it.

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway drew the knife along the seam of the shirt with the patience of someone opening a letter they already knew the contents of. The fabric split along the thread rather than the blade — she'd been cutting the stitch, not the cloth. Stupid to dull a blade on cotton.

"Closer with the lamp," she said. "Not closer with you. Lamp only."

She peeled the shirt back from the reversed forearm and held it open like a page.

The skin underneath was wrong before it was damaged. That was the first thing — wrong before the break, which meant the break wasn't the origin. The forearm was too smooth. Not smooth as in unblemished, smooth as in *uniform*. No hair, no pores, no freckling or scarring or the thousand small failures that a person accumulates over a life. It looked like something made from one material rather than assembled from many.

"Skin's wrong," she said. "See it? Not injured — wrong from the start. No hair, no marks. Whatever this was wearing before it was a person, it was wearing it as skin."

She moved the light down to the break itself.

The elbow had separated backward — the olecranon process forced through skin that should have held it. Around the wound, the tissue was dark but not bleeding. Not *anymore*. The wound had been made and the body had stopped responding to it, which meant the cardiovascular system had shut down at some point between the injury and now. She pressed two fingers above the wound, not touching the exposed joint, feeling for the firmness of muscle that hadn't yet begun its work.

"Smell," she said. "Come up when I tell you to and don't you dare do it early."

She leaned in first herself. The water had its own smell — standing water, mineral, faintly sweet where the cellar floor was brick and old. Underneath it, something else. Not putrefaction. Putrefaction had a specific architecture: it built from the gut outward and announced itself early and loud. This was wrong in a different direction. Acrid, almost metallic, with an undertone she recognized from situations she didn't want to describe to Pike on a first night.

"Copper and something like wet slate," she said, pulling back. "That's not rot. Rot comes later. That's whatever replaced what was inside him, still reacting with the air." She paused. "Smell it now if you're going to."

She waited, then nodded as Pike presumably did whatever Pike did.

"记住 that smell," she said in English, switching back without apology. "记 sorry — remember it. That's the smell of the thing before it's had time to become a corpse. In a week, rot takes over and you lose it. But if you smell that in a cellar again, you know something *changed* and it was recent."



She cut further down the arm, exposing the forearm to the wrist. The dislocation at the shoulder was higher — she'd need to cut the sleeve entirely off for that, and the torso still lay under water.

"There's no bruising," she said. "That's the detail I want you to hold onto. A break in a living person bruises — blood leaves the vessels, tissue swells, the color tells you the timing. This wound has no bruising at any margin. Which means either the body had no blood left when the break was made, or..." She trailed off, examining the exposed joint with the lamp held at an angle that flattened the shadows. "Or what's in there isn't blood."

The joint cavity was visible. She angled the light.

Inside, where marrow should have been — white and dense and identifiable — there was a void. Not hollow, not empty. Filled with something dark and granular that shifted when the water lapped against the arm, the way wet sand shifts.

"That's what's under the skin," she said. She kept her voice level because level was the only way to say it. "Where the marrow should be, there's something else. It's been there long enough to fill the cavity completely — the bone isn't hollow anymore. It's packed." She paused. "Whatever was inside him when this was made, it didn't take the bones. It *inhabited* them."

She cut one more inch, found the wrist, and stopped.

"That's as far as I go tonight." She sheathed the knife. "What I know now that I didn't an hour ago: the thing wearing this body wasn't born into it. The skin was wrong before the injury. The break had no bruising. The marrow is replaced with something that responds to water movement. And the smell — that smell — is chemical, not biological, which means the thing underneath is still *doing* something even though the body stopped moving."

She sat back on her heels and wiped her hands on her trousers, which accomplished nothing except the ritual of it.

"Your gut said the thing isn't done. Here's what I'd add to that." She looked at Pike. "It's not that the thing isn't done. It's that the thing is still *in there*. The body stopped, but whatever packed the bones didn't get the memo." She let the lamp hiss. "So when we come back — and we are coming back — we don't bring a stretcher. We bring fire."

She stood, knees cracking, and offered Pike a hand up the last two steps without ceremony.

"Anything else you need to know while we're still close enough to know it? Because after this we're going upstairs, and I'm going to want a drink that isn't water from a cellar with something in it."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway looked at the thing again — not with fresh eyes, because she'd already done her seeing, but with the specific attention of someone checking a box she'd hoped to leave blank.

"Recently, no," she said. "There's no swelling. No gas. The water's clean around it, or as clean as cellar water gets. If this were a person who'd died this week, the water would be doing things it isn't doing."



She let that sit for a moment.

"Waxy like that, though — that's soft tissue that's been *worked*. Something's taken it apart and put it back. The joints your eye caught, those aren't joints. Those are seams. Whoever — whatever — built this thing didn't have the bones right, so it's folding where it shouldn't, and it's stiff where it should flex."

She crouched slightly, bringing the lamp lower so the light hit the waterline. The reflection trembled.

"Was it a person once? Maybe. Long enough ago that the shape's worn off. But I'll tell you what I *can* tell you." She paused, and her mouth did something that wasn't quite a smile. "It's not dead. It's just finished."

She straightened up and looked at Pike sidelong.

"So. Floor's yours. What do we do with a thing that isn't dead and isn't moving? Think about it, because I'd rather you get it wrong in words than wrong with your hands."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway stopped on the third step from the top and stood there, water streaming off her trousers, lamp held steady at her side. She didn't turn around yet.

"You want to know what's under the skin," she said. "That's the right question. I'm going to tell you what I can see and what I can't, and I need you to hear both parts equally."



She turned then, leaning against the wall, and set the lamp on the step above her so both her hands were free. She held up one finger.

"Dislocated shoulder, pulled straight. That took force in a direction — someone grabbed the arm and *extended* it. Not a flail, not a fall. A grip. Which means the thing that did this has hands, or appendages that function like hands, and enough strength to separate a shoulder joint cleanly without tearing the arm off at the socket. That's controlled force." Second finger. "Forearm broken backward at the elbow. Same thing — controlled, specific, *past* the natural stopping point. A predator feeding doesn't bend arms. A person breaking someone's arm for compliance bends it that far. This wasn't feeding. This was *dismantling*."



Third finger. "Three points of damage, limb by limb, each one isolated. No crush injuries, no drag marks along the skin I can see, no tearing of flesh. If something was eating him, you'd see it in the limbs first — they're the most exposed. There's no evidence of that." A pause. "What there *is* evidence of is someone — something — working through him methodically. Joint by joint. Which means at some point he was held still enough for that to happen, which means either he was dead before it started or he was restrained. Both options are worth knowing."

She held up a fourth finger and then lowered it.

"That's what I can see. Now the part where I stop."

She picked up the lamp. "What's under the skin — what it *took*, how far it got — I can't answer from here. That information is in the torso, and the torso's under the water with the head. Until I get eyes on the chest and the abdomen, I'm giving you inference, not fact. And inference is how people get killed."

She began climbing the rest of the steps.

"But here's what thirty years has taught me about things that take things." She paused at the top, turned back. "Whatever it was doing to him, it started with the limbs and worked inward. Limbs first means it wasn't interested in the organs yet. Organs come second — they're what you take when you're *hungry*. Limbs come first when you're either restraining or when you're *taking the arms for something*." She let that sit. "If it had finished, we wouldn't be looking at a body with a shirt still on it. It got interrupted, or it got full, or it got scared."

She stepped onto dry ground and wrung water from her sleeve with clinical disinterest.

"So when you meet another one — and you might — what you know is this: it grabs, it extends, it breaks, it works in order, and it stops before the torso. That tells you it can be interrupted. That tells you it has a sequence. And things with sequences can be disrupted at the wrong step."

She looked at Pike steadily.

"Now your gut. What's it saying?"

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway leaned against the wall opposite, arms crossed, and looked at Pike sitting there with the lamp in her hands — not doing anything with it, just holding it the way people hold things when their hands need a job that isn't thinking.

"Finish it," Halloway repeated. "You want the whole thing. Not the parts I've been giving you in order. The whole thing, the way I'd write it up if anyone ever asked me to write things up."

She looked at the cellar door. Looked back at Pike.

"Right. Sit with it, then."

She slid down the wall until she was sitting too, back against stone, and folded her hands in her lap with the air of someone opening a file they'd rather not open.

"Full account. I'll tell you what I saw, what I didn't, what I've inferred, and where the line is between the three. You stop me if you need me to say something again. You stop me if something doesn't make sense. And you *don't* stop me because it's unpleasant, because you asked for it and I'm going to give it to you properly."



She took a breath.

"First: the body. Male, based on the bone structure I could see at the wrists and what the shirt tells me about shoulder breadth. Broad-shouldered, which means whatever got him had to work against mass. Age is difficult — the skin was wrong from the start, so I can't use it. Bone density suggests somewhere between thirty and fifty, but I'm guessing. I'll know more when I can get to the hips, which are under the water." A pause. "Height I can't tell you either, because one arm's pulled out of socket and the other's bent the wrong way, and neither of those gives you a reliable line to measure against."

"Noted and moving on."

"The injuries. Three, all in the upper limbs, none of them defensive — no wounds on the forearms that would indicate blocking, no scraped knuckles, nothing that says he raised his hands to protect himself. Which tells me one of two things: either it happened too fast for him to react, or he was already compromised when it started. Paralyzed, drugged, unconscious — something. A man with a broken shoulder and a shattered elbow would have marks on his hands from fighting back unless he *couldn't* fight back. There are no such marks. So he couldn't."



She let that sit.

"Dislocation at the right shoulder. The humeral head was forced anteriorly and inferiorly — out the front and down. That's what happens when someone grabs an arm and pulls it straight past its range, which means the thing that did this was standing in front of him, facing him, gripping his arm with both its hands or whatever it has. It wasn't behind him. It wasn't ambushing from the side. It was *facing him* when it did this."

Halloway unfolded one hand and held it up, fingers spread.

"Break at the right elbow. Olecranon forced posteriorly — the bone pushed through the back of the joint until the skin gave way. The break itself is clean, which means it was fast. A slow break tears. A fast break snaps. This was fast. Which means once it had the arm where it wanted it, it bent it in one motion. No hesitation. No adjustment. It knew exactly how far to go and it went there." She closed her hand. "That's not something that's learning. That's something that's practiced. Or something that's built to do exactly that."

"Left arm was next, if we're reading the order of operations from the extremities inward. The skin there was intact where I could see it, but the musculature had a density to it that was wrong — too uniform, the way the forearm on the right was too smooth. And beneath that skin, at the wrist, I could see where the tissue had a faint pattern to it. Almost like grain. Like wood. Like something that had a structure and direction to it rather than the random mess of muscle and fat you'd find in an arm."

"I didn't open that one. You should know that. I stopped at the wrist on the right arm and I didn't cut anything on the left. What I'm telling you about the left arm is from sight and touch — pressing on it through the skin. That's inference, not observation. I'm flagging it because you asked me not to leave anything out, and one of the things I could leave out is the part where I'm not sure."

"The torso. Still under the water. I could see the outline — ribs, the suggestion of a sternum, the flat plane of the abdomen — but the water distorted it enough that I couldn't commit to any detail. The head is beneath the surface as well. Based on the position of the shoulders and the angle of the visible limbs, I'd estimate the torso is lying face-down, which is why we can't see the head — it's under the body, not beside it."

"That matters for a reason I don't love. If the face is down and the head is beneath the body, then whatever was on his face or in his mouth is pressed against the cellar floor. If there's something *in* his mouth — something that got in, or something that was put in — it's been sealed against brick for however long he's been down here, which means whatever is inside him that likes a sealed dark space has been in its ideal conditions. I don't know if there's anything in his mouth. I'm telling you it's a possibility because you asked for everything and I'm including the possibilities alongside the facts."

She shifted her back against the wall. Stone was unforgiving after the first few minutes.

"Smell. I described it earlier but you asked me to finish, so I'll go deeper." She paused, choosing words with the care of someone laying out tools. "The primary note is copper. Not iron — people say iron when they mean blood, but this wasn't blood. Blood has a specific smell when it's been in contact with air for more than a few hours — it goes sweet, then sharp, then it becomes recognizable as decay. This was sharper than blood. Brighter. Like a coin in your mouth."

"Underneath the copper: wet slate. Mineral. The kind of smell you get from a cave where water has been moving over stone for a thousand years. That's the cellar's smell, but *concentrated* — as though the body were producing it rather than sitting in it. Which means whatever's packed into those bones is actively reacting. Not decaying. Not breaking down. *Reacting*. Doing chemistry. The way a hot coal does chemistry when it sits in open air."

"And underneath *both* of those — this is the part that made me decide we come back with fire rather than a shovel — there was something I've smelled exactly four times in thirty years. I'm not going to tell you what the four times were because they're not relevant and it'll take too long, but I'll tell you what it smelled like because you asked. It was sweet. Not rot-sweet. Not fruit-sweet. Sweet the way a flower is sweet — the smell of something that wants to attract. Something that was *calling*."



Halloway stopped talking. Looked at Pike. Looked at the lamp in Pike's hands, at the steady light of it, and seemed to find some reassurance in the fact that it was still just a lamp.

"I don't know what called what," she said. "I don't know if the smell was meant for something in the cellar or something above it or something that was supposed to come *through* the cellar. I only know that four times in my career, when I've smelled that particular chemical sweetness coming from something that was supposed to be dead, there was a second one. Not a second incident — a second *body*. A second thing in a state of being not-quite-right. Because whatever packs the bones doesn't do it alone. It has company. Or it sends for company."

She held up a hand.

"That's inference. Strong inference, but inference. I'm giving you the fact and the read separately because you asked me not to blur them."

"The things I don't know. I'll list them so you have the shape of the gap." She ticked them off. "One: what's in the torso. Two: whether the head is intact. Three: what's under the water besides the body — I felt the cellar floor with my feet the entire time and it was brick and silt, nothing else, but my feet only cover so much area. Four: whether what's packed into the marrow is uniform throughout the skeleton or localized to the limbs I could feel. Five: how long the body's been in the water — no insect activity I could see, which in a cellar this cold and wet could mean days or could mean weeks. Six: who this was, and what they were doing in a cellar that somebody dug for a reason I haven't been told."

She stopped ticking.

"And seven — the one I've been sitting with since the first ripple, the one that made me keep the lamp at a distance instead of walking straight in. The thing that's under the water that isn't the body. I saw it once. It moved once. It's been still for..." She checked. "...close to an hour now. That stillness could mean it left. That stillness could mean it's waiting. What I *will* tell you is that I've been watching the far end of the cellar for the last twenty minutes while I talked to you, and the water surface at the far end is not the same as the water surface at the near end. Near end: still. Far end: a slight, continuous vibration I can feel in the steps when I press my palm flat against them. Something is humming down there. Not moving — *humming*. Like a frequency. Like something vibrating at a speed too fast to see and too slow to hear."
