rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway made a short, dry sound, not quite a laugh and not at all warm.

“Plainly,” she said. “Plainly is what people ask for when they want me to take the teeth out of the story. I won’t.”

Her eyes stayed on the edge of the dark shape, where the still water met the pale suggestion of form. The pinch of salt, iron, and bell-ash remained between her fingers, poised and small.

“If I were making a report to a magistrate with weak nerves,” she said, “I’d say a person died, the body was placed in the cellar, and the flood has preserved it badly. If I were making a report to someone who intends to live through the night, I’d say the body was not merely placed there. It was arranged.”

She gave the faintest nod toward the far end of the cellar.

“The water should have done something by now. A body in water makes a bargain with the water. It swells, it leaks, it floats, it settles, it loses its dignity in stages. This has done none of those things. The surface is too calm. The shape is too compact. The shoulders are raised because something underneath has been forced upward, or broken back, or folded where it should not fold. The head is absent because it was removed, hidden, or never completed.”

Her voice stayed level, practical, almost offended by the inefficiency of the thing.

“Recently? Yes, I’d say recently. Not fresh in the honest sense. Not bleeding, not newly dead in a way that would stain the water. But recent enough that the shape still remembers having been a body. That’s why your eye keeps catching on it. It has the grammar of a person, but the syntax is wrong.”

Then she opened her fingers a fraction.

The pinch fell.

It struck the water without a splash. That was the first bad thing. The second was that the grains did not scatter. They lay on the surface like tiny chips of bone, motionless, then slid inward a finger’s width toward the shape without making the smallest ripple.

Halloway’s expression did not change, but her shoulders settled.

“There,” she said. “The whole surface is connected.”

She closed the paper twist carefully, though she did not put it away.

“What happened to it, plainly? Someone died. Likely by ordinary means first—struck, strangled, stabbed, drowned, frightened to death, it doesn’t matter yet. Then the body was brought here, or the body was found here, and something else got to work on it. Not a butcher. A butcher leaves honest pieces. This was someone, or something, trying to make a body into a container.”

The lamp flame leaned again, though no draft had passed them.

“The head may have been taken because heads are where people look for intention. No face, and you can’t tell if it’s pleading. No face, and you can’t tell if it’s laughing. No face, and you start lending it your own expressions. That’s dangerous. Sentiment gets people killed.”

She shifted her weight just enough to keep the cellar stairs between them and the water.

“It stopped moving because it knows we’re here. It may not know our names, but it knows light, sound, and fear. It’s deciding whether we’re useful. If it stays still, we may come closer. If it moves a little, we may stay longer. If it moves too much, we may run, and running is often when things learn exactly how fast they need to be.”

Her mouth tightened.

“So, plainly: it was probably a person once. It has been revised. The water is either its tool, its nest, or its body. And we are currently standing near enough to be considered a suggestion.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway’s mouth flattened, not in distaste, but in the way of a woman being asked to hand over a tool she knew would cut the person holding it.

“Exactly is not mine to give,” she said. “I’ll give you likely. Likely is what keeps you alive when exactly gets you killed.”

She kept the lamp low and her body angled toward the stairs. The dark shape at the far end of the cellar had not moved, but the stillness around it seemed to have thickened, as if the air itself had decided to hold its breath.

“If it was a man,” Halloway said, “and I’ll grant you that for the sake of grammar, then the first thing to understand is that the body was probably dead before the real work began. Not necessarily long before. Minutes, perhaps. Enough that the blood had stopped making decisions. Enough that the thing inside could take the frame without being argued with by a living heart.”

Her eyes tracked the high, wrong line of the shoulders.

“The outer skin is mostly intact. That’s deliberate. It wanted a container. You don’t keep the skin if you only want meat. You keep it because skin holds shape. Skin makes people hesitate. Skin makes you think there’s still somebody in there.”

She gave the faintest nod toward the waterline.

“Under it, I’d say the ordinary furniture has been removed or dissolved. Lungs, heart, gut—gone, or reduced to something no longer useful as organs. There’s no bloat. No purge. No honest rot. That means it either consumed what it didn’t need, or it pushed it out through some opening we can’t see and replaced it with itself.”

The lamp flame gave a small, uneasy lean. Halloway did not follow it with her eyes. She kept her gaze on the shape.

“What’s under the skin now is not muscle in the way you understand muscle. It may be strands. Threads. Wet cord. Something that can tighten, loosen, and imitate the pull of sinew without needing bones to anchor to. If you cut it, it would probably part like wet hair, then close again. If you pressed it, it would press back.”

Her voice stayed flat, surgical, stripped of comfort.

“The bones are the next problem. Some may still be there, but not in their proper stations. Look at the shoulders. Too high. Too sharp. That suggests the collarbones have been forced upward, or the shoulder blades have been turned inside the frame to make hooks. It doesn’t need the skeleton to walk the way a man walks. It needs the skeleton to suggest a man. That’s why the shape is close enough to fool you at a distance and wrong enough to make your stomach rebel.”

She paused just long enough to let the cellar’s silence press against the words.

“The three limbs you see are likely three different mistakes. One may be the original arm, or what’s left of it. One may be a limb made from the body’s own lining, turned outward and stiffened. The third may be folded under, or growing from the torso, or only pretending to be separate. Things like this don’t obey number. They obey need. If it wanted to brace itself, it made a brace. If it wanted to reach, it made a reach. If it wanted to look human, it kept enough human parts to make you feel guilty for suspecting otherwise.”

A thin, humorless line touched her mouth.

“The head is the clearest thing it took. If the head was removed cleanly, we’d see a cut. If it was torn, we’d see ragged tissue. From here, the neck looks more closed than severed. Pinched. Drawn in. Like the mouth of a sack after the contents have been shifted.”

She let that sit for a moment.

“It may have taken the head because the head is where identity collects. Eyes, mouth, voice, expression. Those are tools for dealing with people. If it doesn’t yet know how to use them, or if it lost them in the making, it may have withdrawn them rather than present a bad copy. A missing head is less dangerous than a wrong face. A wrong face makes you call out. A missing head makes you step back. It may have chosen the better option.”

Her thumb brushed the pocket where the paper twist rested, then stilled.

“How far it got? Far enough to use the torso. Far enough to move limbs. Far enough to settle into the water and make the water behave like part of it. Not far enough to finish. That’s the important part. It still lacks a face. It still lacks honest weight. It still has to borrow from us if it wants to complete the shape.”

Halloway’s voice lowered, not with fear, but with the kind of precision that came from having seen too many things finish themselves in other people’s presence.

“If I had to put it plainly for another encounter, I’d say this: it hollows the dead and wears them as a draft. It takes what it needs for structure and leaves what it needs for deception. It may remove the organs because they decay, or because they get in the way, or because it has no use for wet, stupid meat. It may keep the skin because skin is persuasive. It may keep the hands because hands can grasp. It may leave the face for last because faces are difficult, and a bad face is a confession.”

She gave the water one last, unimpressed look.

“If you meet another, don’t look for the person. Look for the errors. Shoulders too high. Joints bending where they should brace. Water too still around the body. No insects, if there should be insects. No smell, if there should be a smell. Or the wrong smell—sweet, mineral, like old rain in a closed cup. If the skin moves without the bones beneath it, don’t wait to see what the bones are for.”

Her jaw set.

“If it speaks, don’t answer. If it cries, don’t pity it. If it uses a voice you know, treat that as theft, not recognition. If it reaches, don’t let it touch you. If it gets under your skin, don’t try to cut it out with a kitchen knife and a prayer. Burn the limb if you can. Burn the whole thing if you must. Better one body lost than two bodies made.”

The faint, grim smile returned for only a moment.

“And if you find one that has finished its face, Pike, don’t admire the workmanship. That means it has had enough practice to get it right.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway had already made the first cut by the time the words left Pike’s mouth, a shallow, deliberate line across the pale rise that might once have passed for a shoulder. The blade was not long, but it was sharp, and she used it the way she used everything: without ceremony.

The skin parted wrong.

It did not split like flesh. It separated like waxed cloth over wet cord. There was no fat beneath it, no yellow give, no honest red. Only a slick, gray-white membrane stretched tight over something arranged too neatly to be anatomy.

“No blood,” Halloway said. “That’s the first thing you remember. A body used recently will still leak somewhere. Bruise, seep, stain. This one’s been emptied or sealed from the inside.”

She drew the blade a little farther, not deep, only enough to lift the outer layer. The lamp light caught the underside of the skin. It looked too smooth there, almost polished, as if it had been scraped clean and then pressed back into service.

“Under the skin, there’s another skin,” she said. “A caul, or something like it. That’s what’s holding the shape together. Cut the outside and the inside still keeps the outline. That’s why it can move without bones doing all the work.”

The second layer gave with a faint, fibrous resistance, like wet hair pulled through a narrow ring. The smell rose then.

Halloway did not recoil. She only narrowed her eyes.

“There,” she said. “That smell. Not rot. If it were rot, I’d trust it more. Rot is honest. This is preservation.”

It was cold and faintly sweet, like old rain standing in a closed room. Under that, there was a mineral sharpness, copper without blood, and something else beneath both: tallow, or wax, or the ghost of a lamp just blown out. It did not smell like a cellar. It did not smell like a corpse. It smelled like a place where a corpse had been used as a pattern.

“No bowels,” she went on. “No purge. No stomach contents. That means the gut was taken early, or dissolved, or folded into whatever this is. The chest cavity’s not empty, though. Look past the membrane. It’s lined.”

Inside the opened seam, thin strands lay packed together in pale coils. They were not muscle. They were too even, too pale, too wetly braided. Some were slack. Some were drawn tight. They crossed one another in angles that suggested use rather than growth, like rigging inside a sack made to imitate a torso.

“Threads,” Halloway said. “Or cords. Wet sinew without the bone to justify it. If you cut one, it contracts. Not because it feels pain. Because it keeps tension.”

She touched the flat of the blade to one strand and pressed.

It tightened at once.

The shape at the far end shifted by less than a breath. The water around it finally remembered itself and made a small, oily ripple.

Halloway’s mouth thinned.

“There,” she said. “It can keep the surface still until you touch the inner work. That’s the second lesson. The outside lies. The inside reports.”

She eased the blade back but did not withdraw it.

“The bones are partial. Some are still human. The ribs, most of them, are in place, though the lower ones have been bent inward. Not broken outward the way a struggle or a fall would do. Pulled in. Made into a cage for whatever’s sitting in the chest instead of a heart.”

The blade moved again, careful now, tracing the line where the cords gathered beneath the sternum.

“There’s no heart,” she said. “No lungs. No liver. Nothing that would demand oxygen or make a mess. What’s in the middle is a knot. A core. Call it what you like. It’s where the strands meet. It’s not beating, but it is adjusting. Small pulls. Small slackening. It’s balancing itself against the water.”

Her voice stayed flat, almost tedious, as if she were reading inventory from a drowned storeroom.

“The shoulders were the first obvious cheat. The collarbones have been forced up. The shoulder blades are turned wrong. It doesn’t need them to lift arms the way a man lifts arms. It uses them as anchors. Hooks. Points to hang the shape from.”

She cut another careful inch along the pale mass, nearer where one of the visible limbs folded into the body.

“This one,” she said, “is probably the original arm. Or part of it. The bone’s there, but the joints have been packed with cord. It won’t bend like a living arm. It’ll bend like a wet rope being asked to imitate one.”

She indicated another fold without pointing.

“That second thing you counted as a limb isn’t. It’s a flap of skin stiffened inside. A brace, maybe. Or a lure. If it wanted to look like an arm reaching, it could make that move. If it wanted to look like a man half-drowned and begging, it could make that too.”

Her eyes went to the third shape, darker and less defined where it curved beneath the waterline.

“The third is the worst of the three. That one’s not finished. It may be a leg, or a tail, or a root. It’s anchored lower. That’s why the body sits so still. It’s not resting. It’s attached.”

The blade lifted a little more of the outer skin. Beneath it, the gray-white caul seemed to draw inward, as if resenting the air.

“It smells sweet because it’s keeping itself clean,” Halloway said. “No digestion. No waste. Whatever got inside either ate what would spoil or pushed it out through the water. That’s why there’s no bloom on the surface. No film. No honest corruption. If you find another one and it smells like this, don’t wait for it to move. Sweetness in a body is a warning. Rot is bad, but sweetness is intent.”

She paused only long enough to change the angle of the cut.

“The neck’s the clearest evidence. See how it closes? Not cut. Not torn. Gathered.”

The place where a head should have been did not gape. It narrowed into a tight, puckered seam, like the mouth of a bag drawn shut. There was no spine visible there, no ragged pipe of throat. Only that closed, patient circle.

“It took the head,” Halloway said, “but it didn’t leave the neck open. That’s important. Things that take heads and leave the neck open are feeding. Things that close the neck are building. It wanted the head gone because the head would have betrayed it. A bad face is worse than no face. No face buys time.”

She let the blade rest against the seam without pressing through.

“There are membranes in there. Thin ones. Like skin stretched over a drum. If it wanted sound, it could push water or air through them and make something like a voice. Not a real voice. A shape of one. Enough to call a name. Enough to make a fool turn around.”

The water moved again, very faintly, not from the cut but from somewhere deeper.

Halloway saw it and went still for half a heartbeat.

“It knows we’re learning,” she said. “Not hearing. Learning. It felt the blade where it matters.”

She did not step back. She did not raise the lamp. She only adjusted her grip and made one more cut, lower, near the place where the torso should have met the hips.

That part was less finished.

The skin there was thinner, and beneath it the strands were looser, not woven into the same tight order. There were suggestions of legs, but no honest knees. A mass of cord where a pelvis should have been. Something that might have been feet if the thing had cared enough to complete them.

“It got as far as the torso and one working arm,” Halloway said. “Maybe less. The lower body’s a draft. It hasn’t decided whether to walk, crawl, or drag itself. That’s why it stayed in the water. Water hides unfinished work. Water makes every shape look possible.”

She lifted the blade a little, letting the light touch the opened places.

“Under the skin now, there is no man. There is a frame borrowed from one. Some bones remain where they were useful. The rest is packing, tension, and imitation. It took the organs because organs are weak. They spoil. They demand. It kept the skin because skin persuades. It kept enough limb to reach. It took the head because the head would have required skill it does not yet have.”

Her voice hardened by a degree.

“How far it got? Far enough to move. Far enough to listen. Far enough to use the water as an extension of its own surface. Far enough to make a voice if it gets enough material from us. Not far enough to survive fire if fire is used properly.”

She closed the cut with a practiced movement, not because the thing needed mercy, but because the opened layers had begun to draw together on their own, the strands beneath tightening like something trying to heal without blood.

“It’s closing,” she said. “Not healing. Reordering. If we left it, by morning the cuts would be hard to find. That’s the last lesson. It does not remain wounded the way a body does. It treats damage as information.”

Halloway wiped the blade once on the edge of her coat, though no blood had touched it.

“If you meet another,” she said, “look for the shoulders first. Then the water. Then the neck. If it smells sweet and the surface is too still, you are not looking at a corpse. You are looking at a workshop.”

Her eyes stayed on the closed seam where a face should have been.

“And if it has finished its face by then, don’t waste time admiring the craft. Burn it while the face is still new enough to be proud of itself.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
She exhaled, just slightly, through her nose—the closest she ever came to showing impatience with the ritual. "The blade entered cleanly between the third and fourth ribs on the right side," she said, her voice deliberate. "Pierced the lung. He would have drowned in his own blood within minutes." Another pause. "Not quick. But inevitable." 

Her fingers flexed once around the hilt of her sword. "The body is largely intact. No other wounds to complicate burial."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren's gaze flicked briefly to the blood-darkened ground. "Four paces from where you stand now," she said, precise as ever. "He fell forward, left arm outstretched." 

She didn't add that his fingers had twitched—that wasn't part of the accounting, merely an observation that clung unwanted to the edges of her thoughts. 

"The blade came free cleanly when he went down," she continued, voice steady. "No secondary wounds from withdrawal." A beat. "That's all that needs saying."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren stopped mid-stride, her shoulders rigid beneath her coat. The request was valid—painfully so—but that didn’t make it easier.  

When she turned back, her expression was carefully blank. "He took eighteen minutes," she said, the words like stones dropped one by one. "Called for his sister twice. Then his breath started hitching. There was blood in his mouth by the end."  

Her fingers flexed once at her side, restless. "His hands kept clutching at his shirt. Like he thought he could press the bleeding shut." A pause. "He couldn’t."  

The last detail came out flatter than the rest. "His eyes didn’t close when he died. You’ll need to do that for him."  

She held Del’s gaze, unmoving. "That’s everything. Now the account is closed."  

This time when she walked away, she didn’t stop.

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway did not treat the words as a request. She let them settle into the cellar with the same expression she gave a lock that had lied about being simple.

“Finish,” she said. “A tidy word for untidy work.”

She wiped the blade again, though there was nothing on it to remove, and laid it across the dry stone of the step within reach. The lamplight gave her enough. It gave her too much, in fact: every pale fold of the thing, every wrong line of shoulder and limb, the closed seam where a head should have been, the black water pretending to be a floor.

“Then we’ll finish it the way one finishes spoiled meat,” she said. “Not with argument. With heat, caustic, and insult.”

From the deep pockets of her coat she brought out the rest of her working kit, arranging it with no hurry and no ceremony. A squat black bottle, stoppered with wax. A small tin, sealed against damp, marked with a scratched circle and a line through it. A length of waxed cord, dark and stiff. A short iron hook, blunt at the point but cruel at the curve. Three twists of oilcloth, already greasy. A stub of taper. A brass tinderbox, battered at the corners. The last of the paper packet of salt, iron filings, and bell-ash.

She looked at the arrangement once, then at the shape.

“You like stillness,” she said. “We’ll see how you like chemistry.”

She broke the wax on the black bottle with her thumb and sniffed it without sentiment. Lamp oil, old and sharp. Good. It would float. It would carry flame where water would not. She poured some of it over the oilcloth twists, soaking them until they glistened, then set them aside on a dry stone. She did not light them yet.

Next she took the paper packet and opened it fully this time. She did not drop a pinch as a question. She cast the mixture in a narrow line across the water between the stairs and the dark shape, flicking it from her fingers with the practiced contempt of someone sowing seed in bad ground.

The salt and iron and ash struck the surface and did not sink.

For a heartbeat they lay there, tiny black and gray specks on the skin of the water. Then they began to burn.

Not with flame. With refusal. The surface dimpled at each grain, shivered, and pulled back from it as if the mixture had become a hot thing. The perfect, lying smoothness of the water broke into a fine tremor. It was not honest rippling yet, but it was a start.

The shape at the far end shifted.

Not much. One of the high shoulders rose a fraction, then lowered. The pale seam of the neck tightened.

Halloway’s mouth thinned.

“There,” she said. “You can feel a boundary when someone spends it properly.”

She struck the tinderbox.

The first spark failed. The second caught the waxed taper, and a small yellow flame stood up in the cellar, ordinary and brave. The dark water seemed to draw back from it by no more than a suggestion, but Halloway saw that too.

“Fire,” she said. “The oldest answer. Still one of the best.”

She touched the flame to the first oilcloth twist. It caught with a soft, hungry breath. She did not throw it yet. She let it burn for one second, two, three, watching the shape.

The water around the thing thickened again, trying to become calm.

Halloway threw the burning twist.

It struck the surface short of the shape and did not sink. The oil on the cloth spread at once, running outward in a blue-black vein. Flame followed the oil with a quiet hiss, crawling across the water in a line no honest cellar flood should have allowed.

The thing moved.

It did not lunge. It did not rise. It contracted, all at once, like a hand closing under a cloth. The three visible limbs drew inward. The false shoulder lifted. The water finally rippled, but the ripple was wrong: it moved away from the shape, then back toward it, as if the surface could not decide whether to flee or obey.

Halloway lit the second twist and threw it wider.

It landed near the pale mass and burned at once. The flame there went low and green at the edges, then settled into dirty yellow. The smell changed. The cold sweetness turned under itself and became scorched wax, wet hair, hot mineral, and something like burnt skin stretched too tight over a bowl.

“No bloat,” Halloway said, almost to herself. “No purge. No honest rot. Let’s see what you do when your preservation is cooked.”

She opened the sealed tin.

Quicklime. Dry, pale, caustic. She had carried it for years and used it less often than she should have, because quicklime was rude and because it asked questions of the user as well as the target. In a sealed tin it was merely dangerous. In water it became an argument.

She took a careful handful and cast it into the burning path.

The lime struck the water and began to boil.

Not like a pot. Like a wound. White plumes rose from the surface, hissing and spitting. The black water turned milky where the lime touched it, then curdled. Heat rolled upward in a sharp alkaline cloud. The cellar air grew bitter. The flame along the oil line flared brighter, fed by disturbance.

The shape jerked.

It was small, but it was real. One limb — the one that might once have belonged to a man — lifted from the water and bent at a joint that had no business bending that way. The limb had fingers, or the memory of them. They spread, then clenched, then dissolved at the tips into pale strands that whipped back toward the body.

Halloway did not step back.

“Function,” she said. “Pattern. Skin. You took what was useful. Now see how useful boiling is.”

She threw more lime, not at the center but at the edge where the thing met the wall. The water there hissed violently and drew away, leaving a slick black line on the stone. The shape twisted. For the first time, the whole of it seemed to understand that the cellar was no longer a hiding place.

It made a sound.

It was not a voice. It was the shape of a voice pushed through wet membranes: a thin, bubbling note that might have been a moan if it had belonged to a person. It had no grief in it. It had no pain, exactly. It had imitation. It was trying the sound on, seeing whether it would make the living things hesitate.

Halloway’s face did not change.

“No,” she said.

She took the iron hook and the waxed cord, tied the end fast with a knot that would hold when wet, and tested it once with her hand. The hook was ugly and practical. It had been made for dragging things out of wells, ditches, and worse.

She cast it.

The first throw caught the false limb, the one that had counted as an arm. The hook bit into the stiffened flap and tore it loose with a wet, fibrous snap. The thing came away in Halloway’s hand: a length of skin and cord, lighter than it should have been, no bone inside, no honest weight. It twitched once on the stone, then lay still.

She looked at it without interest.

“One apology,” she said.

She threw it into the burning oil. It flared at once, curling like paper.

The shape in the water shrank tighter. The remaining limbs folded inward. The closed neck seam puckered so hard it looked as if it might draw itself into the body and vanish.

Halloway cast the hook again.

This time she aimed for the neck.

The iron caught the gathered seam and held. She did not yank immediately. She let the hook sit there, biting into the closed circle, while she braced her boots against the lower step and took the cord in both hands.

“You wanted to be a container,” she said. “Let’s see what you’re holding.”

She pulled.

The seam stretched.

It did not tear at once. It drew out like the mouth of a wet sack, pale and tight, with dark strands moving beneath it. The water around it boiled where the lime had touched, and the oil fire crawled closer, eating the surface. The shape resisted, anchored somewhere below by the unfinished third limb. Halloway felt the pull run through the cord and into her shoulders.

It was strong.

But it was not heavy in the honest way. It had mass only where mass served it. It had weight only where weight could deceive.

She pulled harder.

The anchor held.

Halloway glanced at the lower part of the shape, where the dark water was thickest. The third limb, the unfinished one, disappeared into the flood near the wall. It was not a leg. It was more like a root, or a cable, pale where the firelight touched it and black where it sank into whatever hole it had found.

She took two quick steps along the edge of the stairs, still holding the cord, and threw another handful of quicklime into the water above that lower anchor.

The reaction was immediate.

The water churned white. Something beneath the surface writhed, thin and pale, like a bundle of cords pulled through a fist. The anchor loosened. The shape gave a sound again, higher this time, wet and clicking, and the closed neck seam tore a little under the hook.

Halloway hauled.

The thing came free.

It did not float upward. It slid across the surface, drawn by the hook, leaving a burning trail of oil and lime behind it. The water, no longer perfectly obedient, broke into ugly, ordinary ripples. Black flakes rose from where the fire had eaten the skin. The sweet smell had turned to something charred and sour underneath, and that was better. That was closer to death. That was closer to truth.

She dragged it until it lay within reach of the stairs.

Up close, it was worse.

The skin had begun to blister from the heat, but the blisters did not fill with fluid. They filled with fine white strands that moved under the surface like worms under glass. One of the shoulders had collapsed inward, revealing that the bone beneath was not bone at all but a lattice of hardened cord, pale and wet, shaped into the idea of a clavicle. The chest still held the outline of ribs, but they shifted when the fire touched them, opening and closing by tiny increments.

Halloway took the blade in her right hand and the hook cord in her left.

“You had your chance to stay a mystery,” she said.

She cut.

The first cut reopened the seam she had made before. The outer skin parted with that wrong, waxed resistance. The inner caul beneath it had tightened in the heat, but it was weaker now. Halloway hooked the edge of the membrane with the iron point and dragged it upward.

The chest opened.

There was no heart. There had never been one, not in any sense that mattered. What sat inside the rib cage was a knot.

It was perhaps the size of a man’s fist, but it had no fixed shape. It was made of pale cords, wet threads, thin membranes, and darker strands all wound through one another in constant small adjustment. Some cords ran into the shoulders. Some ran down toward the ruined lower body. Some ended in the neck seam. Some were loose, trembling, reaching for patterns they had not yet caught.

The knot turned toward the fire.

Not physically. Not exactly. But the strands shifted, and Halloway felt the attention in it. It knew where the heat was. It knew where the air was. It knew where living breath might be.

She poured oil directly into the opened chest.

The oil ran down the cords and pooled in the center of the knot. The thing’s limbs twitched. The false arm curled against its body. The torn flap that had been a limb burned somewhere behind them on the water, sending up a greasy black thread of smoke.

Halloway took a second twist of burning oilcloth and dropped it into the chest cavity.

The flame caught the oil at once.

Fire bloomed inside the rib cage.

The sound that came out of the thing was not a scream. It was worse. It was a collection of sounds: a breath drawn through a wet throat, a syllable without a tongue, the small click of teeth that were not there. It tried to make a face. Halloway saw the membranes in the neck swell, saw the closed seam push outward as if something behind it was shaping a mouth.

She drove the blade into the center of the knot.

“No face,” she said.

The cords clenched around the blade. Not hard enough to trap it. Hard enough to show that it felt pressure. She twisted the edge and cut sideways, opening the knot from the inside. Pale strands sprang apart. Some burned. Some drew back. A black fluid, not blood, leaked from the deepest part of the mass and hissed where it touched the fire.

Halloway took more quicklime and poured it into the burning chest.

The reaction was violent. The oil fire flared white. Steam burst upward, carrying the bitter smell of hot lime and ruined sweetness. The thing arched, if a thing without honest spine could be said to arch. Its remaining hand — if it was a hand — came up toward her, fingers spreading in a gesture so human that it was almost convincing.

Almost.

The fingers had too many joints.

Halloway caught the wrist with the hook and tore it back.

“Not today,” she said.

She cut the wrist.

The limb did not bleed. It frayed. Pale cords snapped and curled away from the blade like singed thread. The hand fell into the water and immediately began to dissolve into strands, each strand moving as if it still remembered being part of a finger.

Halloway did not watch it for long. She had learned long ago that severed pieces of things like this liked to attract pity, or curiosity, or the toe of a boot.

She turned back to the chest.

The knot was burning, but not fast enough. It was trying to reorder itself even in the fire. Strands pulled away from the flame and tried to weave themselves into a new center. The membranes around it inflated and collapsed, testing whether they could become lungs, throat, mouth. The closed neck seam stretched outward again, forming a pale bud of skin that might, given time and enough stolen pattern, have become a nose. A jaw. An eye socket.

Halloway felt no awe. She felt only the old, cold irritation she always felt when something tried to make a person into raw material.

She took the last burning twist and pressed it into the neck seam with the flat of the blade.

The skin there burst.

Not with blood. With air. A wet, whistling breath escaped the thing, carrying the smell of old rain, wax, and copper. The sound shaped itself into something horribly close to a word.

It was not Halloway’s voice.

It was not Pike’s.

It was no one’s, which made it worse.

Halloway did not answer it. She did not even give it the dignity of flinching.

She cut the neck open from seam to shoulder.

The pale bud that had been trying to become a face split apart. Inside it there were no eyes. There were only thin membranes stretched over hollows, vibrating with the effort of making sound. Halloway drove the hook into those membranes and dragged them out.

They came away in a wet cluster, translucent and trembling.

She threw them into the fire.

They burned with a high, thin hiss.

The thing in the water went still.

Not the patient stillness from before. Not the listening stillness. This was the stillness of structure failing. The cords in the chest loosened. The ribs sank inward. The shoulders dropped, and the wrong sharp line of them finally became merely broken. The skin blistered, blackened, and began to peel away from the inner caul in long strips.

Halloway did not trust it yet.

She took the black bottle and poured the last of the oil over the burning remains. She took the last of the quicklime and scattered it across the water around the shape, making a pale ring of caustic heat. She took the tinderbox and struck it again, though there was already plenty of fire, because habit had kept her alive longer than cleverness ever had.

The flame leapt higher.

The water around the thing began to boil in earnest. The oil burned on the surface, and the lime worked beneath, and the remains of the false body curled in on itself like a draft being thrown away. The chest knot gave one last adjustment. A strand reached upward, thin and pale, as if trying to catch the shape of the hand that had cut it.

Halloway caught the strand with the blade and held it in the flame until it blackened.

“Pattern,” she said. “You can have that one.”

The strand broke.

It fell into the fire and did not move again.

She waited.

The fire burned lower. The oil spent itself. The quicklime worked the water into a milky, bitter slurry. Black flakes drifted across the surface, ordinary in their ugliness. The smell changed again. The sweetness was gone. What remained was char, hot stone, burnt oil, and underneath it the first honest note of rot.

Halloway watched the edge.

The edge did not climb. The water did not become a skin again. The ripples moved the way ripples should, clumsy and caused by nothing more sinister than heat and disturbance.

She reached out with the hook and turned the largest blackened mass over.

It had no shoulders now. No suggestion of arms. No closed neck seam pretending to modesty. It was a lump of burned membrane, half-melted cord, and charred skin. Something in it might once have been a rib. Something else might have been part of a human hand. They were impossible to separate now, and that was as it should be.

Halloway took a pinch of salt from the last torn corner of her packet and dropped it onto the remains.

The salt lay there.

It did not slide inward. It did not vanish into tiny mouths. It sat on the blackened surface like salt on any burned thing.

She let out a slow breath through her nose.

“Finished,” she said.

She wiped the blade on a clean corner of her coat, inspected the edge, and put it away. The hook she cleaned less carefully, scraping it against the stone until the worst of the black residue came off. The cord she coiled, though it stank. The tin and bottle she sealed again, even empty, because empty containers were useful and habits were cheaper than funerals.

Only then did she look at the lamp.

Its flame had burned down, but it was still steady. Good. Light was not a comfort, but it was evidence. It showed the water as water now: filthy, scorched, fouled with lime and oil, but no longer listening.

Halloway stood there a moment longer, letting the cellar settle around the smell of fire and caustic.

“If it grows a face in the night,” she said at last, “don’t be flattered. Burn it again. If it grows a better face, fetch a priest and a shovel, not necessarily in that order.”

She looked once more at the blackened remains.

“And if anyone asks what happened down here,” she added, “tell them the body was in poor condition and we were forced to improve the ventilation.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren exhaled through her nose, the faintest tightening around her eyes betraying her irritation. "Through the lower abdomen," she said, each word measured. "Blade angled upward, perforated the liver. Death would have taken less than an hour, but it wouldn’t have been painless." 

She turned her wrist slightly, as if demonstrating the motion, though her gaze remained fixed on Del. "He bled out internally. No visible exit wound." 

A muscle in her jaw worked briefly before she added, flatly: "No one rallies from that. If he had people, tell them he didn’t linger." 

That last was as close to mercy as the accounting allowed.

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Auren didn’t turn.  

But she stopped walking.  

For a long moment, the only sound was the distant call of a street vendor and the rustle of her coat settling around her. Then, voice low and deliberate—each syllable sharp enough to draw blood—she spoke.  

"Entry wound: two inches below the ribcage, left side. Blade angled upward at fifteen degrees. Pierced the diaphragm, nicked the spleen. Secondary cut to the stomach wall when he twisted away." A pause. "He vomited blood before he started begging."  

Her fingers curled into her palm, nails biting flesh. "His last words were *please*, repeated seven times. The eighth time, it choked off halfway. His fingers left marks on the ground where he clawed at it."  

She swallowed once, hard. "Death took him at nineteen minutes. His eyes were open. His mouth was full of blood. The body is intact enough for viewing."  

Auren tilted her head just slightly, still not looking back. "That is the accounting. Unsoftened. Unspared."  

Then, quieter: "Now let it be done."  

And this time, when she walked away, no one called her back.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren did not treat the question as repetition, because it wasn't one. She had given the account in the language of the code and the language of the fence; the second was asking for the language of the body, and that was a different tongue, one she spoke just as carefully.

"Plainly, then," she said, and raised her hand to her own chest, setting two fingers below her left collarbone, a hand's width in from the point of the shoulder. She held the touch so the courtyard could see it.

"Here. Front of the body, left side, two finger-widths beneath the bone. The point entered at this angle—" she tilted her hand upward and slightly inward, toward the base of her own throat, and held it steady "—rising and turning toward the center of the chest. Four inches of blade went in after it. The blade stopped inside. There was no exit wound; the point stayed within the lung. Any witness who needs the geometry can mark my hand as it stands."

She lowered her hand and gave the rest without the fence's vocabulary at all.

"In plain words: I put the point of my blade into the front of his chest, below the collarbone. It cut through the artery that runs beneath that bone, and then the top of the lung beneath it. That is where it landed, and that is the whole of where. There was no other mark on him — no cut, no graze, no bruise from the hilt. One entry. Nothing else. Let that be recorded plainly, since it was asked plainly."

She paused, then added the part she had learned to add, because families deserved to know what words were being withheld from them as much as what words were being given.

"You'll notice I don't say the wound was clean. Duelists say that to families. It's a courtesy and it's a lie — no wound that kills a man is clean. She knew the shape of it the way she knew the shape of her own guard.

She turned a half-step so her voice carried to the courtyard's edges, and she did not hurry.

"I am Auren, victor in this matter, and I speak the killing wound before witnesses, that it be recorded and not embellished."

The formal register. Flat, clear, each word set down like a stone.

"The duel was fought on the terms agreed by both parties. At the fourth exchange, the deceased lunged in a true and sound line. I parried in octave and answered with a riposte to the outside shoulder, intended to wound and conclude the matter. The deceased recovered faster than I credited and turned into the thrust. The point entered below the left collarbone, at an upward angle, to a depth of four inches. It pierced the subclavian artery and the upper lung. It was the only wound dealt in the exchange — no earnest stroke before it, none after. Death followed within moments of the touch. He did not yield, and no opportunity to yield was given or could have been taken."

She kept her hands where the code required them and finished the part that was hers to carry.

"I state for the record that the stroke which killed him was not the stroke I intended. I record this because the code demands the account be true, and truth includes my error. He died because he fought well. Let any surgeon present examine the wound and confirm or dispute what I have said."

She let one breath pass, then spoke the closing words, the ones that ended it whether anyone wanted them to or not.

"The account is spoken. Let it stand as given. If any witness disputes it, let them speak now or hold their peace."

The courtyard said nothing. It rarely did.

Only then did she turn back to the second, and her voice came down from the formal register to something merely level.

"The code is met," she said. "From this moment I stand at your disposal — for the family, for the arrangements, for whatever the house requires of me. I won't leave this courtyard until you release me. That isn't in the code either. It's simply what I'll do."

rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren adjusted the weight across her shoulders and did not slow her pace, because the road was not the place for slowing, and the question was not one that needed gentleness. It needed accuracy.

"Then precisely," she said. "The blade went in below the left collarbone, angled upward toward the center of the chest. It cut the subclavian artery first — the vessel that runs beneath the collarbone, feeding blood to the arm and receiving it back from the body. When it was cut, blood left the circulation at pressure. Not a leak. A rupture. The artery was still pumping when it was severed, so blood was being driven out of the vessel and into the chest cavity with each beat of his heart. The lung was next — the top of it, the apex, pierced through its outer membrane and the tissue beneath. When the lung was pierced, it collapsed. Not gradually. A pierced lung goes down like a sail with the wind knocked out of it, and his did. The chest cavity on that side began to fill with his own blood at the same time the lung was failing to inflate. He had a heart still beating, blood still moving, and nowhere for either to go. That is what the blade did, and that is what it did it to. A man's artery and a man's lung, and the space between them that was never meant to hold blood at all."

She let a few paces pass before she continued, because the next part was hers to say or not say, and she had decided long ago that it was hers to say.

"He would have felt the entry. It is not painless, a blade through the chest — I won't pretend it was. But it was also not the worst of it. The worst of it was the suffocation, and that arrived fast and finished faster. His body would have tried to breathe and found it could not, and that struggle is brief in a case like this because the blood pressure drops so quickly that consciousness goes before the struggle can amount to much. He lost blood into his own chest at a rate his heart could not sustain. He lost the ability to draw air at nearly the same moment. The two failures together did not leave him time to suffer at length. That is the precise truth of it — not painless, but brief, and the brevity was not a mercy I designed. It was the arithmetic of the anatomy. I can take no credit for it and no blame."

She walked on, the weight steady, her voice still pitched low and even.

"You asked for precisely, not tactfully, so here is the last of it. He was alive for perhaps ten seconds after the point landed. I say perhaps because I was counting but counting is not always exact under those conditions. In those ten seconds his heart was already failing, his lung was already down, and his body was already doing what bodies do when the blood goes out of them — going grey, going cold at the extremities, the color leaving his face from the top down. He was not conscious for all of it. He was conscious for some of it. I won't tell you which part he was conscious for, because I don't know, and I won't guess at it to make either of us feel something particular."

She turned her head slightly, enough to be heard clearly, not enough to disturb the carriage of the body.

"That is what the blade did and what it did it to. If the family needs it in writing, I'll write it out by hand tonight and seal it. If you need it said again on the road, I'll say it again. But that is the whole of it, precisely, and I'll not make it prettier than it was, because it was what it was, and he was owed better than a pretty version."

rows.reply:
Auren did not slow. She had promised the pace, and the account would not change it. The dead man across her shoulders had already heard everything she was about to say; the living deserved it at a walk as much as at a stand.

"Then all of it, in order, from the touch to the stillness. Nothing left out, nothing added."

"The thrust first, and what my hand felt, because the hand knows before the eye does. Cloth. Then the give that is flesh. Then, beneath it, a deeper give that is lung — there is a texture to lung through a grip that is not muscle and not bone, and I know it, and I'll not describe it further because there are no words that make it better. Then the drag — because he was already turning, and his turn carried him along the steel. Understand this plainly: my thrust was four inches, aimed at the shoulder. His recovery put his body onto it, deeper, and at the angle that killed him. The depth was half his doing. I want that standing in the record beside my error, because both are true, and neither excuses the other."

"His weight came onto my arm for a heartbeat. That is how a duellist knows a wound is mortal before the eye confirms it — the blade tells you the chest is open. His body came off the steel as he fell, the fall doing the withdrawing. I recovered my guard before I moved to him, and I'll own to that half-second, because a victor who drops her blade over a falling man deserves what she gets. I was at his side inside two seconds."

"He landed on his back, half-turned toward me, his sword arm flung out. He had not dropped his blade. His grip was still closed around it, and it stayed closed — it loosened by degrees afterward, but it never opened, and I did not open it for him."

"What he said. Nothing, and I'll give you the sounds precisely so that nothing hides in the word. The fall drove the last of his breath out of him in a single push — that was the sound I told you of, and it was air, not voice. On the ground, the lung tried to work twice. A catch, wet, the second smaller than the first. Those are every sound he made. No words at the touch, none in the fall, none after. I've heard men die loudly and I've heard them die quietly, and I won't tell you which is courage. But his was quiet."

"The seconds, as I counted them. The first took him off his feet. The second, I was moving. By the third I was kneeling at his shoulder and his eyes were already past me — the sky, or nothing. The fourth through the sixth: the two attempts at breath, and the color leaving his face from the top down, lips first. His sword hand was opening by degrees through those seconds — a grip becoming a hold, a hold becoming nothing. The seventh and eighth: no more attempts. His chest moved once more, and not with air — the heart can shift a pierced chest after the breath is done; any surgeon here will confirm it. The ninth: the stillness. The tenth: my hand on his eyes."

"What it looked like at the end. There was less blood than anyone expects, and I'll tell you why, because if the family is shown the body, the near-clean shirt will confuse someone, and confusion turns to doubt, and doubt turns to accusation. The wound bled outward only a little — a dark line at the entry, no spurt — because the artery was cut on the deep side of the bone and the blood went where there was room for it. Inward. Into the chest. He drowned in his own blood where no one could see it. The clean shirt and the dead man are the same fact."

"His face. At the touch it held the fencing in it — I've said that. On the ground it went from occupied to empty, and the difference between those two things can't be told to anyone who hasn't seen it. But I'll say this much: the last thing on his face was the interruption of a plan. Not pain arriving. Not fear. A man mid-recovery whose feet had stopped answering him. Then the face stopped being about anything at all, and that is what the end looked like. It looked like a man going from mid-motion to finished, without ever standing still in between."

She adjusted the weight once, and her voice stayed level.

"One thing more, since it's part of all of it. When I took him up just now, his blade was still in the loosen of his hand, and I left it there. Some seconds pry the sword away before the family sees. I never have. He carried it through the whole of it. Let him carry it home."

The rise was close now, the house beyond it.

"That is everything. Every second I counted, every sound he made, everything the blade told my hand and my eyes told me. Nothing withheld, nothing softened, nothing added. The written account will match this word for word, because I'll write it tonight from what I've just said. The code is met — and more than the code, because you asked for all and all is what you have."

She kept the pace she'd promised, even, unhurried.

"It's a hard thing I've handed you, and I know it. Take whichever parts of it she can use, and leave the rest with me. I've room for it. I've been making room for eleven of these."

Both of those things would have been discourtesies of different kinds. Instead she gave the confirmation what it required: the formal close, spoken level, so that the record ended in order even if the voices carrying it did not.

"Confirmed by the second, witnessed on the road, the account stands as given. All of it. Every second, every sound, every particular of the blade and the body. Nothing withheld, nothing softened, nothing added. The code is met, and met fully, and I'll not speak the account again unless it's asked for."

She let a few paces pass, the gravel crunching under her boots and the weight across her shoulders held steady, evenly, the way she'd promised.

"Now hear the last thing I'll say about it today, and then I'll be quiet unless you want otherwise. You asked for all of it, and you took all of it standing, and you confirmed it with your voice doing what voices do when they carry something this heavy. That's not weakness. That's the correct cost of the thing, paid by the person with the right to pay it. I've stood before seconds who took the account stone-faced and went home and broke where no one could witness them breaking. I've stood before seconds who wept openly and were better for it by nightfall. I've never once stood before a second who confirmed it wrongly. The code doesn't ask you to be unmoved. It asks you to be accurate, and you were."

The rise came and she took it without shifting the pace, adjusting the weight at the crest so the carriage stayed dignified through the change of grade, and when the house showed itself below — the roofline, the gate, the windows that would be holding people who already knew or were about to — she stopped where a stopped person could not be seen from the door, because the family deserved the choice of how the arrival looked, and a victor pausing at the last rise to let the second compose himself was a courtesy the code had never named but she performed every time.

"I'll stop here until you say go on," she said. "The house won't see us wait, and you can take whatever time the rise gives you. When you say go on, I'll carry him the rest of the way at this pace, to the gate and past it if the family allows, and I'll set him down myself, properly, with hands that will be careful with it. And then I'll stand wherever the house wants me — inside, outside, at the door, in the yard — until you or the family release me. I've said it and I mean it and there's no hurry in any of it."

She looked at the road behind them once, the whole length of it, the courtyard long out of sight, the witnesses scattered to their own accounts of the day, and then she looked back at the house.

"You did well by him," she said. "Both of you did. He checked his footing first, and you kept your eyes open through all of it, and neither of those things is in the code. They're just the things people do when they mean to see something through. I'll write the account tonight, all of it, by my own hand, brevity included, the footing and the fear included, sealed and in your hands by morning for his sister. And if she wants my mouth instead of my ink, send for me. I'll come."

The weight sat on her shoulders and the number sat with it, ten, still with weight to it, and Auren stood at the rise and carried both, and waited for the word to go on.

rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren looked at the pen on the stone and did not pick it up. Not yet. She understood what he was asking, and she understood that the asking was right, and the rightness of it meant she had to stop and think before she spoke, because precision was not something she could summon on demand. It was something she owed, and owing meant working.

"The blade did three things," she said. "And I will say them in order, because the order is what a physician or a magistrate would ask for and I would rather say it once."

She held up one finger.

"The blade entered the body. It passed through skin and superficial muscle at an angle of twelve to fifteen degrees above horizontal, entering four fingers' breadth below the left nipple line, between the seventh and eighth ribs. There was no bone contact on entry. The blade was four inches of steel — I use the short guard blade, not the duelling sabre, and the witnesses know this — and approximately two and a half inches of that length passed into the thoracic cavity."

She held up a second finger.

"The blade traveled upward and slightly medial through the intercostal space and contacted the pericardium. It opened the pericardium and entered the left ventricle at the apex and drew a laceration approximately one inch in length along the ventricular wall. There was no exit wound. The blade did not contact the sternum, the spine, or the opposite lung. The heart was the only organ the blade touched."

A third finger.

"The blade was withdrawn along the entry path. Withdrawal was clean. The wound channel collapsed behind it and hemorrhage began internally and externally, externally meaning a quantity of blood sufficient to mark the ground beneath and beside where he stood, which you have all seen. He was upright at the point of withdrawal and for some seconds after. He took two steps — one forward and one to his right, which is away from me, which is what a body does and is not evidence of intention — and then he sat down, and then he lay down, and then he did not get up again."

She lowered her hand.

"That is what the blade did," she said. "And what it did it to was a man's heart, and a man's pericardium, and the intercostal tissue between his seventh and eighth ribs on the left side, and the skin and superficial muscle overlying them. It did not touch his arm. It did not touch his guard. It did not touch anything he offered me and I accepted. It touched the thing that was behind the thing he offered."

She stopped and looked at the pen.

"That is the blade, and that is what it did it to," she said. "I have left out what he was doing when it happened, because you asked me what the blade did and the blade has no intentions. If you want the man's part of it, that is a separate line, and I will write it separately, because putting them together is how accounts get muddled and the dead deserve better than muddle."

She gestured at the sheet with her open hand.

"Write your name where you saw the turn," she said. "And then, if you will, write beneath it what you saw the body do — not what you think he meant. Only what the body did. *Entered, rotated, took the wound inside the line.* If that is what you saw. If it is not what you saw, write what you saw and I will stand corrected before these witnesses and think none the less of either of us."

She picked up the pen again and held it out to him a second time, and this time her hand was very steady, because steadiness here was the whole of what she had left to give.

"The code does not ask for tact," she said. "It asks for the truth in the order the truth happened. I have given you the blade. Now give me the man, and we will have the whole of it, and then I can write his second a letter that does not lie to him."

rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren set both hands flat on the stone and looked at him, and there was something in her expression that was almost gratitude, because he had asked the right question and the right question was a relief after the wrong one.

She turned and pointed, not at the body, but at the air where the body had been standing, which she could still see as plainly as if the man were still in it.

"Here," she said. "Left side. Beneath the ribs. Not beneath the floating ribs — beneath the true ones, and low, and I will tell you plainly because you are right that the witnesses need it and so do I." She traced the line in the air with one finger. "The entry was four fingers' width below the nipple line. The angle was upward — not steeply, but unmistakably. Twelve degrees, perhaps fifteen. The blade went between the seventh and the eighth rib, which means it did not strike bone on entry, which means it was not deflected, which means the angle I found is the angle he gave me."

She held her hand where the entry had been, and did not move it.

"If he had stood still and I had struck where I was already committed, the wound would be here." She moved her hand out to the left and down, to the air where his upper arm would have been. "Outer arm, below the deltoid, angled down and through. That is a wound a man lives with. That is the wound I intended." She brought her hand back to the ribs. "This is not that wound. This wound is one a man makes by turning *into* the line, and turning into the line is not what a feint high does to a body. A feint high pulls a man back and up. His guard drops, his weight goes to the rear foot, his chest opens to the sky. A feint high does not drive a man forward and sideways onto a low blade."

She finally lowered her hand.

"He came inside the arm," she said. "Low. Rotating toward me, not away. That is what the angle says, and the angle is the only witness I trust completely, because it does not have intentions and it cannot be frightened." She looked along the rail at the witnesses. "You all heard it. The wound is consistent with a man who moved into the strike and not away from it. That does not prove he meant to die. But it is now a fact in the record, and it sits beside the fact of the feint, and together they are not nothing."

She looked back at Del.

"Plainly," she said. "That is plainly. If his second tells me the feint was only a feint, then I have killed a man through my own error and I will say so before these same witnesses. But if his second tells me the ninth pass was arranged — then the wound I gave him is the wound he came for, and I will not carry it as a mistake." She paused. "I will carry it as something else. I do not have a word for that yet either."

Auren's hands stopped on the clasp.

She did not turn around immediately. She stood very still for a moment, and the yard held its silence the way it had held it for the accounting — but this silence was different. This was the silence of something not fitting.

Then she turned and looked at Del with an expression that was not quite confusion, because Auren did not permit herself confusion in a duelling yard, but was something adjacent to it — the careful, flat attention of a woman who had just been asked to account for something she had already accounted for.

"It has been spoken," she said. "And witnessed. And confirmed by the second — which is you." She let that sit. "The form was satisfied. You stood and heard it. The witnesses nodded. If I speak it again, I do not give the dead his due twice. I give him a repetition, which is not the same thing and is, in fact, a discourtesy."

She studied him for a moment longer than was comfortable.

"Unless you mean to tell me you did not hear it," she said, and her voice was careful and entirely without edge, because she had known seconds to be struck deaf by the hour and she would not shame a man for that. "In which case I will say it again and I will not think less of you for needing it. But I would know which it is before I speak, because the code does not ask me to perform. It asks me to account."

rows.reply:
Auren set the case down again. She had picked it up three times now and set it down three times, and she was aware of this and did not care, because the evening had become something that required her hands to be empty.

She stood with her arms at her sides and looked at the ground between where she stood and where Del stood, and she began.

"The engagement lasted nine passes," she said. "The first eight took approximately four minutes. I have not timed it — I never time it — but the light had not moved on the wall and the lamp was still at the height it was when we took our marks, and a lamp drops roughly a finger's width in a quarter hour, so four minutes is what I will say and I will say it as an estimate and not as a fact."

She paused. This was the part where precision required her to admit what she did not know, and admitting what she did not know was harder than any wound.

"He spoke once," she said. "At the beginning, before the first pass. He said: *I would prefer we did not prolong this.* I took that at the time as impatience. I have since wondered what else it might have been, and I have not resolved that either. He did not speak during the engagement. He did not speak after the wound. Not a word. Not a sound I could distinguish. If he made a sound, it was beneath the sound of the yard, and I will not invent one to make the account more complete than the truth is."

She breathed once, evenly, the way she breathed before a pass.

"The first two passes were feeling passes. Testing distance, testing reactions. He was good — better than his reputation, which is rare; men are usually worse than their reputation and twice as loud about it. His footwork was clean. He held the low guard, which is defensive, which is not what a man holds when he means to end a thing quickly. I noted that at the time. I noted it and I did not think about what it meant, and that is a failure I will own."

She held up her hand again, counting, because counting helped her keep the shape of the thing from collapsing into the one moment she could not stop seeing.

"Third and fourth pass, he began to press. Not recklessly — with intent. He came at my left twice, which is my weak side, and he knew it was my weak side because I had shown it to him in the second pass when I let my line drift, which was a deliberate drift and not an error, and he read it correctly, which told me he was reading me well. Fifth pass, he drew blood." She touched her left forearm, where a shallow cut had been wrapped beneath her sleeve. "A scratch. It was meant to be a scratch. He was marking me and not trying to end me, and again, I noted it and did not think about it."

She let her hand drop.

"Sixth and seventh pass, we were equal and we both knew it. He was not pressing anymore. He was waiting. I mistook that for fatigue. It was not fatigue. A tired man's guard sags. His did not sag. It *settled*. There is a difference and I know the difference and I did not see it in time."

"Eight pass — " She stopped. Corrected herself. "Eighth pass. I was the one who pressed. I came at his right and drove him back two steps and I was pleased with myself, which is a thing I am never permitted to be and should not have been then, because he gave me those two steps. He did not have to give them. He walked backward with a clean retreat and he set his feet at the end of it in exactly the position he wanted to be in, and I did not see that either."

Her voice did not change. Her voice had not changed through any of this. But the pace of it slowed.

"Ninth pass. He dropped his guard. The feint came high — head and shoulders, the shape of an attack to the face or the collarbone. I responded the way I am trained to respond. I committed to the arm. Outer arm, below the deltoid, angled down and through. I was already moving when he turned. I could not have stopped. I want that in the record — I could not have stopped. The turn took less than half a second and I was inside it before I understood there had been a turn."

She looked at her hands.

"The blade went where I have described. Four fingers below the left nipple line. Between the seventh and eighth ribs. Upward. Into the heart. I felt it go in, which is a thing I have never said aloud and I will say it now because you asked for all of it. I felt the blade go in and I knew before I saw his face that I had killed him, because a blade does not feel like that in muscle. It feels like that in a room it should not be in."

She closed her hands.

"He took two steps. The first was forward and the second was to his right, which is away from me, and which I have already said is what a body does. He was upright. His hand was open — his sword hand. The sword was already on the ground. I did not see it leave his hand. It was simply on the ground and his hand was open and he was walking, and he was not walking toward anything. He was walking the way a man walks when he is leaving a room and does not know where the door is."

Her voice held. It held because she made it hold.

"He sat down. Not collapsed — sat. He put one hand on the ground behind him and he lowered himself, and there was something almost deliberate in it, and if I had not known what had just happened to his heart I would have said he was resting. Then he lay down on his left side, which is the side the wound was on, and I have wondered since whether that was the body's choice or gravity's, and I do not know, and I will not say I know."

"He was still for a while. I do not know how long. Long enough for the witnesses to start moving. Long enough for someone to say his name twice. I do not know who said it or what name was said, because I have told you I did not know his name and I did not hear it in the moment, and that is the truth and it is an ugly truth and I am not going to soften it."

She looked at Del.

"He did not speak," she said again. "He did not look at me. He looked at the ground. He was looking at the ground when he stopped breathing, and I know when he stopped breathing because I was watching his shoulders, and the shoulders stopped, and that was the end of it. It was quiet. The whole of it, from the ninth pass to the shoulders stopping, was — " She searched. "Under a minute. It was under a minute. He died in less time than it takes to cross this yard."

She stopped.

"That is all of it," she said. "The passes. The blood he took from my arm. The two steps. The sitting. The lying down. The looking at the ground. The shoulders. There is nothing else and I have not left anything out and I have not put anything in." She held his gaze. "Now. His name. Say it plainly. I have given you all of mine."

"Then hear it," she said. "The whole of it. Not the wound alone. Not the passes alone. The account. She drew one breath. She had drawn one breath before every account she had ever spoken and she drew this one the same way, and she did not look at Del while she drew it, and she did not look at the witnesses. She looked at the ground where Kaelen had fallen, because that was where the account had happened and that was where it should be read from.

"This is the accounting of Kaelen, as witnessed in the duelling yard on the evening of the ninth pass engagement," she said. "Spoken by Auren, duellist of record. Confirmed by the second who stood and did not look away. Witnessed by those present at the rail, whose names will be entered in the hand of the magistrate's clerk."

She paused. Not the pause of the wound. The pause of a woman turning a page.

"The engagement was called and set. The terms were met. Kaelen and I took our marks. Before the first pass, Kaelen said: *I would prefer we did not prolong this.* I took that for impatience at the time. I do not take it for impatience now. I record it as spoken and I leave its meaning open."

"The engagement ran nine passes. The first eight took approximately four minutes by the fall of the lamp, which is an estimate and not a measurement. The first two passes were feeling passes. Kaelen held the low guard, which is defensive. The third and fourth passes, Kaelen pressed at my left, which is my weak side, having read the drift I showed him in the second pass. The fifth pass, Kaelen drew blood — a scratch to my left forearm, shallow, delivered as a mark and not as an attempt on my life. I carry it still beneath my sleeve. The sixth and seventh passes, we were equal. Kaelen's guard settled and did not sag. I mistook the settling for fatigue. It was not fatigue."

"Eighth pass. I pressed at his right and drove him back two steps. He gave me those two steps and set his feet where he wanted them. I did not see that he had chosen the ground. I believed I had won it."

"Ninth pass. Kaelen dropped his guard and feinted high. I committed to the arm — outer arm, below the deltoid, angled down and through, which is a disabling wound and not a killing one. I was already moving. I could not have stopped."

Her voice did not break. It had never broken and it did not break now. But it slowed to the pace of something being set down very carefully, one piece at a time, on a surface that might not hold.

"Kaelen turned. Into the line. Not away from it. The second saw the turn and has written it in his own hand upon this record. The wound angle confirms it. A feint high pulls a body backward and upward. Kaelen came forward and low and rotated toward me, and the blade entered where the arm should have been."

"The killing wound was to the left side beneath the true ribs. The entry was four fingers' breadth below the left nipple line, between the seventh and eighth ribs, at an angle of twelve to fifteen degrees above horizontal. No bone was struck on entry. The blade was the short guard blade, four inches, and approximately two and a half inches passed into the thoracic cavity. The blade traveled upward and slightly medial through the intercostal space and opened the pericardium and entered the left ventricle at the apex, drawing a laceration of approximately one inch along the ventricular wall. There was no exit wound. The sternum was not contacted. The spine was not contacted. The opposite lung was not contacted. The heart was the only organ the blade touched."

"I withdrew along the entry path. The withdrawal was clean. Hemorrhage began internally and externally. Kaelen was upright at the point of withdrawal and for some seconds after."

"He took two steps. The first was forward. The second was to his right, which is away from me, which is what a body does and is not evidence of intention. His sword was on the ground. I did not see it leave his hand. His sword hand was open. He was upright and he was walking and he was not walking toward anything."

"He sat down. Not collapsed. He put one hand on the ground behind him and lowered himself, and there was something in it that I will call deliberate because I do not have another word that is true. Then he lay down on his left side, which is the wound side, and whether that was the body's choice or gravity's, I do not know."

"He did not speak. He did not make a sound I could distinguish. He did not look at me. He looked at the ground. He was looking at the ground when he stopped breathing, and I know when he stopped breathing because I was watching his shoulders and the shoulders stopped."

"From the ninth pass to the cessation of breath was under a minute. He died in less time than it takes to cross this yard."

She stopped.

The lamp had dropped further. The witnesses at the rail had not moved. The yard was the kind of quiet that has weight to it.

"That is the accounting," Auren said. "Name. Engagement. Passes. Wound in full, with measurements and path and organ. Withdrawal. The body's movement after. The manner of death. The time it took. The words he spoke before it began and the silence he kept after it ended. The second's corroborated observation of the turn. The open question of intent, which I hold open and do not resolve, because the code does not ask me to resolve what I do not know and I do not know it."

She looked at Del.

"I have not left anything out," she said. "I have not put anything in. That is the whole of it as I have it and as I will write it and as I will stand by it, amended or not, when Corrin's reply comes." She paused. "Confirm it or do not. But if you confirm it, confirm it as a man who heard all of it, and not as a man who heard the wound and let the rest go past him."

She stood with her hands at her sides and she waited.
