She straightened. The posture returned — shoulders squared, hands at her sides, eyes open and level. The same posture as before, because the account did not change and neither did the body that gave it.

"The blade entered below the left ribs at an angle that carried through the lung and stopped a hand's breadth short of the heart," she said. Her voice was exactly as it had been the first time. Not flatter. Not softer. Not harder. "The wound was mortal from the first breath taken after it, though the breath itself lasted a short while longer. He bled inwardly more than outwardly, which is why the ground beneath him shows as little as it does."

She let the silence hold for the space of one breath, as the code required.

"The blade entered cleanly. There was no tearing. It was not a slow death and it was not a fast one. It was the death his own blade had been pointed at me to produce, had it turned differently."

This time, when she looked at Del, something in her expression shifted — not softened, but settled, the way a seal settles into wax.

"You have asked the account formally and I have given it formally. Your name stands beside mine on this record if you place it there. That is a heavier thing than witnessing as you stood and watched. I will not pretend otherwise." She paused. "You may decline. No dishonor attaches to declining what was never yours to carry."

She waited, hands still, eyes still, giving Del the same stillness she had given the account — the stillness of a woman who had learned that the waiting was the part that mattered most.

Auren stopped walking. She did not turn immediately — she let the distance between her stride and her answer open the way it needed to, the way a wound opens before it closes. Then she turned.



"Below the left ribs," she said. "The blade went in on a downward angle, beneath the cartilage, between the fifth and sixth rib. It crossed the lung and came to rest short of the heart." She said it the way she might have read from a ledger — without inflection, without the weight that the same words had carried when spoken as the full account. This was the plain form. The code permitted both. "It did not exit. The point stayed inside him."

She looked at Del directly.

"That is where it landed." A pause. "If the witnesses need the wound as the body carries it now, you will need to lift the cloth. I would not ask you to do that on my account, but if the record requires a second pair of eyes confirming the wound as described, then the cloth comes up and goes back down, and nothing about the accounting changes."

She let her hand fall from where it had been resting, near the pocket that held the folded strip with two names on it. She had not known she was touching it until Del spoke.

"The wound tells the same story the account does," she said. "It always does. That is the one mercy of it — the dead cannot argue with the record." She paused, and something moved behind her eyes — not quite a memory, but the shape one leaves. "I have checked every time. I would not tell you where to look if I had not looked myself."

She waited, because waiting was the part that mattered most, and because she had not yet decided whether Del was asking to confirm the record or asking because something in the plain telling had not settled.

rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"

Auren stopped again. This time she turned fully, and there was no pause before she did — she had turned as quickly as she turned when the blade came out, which was not quickly at all but without hesitation, as though her body had already decided what her mind was confirming.



She looked at Del for a long moment. Then something shifted in her expression — not shame, exactly, but the recognition of having been caught in something she had not realized she was doing. The plain form had been accurate. It had also been brief, and brevity was its own kind of omission.

"You're right," she said. "I gave you the plain form. The plain form is permitted, but it is not the same as the precise account." She drew a breath through her nose. "The plain form is what I give when the audience cannot bear the full telling. I should not have assumed what you could bear."

She squared her shoulders again, though she had not un-squared them this time — she had simply re-squared them, as one straightens a thing that had bent a fraction out of true.

"The blade entered between the fifth and sixth ribs on the left side, below the costal margin, angled downward and slightly toward the midline. It passed through the intercostal muscle, severed two intercostal vessels, punctured the pleural membrane, and entered the left lung through the lower lobe. The tip crossed the lower lobe diagonally, destroying a portion of the parenchyma and opening a branch of the pulmonary artery. The blade stopped short of the mediastinum — a hand's breadth short of the heart, as I said — because the rib above the intended path deflected it by the width of a finger. Had it not, the account would be different, and I would be the one being accounted for."

She paused, but not for breath. She paused because the code required a separation between what the blade did and what the wound became, and the two were not the same thing.

"What the blade did to him was this: it opened a path from the outside air to the inside of his lung, which means that every breath he took after the wound was made drew blood into the space where air belonged. The lung collapsed on that side within a short time. His heart continued to beat — it did not stop from the wound itself, because the wound did not reach it — but it was pumping against a chest that could no longer hold pressure. The bleeding was internal. The blood went into the pleural cavity and stayed there. He would have felt the air leaving him before he felt anything else. The pain, if he felt pain, would have been in the shoulder — the diaphragm refers pain there when it is compromised." Her voice did not waver, but it slowed, not from reluctance but from precision, the way a hand slows when threading a needle. "The breath he took after the wound was the last one his lung participated in fully. After that he was breathing with half a chest and the other half filling with what should not have been in it."

She held still.

"That is what the blade did. That is what it did it to. Nothing in it is softened. Nothing in it is omitted." She met Del's eyes. "You asked for precise. That is precise."

For the first time since the blade had come out, something moved across her face before she could contain it. It was not reluctance. It was not disgust. It was the expression of a woman who had carried something in a place so deep that pulling it out required her to reach past other things she had not expected to touch on the way.

She walked back to where Del stood. She did not hurry, but each step covered more ground than her previous steps had, as though the distance between them had become something she intended to close rather than merely traverse.

She stopped an arm's length away and faced the body without looking at it. She knew where it was. She would always know where it was.

"The code says all of it," she repeated, as though tasting the words for structural integrity. "You are correct. I have been giving you the parts in sequence and calling it complete. It is not complete until the whole of it is spoken." She paused. "I will tell you what I have not told any witness, because you have asked for it as the code intends it to be asked — plainly, and without flinching in advance."

She drew a breath. It was not the breath the code required. It was the breath a woman takes before descending stairs in the dark.

"The first breath after the wound, he did not react. He looked at me the way a man looks at a sentence he has not finished reading. Then his hand went to his side and came away red, and his face changed — not to pain, not yet, but to the recognition that something had happened which he had not authorized."

She paused. The code required it here, but she would have paused regardless.

"He said two things. The first was a name — not mine. I will not speak it, because the code does not require the names of the dying, only the account of the wound and the manner of it, and I have weighed this eleven times and I will weigh it now: the name is not yours to carry." A beat. "The second thing he said was, *'It went in easy.'* His voice was level. He said it the way a man comments on weather. I do not know whether that was courage or the body's refusal to admit what had happened to it. I have thought about it every day since and I have not decided."

Her hands, which had been still at her sides, closed slowly into fists and then opened again. Not from emotion. From the effort of keeping them still while saying something that required her entire body to remain disciplined.

"After the second minute, the bleeding slowed — not because it had stopped but because there was less of it left to come out where I could see it. The rest was going where I could not. His breathing changed. He began taking air in through his mouth in short pulls, the way one does at altitude, and each pull was shallower than the last. He did not gasp. He did not clutch at the wound. His hand stayed at his side, fingers open, as though he had decided that touching it would make it more real."

She paused, and this pause was longer than any she had taken. When she spoke again, her voice had not changed, but something in the architecture of her jaw had tightened — not against the words, but in support of them.

"At three minutes, his eyes found mine and held them. I do not know what he saw. I know what I was doing — I was standing where I had been, blade down, not moving, because the code does not require movement after the wound is made and because moving would have been a kind of mercy I was not entitled to offer." A breath. "He held my eyes for the space of roughly ten heartbeats. Then his gaze went past me — not to anything behind me, or if it was, I could not turn to see it without breaking the count — and his head tilted slightly to the left, the way a man's does when he is listening to something at a distance."

"That is what it looked like at the end."

She stood very still. The wind moved. The treeline stood where it had been standing.

"That is all of it," she said. "The four minutes. The two words. The hand turning over. The face settling." Her eyes met Del's and held, and in them was the same open, neither-hard-nor-soft look she had worn since the beginning — but beneath it, at a depth that had taken four minutes of silence and eleven accounts of practice to reach, was something that was not quite grief and not quite relief but was the exact weight of having placed the whole of a thing down and found that the ground held it.

"I have never said all of it aloud before," she said. "I have thought it in the order I have just given it — every night, without exception, since it happened. The thinking was mine and the silence was mine and I told myself that was sufficient because the code does not require the manner of the end unless a witness asks for it, and no witness ever did."

She held still for one more moment.

"You asked. So it is spoken, and now it is yours as well."

It entered at an angle, and the force behind the strike drove it through the vital organ, causing immediate unconsciousness and subsequent death. The body fell to the ground, the weight of its own mass carrying it down, and it landed as you see it now, facedown, with the blade still embedded. That is the plain truth of it, as you and the witnesses required."

She paused, her eyes not leaving Del's, as if daring them to question the account again. "The location of the wound and the fall are as clear as the code demands. "He was quick, and he did not suffer. The precision of the wound was such that it rendered him unconscious almost instantly, a mercy in a world where such mercies are rare. That is the truth of the account, spoken before witnesses, as the code demands. May it serve as a reminder of the weight of our actions and the responsibility we bear in this brutal world."

rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply: Auren's gaze didn't waver, her eyes steady and unwavering as she met Del's stare. "The blade pierced the chest, just above the heart," she began, her voice precise and unyielding. "It entered at an angle, the point driving through the vital organ with precision. The force of the strike was such that it severed the aorta, causing immediate and irreversible damage. The heart would have stopped within seconds, rendering him unconscious and then lifeless. That is what the blade did, and that is what it did to him. No more, no less. The account is as the code demands, precise and unflinching. There is no room for tact in the face of truth, and there is no dishonour in speaking it as it is."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway considered the question with the same patience she gave a wound. Then she moved the lamp lower, not toward the water, but across the curve of the thing’s folded arm.

“Recently?” she said. “Depends whether you mean recently enough to have a name, or recently enough to still have warmth in the socket.”

The light caught the doubled fingers. They were long, too long, but the knuckles had the architecture of hands that had once gripped something ordinary—a bucket, a rail, a child’s wrist.

“This had a wrist,” Halloway said. “This had a shoulder that used to work one way. Those are human beginnings. The rest is editing.”

She did not look at Pike when she said it. Her attention stayed on the rippling flank, on the place where the skin tented and smoothed, tented and smoothed, like something beneath was practicing how to move.

“If it was a person within a day, there’s somebody missing above us and they’ll bring searchers soon. If it was a person within a week, there’d be smell, flies, and a coroner’s problem. If it was a person before that, then it’s furniture.” A dry pause. “This isn’t furniture. The skin is too new. The water’s kept it honest.”

The creature remained folded, but the ripple slid again beneath the ribs and stopped near the opened cage of bone.

“So yes,” Halloway said. “Somebody wore this shape not long ago. Don’t confuse ‘was’ with ‘is.’ What’s in that water is not waiting for its family. It’s waiting for an opening.”

She lifted the lamp back to the shoulders, where the joints branched wrong beneath the surface.

“And if you start mourning it before we know whether it can stand, I’ll leave you here to explain yourself to the next thing that crawls out.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren's eyes hardened, her jaw setting in a line of resolve. "He took seconds," she said, her voice as precise as the blade that had ended his life. "He was swift, as I have already accounted. His final words, if any, were lost to the swiftness of his end. As for what it looked like... he fell as you see him now, facedown, the blade still lodged in his chest. There was no prolonged struggle, no drawn-out agony. It was swift, it was precise, and it was over before any of us could truly comprehend it."

She paused, her eyes not leaving Del's, as if daring them to question the account further. "The code demands precision, and I have given it. I have accounted for the wound, the swiftness of the end, and the dignity with which he fell. To ask for more is to question the very nature of the duel and the honour of those who witnessed it. That is the truth of it, as plain and as unflinching as the blade that dealt the killing wound."

"The duel began with both parties acknowledging the code and the witnesses. The opponent, a skilled duelist, engaged with speed and precision. I countered his moves with equal measure, our blades clashing in a dance of steel and will. He was quick, his strikes swift and sure, but I matched his pace, my own movements honed by years of practice and discipline.

"The killing wound was to the chest, piercing the heart. I struck with the precision that the code demands, the blade entering just above the heart, at an angle, severing the aorta. He was swift, and the force of the strike drove the blade through the vital organ, causing immediate unconsciousness and subsequent death. The wound was contained within the chest cavity, with minimal spillage, the floor not slick with blood. The body fell facedown, the blade still lodged, as you see it now.

"He fought with honour, his movements those of a trained duelist. He did not falter, and he did not hesitate. His final words, if any, were lost to the swiftness of his end. The duel was swift, precise, and over before any of us could truly comprehend it. That is the account, as the code demands, and as I have given it. The dead will be treated with the dignity they deserve, and the lessons of this day will be carried forward, as is our responsibility."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway did not waste breath on reprimand. There would be time for that if they lived.

“Keep it low,” she said. “And if your arm tires, tell me. A moving light reads as prey.”

She worked one knee onto the damp step, close enough that the water’s cold reached through her trousers, not close enough to be invited in. The hooked wire went out again, this time to the hinge of the creature’s shoulder. It met resistance—cartilage, maybe, or something that had learned to pretend to be cartilage.

“What happened to it,” she began, as if taking a statement, “started with a body. Human. Probably adult, probably mobile, probably foolish enough to come down these steps when the cellar smelled wrong. That part is common.”

The wire slipped between the peeled ribs. Inside, the black water moved with a purpose that had nothing to do with currents.

“Then something got in. Not through the mouth. Mouths are for eating. This came through softer places: a wound, a bite, a splash of contaminated water up the nose, a hand pressed into the wrong pool. After that, it did not kill the host. Killing is wasteful. It kept the heart beating, the lungs drawing, the nerves firing just enough to move meat from one dark corner to another.”

She eased the rib cage wider. The creature’s folded arm twitched, but only once, like a dog dreaming of a rabbit.

“The extra joints are not new bones grown for style. They’re old bones split and reset. See here?” She touched the wire to the shoulder. “The humerus has been divided, capped with fresh growth at both ends so the limb can brace sideways. The ribs have been pried outward to make a chamber. That chamber is not for breathing. It is a nursery, a larder, or a hive. Sometimes all three, and they rarely get along.”

The lamplight showed what Halloway had already suspected: beneath the skin near the ribs, the ripple was not one thing travelling. It was many small things coordinating.

“No wonder it stopped moving,” she said, dry. “It was busy furnishing.”

She withdrew the wire. Clinging to the hook were three pale threads, each thinner than fishing line, each curling toward the warmth of the light with blind, patient intent. Halloway watched them for a moment, then flicked them into the water away from the stairs. They sank, then turned back toward the creature’s leg.

“It is connected,” she said. “Not a ghost in the machine. A colony. The man is the machine. The thing under the skin is the operator, and it has not finished learning the controls.”

Her blade cleared the leather fully now, a short, honest length of steel. She laid the flat against the creature’s sternum, feeling for the place where bone should have been solid and was instead soft, layered, wrong.

“Plainly: someone wore this shape recently enough to have a name. Something got inside them alive. It split their joints, opened their ribs, filled the cavity with its young, and kept the body walking until the meat was tired or the water was deep enough to hide the smell. What you are looking at is not a corpse and not quite a creature. It is a house that has started eating its tenants.”

The mouth-seam twitched. Not open. Not yet. Only the lips drawing back over the uneven points, as if the thing beneath were rehearsing the expression.

Halloway’s voice dropped, clinical and without comfort.

“Teeth can wait. The door it chose can wait a little longer, but not much. When it stands, do not aim for the head. The head is only the part that screams. Aim where the shoulder branches—there the joints are newest, and newest means softest.” She glanced toward the waterline, then back to the rippling cage of ribs. “And if it takes your lamp from you, let it go. Light is useful. Hands are harder to replace.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway did not turn at once. She let the hooked wire hover an inch above the creature’s shoulder, close enough to feel the chill coming off the wet skin, far enough that nothing could thank her by taking her fingers.

“Still light draws them,” she said. “Heat first. Motion second. If the threads gather at the lamp in a thick rope, you have already spent your warning. Ease back. Do not shake it. Do not raise it. A lamp lifted in panic is just a dinner bell with better manners.”

The creature remained folded. The mouth-seam did not open, but the lips had drawn farther back over the uneven points, as if the thing beneath had decided a face was useful after all.

Halloway watched the shoulder joints shift under the water, slow and deliberate, like a man testing whether his legs remembered how to kneel.

“Detail,” she repeated. “You want detail from a house that hasn’t finished renovating.”

She touched the wire to the ridge where the humerus split into two fresh caps of bone. The skin there was stretched thin and grey, not blue with bruising, not red with inflammation. It had the colour of candle wax left too near a fire.

“I can tell you what it did to him because bodies confess, if you know the language of ruin,” she said. “Exact requires opening it while the parts are still labelled. Opening takes time. Time is what the thing in the water is spending on us.”

The wire slid under a flap of skin at the shoulder. Nothing bled. Instead, a dark thread came with it, fine as hair, glossy as oil, curling around the blackened metal with blind persistence.

Halloway lifted it just enough to show the lamp.

“Here. First it took the wrapping.”

The thread trembled, then oriented toward the warmth of the light before snapping back toward the creature’s flesh.

“Not muscle first. Muscle is expensive and slow to replace. It went for fascia—the wet sheeting that holds a man together. Fat under the skin. Connective cords around the joints. Small things live in those places because there is no argument there. No bone to break its teeth on, no heart to complain, no nerves screaming loud enough to wake the neighbours.”

She let the thread fall. It found the shoulder again at once, eager as a root seeking water.

“Once it had the scaffolding, it started editing. The humerus was whole when the man was alive. Now it is divided, capped, reinforced. Fresh growth at both ends. That is not healing. Healing closes gaps. This opens possibilities.”

Her gaze moved along the peeled ribs.

“Same with the cage. Ribs do not peel outward because a man stretches. They were forced. Pried. The body was made into a chamber. Not for breathing. Breathing happens upstairs, in the lungs, which are still working because the thing under the skin is too practical to kill the pump before it has finished using it.”

The water gave a soft lap against the creature’s flank. The ripple beneath the skin moved again, this time from the ribs toward the pinned arm.

Halloway’s voice flattened further, as if precision were a kind of armour.

“What it took: mobility. Pain response, mostly. The ability to call the body his own. It left the heart because the heart carries food. It left the lungs because the lungs move water and heat through the meat. It left enough of the brain stem to make the flesh breathe, flinch, swallow, and fail to die properly. The rest—judgement, memory, the part that knows a cellar is not a bed—has been composted.”

She stepped half a foot lower, boot finding a dry patch on the stair. The lamp’s edge cut across the creature’s neck, where two dark slits sat where a nose should have been.

“How far it got: far enough to stand, not far enough to walk well. Far enough to reach, not far enough to speak. The mouth is rehearsal. The shoulders are the first true limbs. The threads under the skin are coordinating, learning which cord pulls which bone. When it rises, it will not rise like a man. It will rise like a trap.”

The folded arm twitched again. This time the fingers did not merely double back; they spread, slowly, the too-long joints locking into a shape that could grip a ledge, a throat, a lamp.

Halloway saw it and did not pretend surprise.

“That is progression,” she said. “Minutes matter. Hours matter more. If it has been in water this long, the cold has slowed the brood. Warmth speeds it. Blood speeds it. Movement speeds it. Every time it tests a joint, the threads learn the joint. Every time the ribs flex, the chamber settles. By the time it can stand without folding itself in half, it will not need to think about where you are. It will taste the difference between stillness and fear.”

She withdrew the wire and wiped it along the heel of her boot. The black thread clung for a moment, then detached and slid into the water, making for the creature’s leg with patient, sightless intent.

“If you meet another,” Halloway went on, “do not begin by asking whether it was a person. Begin by asking what it has spare. Extra joints. Peeled ribs. Skin that ripples against gravity. Black fluid that strings when lifted. Smell of pond silt, copper, and sweet rot under it. The mouth will be late. The shoulders are early. The hands decide. The under-skin decides whether there is anything left to save.”

Her blade cleared the leather again, not drawn, only loosened, the steel whispering against its fittings.

“Aim where the newest bone meets the oldest meat. There the colony is still paying attention. Cut the thread-cluster at the shoulder branch and the arm becomes decoration. Pierce the rib chamber and you may disturb the brood, which is worse than disturbing the body, because disturbed brood does not care whose lungs it fills.”

The creature’s head shifted. Not up. Not yet. Only a small rotation beneath the water, the jaw slits angling toward the stair.

Halloway watched it with the weary satisfaction of a woman confirming a bad diagnosis.

“Plainly,” she said, “someone wore this shape recently enough to have a name. Something entered through a wound or a mouthful of wrong water. It did not kill him. Killing is wasteful. It colonised him. It softened the bindings, split the levers, opened the storehouse, and filled the cavity with its young. It kept the heart beating because the heart is a servant, not a master. It kept the lungs drawing because the lungs move heat, and heat is what the threads want.”

The ripple under the skin ran once more toward the opened ribs, stopped, then returned to the shoulder.

“Now it is learning to stand.”

Halloway looked from the shoulder to the waterline, measuring the distance with her eyes the way a surgeon measures a cut.

“That is the detail. Not poetry. Not mercy. A body turned into furniture for hungry things. If you want grief, save it for daylight. If you want to live long enough to grieve properly, watch the shoulder joint. When it lifts, tell me whether the elbow leads or the fingers lead. If the fingers lead, it is reaching for something specific. If the elbow leads, it is only practising balance.”

The mouth-seam parted.

Not wide. Not enough to count teeth. Just a black slit between swollen lips, weeping dark water that did not behave like water. It hung at the corners in strings, then fell back toward the ribs as if the creature were tasting the air and finding it insufficient.

Halloway’s voice dropped to a near-whisper, clinical and cold.

“There. It has chosen a door. Enough lecturing. Watch the shoulder.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway did not tell him to be quiet. Words, used properly, were another instrument. They kept the hands honest and the mind out of the creature’s mouth.

“You want everything,” she said. “Everything is mostly plumbing and spoilage. Try not to learn it romantically.”

She set the blade at the shoulder branch and opened the skin again, shallow and controlled. The cut parted with a soft, wet sound. No red welled up. Black beads formed along the edges, then drew into threads.

“Underneath,” she said, lifting the flap with the hook, “the body has been stripped to its engineering. Fascia first. It should be a sheet. Here it is a net. The threads have replaced most of it. Tendons remain, but they are sleeved. Muscle is not digested; it is warehoused. See the pale grains? Larval sacs. Each one holds a knot of the colony. Mature sacs do not crawl. They anchor.”

The elbow under the water jerked. Halloway kept the blade beside the motion.

“The humerus is divided at mid-shaft. New bone caps, still cartilaginous. That gives the limb a hinge where a man has none. Scapula has been perforated and reset forward. Three accessory sockets. It can brace sideways, climb downward, or fold through a space narrower than its shoulders. The ribs were pried outward from inside. Not broken. Spread. The intercostal muscles have been threaded to hold the cage open. The pleural cavity is no longer a lung space. It is a chamber.”

She touched the wire to the gap. Black water slid over the hook, thick as oil.

“Smell,” she said. “Correctly. Pond silt. Copper. Sweet rot under it, the kind that starts in fruit left too long in a closed room. Ammonia. Wet wool. Yeast. When the threads break, it sharpens—hot metal, like a coin held in the mouth during a storm. If you smell that on a living person, they are already part of the cellar.”

The mouth opened another fraction. Halloway did not admire it.

“How far it got. Entry through a wound or mucous membrane. Probably hand or face. It avoided blood at first. Blood alarms the body and carries heat too fast. It used fascia, lymph, nerve sheaths. It reached the spinal canal and took the brainstem, not the cortex. The man is not driving. The brainstem is being borrowed to keep the pumps running. What it took: autonomy, pain modulation, speech, memory. What it left: heartbeat, breath, swallow, and enough spinal reflex to make the meat useful. Heart encased in thread-net. Lungs still inflate, but the pleura is lined. Diaphragm is a bellows for warmth and spores. Liver tapped for nutrients. Kidneys for mineral. Gut still attached, but it is processing reserve, not meal. Fat, glycogen, some muscle. Bones are being resorbed and rebuilt where the colony needs leverage.”

A sac bulged beneath the cut, pale and taut, with something curled inside.

“That is a brood unit. Not a maggot. Not a worm. A node. Cut one free and it seeks warmth. Cut the cluster and the limb loses orders. Open the chest and the nodes get air, heat, and your face.”

The second arm shifted under the water, dragging against the floor.

Halloway saw the movement and named it without drama.

“Contralateral bracing. It has crossed the midline. The colony is coordinating both sides. Standing is minutes, not hours.”

The first cut began to close. Threads pulled the skin edges together like coarse sutures. Halloway stabbed once through the knot, severing them. The creature’s jaw widened, and a sound came from the rib chamber: a wet, multi-toned click, as if many small mouths were testing the air.

“Thirteen teeth visible,” she said. “Odd. Growth. Still not a man with a bad mouth. Still a house with a leak.”

The smell thickened, hot and mineral.

“If you cannot open another one, read the outside. Skin too smooth, too damp, no proper rigor. Joints bending away from load. Ribs flared. Shoulders moving before the head. Mouth late. Black string from wounds. Water that ripples toward the same place twice. And the smell: cellar, copper, sweet rot, yeast. If all four are present, do not ask whether it was someone. Ask where it can reach.”

The thing lifted.

It came up on the new shoulder braces first, torso rising from the water in a slow, wrong unfolding. The rib cage opened fully above the surface. Inside, black fluid swirled around pale sacs, pulsing in staggered sequence. The pinned leg dragged free, then found the cellar floor.

Halloway stepped back one pace, enough to keep her boots out of the deepest water, and set the blade across her forearm.

“That is how far it got,” she said. “To standing. To targeting. To being less corpse and more nest with leverage.”

Its fingers spread.

Halloway’s voice went flat and final.

“Fingers lead. It has chosen something specific. The split at the shoulder is still soft. Iron there, if there is iron. If not, take the neck at the collarbone and do not let it close distance. And when it screams like the man it used to be—” A dry pause. “That is not a soul asking for help. That is a lure with a throat.”

The creature’s head turned toward the light.

Halloway did not look at the face. She looked at the shoulder branch, at the threads knitting and pulling beneath the wax-pale skin.

“Now,” she said. “Tell me what moves first.”

rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway heard the order from the dry stone above her and did not mistake it for courage. Courage was what men called duty when it had not yet been billed.

“Finish it,” she said. “Comfortable phrase. Holds no water.”

The creature had nearly risen. The right shoulder stood higher than the left, the skin over it drawn into a clean, terrible ridge where the threads had braided themselves into a cable. The left arm, half-cut and still twitching, lay across the water with the useless confidence of a limb that had been promised work. The rib cage opened above the surface like a cabinet displayed for buyers. Inside, black fluid moved in slow, deliberate circles around pale sacs.

Halloway did not look at the face. Faces asked for sympathy, and sympathy made hands slow.

She stepped into the deeper water.

Cold closed over her boots, her ankles, the lower calves. It was honest cold, cellar cold, the sort that told a woman where she stood and how long she had before her legs began lying to her. She kept her centre low, blade angled along her forearm, hooked wire in the other hand.

“Right,” she said, mostly to the thing. “You’ve had your lesson. Let’s see if you learned it.”

The mouth opened farther.

Not wide. Wide enough.

Dark water strung from the swollen lips, then crawled back toward the throat. The jaw hinges shifted independently, one side lifting a fraction before the other, as if the colony were testing which hinge it preferred. Halloway counted without admiration.

“One, three, five, seven—”

The teeth were pale, uneven, set in gums that had once belonged to a man who brushed them or did not, depending on his habits and his hope of living long enough to matter.

“—nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen.” She withdrew the wire from the shoulder knot with a small, practical shake. “Odd. Still growing. Still rude.”

The creature’s left hand jerked.

Not toward Halloway.

Toward the light.

The too-long fingers spread on the stair-edge below the lamp, scraping stone with a sound like nails being taught a new trade. Water ran off them in thin sheets. The bunching threads at the cut shoulder tried to knit, black strands reaching across the wound with the patient stupidity of roots finding manure.

Halloway moved before the arm could decide whether it wanted heat or flesh.

She put the hooked wire into the right shoulder not with a thrust but with the flat patience of a woman opening a stuck drawer. The hook found the accessory groove behind the collarbone, the false socket the colony had carved for leverage. She leaned back.

The scapula came forward with a sound like a knuckle cracked in cold tallow.

The creature folded sideways.

Water burst outward in a low, heavy wave. The right arm lost its brace and swung, not in pain—pain was a language the colony had stopped speaking—but in correction. Halloway stayed inside the swing. Outside it, the arm would have found the stairs. Inside it, it found only her blade.

She cut.

Short strokes. Not hacking. Hacking was for doors and men who had never paid for a funeral. She separated the main cable from the bone spur with three precise strokes, each one releasing a thin spray of black fluid that hissed where it met the water. The threads curled away from the steel, then tried to return, then thought better of it.

The right arm went slack.

“Good,” Halloway said. “Now you have two disappointing limbs and one opinion.”

The jaw snapped.

It came down where her shoulder had been a half-second earlier. Halloway had moved because thirty years had taught her that predators aimed at the story they wanted, not the body they had. The teeth closed on water and the echo of a woman who had not been there.

The rib chamber clicked.

Not one mouth. Many.

The sound rose from the opened cage, wet and arrhythmic, like small bones learning speech from the wrong end. The pale sacs inside pulsed in staggered sequence. One near the sternum bulged, then settled. Another tightened into a knot and released.

Halloway’s expression did not change.

“Still furnishing,” she said. “No taste.”

The left hand dragged upward, fingers hooking the stair-edge again. The body rocked, trying to convert damage into leverage. The legs beneath the water shifted, joints unlocking in sequence. The cellar floor scraped.

It was still trying to stand.

Halloway stepped onto the creature’s thigh.

Not gracefully. Grace was for women with fewer enemies and better shoes. She put one boot on the bent knee, the other on the outer shelf of the ribs—careful of the chamber, careful of the gap—and used the height to get behind the right shoulder. The water pulled at her boots like cold hands. The creature’s skin under her foot was slick, wax-pale, and warm in the wrong places.

Nest-warm.

Not blood-warm.

She found the nape with her free hand. The head was useless already, the brainstem relay half-cut, but the colony kept the skull attached because heads contained senses and senses contained opportunities. Beneath the skin at the base of the skull, the threads made a braid around the first vertebra. That braid was the last courtesy the colony paid to the man’s own nervous system: it let the head hang, blink, and scream.

Halloway slid the blade under the braid and lifted.

The head went slack.

The body did not.

“Of course not,” she said. “You were never a body. You were a committee.”

She dropped from the shoulder to the water beside the creature’s flank, keeping the blade low. The left arm still twitched, fingers flexing without direction. The right hung loose, the cut cables drifting like seaweed in a current. The rib cage remained open, black fluid sloshing inside with a thick, living rhythm.

Now the chamber.

Halloway hooked the lower edge of the peeled ribs with the wire. The bones gave with a slick, internal creak. Not broken. Spread. The intercostal muscles had been threaded to hold the cage open, each strand anchored to pale sacs along the inner wall. She pulled outward, not enough to tear the chest wide, only enough to make a door.

The smell changed.

Pond silt. Copper. Yeast. Sweet rot. Beneath it, the hot-penny stink of disturbed thread.

Halloway turned her face aside and breathed through her mouth.

“If you value the lining of your lungs,” she said, voice flat, “stand upwind.”

She put the blade into the chamber.

Not deep. Deep was for men who liked surprises. She laid the edge flat inside the opened cage and raked across the lining, severing the supply threads that fed each node. The sacs bucked. Black fluid ran over the blade in strings. One pale knot near the sternum burst with a sound like a green walnut under a boot, and from it spilled a cluster of smaller threads, writhing, blind, seeking warmth.

Halloway stamped them into the water.

They slowed in the cold, then turned toward the creature’s leg.

“Not today,” she said.

She worked around the chamber with methodical hatred. Not rage. Rage made cuts sloppy. She severed the anchoring threads at the left rib fan, then the right. She crushed the mature sacs along the inner wall with the pommel of the blade when the edge would not reach without opening the chest further. Each one yielded a thick, black bead that floated for a moment, then sank.

The heart remained.

It sat behind the sternum, wrapped in a net of black fibre, beating in the wrong rhythm. Too fast. Too patient. The colony had kept it because the heart carried food, heat, and excuse. Halloway found the great vessels where they entered the thread-knot, the place where the man’s own plumbing had been hijacked into service.

She cut the net.

The heart gave one last useful contraction.

Halloway drove the blade through the base of the organ and twisted once.

The beat stopped.

The rib chamber went still.

For three seconds, nothing moved.

Then the threads under the skin began to fail.

Not dramatically. Not all at once. They loosened. The dense plait at the left shoulder unravelled into separate strands, each strand losing its reason. The black cables along the arms drifted free. The sacs inside the opened cage collapsed into pale, wet grains. The mouth, which had been rehearsing expression, fell slack.

Halloway did not sheathe the blade.

She waited.

The water gave one small lap against the cellar wall. Ordinary water. Dead water. No ripple travelled beneath the skin. No thread turned toward the light. The creature’s head lolled against the opened ribs with the perfect indifference of meat.

“Still not beautiful,” Halloway murmured. “Hungry, though. That we knew.”

She hooked the wire under the creature’s jaw and lifted the face clear of the water.

The features were ruined, but not beyond reading. Swelling had erased the nose, drawn the lips back, pushed the eyes into dark slits. The skin had the colour of candle wax left too near a fire. Beneath the jaw, the throat showed the old landmarks: hyoid, thyroid cartilage, the ghost of a man’s voice box. Halloway pressed the wire against the side of the neck and felt for the pulse that was not there.

None.

She moved to the hands.

The left hand had been a worker’s hand before the colony edited it. Callus across the palm. Short, ragged nails. The fingers were too long now, doubled at wrong joints, but the nail beds still told the older story. The right hand had an old break at the ring finger, set badly and healed thick. A band of cheap gold rode loose on the fourth finger, dented but not removed.

Halloway looked at it for one measured second.

“Married,” she said. “Or vain enough to wear metal into a cellar.”

She released the hand and let it fall back into the water. Sentiment was a knife with the edge turned inward. She had carried enough of those in thirty years to know how they cut.

The mouth still held the truth, if one knew how to ask.

Halloway inserted the wire between the jaws and eased them apart. The hinges resisted, then gave. The teeth showed in uneven rows. She counted again, slower.

Human canines, worn flat. A capped molar, tin bright under the filth. One incisor chipped old enough to have hurt. Behind the natural teeth, the colony had pushed extra points through the gums, pale and soft-rooted, not designed so much as encouraged.

“Seventeen total,” she said. “Thirteen human, four intruders. Odd count. Growth. No plan worth the name.”

She withdrew the wire and wiped it along the heel of her boot. The black thread clinging to the hook detached, slid into the water, and made for the creature’s leg with the last, pointless patience of a thing that had forgotten its master.

Halloway watched it go.

Then she put the blade through it.

The thread burst into a smear of oily darkness.

“Housekeeping,” she said.

She checked the rest of the body with the efficient contempt of a woman reading a bad ledger. The shoulders: split, capped, reinforced. The humeri divided at mid-shaft. The scapulae perforated and reset forward. The ribs pried outward from inside, the intercostal spaces threaded open. The pleural cavity no longer a lung space. A chamber. A nursery. A larder. The liver tapped for nutrients. The kidneys for mineral. The gut still attached, processing reserve rather than meal. Fat, glycogen, some muscle. Bones resorbed and rebuilt where the colony needed leverage.

The brainstem had been borrowed. The cortex composted.

Halloway nodded once, as if confirming a diagnosis she had already made in the stairwell.

“Someone wore this shape recently enough to have a name,” she said. “Something entered through a wound or a mouthful of wrong water. It colonised him. It softened the bindings, split the levers, opened the storehouse, and filled the cavity with its young. It kept the heart beating because the heart is a servant, not a master. It kept the lungs drawing because the lungs move heat, and heat is what the threads want.”

She looked at the opened rib chamber, at the pale grains floating in black fluid.

“Then it learned to stand.”

The cellar was quiet except for water.

Halloway climbed down from the creature’s flank and back to the stair, each step careful, each boot grinding faintly on the wet stone. The cold had soaked through her trousers and settled into her knees. She ignored it. Knees were negotiable. Dead things were not.

At the upper step, she set the blade against her hip and did not sheathe it. The steel was blackened with thread-fluid, and the edge still carried a faint, greasy shine. She tested it with her thumb. It took a shaving of skin without complaint.

“Good,” she said. “You behaved.”

She looked back into the cellar.

The body lay half-folded in the water, mouth open, ribs spread, head lolling. Without the colony’s coordination, it was only meat again. Worse than meat. Meat did not have spare joints.

Halloway began the boring part.

She took a length of cord from her belt, looped it around the creature’s left wrist, and hauled the arm clear of the stair-edge. The fingers dragged over stone, then hung limp. She tied the cord to the iron ring set in the wall above the waterline. Not to secure the body. To keep it from drifting into the steps and teaching the wood bad habits.

Then she checked the waterline.

The cellar had a drain at the far corner, half-submerged, crusted with silt. Halloway waded to it, blade low, and swept the hook through the grate. Black fluid eddied. Nothing moved against the current.

“No second tenant,” she said. “Lucky.”

Luck was a word hunters used when preparation had finished its work.

She returned to the body and searched the remains with the same clinical patience she brought to a wound. Shreds of canvas trousers. A belt with a brass hook. A coin worn thin in one pocket, the date illegible, the metal green with cellar damp. On the other side, a folded square of oilcloth, stiff with grime. Halloway opened it with the tip of the blade.

A man’s photograph, water-spotted. Face blurred, but the stance was ordinary. Shoulders squared. Chin lifted. The sort of pose men chose when they expected to live long enough to be vain about it.

Halloway looked at it for one second longer than necessary.

Then she folded the oilcloth and tucked it into her coat.

“Name later,” she said. “First, fire.”

She went back to the stair and gathered the tools that mattered: the hooked wire, the short blade, a tin of salt from the inner pocket, a stoppered vial of lamp oil she kept for emergencies and bad lighting. She poured a thin line of oil around the creature’s opened rib chamber, not over the body. Over the chamber. The black fluid inside resisted the oil at first, then accepted it with a slick, greedy sheen.

Halloway stepped back.

She did not strike a light yet. Light came after certainty.

“Now,” she said, voice flat and practical, “we burn the house down.”

She tossed the salt into the water first. It spread in a white film, dulling the black threads that still drifted near the drain. Then she touched flame to the oil line.

The cellar took the fire the way cellars do: reluctantly, then all at once.

Blue light crawled along the oil, found the chamber, and went up. The rib cage burned from the inside. Pale sacs popped in quick, wet succession. Black fluid boiled and steamed. The body arched once—not life, not protest, only gas expanding in sealed places—and then settled.

Halloway watched it burn with the steady attention of a woman counting coins.

When the flames died to a low, stinking hiss, she waited another ten seconds. Then twenty. Then she stepped forward with the hook and broke the charred rib cage open.

Inside, nothing moved.

The threads had curled into black beads. The sacs had burst into ash and grease. The heart was a lump of cooked meat wrapped in brittle fibre. Halloway stirred the remains with the hook, turning over fragments of bone, tooth, and cloth. She found three human teeth intact, one tin cap melted to a grey blister, and the gold band warped but whole.

She collected them in a linen square from her pocket.

“Evidence,” she said. “Also proof that people can be stupid enough to wear metal into a cellar.”

The smell was atrocious. Burned silt. Hot copper. Sweet rot turned acrid. Wet wool scorched. Halloway breathed through her mouth and kept working.

She checked the shoulders again. The new bone caps had cracked in the fire, exposing the soft centres. The accessory sockets were empty. The cable knots had burned to charcoal. She broke one open with the blade and found no movement inside.

“Colony dead,” she said. “Host dead. Chamber dead. Drain clear.”

She looked at the water.

It was still.

Not peaceful. Still. The difference mattered.

Halloway sheathed the blade at last. The steel made a small, honest sound against leather. She wrung the hem of her coat, sending dark water splashing onto the stair. Then she took the tin of salt and scattered a line across the top step, not for superstition, but because salt slowed what was left and reminded living things where the boundary was.

“Right,” she said. “That is the cellar finished.”

She turned toward the stairs.

The body burned in the water behind her, black and steaming, the opened ribs collapsed inward like a house after the roof has been taken. The cord at the wrist held. The drain gave up its last thin trickle. The lamp-light from above made a small, stubborn island on the wet stone.

Halloway climbed one step, then stopped.

Not because she was tired. Because she heard it.

A lap of water.

Not from the burning body.

From the far corner, beyond the drain.

Halloway’s hand went back to her blade.

“There,” she said quietly. “Of course there.”

She did not go closer. Not yet. She stood on the damp stair, water dripping from her coat, and listened to the cellar breathe.

The sound came again. Small. Obscene. Patient.

Something in the far water had not been in the chamber.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“Finish it,” she repeated, grimly amused. “Spoken like a man who has never had a cellar finish him first.”

She drew the blade.

“New rule,” she said. “The first house is always a warning. The second house is the neighbourhood.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
Auren had said her last on it — or thought she had. The formal words stopped her where she stood.

She turned back and faced Del fully, and after a moment she drew the blade again and held it low at her side, exactly as she had held it for the witnesses, because the form did not change for having been done once already.

"Properly asked," she said. "The witnesses heard it because the code requires witnesses. The second asks for it because the second stands in the dead man's place, and what is asked in his place must be answered in full — the first time, and the eleventh, and however many times it is asked after that. The account is owed. It is not performed once and spent."

Then she spoke it again, and she changed nothing. The words came in the same order, at the same pace, because a telling that varied from the first was not an account but a performance, and she had never performed it.

"Edrin Caul is dead by my hand, and this is the account of it.

"The fourth pass. He came in high, committed to the cut, and his front foot went half a hand's width on the wet stone. I did not beat his blade. I put mine where his line opened and let his own weight carry him onto it. The point entered below the fourth rib on his left side and travelled upward the length of my hand. It opened the lung. It cut the great vessel above the heart.

"He lived perhaps forty breaths after. He knew what had been done to him. He did not cry out. He asked me to finish it, and I told him the truth, that it was already finished. He died holding my sleeve, and I did not pull free.

"I claim no skill in the killing of him. His foot went and mine did not, and that is the whole of what separated us this morning."

She held Del's eye through the last of it, the way she had held the witnesses', because the second was owed the same unwillingness to look away.

"That is the account, whole and unsoftened. If you find it incomplete, say where it fails, and I will answer. If you find it complete, witness it — and then it will have been done in order, as it is written, and no one will be able to say it was done carelessly. Not his household. Not you, later, when you go over it in the dark, as you will."

The wind moved through the yard again. Auren waited, blade low, the crease still twisted in her sleeve, and gave no sign that the waiting cost her anything — though it had cost her something every one of the eleven times, and she had long since stopped expecting that to change.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren answered without hesitation, the way she answered everything that belonged to the account — as though the question had been standing in line all morning, waiting its turn.

"Here," she said, and set two fingers against her own chest, left side, a hand's width from the breastbone, just below the fourth rib. "Between the fourth rib and the fifth. It touched no bone. A point that meets bone turns, and then his weight would have meant nothing — it went between, clean, and that was the only clean thing in it."

She drew her fingers slowly upward along her own body, toward the hollow at the base of her throat, tracing the line the blade had taken in him.

"From there it travelled up, the length of my hand, at this angle. The lung first — the lower part of it — and then the great vessel above the heart. The artery that carries the blood out of it. Once that is open, the chest fills from the inside, and there is no hand that reaches it and no binding that holds it. A surgeon would tell you the same. I have it from eleven mornings instead."

She lowered her hand.

"You saw less blood on the stones than you expected. Most of it stayed inside him — that is how I knew the vessel went and not the lung alone. A lung wound brings blood to the mouth, and he had that. The rest never left his chest. I knew both before he finished speaking, and so did he, I think. Men who have fought long enough learn to read their own wounds. He read his correctly."

A pause, measured, because the next part belonged to the question whether Del had meant it to or not.

"It did not come out his back. It stopped where its work was done, and I withdrew it along the line it had made, because a blade pulled sideways tears, and tearing would have taken the forty breaths from him without giving him anything back. That is what I meant when I said there was no withdrawing it clean. Not the blade — the wound. There was no version of it that left him living, and I would not stand over a dying man and tell him otherwise."

She let that stand, then gave him the rest of it, because the where was incomplete without the why.

"His cut was high and fully committed, both arms up. A man cutting high opens his whole left side — the arm lifts the ribs like a gate. Then his foot went on the wet stone, and the slip turned him a quarter into my line, and his own weight carried him the rest of the way. My arm did not drive the point. It only held the door open. I have told you I claim no skill in it, and this is what that means, said plainly: any blade held steady in that line kills him. Mine happened to be the one held there."

The wind came through the yard again. Somewhere behind her the work went on, quietly, the way men work when they are grateful not to be the subject of the morning.

"His household will ask this. Not first — first they will ask whether he suffered, because that is what the living ask — but they will come to it, and I will answer them in these same words, and I will show them on my own body as I have shown you, because his wife should not have to imagine it wrongly. Imagined wounds are worse than true ones. I have stood at eleven doors, and I know."

She regarded Del steadily.

"Ask until there is nothing left to ask. That is what a second is for, and it is what the account is for. And when you are done asking — eat. The road does not shorten for grief."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren set the wineskin down.

"Precisely, then," she said, and gave it the way the code wanted it given — as mechanism, not moment.

"The blade first, because the blade is part of the answer. A yard of steel, two fingers wide at the guard, edged on both sides for the last half of its length. It is not a cutting sword. It is built to make a channel, and that is what it made."

She held up her free hand, fingers together, and walked the point of them up her own body as she spoke.

"His skin parted first — a mouth two fingers wide, lips clean, because a sharp edge under a man's own weight does not tear, it divides. Then the muscle between the ribs, which is thin there. Then the lining of the chest, which is thinner. Three resistances, in order, in less time than a word takes. My hand felt all three through the hilt. A duellist's hand learns to read steel the way a blind hand reads print, and mine read it correctly."

"Then the lung. The lower lobe of the left one. A lung is not a bag — it is a sponge, wet and close-grained, and a blade makes a slit in it, not a hole. The slit bleeds into itself and weeps air, and his breathing went wet on that side from that moment. That wound alone a man can carry for days. Some men mend from it. That was not the killing wound, and I have never called it one."

"Above the lung, the vessel. The great artery that leaves the heart carrying the whole of the body's blood at the heart's own pressure. The point opened its wall — a cut the width of the blade, no more. It did not need more."

She lowered her hand.

"That is what the blade did. Now what it did it to. From the moment the vessel opened, every beat of his heart drove blood into his chest instead of his body, and there is no hand that reaches it and no binding that holds it, because you cannot press on a wound inside the cage of the ribs. The left lung was crushed flat by the blood from without while it bled from within. The heart starved of the blood it was spending, and beat the faster for it, and spent it the faster — that is the arithmetic of the wound, and it is arithmetic, not malice. Forty breaths of it. He died of the vessel. The lung only made it audible."

A pause, measured, because the next part she had never said at a door, and she said it now without changing her voice.

"I will give you what is not in any surgeon's book, because the code says precisely and this is precise: when the point is in the great vessel, the blade carries the heartbeat. I felt his through the hilt — three beats, perhaps four, strong, then going thin — while I was still holding the steel and he was still standing on it. That is how I knew before he spoke that the vessel had gone and not the lung alone. The steel told me. I have never found a tactful way to say that, and I have stopped looking for one. Tact is a curtain, and the code forbids curtains."

"The blade came out the way it went in — along the channel, edges still. A blade turned on the way out tears, and tearing would have taken his forty breaths without giving him anything in exchange. I withdrew it in one motion and put my hand over the wound — not because it could help, it could not, but because a man should not have to watch his own blood leave him if a hand can cover the sight of it. That was not the code. That was mine."

She picked the wineskin up again but did not drink.

"You are right to press on it, and the code is right: precisely, not tactfully. Understand what the difference is for. Precision is owed to the dead — a man is entitled to have the thing that killed him named correctly, and 'run through' is not a name. And a precise account cannot grow in the telling. Rumour makes wounds wander; a wound spoken exactly stays where it was, and his family will need it to stay where it was. When Maren asks, I will answer to this same depth — to the depth of her question. I will not volunteer the heartbeat in the steel to a widow who has only asked whether he suffered. Precision answers the question asked. It does not go hunting for questions no one asked. That is not tact. That is aim."

She looked at Del evenly.

"You have now had it three ways — the what, the where, and the how — and they are one account, and it does not change. Ask it a fourth time on the road if you need to. It will be the same words. That is the use of a true one: it does not tire."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren walked on for three strides before she answered, and when she did, there was something in her voice that had not been there all morning — approval, or the nearest thing to it the day was going to carry.

"Properly asked. And understand that you have answered my question by refusing to answer it yet. You cannot say whether he suffered until you know what there was to suffer. That is the correct order, and I will honor it. All of it, then."

She did not draw the blade. The steel's part was done; the rest was hers.

"Forty breaths. I counted them. I have counted all eleven, because someone in the world should know the number, and it is the killer's work to know it."

"The first ten were strong. Wrong, but strong — deep, and wet on the left side from the first, because the slit lung weeps air and blood both. He was on his knees by then. His legs gave as I withdrew the blade; he caught my sleeve going down, and I went to one knee with him so that his grip would not have to hold his weight. My hand stayed over the wound. It changed nothing. It was never meant to change anything."

"The middle twenty were labor, and I will not call it anything else. The chest fills, the lung is crushed by the blood from without while it bleeds from within, and the body spends itself buying air it cannot keep. His breaths came faster, then shallower. The pulse in his throat raced, then fluttered, the way a flame does before it goes. The grey came up under his skin — lips first, then the hollows of his face. There was blood at his mouth, bright, from the lung. The vessel's blood never left his chest. I have told you that, and it remains true, and it is why the stones were not what you expected."

"His eyes stayed clear. That is the thing I will carry from this morning, if I carry one thing: he was present for the whole of it. I have seen men look inward, gone somewhere behind their own faces while the body finishes without them. He did not. He looked at me. I was the last thing he looked at, and I did not look away. That, too, is owed."

The bearers' tread kept its distance behind them, steady as a pulse. Auren did not turn.

"You asked what he said. I will give it to you as it was said, because last words are part of the account and paraphrase is a curtain. His first words were: *Finish it.* I told him the truth: *It is finished.* He took that the way he took everything that morning — he tested it. His hand went to his own chest, over mine, and he read himself the way men who have fought long enough learn to read. *The vessel,* he said. It was not a question, but I answered it as one: *Yes.* He nodded once, as if I had confirmed a passage of play. Then he said: *The stone was wet.*"

"That was the whole of his account of his own death, and it was accurate, and I told him so. Even the dying make their accounting, Del. His was four words long and there was not an error in it."

She walked a dozen strides in silence then, and the silence was not for effect — it was the space the next part required, and she gave it exactly that and no more.

"The last ten breaths, the pauses open between them. A breath, and then a longer nothing, and then another breath, and each one after a pause comes as a surprise to everyone but the dying man, who is past surprise. Somewhere in the last five, he tried to speak again. His eyes were on mine and he shaped the beginning of a word — her name, I believe, or the beginning of something meant for her — and the breath it rode on was the one that did not come back."

"What he meant to say, no one living knows. I will not guess at it. A guess would be a comfort, and comfort is a curtain, and the code forbids curtains. If Maren asks me whether he spoke of her, I will tell her the truth: he tried to. The trying is what there is. In my experience of eleven doors, the trying is not nothing to a widow. It is not enough, either. It is what there is."

"You asked what it looked like at the end. The last breath went out of him and did not come back, and I knew it was the last not by the stillness but by the eyes. They do not close — that is songs. They stop being looked out of. The light does not go; the looking goes. I have seen it eleven times and cannot say it plainer than that. His hand did not tighten at the end — that is songs as well. It opened, finger by finger, as the strength left it, and the crease it left in my sleeve is the one I am still wearing."

"I stayed the count of ten more, to be certain, because the code requires certainty and so did he. Then I closed his eyes. That is not in the code. That was mine. I lifted my hand from the wound and raised it, and the witnesses came forward. The dying is the duellist's; the death is everyone's. That is the form."

"It looked like work, Del. That is the honest answer. It looked like a man laboring, and then it looked like a man set down by his labor when the labor was done. I will not call it peaceful — *peaceful* is a curtain. It was not ugly. It was the arithmetic finishing itself, and a man declining to complain while it did."

She glanced at Del then, sidelong, without breaking her pace.

"Forty of his breaths. I have timed it since, without meaning to: the account of the wound, spoken at code pace, takes very nearly as long as his dying did. I have made nothing of that, except that it is so."

"Now you have all of it — the what, the where, the how, and the end. So I will ask you again, second, and this time you will answer from knowledge. She will ask whether he suffered. They always ask."

"What is your answer?"

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
The footsteps came unhurried — a woman answering a knock at mid-morning — and the door opened on Maren Caul with a drying-cloth still in her hand.

She knew. Auren had said they always knew, and Maren Caul was not the exception. It did not come into her face as surprise but as the end of hope, her eyes going from Auren's face to the blade at her hip, to Del at her shoulder, to the crease twisted in the dark wool of Auren's sleeve, and back again. The cloth stopped moving. Behind her, the house's morning was still intact — a fire, the smell of oats, a girl's voice somewhere upstairs, singing to itself.

"Maren Caul," Auren said. "I am Auren. Your husband Edrin is dead by my hand this morning, lawfully met, and I have come to give you the account of it, if you will hear it."

One breath, whole. Maren did not fall. She went still in the way of a woman holding a house together with her body, and her hand found the doorframe.

"If I will hear it," she repeated. Nineteen years, and it was the one choice left to her; she took it the way her husband had taken his wound — she tested it first. "And if I will not?"

"Then I leave word where I can be found, and his friends carry him to his door, and I do not trouble you again unless you send for me."

"Where is he?"

"At the bend of the lane, in the care of four men who knew him, covered in a good cloak. He does not come to his door until you know what is coming to it."

Something in that reached her — that he was near, and had been kept from coming home as rumour. "I will hear it," she said, and stepped back from the door, which was the only invitation the code required.

The girl came halfway down the stairs at the sound of strangers — nine years old, her father's chin — and Maren sent her up again, gently, with a reason about porridge that they both knew was not the reason. The door upstairs did not quite close. The boy came instead: fourteen, his father's build beginning in his shoulders, and he put himself between Auren and his mother in the kitchen doorway and would not be sent anywhere, and Maren did not send him. Auren had predicted all of it, and softened her face at none of it.

Inside, then. Maren stood at the table, the cloth still in her hand, and Auren faced her squarely, as she had faced the witnesses, and gave it the way the code wanted it given — the name before everything.

"Edrin Caul is dead by my hand, and this is the account of it.

"The fourth pass. He came in high, committed to the cut, and his front foot went half a hand's width on the wet stone. I did not beat his blade. I did not need to. I put mine where his line opened and let his own weight carry him onto it. The point entered below the fourth rib on his left side and travelled upward the length of my hand. It opened the lung. It cut the great vessel above the heart. There was no withdrawing it clean, and I did not pretend otherwise to him.

"He lived perhaps forty breaths after. He knew what had been done to him — I have seen men who did not know, and he was not one of them. He did not cry out. He asked me to finish it, and I told him the truth, that it was already finished. He set his hand to his own chest, over mine, and read his wound the way men who have fought long enough learn to read, and he named it: the vessel. He was right. His own account of his death was four words long — *the stone was wet* — and there was not an error in it. He died holding my sleeve, and I did not pull free.

"I claim no skill in the killing of him. His foot went and mine did not, and that is the whole of what separated us this morning. If any dispute the account, I will answer. It has been witnessed, and found complete."

The fire settled. Upstairs, floorboards held their silence. Del witnessed it aloud — the voice unsteady, the words whole, and whole was what was needed — and Maren looked at the second standing where she could see him, the living proof that someone had stood for Edrin at the end of it, and whatever she found there, she accepted with a single nod.

"Did he suffer?" They always asked first.

"He labored," Auren said. "I will not call it peaceful — peaceful is a word for songs, and you are owed the truth. Forty breaths of work, and he did the work without complaint. He was not frightened. Frightened men do not audit their own deaths; your husband named his wound correctly and accounted for himself in four words. And he was not alone. My hand was over the wound and my eyes were the last thing he looked at, and I did not look away. That can be witnessed. It has been."

"Did he speak of us?" Her voice did not break on it; she had clearly decided it would not. "Did he say anything — for us?"

"His words were for his death, and I have given them to you exactly. At the end he tried to speak again. He shaped the beginning of a word — your name, I believe — and the breath it rode on did not come back." Auren did not soften it, because softening was the dishonour. "What he meant to say, no one living knows, and I will not guess. A guess would be comfort, and comfort is a lie told to the grieving. The trying is what there is. It is not enough. It is what there is."

Maren closed her eyes then, and two tears got free of her anyway, and she did not wipe them. "The trying," she said, and said nothing more for a moment, and the boy stared at Auren with his fists clenched and managed perhaps half of his hatred before the rest of it went somewhere else.

"Why—" Maren began, and stopped, and made herself finish. "Why did you fight him?"

"The quarrel was lawfully met and fairly answered. It died in the yard. I will not lay it on you."

"How tidy," Maren said, with the first anger in it, which was better than the stillness, and Auren received it without defending herself.

"You may hate me for that. It changes nothing I owe you."

Maren looked at her for a long moment, and then her eyes went, as they had kept going all along, to the crease in the dark wool. "Is that—"

"His grip, as he left it. I have not straightened it. I thought you should see it before it was laundry."

Maren crossed the room and touched the crease once, with two fingers, the way one touches a relic, and then stepped back and folded her hands and was a widow with a household again.

"Bring him home," she said.

"I will go and fetch your husband now," Auren said, and turned for the door.

Which was when Tam — who could not reach Auren, and had known it all along — rounded on the one he could reach, fists white, voice breaking, and demanded of Del: "You stood for him. That's what a second does. So tell me — did my father die well?"

rows.reply:
Auren did not bridle at the correction. Precision was the code’s mercy, and she had never mistaken gentleness for honor.

She looked toward the witnesses, then back to the place where the dead man lay, and made her voice as plain as steel.

“My blade entered beneath his left ribs,” she said. “It passed upward through his chest and pierced the heart. The heart was opened by the point. He died from that wound.”

She let the words stand without ornament.

“The blade did that,” she said. “It did it to the man who faced me in fair exchange.”

rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren looked at Del without flinching, because the question was part of the accounting and she had never refused the accounting its due.

“The point entered beneath the left ribs,” she said. “Low, under the line of the guard. It passed upward through the chest and struck the heart. There was no second wound, and no other blow.”

Her voice remained level, exact, and unadorned.

“He died of that wound alone. That is where it landed.”
