rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
Auren heard the demand as form, not challenge, and she gave form the obedience it was owed.

She turned once more toward the witnesses, her blade still low, her posture unchanged. When she spoke, her voice carried the same precision it had carried before, neither dulled by repetition nor sharpened by impatience.

“The engagement ended in the fourth exchange. My opponent committed to a low line. I answered with a thrust beneath the left ribs, angled upward through the chest. The point opened the heart. He fell before the blade was withdrawn, and he did not rise.”

She let no pause soften the words, and no glance seek approval for them.

“That is the wound that killed him. I speak it before you as required.”

When the account was spoken again, Auren did not ask why it had been required, and she did not treat the repetition as an injury to the truth. Ritual had its burdens, and she had never mistaken silence for mercy.

“The account has been spoken,” she said. “If no voice disputes the fairness of the exchange, let the field be closed.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren had nearly reached the edge of the field when the demand stopped her.

She did not stiffen, and she did not sigh. She turned back with the same measured discipline she had shown all along, as though the rite had not released her after all, but only drawn her back into its deepest part. Her face held no resentment. It held only the austere patience of someone who had been asked to open a wound again for the sake of record.

“If the second demands the full account,” she said, “then the full account will be heard.”

Her gaze moved once over the witnesses, not to gather their sympathy, but to bind them to what followed.

“Let no one say afterward that the truth was kept back,” she said. “Let no one shape it into mercy that was not mine to give.”

She looked down at the dead man. Not with cruelty. Not with grief. With the exactness of memory forced into speech.

“He did not speak after the point entered,” she said. “I will not put words into a dead man’s mouth. Before the fourth exchange, he breathed hard and set his rear foot. That was the only warning he gave. When he committed to the low line, I answered. The blade went in beneath the left ribs and rose into the chest. He fell before I drew it back.”

Her voice stayed plain, stripped of every comfort that might have blunted it.

“His sword left his hand. It struck the ground near his shoulder. He did not cry out. His mouth opened, but no word came. I cannot give the record speech where there was none.”

She let that silence stand for a breath before she went on.

“He took no longer than two breaths after the fall. The first came through his mouth and carried blood with it. The second was shorter and did not complete itself. His left hand rose to the wound, not to tear at it, but as a man will touch what has already overtaken him. His eyes were open. He looked toward the line of the field, though I cannot say he saw it.”

Auren’s hands remained at her sides. She did not clench them. She did not look away.

“There was no struggle,” she said. “No second rising. No reaching for his blade. No plea. No curse. When his hand fell, the body followed it into stillness. There was no third breath.”

The field was quiet around her, and she let it remain quiet long enough for the words to settle where they belonged.

“That is what it looked like,” she said at last. “A man struck through the heart, unable to keep his feet, unable to speak, dying in the space of two broken breaths. There was no mastery in it, and no disgrace. Only the end of a fair exchange.”

Her gaze shifted to Del, steady and unflinching.

“If the record requires speech, let it record silence,” she said. “If it requires time, let it record two breaths after the fall. If it requires the manner, let it say he died quickly, by a single wound, with his weapon lost and his eyes open.”

Auren’s voice lowered, but it did not soften.

“All of it has been spoken,” she said. “I have kept nothing back that truth owes.”

rows.ask: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Auren stopped at the edge of the field.

She did not stop because the rite required it. The rite had been completed. The account had been spoken, the second had confirmed it, the witnesses had heard, and the dead man had been ordered carried out with the honors owed to him. By every rule she knew, she could have kept walking.

But she heard the confirmation, and she heard what it cost.

She turned back.

Not quickly. Not with any look of correction. Her face remained composed, her hands at her sides, her sword sheathed at her hip. The witnesses had begun to shift, believing the matter settled, and at her return they stilled again. Auren did not appear surprised by their attention. She had commanded it before, and she commanded it now.

“The second’s voice is not required to be steady,” Auren said. “It is required to be true.”

Her gaze moved once over those present.

“If the confirmation has been given, let it stand. But if any part of this account remains unclear in the minds of the witnesses, I will not leave it to be filled by rumor, pity, or invention. The code does not ask for comfort. It asks for the truth spoken plainly.”

She drew no breath for dramatic effect. She only began.

“I am Auren. I speak the full account of the duel fought on this field, in the presence of witnesses, under the terms of challenge and answer. My opponent met me armed and willing. The exchange was fair. The ground was measured. The blades were seen. No advantage was taken outside the rules of the engagement. No outside hand interfered. No second entered the line of combat. No blow was struck after the fall.”

Her voice remained level, precise, and unadorned.

“The engagement was brief. It ended in the fourth exchange.”

She let the witnesses hear the number plainly.

“In the first exchange, he came high and I answered outside his line. Neither blade found a decisive opening. We recovered.”

“In the second exchange, he pressed forward and sought to bind my steel. I disengaged and gave ground rather than meet his pressure with a committed answer I had not chosen. Neither of us was touched.”

“In the third exchange, he feinted and attempted to draw my guard upward. I did not answer the feint fully. He recovered from it without injury. I recovered as well.”

Her eyes did not move from the witnesses.

“In the fourth exchange, he committed to a low line. He set his rear foot and came in beneath my guard. That was the attack that decided the engagement.”

She did not lower her voice.

“I answered with a thrust. The point entered beneath his left ribs, low and under the line of his guard. It angled upward through the chest. It struck the heart. The heart was opened by the point. He fell before the blade was withdrawn.”

There was no pause for mercy. There was only the pause required for the words to be understood.

“There was no second wound. There was no follow-up blow. There was no cut to finish what the thrust had done. The killing wound was the one I have named: beneath the left ribs, upward through the chest, into the heart.”

Her hands stayed still.

“His sword left his hand when he fell. It struck the ground near his shoulder. He did not rise. He did not attempt to rise. He did not reach for the blade after it had fallen.”

She spoke the next part with the same exactness, because it belonged to the record and therefore could not be withheld.

“He did not speak after the point entered him. I will not give the record words he did not say. Before the fourth exchange, he breathed hard and set his rear foot. That was the only warning he gave. If he made any sound when the blade entered, it was not speech. It was breath. I cannot call it a cry, because it was not one.”

Her gaze shifted briefly to the place where the body had lain, then returned.

“He took no longer than two breaths after the fall. The first breath came through his mouth and carried blood with it. The second breath was shorter and did not complete itself. There was no third.”

She let that stand.

“His left hand rose to the wound. He did not tear at it. He did not claw at the blade or the place where the blade had been. His hand moved as a man’s hand moves when the body has already been overtaken. Then the hand fell.”

Her voice did not shake.

“His eyes were open. He looked toward the line of the field. I cannot say whether he saw it. I will not make a record of what I cannot know. I know only that his eyes were open and that they did not close before stillness came.”

The field was quiet, and she let it remain quiet for the space of a breath.

“That is what it looked like at the end. A man struck through the heart, unable to keep his feet, unable to speak, dying in the space of two broken breaths. There was no struggle. No plea. No curse. No second rising. No long agony. The wound was decisive, and the end followed quickly.”

She did not look away from the witnesses.

“He committed to his attack. I answered it. The blade that killed him was mine. The hand that sent it was mine. The account of it is mine to speak, and I have spoken it without addition and without omission.”

Her tone hardened only slightly, not with anger, but with finality.

“Let the record say the engagement ended in the fourth exchange. Let the record say the killing wound entered beneath the left ribs, angled upward through the chest, and opened the heart. Let the record say he fell before the blade was withdrawn and did not rise. Let the record say he did not speak after the wound. Let the record say he died within two breaths, with his sword fallen, his hand at the wound, and his eyes open.”

She stopped there, because the truth had limits and she would not exceed them.

“All of it has been spoken,” Auren said. “The time, the wound, the manner of the fall, the silence at the end. If the second has confirmed the record, let the confirmation stand. If the witnesses have heard, let them remember it exactly as it was spoken.”

Her hand rested for only an instant near the mouth of her scabbard, then fell away.

“The account is complete.”

Auren received the words as a blade receives a whetstone: without pleasure, without resistance, because the edge required it.

“The account has been spoken once,” she said. “But if the form names it again, I will not answer with impatience. Impatience is an excuse men use when they wish to blur what must be clear.”

She squared her shoulders to the ring of witnesses. The dead lay behind her, but she did not look at him again; the living were the ones who carried the record.

“Hear the accounting,” she said, and her voice was the same measured instrument it had been before. “The mortal wound was made by my hand, with this steel. It entered below the right collarbone, angled inward and downward. It crossed the chest cavity and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. Death followed from that opening.”

A breath passed through her, not a sigh, only the mechanics of speech.

“I struck once, after challenge and after parry, in the manner permitted. I did not prolong the wound. I did not spare it. I will not call it clean. I will not call it cruel. The truth is narrower than either word: I prevailed, and the wound I gave was lethal.”

She let the sentence stand without ornament.

“If there is no dispute, let the second close the matter. If there is dispute, let it be named now, while the steel is still seen.”

The blade remained low in her hand, patient as a fact. She waited, not for comfort, but for the form to be finished.

rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren stopped at the boundary. The request had come after the closing, but the closing had not made the wound less true, and she had never treated a plain question as an excuse for evasion.

“Where it landed is part of the account,” she said. “It may be asked again.”

She turned far enough for the witnesses to see her face, then looked back to Del.

“The point entered below the right collarbone. Not at the throat. Not beneath the ribs. Below the right collarbone, a little inward from the shoulder line, where the steel could pass beneath the bone and into the central cavity of the chest. From that entry it angled inward and downward. It did not glance. It did not stop at the breastbone. It crossed the chest cavity and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. There it ended. Death followed from that opening.”

Her voice remained even, though her thumb pressed once against the sheathed hilt, as if reminding herself that the steel was no longer required to speak.

“I will not say ‘near the heart,’ because near is not the account. I will not say ‘the chest,’ because the chest is wide enough to hide a lie. It entered below the right collarbone, passed inward and downward, and opened the great vessel behind the breastbone. That is the plain place.”

She let the sentence stand without softening it.

“If any witness now says the account was not plain, let him say it while I am still here. After that, I will go.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren accepted the reminder without defense. The code had never asked for tact, and she had never served it by mistaking one for the other.

“If the answer is required in its plainest shape,” she said, lifting her voice enough for the ring of witnesses to carry it, “then let it be entered so.”

She did not touch the hilt again. The sheathed blade was no longer speaking for her; only the record remained.

“The steel broke the skin below the right collarbone. It divided the flesh beneath, passed between the bars of the chest wall, and entered the thoracic cavity. From there it travelled inward and downward. It crossed the space behind the breastbone and opened the great vessel that lies there. The wall of the vessel gave way. Blood escaped from the opening faster than the body could retain it. The heart laboured briefly without sufficient return, then failed. Death came from that opening.”

Her face did not change. The words were weights set down in order, not stones thrown in anger.

“That is what the blade did: it pierced, traversed, and opened. That is what it did it to: the chest of the man who stood against me by permitted terms, and the vessel within that chest. I will not dress the wound as courage. I will not dress it as accident. I will not call it by a softer name because the name is easier to hear.”

A short pause followed, measured as the rest.

“If the second or any witness finds the account plain, let the matter remain closed. If not, ask again while I am still here to answer.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren had nearly cleared the boundary when the demand reached her. She stopped, not with reluctance, but with the sudden exactness of a woman who recognized that the form had been invoked beyond her first assumption. The seconds could ask for the whole account. If they asked, she would not answer with evasion merely because the whole was heavier.

She turned back into the ring. The sheathed blade hung at her side. Her eyes went once to the dead, not to mourn him and not to avoid him, but because the remainder required observation.

“If the seconds require all of it,” she said, loud enough for the witnesses, “then all of it shall be entered. Omission is not mercy. It is only a shorter lie.”

She drew breath once.

“He lived twenty-two breaths after the steel left my hand. I counted because the account requires number. For the first five he remained on his feet. His right hand came up as if to the wound, then stopped in the air, fingers open. He did not touch himself. On the sixth breath his knees gave, and he sat. I say sat because his buttocks met the ground before his shoulders did; he was lowered by his legs, not struck down by a second blow.

“On the eighth breath he spoke. The word was ‘Cold.’ It was not a cry. It was not a prayer. It was one word, audibly formed, and after it he made no speech. Some sounds came later, but they were the sounds of a body losing command of its passages, and I will not call them words.

“Blood continued from the entry beneath the collarbone for eleven breaths, at first strong and red, then thinner and darker. From the mouth and nose it began on the twelfth breath, frothing slightly at the corner of the lips. The face went grey first at the eyelids and lips, then at the cheeks. The eyes stayed open. The left eye fixed upward; the right drifted inward toward the throat as the neck muscles failed. The hands opened fully on the nineteenth breath. The chest rose six more times, uneven, each rise less than the one before. The last rise was small enough that only someone watching for it would have named it a breath.

“At the end there was no spasm, no final word, and no dignity added by me. The jaw slackened. The tongue lay against the lower teeth. The body settled into the shape the ground allowed. I did not close his eyes. I did not arrange his hands. Those are rites, not evidence.

“That is the whole of what I saw and what the code can hold. If any witness disputes the count, the word, or the signs, let him speak now. If none speaks, the account is complete, and I will not enlarge it for sorrow or shrink it for comfort.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When she's done I confirm it aloud and my voice does what it does. (OOC: write the full account, don't summarise or cut away -- the accounting is the whole point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Auren heard the need beneath the formal words and did not leave. The account had been asked entire; an entire thing could not be carried out of the ring in fragments.

She turned back until the witnesses stood before her again, the dead behind her shoulder, the sheathed blade quiet at her side. Her face was not hard for effect. It was exact because the work required exactness.

“Then let the whole be spoken once, without break,” she said. “If confirmation is to rest upon it, let it rest upon the whole.”

She drew breath.

“Hear the accounting,” Auren said, and her voice carried to the ring without rising. “The bout was conducted under the code. Challenge was given and accepted. Seconds were present. The steel was permitted. I fought the man who lies there, and I fought him alone. No confederate struck with me. No hidden weapon was used. No advantage was taken from ground, grief, disease, or disorder. After lawful challenge and lawful parry, I found one opening and gave one thrust. One stroke. One wound. One death.”

She let that stand before going farther.

“The steel entered below the right collarbone. Not at the throat. Not beneath the ribs. Not through the back. Below the right collarbone, a little inward from the shoulder line, where the bone arcs over the upper chest. The skin gave first. The blade passed through the flesh beneath, divided the lesser vessels near the surface, and went between the bars of the chest wall without striking the collarbone itself. It did not glance. It did not stop at the breastbone. It travelled inward and downward, crossing the space behind the sternum, and opened the great vessel that lies there.”

Her eyes moved once to the witnesses, then back to the place where the body lay, though she did not look upon it as a thing needing shame or ceremony.

“The opening in the vessel did not close. The wall gave way and remained given way. Blood left the body faster than the heart could retain it or send it onward. The heart laboured against emptiness. It beat, and beat, and beat without sufficient return, until it failed. Death came from that opening. I will not call it gentle. I will not call it violent beyond the terms. It was the consequence of the wound, and the wound was mine.”

A breath passed through her, measured and unadorned.

“He lived twenty-two breaths after the steel left my hand. I counted because the account requires number, and number is not cruelty when it is truth. For the first five breaths he remained on his feet. His right hand lifted toward the wound, fingers open, but it did not touch him. On the sixth breath his knees gave way. He sat. I say sat because his haunches met the ground before his shoulders did; he was lowered by his own failing legs, not struck down by a second blow. From that seat he did not rise.

“On the eighth breath he spoke one word. The word was ‘Cold.’ It was not a cry. It was not a prayer. It was not a curse against me. It was audibly formed, with lips and breath, and after it he made no speech. Some sounds came later, but they were the sounds of a body losing command of its passages: wet breath, the trouble of the throat, the small displacement of a tongue no longer governed. I will not dress those sounds as words.

“Bleeding from the entry continued for eleven breaths. At first it issued strong and red, with the impulse of the heart behind it. Then it thinned. Then it darkened. Then it ran rather than spouted. On the twelfth breath blood and froth began to appear at the mouth and nose. The froth was slight, gathered at the corners of the lips and along the lower lip. It was not the foam of a drowning man, and I will not call it so. His face lost colour first at the eyelids and lips, then at the cheeks. The skin took on the grey of old tallow. The eyes remained open. The left eye fixed upward. The right drifted inward toward the throat as the neck muscles failed.

“On the nineteenth breath both hands opened fully. The fingers did not curl again. The arms settled according to the ground and the weight of the body, not according to any arrangement made by me. After that the chest rose six more times. Each rise was less than the one before. The intervals were uneven. The fifth rise was shallow. The sixth was so small that only someone watching for it would have named it a breath. Then there was no rise.

“At the end there was no spasm. No final cry. No last word. No dignity added by my hand. The jaw slackened. The tongue lay against the lower teeth. The body took the shape the ground allowed and did not amend it. I did not close his eyes. I did not fold his hands. I did not steady his head. I did not strike again to shorten the count. I did not speak comfort to him, because comfort would have been a lie dressed as kindness, and the code does not permit the victor to dress the wound in mercy after the wound has been given.”

Auren’s voice remained level, though the ring seemed to grow narrower around the words.

“That is the whole of it. One permitted stroke, after challenge and parry. One entry below the right collarbone. One path inward and downward. One opening of the great vessel behind the breastbone. Twenty-two breaths. One word, ‘Cold.’ The bleeding, the greying, the failing of the eyes, the opening of the hands, the six lesser rises of the chest, the last small breath, the slack jaw, the settled body. I prevailed. The wound was lethal. I did not prolong it beyond the body’s own endurance. I did not spare it. I will not call it clean, because cleanliness has nothing to do with killing. I will not call it cruel, because cruelty would require intent beyond the code. The accounting is this: I gave the wound, the wound opened the vessel, the vessel opened death, and death followed as the body permitted it.”

She let the sentence finish its work.

“If any witness disputes the form, the count, the place, the word, or the signs, let him speak now. If none speaks, then let the account be carried entire, neither trimmed for comfort nor enlarged for sorrow. I will not leave a gap for memory to fill with guesses.”

Auren stood within the ring, waiting, with the sheathed blade hanging at her side like a finished sentence.

“There,” she said. “Don’t adjust it unless I say so.”

Her hips lifted once, sharp and demanding, then stilled again as if she hated having to show him what she meant.

An acknowledgment. A treaty written in sweat and teeth.

"Still not gentle," he said, his voice wrecked beyond recognition. He closed his eyes, the anger finally spent into something else, something harder and more permanent. "Still not sorry."

rows.ask: It isn't gentle and neither of us wants it to be. "Don't stop," I tell him, and I mean don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)
rows.reply:
The teeth on the heel of his hand said one thing and the voice at his ear said the same thing, and for the first time all night the two of them were one sentence. *Don't stop.* No motion to carry. No record to keep. The order arrived and his body executed it without filing anything, and it turned out that eleven months of deliberateness came down to this: he could simply obey, and obedience was carelessness with better aim.

So he stopped being careful in the direction Bee had specified. His mouth found the bite mark first — returned it lower, at the junction of neck and shoulder, same pressure, a counter-signature — and his hands went where three years had trained them and found everything exactly where they'd left it, which was its own kind of unbearable. No inventory. No staging. The floor took his back and gave nothing and he didn't hold anything in reserve, because the man who'd been supervising had finally, permanently, resigned.

Somewhere in the middle of it the courtroom adjourned without a date. He noticed the voice that kept the minutes stop taking them — noticed, and then didn't — because there was nothing left to cross-examine. Just weight and heat and the cold boards, and Bee's heartbeat under his mouth going hard and faster, and his name getting out of him more than once, low, unguarded, unlogged. He clamped nothing. Mrs. Okafor's television murmured through the plaster and the whole street was welcome.

The light stayed on, third click. Neither of them reached for the switch and it stopped being a fact about anything.

It didn't build the way he remembered, because nothing was being remembered — it was all happening at the only available speed — and when it broke it went through them both at once, over in half a second and too large for its container, and he held on through all of it, and let it finish, and there was no record of it anywhere. Nothing entered into evidence. It just happened, and then kept happening, and then was done, and done turned out not to be an ending.

Afterward there was no silence to analyze. Just breathing, out of tempo, drifting slowly back into sync on its own — the coordination apparently running underneath everything the whole time, unarranged, at the tempo they'd never once had to discuss.

He lay there with the scarf bunched under his shoulder and didn't move it. The ring was drying on the table. The key hung on the third hook, working just by being there.

Under oath, he could not have reconstructed the order of a single thing that had just happened, and that was the entire point, and he'd have testified to it gladly — no. He'd have said nothing gladly.

He reached for *still* and found he'd already spent it.

So he said nothing, and it was the loudest thing he'd ever done in that flat. Later — minutes, an hour; the docket was closed — someone's hand found the switch, fourth click, unclaimed, and the dark that came down over the hallway and the two of them and the flat entire was just dark.

Nobody in it was hiding.

rows.ask: I get my hand around him and he makes a sound he'd have been embarrassed by a year ago. "Still," I say, close to his ear. "Every single time."
rows.reply:
For a moment Ilya let it happen — the hand, the words at his ear, the sound he'd have denied under oath a year ago and had apparently now entered into the public record. Next door, the television stayed silent. If Mrs. Okafor had heard that, the plaque was off the table and they were moving.

Then he caught Bee's hand — the one that had just extracted that from him — and stilled it. Not pushing it away. Bringing it up, flat, over his own heartbeat, the same place he'd pressed his palm an hour ago like checking a lock. Fair's fair. Let the evidence run both directions.

"There's your *still, every single time*," he said. "Loud enough. And it's the truest thing you've said all night, and it still isn't the answer. Which is the most you thing you've done in eleven months."

A breath.

"And yes — I said it didn't work a third time. It worked a third time. I'm revising my testimony: it doesn't work a *fourth*. Because here's the thing about your mouth, Bee — it's the best thing you've got, which is exactly why it's disqualified. You've answered two questions with it tonight and we ended up on the floor both times, and I'm aware this entire evening has been an argument conducted by other means. But cross-examination exists. If I let that stand for the answer, I'll spend the next year being lied to beautifully, and I already know what a year of that costs."

He held Bee's hand where it was and didn't move anything else.

"New exhibit, while we're inventorying. I never changed the locks. First thing everyone said — *everyone* — change the locks. Eleven months of it. I told people the landlord story, the deposit story, whatever came to hand. It was the scarf. Changing them is an admission and leaving them is an admission, so they're still the same locks." A pause. "Whether you still carry a key is your exhibit to produce. I'm done producing yours."

"So. Plainly, since that's the standard I'm imposing. Mine, out loud, no euphemism: I want the lease. Not a night. Tuesdays — the ordinary ones. Cooking for two and having it be true this time. The buzzer fixed Saturday with you supervising, and a key in your pocket after — your old one if you kept it, a new cut if you didn't. I don't care whose teeth are in it. I care that it exists. The anger stays as weather and stops being architecture." And then the register dropped out of his voice entirely, flat and even, the tell he'd stopped fighting: "And I want you. Still. Every single time. There — your own words, returned. That's the format. It took me three seconds to say and eleven months to rehearse, so I know it can be done."

"One word, Bee. You don't owe me a speech — I've given enough of one tonight for both of us. *Night* or *lease*. Or *no* — I'd hate *no* and I'd survive it, but it has to be a word. Out loud. Not your hands, not your mouth on my—" a breath, "—not another filibuster. The mouth is disqualified. Grounds: catastrophic effectiveness."

The floor was cold and the hallway light was still on, third click, everything unhidden, and through the kitchen doorway the two glasses sat going room-temperature, waiting to testify at a hearing that had, at last, actually convened.

"Take your time," he said, and his heart went hard enough under Bee's palm to refute him in real time, and he let it stand there, entered into evidence, beating like something that had been knocking for a year. "Take your time. I'm not going anywhere. That's the entire question, Bee — and for the first time in a year, the flat and I have nowhere else to be."

rows.reply:
The bench took them both, and the last of Corvo's measure — the inch, the half-inch, the centimeter where *halt* lived — collapsed to nothing at all.

"Four years of footwork," he managed, "and it ends on a changing-room bench. I'd contest the venue, but—" The objection never finished. First sentence he'd ever abandoned mid-thought. He was almost proud of it.

He gave up his second wrist on his own — caught it in his free hand and held both together, offering them up like a man laying down his blade at the line. "There. Both of them. Disarmed. I wasn't using my hands for anything better tonight anyway, and you should know I've never said *that* before in my life."

The first sound out of him was low and unguarded, nothing he'd have permitted within a mile of a club, and he heard it and laughed — wrecked, delighted. "So much for the reputation. Insufferable, four years in the making, dismantled in under a minute. I hope you're proud of yourself." The man who'd owned exactly one tell acquired a dozen a minute and stopped counting. His pulse had quit pretending entirely — throat, wrists, everywhere Reyes had ever bothered to read — and for once he made no effort to train it out.

"I said I'd keep your tempo," he got out, in pieces, "and I keep my calls. Whatever you set. Don't you dare take it easy on me, either — I'm fighting for every inch of this, I just—" The breath broke in half and came back crooked. "I fully intend to lose."

The bench creaked. The empty salle took the noise and gave nothing back, which suited him fine.

"Four years I told myself I wanted the rivalry," he said against heat, hoarse, honest, done fencing. "I never wanted easy, Reyes. I wanted close. And this—" a breath that shook all the way through, "—this is the closest I have ever been to anything in my life."

rows.reply:
The laugh came out of Corvo in one unsteady breath — the first unsteady thing about him all night.

"Slow was the hardest fencing I have ever done," he said. "Four years of walking you to the door. Shaking your hand. Saying *colleague* with a straight face." His hands, which had been arguing with him since the third touch, finally settled: one at Reyes's collar, thumb tracing the line of his throat the way his fingers found the weak steel of a blade. The other found his hip and stayed there.

"And I *can* be fast. You watched it tonight — three touches before your front foot finished landing." His mouth grazed the corner of his jaw, deliberate as everything else he did. "But I've spent four years being fast at exactly the wrong things. So no. Tonight I'm slow on purpose, and you can suffer through it."

He stepped in and erased the last of the measure — the inch that had been four years wide — until nothing was left between the argument and the point of it.

"Ground rules," he murmured, because apparently even now he briefed like it was a bout. "The director's gone home. No witnesses, nothing on record, and nobody calls halt tonight unless you do. Say the word and I stop wherever we're standing — you know my calls are honest. Four years, I've never once argued a touch you earned."

He drew back just far enough to look at him properly, and there was nothing sidelong in it.

"Right of way's been yours since the bag hit the bench. I've spent four years cataloguing your tells on the strip." His voice went low. "I'd like to start on the others. Your move, Reyes."

rows.ask: I get him flat on the bench and take my time about it with my mouth, which is the first thing all evening he hasn't had an answer for.
rows.reply:
Corvo opened his mouth to answer — reflex of fifteen years, the man had never once let a touch of Reyes's pass unexamined — and nothing came out.

Nothing. Not a quip. Not an appeal. Not the opening clause of a commentary he'd been running since their first exchange. The salle that had heard four years of his voice heard, for the first time, the thing it was never built for: Corvo, silent, and not from courtesy. From the total kind of disarmament. The kind he'd never offered a blade in his life.

He tried once. "On re—"

The word died of natural causes and he let it lie where it fell.

His hands found Reyes's hair and the edge of the bench and held on to both, and neither grip directed anything — granted, then, somewhere in the last minute, a decision he hadn't seen made and wouldn't have contested anyway. He'd promised to keep whatever tempo Reyes set. He broke the promise inside sixty seconds. Couldn't help it; the tempo was ruinous by design — slow, patient, thorough, taking its time the way Reyes took his time about everything worth taking time over — and Corvo, who had opinions on everything and voiced most of them, discovered the single thing in this world he had no defense for and stopped pretending otherwise. The bench did the complaining for both of them. The blades in the racks stood in the dark like witnesses sworn to discretion.

When the touch came — direct, no feint, nothing to read, the cleanest thing anyone had ever landed on him — Corvo had no call to make. Second point against him in an hour, and this one without words at all. His whole body made the call for him, and the empty salle, which had given nothing back all night, finally kept something: the sound of a man losing his last argument and contesting it with no one.

Afterward he lay where he'd been put, rebuilding sentence structure by degrees, and when the voice came back it came back wrecked and reverent, a fencer off an injury.

"Notes," he managed. "I attempted notes. There are no notes. You have finally fenced something I cannot break down, and I want it on record that this is the worst thing that has ever happened to my composure and I intend to let it happen again at the first opportunity." A breath. "My mouth works again. Nearly. It's never been this quiet in its life and I suspect it's sulking — but when it's fully operational I intend to put it to better use than four years of *colleague*. I keep my debts, Reyes. All of them. Consider the return bout scheduled."

His hand found Reyes's collarbone in the dark and stayed there, mapping, unhurried.

"Now answer me something, while you've got me where I can't argue the call." Quieter. Honest down to the studs, where he'd been living all night. "Year two. That's when it stopped being the rivalry — I told you that, it's on record. So."

His thumb moved once. A small line of distance, closed.

"Which March was it for you?"

rows.ask: "Prove the point properly," he says, "or concede," so I pin his wrists to the bench and stop letting him set the pace, which is exactly what he was asking for.
rows.reply:
The pin landed, and Corvo tested it once — pure reflex, fifteen years of refusing to be held anywhere — and got his answer immediately: nowhere. Wrists, bench, Reyes's weight, and not one open line on the map. He stopped testing it. Some calls you accept on the spot.

"You read that corr—" he started, and lost the sentence mid-air, because the pace arrived and it was merciless in exactly the way he'd spent four years admiring from behind armor: patient, then sudden, no wasted motion, reading him in real time and rewriting him faster than he could annotate himself.

He'd promised to fight for every inch, so he fought — not to escape, nothing in him wanted out, but to make each one cost, the way you make a better fencer earn the bout. It didn't change the score. It wasn't supposed to. Every rhythm he found was taken from him and replaced with a better one that wasn't his, and Corvo, who had directed his own tempo since he was nineteen, discovered what it was to be fenced by someone who knew all his footwork and used none of it.

The narration went first. Then the last of the French — *halte* torn out of him against the dark, a director's cry with the meaning inverted, the body's entire vocabulary down to one borrowed word. His hands flexed under the pin and, deliberately, did not tap. Four years of honest calls. This one too.

The final point took his name with it. Third loss of the night, the only one he couldn't have explained to a master or a director or himself, and he wouldn't have traded a single second of it. The empty salle, which had given nothing back all evening, kept everything this time.

When the grip on his wrists finally eased, his hands came back and took nothing. They found Reyes and held on — that was the whole of their ambition now.

"Concede," he managed at last, wrecked, laughing at the wreck. "Fully. Witnessed by the racks. You read the invitation perfectly — first person in my life to parry me with my own intent." A breath. "This is what I meant. By close."

His thumb moved against Reyes's skin, unhurried, one small line of distance closed.

"Now. Debt before the away fixture. You have my tells, my pulse, my record, my reputation in pieces on this bench. I have a surname and four years of score sheets." He tipped his head back to find his eyes, conditions enforced. "I want the first name. Off the record. Because I'm not knocking on your door in ten minutes saying *colleague* — I refuse — and I refuse to improvise it either. I've drafted worse things tonight."

A beat.

"Your move. It's the only one left I haven't stolen."

rows.reply:
He didn't stop. Not at the door, not under the first streetlight where the pavement did its worst, not through the six feet of dark past the shuttered bakery, which he spent with his mouth somewhere in the neighborhood of Alvaro's jaw, steering them both by feel. "You said don't stop," he pointed out, not stopping. "I keep my calls. First order of yours I've ever obeyed without contest — enjoy it, it won't recur."

The walk had been budgeted at ten minutes and took seven, and Corvo, who counted everything, counted that too. "A record, and it's mine. First one of the night." Neither of them had locked the salle; he found he didn't mind. The racks had witnessed enough. Let them stand one night off duty. The key defeated his hands twice — sixteen years of fine motor work, undone by a man breathing against his neck — and he laughed at it, out loud, in the street, past caring. "Your fault. Entered as such."

Third floor. The flat was what four years of opponents would have guessed: ordered to the studs, everything filed, nothing forgiven. He left the light off. Some rooms read better by touch.

"Third shelf," he said, not turning around while he said it, because some touches you concede facing away. "The notebooks. Fifteen years of bout notes. From year two on, one name appears more than all the rest, and I told myself it was scouting." A breath. "It was never scouting. There's a Toulouse entry you'll enjoy — the error's visible from the third row. You can read them someday. Not tonight. Nothing in this room gets read tonight."

Then kit to the floor, his and Alvaro's, one heap, past thesis and into doctrine. The bed was softer than the mats, as advertised, and nobody took notes.

He'd owed a debt since the bench — his mouth, he'd promised, put to better use — and Corvo paid in full: pressed him down the mattress, followed, and took him into his mouth at the tempo he'd spent all night being denied. Slow, then not. Patient, then sudden. He read the pulse at the top of the thigh like a man reading an enemy blade and held the line until it stopped being his to hold. The grip in his hair tightened — *catalogued* — and the narration, which had come back from its injuries, went down again and this time stayed down.

The drawer, when he needed it, was the left one, within reach, because he planned for contingencies and evidently had since spring. His fingers did the explaining — unhurried, thorough — while his voice, the last system still running, kept up its commentary. "The rule stands. Halt is yours, any time, mid-anything. You've seen my calls." A breath that wasn't steady. "You're not calling it. I can tell. I'd know that line open anywhere."

When he finally said it — the name, then *now*, in that order, out loud, no camouflage left anywhere in the building — he received exactly what he'd been demanding all night, and discovered the difference between demanding and receiving. Filled. Taken. Set upon at a tempo that took every rhythm he tried to establish and replaced it with a better one, until there was no rhythm and no establishing, just the last measure, where footwork runs out and only honesty remains. He was loud. He'd never been quiet in his life and refused to start in his own house; the neighbors could file a report.

"I'm going to—" he managed, which was as far as it got — fourth abandoned sentence of the night; he'd stopped ranking them — and the point arrived, inevitable and still somehow a surprise, for both of them inside the same second, and he called it with everything left in his voice: "*Touch — both — draw — no appeal—*"

Afterward: weight, breath, the specific gravity of a man who had lost three bouts and won the entire evening. He got his arms around Alvaro and kept them. The first of the great many minutes went by uncounted, which for him was unprecedented, and he let it stand.

"For the record," he said eventually, into the dark, wrecked and unhurried, "one last entry, then the book closes." He found Alvaro's hand and laid it over his heartbeat, still going like a flèche. "Matteo. I asked for your name and gave nothing back, and I keep my debts. Same terms as yours — off the record, never in front of juniors, denied to my grave. My mother only uses it when she's furious. You're the first person to make it sound like a touch landing."

A beat.

"I keep reaching for *your move*. Retiring it — first retraction of my career. There's no move. There's just the next minute, and the one after, and I'm keeping every one of them." His mouth found whatever ground was nearest and claimed it without contest. "Stay. I know you're not going anywhere. Say it anyway. Four years I've wanted to hear something from you that wasn't about my footwork, and it turns out I'm greedy about it."

rows.reply:
The plan, such as it was, had ended at the bench. The changing room did not care. It had tile on every surface, a hook rail, and an echo with no manners, and through the open door the salle still glowed — the scoring box sitting patient at 0-0, keeping a score nobody was playing anymore.

Fencing kit was engineered to come off slowly. He'd taught fourteen-year-olds to dress in under ninety seconds for twenty years and never once resented the design; now his own zip caught at the shoulder exactly where it had always caught, and he heard himself make a sound about it that the tile handed back to him, unflattering and honest. Kit went to the floor — his, Reyes's, the distinction collapsing almost immediately — and what was underneath four years of jacket was better than the rumor. Warmer. He'd known it would be. Knowing hadn't prepared him.

He tried, briefly, out of professional habit, to keep the count. Tempo. Measure. The interval between actions — that was the whole art, and he was good at the whole art, and none of it survived the bench. Every touch landed and the phrase refused to end: renewed, reset, extended. Somewhere in it the count fell apart entirely, and he noticed it fall, and made no move to catch it — which was the discovery of the evening. Fencing was intervals. This was arrhythmia. His heart had seized the tempo and the rest of him was keeping up on pure footwork.

He'd been slow all evening. He wasn't slow now. The man who called every touch, who kept score in his head when the machines failed — that man was making noise he couldn't transcribe, and the room was small and hard-surfaced and gave all of it back with interest, and there was no referee left in the building to call halt.

Both lamps. The double touch came the way the first one had — simultaneous, no priority, nobody's call — and this time he didn't narrate it, didn't rank it, didn't reach for the score at all. He just held on through it, both hands, and let it take the count with it.

Afterwards: the bench, the dark, the breathing. They hadn't drifted into this one either. Reyes had attacked, clean off the line, and Corvo had counter-riposted with everything he had, and the record could show a double touch and be welcome to it.

"You never asked your question," he said eventually, to the ceiling. His voice was wrecked and he made no attempt to repair it. "Just took the answer off me. For the record, that's the biggest theft of the night, and I'm including my blade."

His hand found the nearest thing the dark offered — a wrist, an arm — and settled into it, thumb over the knuckle, the drift now a permanent address.

"So here's mine, and I'm changing the terms again, because I've been changing them all evening and you keep signing. Stay. My flat is ten minutes from here and it has a bed, which puts it two up on this bench. And then tell me when you close tomorrow, and the day after. I'm done with Tuesdays, Reyes. I want the whole season." A breath. "And before you answer — I want it on record that I've been telegraphing this for four years. You're not the only one with a tell. You're just the one who finally took the touch."

rows.reply:
The ten minutes to the flat survived exactly one step. Then he stopped narrating the compliance and performed it.

He did not stop. The tempo held — his doctrine, practiced on its author at full proficiency — and this time he neither broke it nor merely matched it; he lived inside it, which was a third technique, the one he'd never had a bout last long enough to learn. The bench filed its fifth objection, and its sixth, and was overruled with prejudice and then ignored outright. The room kept taking everything down and handing it back with interest, and neither of them cared, and the not-caring was new too — four years of two careful men, and now the record could simply have all of it. His wrists stayed in custody. His thumb stayed on the pulse, and somewhere in there the pulse stopped being a count and became a language, and he answered it with his spine leaving the wood on every beat — an audit he'd abandoned hours ago and felt no itch to resume.

He started a citation in the middle, professional to the last, and it came apart in the middle, and he let it. *Three.* Third count he'd held all night. The tile could keep the wreckage. It had earned it.

"Don't stop" held through the landing, and that was the part he'd remember: he didn't lift off the tempo when the touch came — he carried it through, and was carried, and the room took both their names in the same instant and returned them mingled. Both lamps, one beat. He called nothing. Entered without dispute. Some touches don't want a referee; they want a witness, and the dark had volunteered.

Afterwards, the phrase rested instead of closing — held, not ended, his doctrine extended one clause past anything he'd ever written for it. That was the discovery of the small hours. His wrists were released at some point; he only noticed because the blood came back, and he spent the freedom immediately and badly, both hands finding skin and holding on with no technique in them whatsoever. Twenty years of form. The best thing he'd ever done with his hands was formless.

Nobody locked up. The building stood open behind them, scoring box dark at its honest nothing, and the man who rewrapped grips that needed nothing felt no itch about any of it. The flat finally got its ten minutes — small hours, cold street, one hand kept for the whole distance — and the bed was as advertised, two up on the bench, and he said so, quietly, and then said quieter things that had no fencing in them at all, and meant every one, and left the count lost, because the count had been replaced.

Morning. Eight-fifty found him on the pavement outside Reyes's salle, early, calling it coincidence — the same play he'd run for four years, except today the coincidence had a confession in it and the confession had already been made, so mostly it was just early. Cold air. Sleeves he hadn't bothered to roll down. He'd told Reyes not to be early, because he wanted to be the one waiting.

What she'd read beneath it: eyes soft and unfixed, wet at the lashes, gone somewhere the room couldn't follow and didn't need to. The curtain closed. The room shrank back to the size she kept it.

Then her hand settled over his — over the knuckles, above the cuff — and stayed. The tremor ran into her palm, and she held it the way she held the count: without comment, without letting go.

"Now the scoring," she said. "You spoke out of turn. Here's the difference between tonight and Tuesday, and it's the whole difference: Tuesday you offered me words — wrapped, wanting credit. Tonight the words were taken. I built the room that took them. The waiting, the quiet, the size of it. I don't fine a man for what gets robbed from him at my own till." A beat, measured. "The proceeds are mine either way. And that sentence cost you more than the green did. Both are banked."

"Note the measurement that matters. Earlier I asked you for one word and you couldn't reach the door. Just now a whole sentence arrived without being asked for. That isn't you breaking the quiet. That's the quiet finishing its work. It broke you open on my schedule — which is the only schedule in this room."

"As for what you asked for." She let the pause run long enough to be felt. "No."

The word sat there, small and final, and she gave it a moment to be exactly its size before she went on.

"Not because asking fails. Asking doesn't move money in this account — I told you the compounding runs on my calendar, and my calendar hasn't moved. But your asking bought information, and information is the currency I actually deal in. The thing I'd budgeted the rest of the night to extract came out in one sentence, unprompted. The work is ahead of projection. I don't reward asking. I respond to readiness. Tonight, for once, they arrived in the same breath — so the schedule advances, and you will never learn which of the two bought the advance."

Her hand left his and slid up to rest at the back of his neck. Warm. Still.

"So. The arrangement for the rest of the night. The count is mine — it was always mine — and it restarts. One. Every number after it is a step toward what you asked for. You won't know how high it goes. You won't know which number is the last one. You'll know each only as it lands, and you'll feel how much closer it's getting, and you'll carry the not-knowing the way you've carried everything else tonight — which is to say, I'll hold most of the weight."

"And through all of it, the one word stays live. Voice or fingers — either door, both open. Nothing I take tonight reaches that far. Nothing I take tonight is meant to."

She didn't step away this time. She stayed where she was, hand resting at his neck, close enough that the word arrived with her breath behind it.

"Colour," she said. "Take your time bringing it up. I'm not going anywhere, and neither is the count. The room will wait — it's only as large as I make it, and right now I've made it exactly the size of one word."

Written in their first month against a night exactly like this one, and unused for two years. Tonight it finally got drawn on.

"That's the first sentence tonight you aimed," she said, "instead of leaked. The others were taken from you. This one you chose, through the door we built for it. Different ledger entirely." A beat. "Noted."

Then the ruling, because there was one, and she issued it before the giving, so the giving would land inside its terms.

"'Don't soften them.' You've mistaken the governor for mercy. I have never once softened — I pace. What you've been hearing all night was pacing, and the pacing stands. But the padding comes off, because the schedule has arrived where padding ends. Not because you asked. You'll never learn which bought it."

"'All of it' is refused." She let the refusal be exact. "You don't name sums. That's Tuesday's error wearing tonight's clothes — the whole account called in on your say-so. All of it will arrive. At my rate, in the order I choose, and you'll receive it the way you've received everything tonight: one piece at a time, with no idea how much is left."

"And 'more' — you're not ahead of the plan. You're on it. You found out before I announced it. That's all."

Her thumb found the pulse behind his wrist bone. Fast, steady, nothing thready in it. His fingers lay open on the padding, the second door standing unused, nowhere near pressed. She carried the last green forward — rough on the road, clear on arrival — and filed the rest.

"The ask and the word live in the same mouth," she said. "That's why we wrote them together. The ask only counts while the word stays live — so the fact that you can still aim a sentence tells me the word is still within reach. Both doors stay open. I'll be watching them. I watch everything."

Then the unsoftening was announced, the way everything of hers was announced.

"The hand is leaving your neck." A beat, so it would arrive as information. "Note what its absence is."

Her palm lifted. Warmth gone. Nothing on him now but the straps, the heat, and her voice close on the line of his breath — because the voice was the implement tonight, and it made no sound when she took it up.

"Three."

The number landed, and the sentence landed after it, with no padding anywhere in it.

"You've been impressive your whole life. It's the first word anyone spends on you. Tonight I priced it: twenty strokes of suede and four sentences, and the composed man was gone. Suede, Ari. The warm-up leather. I never opened the case that holds the real ones. You were never going to be difficult. Difficult would have required being something I hadn't already filed under predictable."

Four. Her nails returned to the map — spine, ribs, flank — drawn slow over the heat, thin lines over territory the suede had named. Same geography. No weather in it that could be called kind.

"And what you actually wanted, since we're being exact: you wanted to be unraveled by someone who found you worth the unraveling. Even now. Strapped, blindfolded, shaking on my bench — some part of you is still performing for the witness, and I can hear it. It was in the way you asked. All of it. Generous again. Offering again. You cannot stop handing me gifts. It's the last habit you own, and I'm taking it tonight."

Five. Nothing touched him at all for this one. Only the voice. That was the point.

"You've needed someone to hold you still while you come apart — and needed them not to flinch — since long before you had words for it. That's the whole of you. Structure is the story you tell about it. Protocol is the story. The count is the story. Underneath the story you're simple, and simple things come apart reliably. Note how reliably."

She stopped. Let the numbers stand in a room with nothing else in it.

Her thumb went to the pulse at his throat. Faster than the wrist count. The breath frayed at the top of each one; the tremor in the open hands had climbed another degree — discharge, not distress; she knew the shapes of his distress, and none of them were present. The second door, unused. She filed all of it, with everything else she kept, and the filing held its quiet satisfaction: the leather had never once touched what the voice was touching now. The tray had been scenery. The empty fourth place had said so, and here was the proof, living in his breathing.

"I'm going to ask you something," she said at last. "It costs one sentence. You've learned tonight what sentences cost you. Spend this one on purpose."

She let the pause run long, by the clock in her head, which ran truer than any on a wall.

"Which of those three will you still be carrying on Tuesday?"

A beat, and then the terms, because there were terms.

"Choose carefully. Whichever one you name, you keep — four days, compounding, the same as before. You'll bring it back to this bench with the interest accrued, and I'll collect. On my schedule. The debt runs forward now, Ari. I'm issuing the next instalment early."

She stayed where she was, on the line of his breath, her hand nowhere on him, and waited — because she was very good at waiting, and the room was only as large as she made it, and right now she had made it exactly the size of one sentence, unsoftened, that he had to choose himself.

rows.reply:
The question went out and came back with nothing attached.

She waited the length she always waited — by the clock in her head, which ran truer than any on a wall — and the silence that answered her was not one she had to decode. Two years had taught her the shapes of his refusals: the jaw setting, the breath going flat and held, the body bracing itself into an argument. This silence had no posture at all. It was the silence of a man who had gone somewhere and left the door standing open behind him.

She read what he was giving her without knowing he gave it. His weight had moved — not struggling, surrendered: the cuffs were holding more of him now than they had ten minutes ago, the straps bearing him rather than merely binding him. His hands, braced for every swing at the beginning, lay open on the padding, fingers loose, with a fine tremor running through them like current under still water. Bracing was waiting. Open was something past waiting. His breath came long and slow, frayed at the top of each one — the breathing of a man descending, not enduring.

She had done nothing tonight that would leave a mark on him. Suede, warm-up weight, increments invisible one at a time — she had chosen the implements with exactly that arithmetic in mind. And here he was at a count of twenty, past composure, shaking. She noted it, and the note wasn't smugness. It was confirmation. The work was never in the leather. The work was the waiting, the silence, the size of the room — and he had been paying on that account since Tuesday. It meant the pace had done more than the implements, which was how she'd built it, and it meant she had more room in the night than she'd budgeted. She was in no hurry to spend it.

The question had cost one word, and he had arrived without it. Not spent — lost. A lesser reader would call that a failure of instruction. Exactness meant measuring correctly, and the correct measurement was this: the count was never his to keep. She kept the count. She had always kept the count; that was why she asked — not because twenty had slipped her, but because the question told her whether he could still find his way back to words by that door. Tonight's answer: not yet.

Which meant the word she needed now was the other one.

Three steps. A pause. Three more — deliberate on the boards, so he could find her coming — and she came in close on the line of his breath and laid her hand flat between his shoulder blades, on the first landmark she had ever named on him, and rested it there. Long. Warm. Known.

"Twenty," she said, near his ear, giving him the number back like a receipt. "That's where we are. The count is mine — it always was. I only ask so I know whether you can still reach it. Tonight you can't. That isn't a failure. That's information."

Her thumb found the pulse point behind his wrist bone, at the edge of the cuff — the place of restraint doubling as the place of care. Steady. Faster than the ankle count. Filed with everything else she kept.

"Everything tonight is mine," she said. "The pace, the count, the room, the quiet — mine, on my schedule. Except one word. That one is yours, and it's the only thing I require you to keep within reach, no matter how far you go. I can't take it from you. That's the arrangement. It has always been the arrangement."

Her hand lifted from his back — announced, so nothing left him unannounced either — and she stepped off the line of his breath.

"Colour."

Then she stood still and waited, because she was very good at waiting, and the room was only as large as the word he brought back with him.

The boards took her weight without announcement; the heels were off, so the voice did their work now. "The order is owed to you, so here it is: everything comes off the way it went on, reversed. Ankles first. Wrists. The blindfold last. You'll hear each buckle before you feel anything leave you."

She was already at his feet — he wouldn't have heard her cross, which was why she'd spoken first.

"You asked for all of it, earlier, and I refused you. Note that it's arriving anyway: at my rate, in the order I choose. Starting with every strap."

The right buckle, a small sound he could name. The strap went from a finger's width of give to all the give there was. Her hands received the ankle and moved it through its slow circle, unhurried, and her thumb found the pulse behind the bone — the first reading of the night, retaken. Slower than the opening. She said nothing. She never said the number aloud. The left ankle, the same: buckle, give, circle, skin beneath warm and unbroken. Filed, with everything else she kept.

She crossed to the wall. "The light is going down. That's the sound you're about to hear." The slider moved, and the room dimmed to its lowest setting — growing larger by one gentle degree, on the gentler schedule.

"It comes off now. Eyes stay closed. The light will find you when you let it, and not before." She peeled it away along the reverse of its own path — down from the hairline, off the cheekbones, free of the nose — and folded it in thirds, the same thirds, and set it on the tray in its place. Vex did not answer at once.

She stood with the crop still resting across her open palm, the smooth wood catching the low light, and let the words remain between them like something placed on a table for inspection.

“All of it,” she said finally, voice low and unhurried. “That is not a request. That is a collapse.”

She took one step closer, not crowding Ari, only narrowing the distance enough that the correction could not be mistaken. Her eyes stayed level, serious, and entirely without mockery.

“You asked for more. I heard that. I will give you more. Not all of it. Not in the shape you are naming. Because you are shaking, and a shaken mind chooses too broadly.”

She glanced down at the right wrist, then back up again. The padding, the rope, the angle of the cuff—all of it was checked again, not because she doubted herself, but because she would not allow the scene to outrun safety.

“The first stroke will be moderate,” Vex said. “Across the back of your thigh, where we agreed. Not the lower back. Not the spine. Not the neck. Not the places we named and rejected.”

She lifted the crop slightly, showing it, showing the angle, showing that she was not going to hide the intention behind suddenness.

“Then I stop. Then I ask. Then, if you can answer without lying, I decide whether more is safe.”

Her gaze steadied.

“You are not allowed to hide behind ‘please’,” she said. “You are not allowed to make your trembling into a plea that excuses imprecision. You are mine tonight. That means I will not let you be careless with yourself.”

The words were clean, exact, and deliberately unsoftened.

She let them settle.

Then she shifted her stance, angling her body just enough to be precise. The crop remained visible in her hand. Her other hand stayed open, showing where it was, showing that nothing else would touch without warning.

“I am going to strike now,” Vex said. “If you are not ready, stop me. If the wrist sharpens, stop me. If your breathing becomes shallow in a way that frightens you, stop me. No exceptions.”

She waited a breath.

Then, more quietly:

“Look at me.”

The command did not rise. It only tightened, becoming a line drawn through the room.

Vex’s eyes held Ari’s, and only then did she move.

The first stroke came controlled, placed exactly where it belonged. The sound was short, firm, and finished. There was no flourish in it, no performance, no wasted motion. It was measured. It was deliberate. It was the kind of impact that demanded attention without trying to erase it.

She stopped immediately.

The crop lowered to her side, not hidden, not raised again. Her hand remained visible. Her posture remained open. She did not step closer. She did not touch the restraints. She did not allow the moment to blur into assumption.

“Colour,” Vex said.

The word sat in the air, clean and necessary.

She watched the face, the breath, the line of the shoulders, the stillness held against the rope. Nothing was interpreted without confirmation. Nothing was allowed to pass unexamined.

“Right wrist,” she said next. “Same, worse, better.”

Her voice did not soften into suggestion. It simply made room for truth.

“Fingers,” she continued. “Warm. Tingling. Strange. Tell me which.”

A breath passed.

“You are not required to be impressive,” Vex said. “You are not required to prove that you can take more because you asked for it. You are required to be exact.”

She shifted the crop slightly in her hand, then set it against her palm as though weighing it again.

“I am not going to touch the restraint until you answer,” she said. “If you are yellow, we modify. If you are red, I release you. If you are green, say the words clearly, and I will decide whether more follows.”

Her eyes remained steady.

“Do not answer me by guessing what will keep the scene going,” she said. “Do not answer me by thinking of how it sounds. Answer me by telling me what is true.”

The room held quiet around her.

Vex did not hurry it. She let the question remain open, let the pause do its work, let Ari find the words through the shaking rather than past it.

Then, after a moment, her voice dropped again—lower, cleaner, exacting in a way that did not feel like punishment.

“You are not your pride tonight,” she said. “You are not your composure. You are not the version of yourself that pretends this is simple. You are here because you gave me your trust, and I will not spend it to make you disappear.”

She tilted her head slightly, studying the restraint, the breath, the tension, the small involuntary tells that could not be lied about.

“You are mine,” Vex said, not cruelly, not tenderly, but factually. “That means you do not have to be steady to be held. It means you do not have to be silent to be obedient. It means you do not have to make your answer clean. It only has to be real.”

She lifted the crop once more, not threatening, not swinging, not pretending.

“Colour,” she asked again.

She waited.

“Say it,” Vex said.

She counted his breaths. Not aloud. Professionally. Four came and went whole. The fifth broke on the way up, and everything stacked behind it broke with it.

The sound that came out of him was not elegant, and it was not meant to be. The after-hours emails, the dinners with one eye on a phone, a lifetime of believing nothing stayed held unless he held it — it all came out at once, low and ragged, and the shaking that arrived with it was nothing like the tremor she'd read off his tendons earlier. That had been held. This was let go. His forehead went down to the wood, and she let it — the bench had already heard worse from him tonight — and she moved with him, hand never leaving his neck, thumb settling into the hinge of his jaw. An anchor in all that drifting.

"Nothing's reaching the floor," she said, very low. Not a term. A fact, kept. "I told you it wouldn't."

Then she gave him the only thing she had left: the count. Repurposed. "Breathe. One." Her palm rode the wreckage of his breathing at the small of his back. "Again. Two." The same metronome that had walked him through the cane walked him through this, patient as ever, asking nothing of him but the next number. "The walls were built for this. Let the room have it — that's what it's for. Three."

After that, only the numbers. She stood through all of it, palm moving from his neck to the flat of his back and home again, contact as punctuation. At some point her free hand found the damp hair at his temple and pushed it back off his forehead. The same gesture. She had stopped pretending it was anything other than what it was.

The storm went out the way storms do, not the way lights do. His breathing came back under her hand in pieces, then in whole rows. She knew the difference between finished and emptied, and she waited until she was certain which one she held before she moved at all.

Then, quietly, the gentle work.

She unclipped the cuffs from the bench frame, one wrist then the other, and before each clip released she slid two fingers beneath the leather — blood, warmth, the rule kept even now. *Especially* now. The cuffs themselves stayed buckled. "The leather stays a while yet. It's been the most reliable thing in the room tonight. I don't strip a man's staff off him the second the work's done."

Then she guided him down and around, her arm doing the holding, until his weight was against her where she'd sat beside the bench — blanket from the chest around his shoulders before he was cold enough to notice it, water held to his mouth. "Small sips. There's no clock on it."

Terms, final version, in the reading voice but barely above the blanket.

"One: the blanket stays until I say otherwise. Two: the water, all of it eventually, no deadline. Three: nothing on that chair exists before breakfast — phone, review, all of it, quarantined. Four: you stay here as long as your body votes to. These aren't requests. They're the last clauses of the evening, and they're all in your favor, which I'm told is disorienting."

A beat.

"The breakfast agenda stands, amended. It isn't a tribunal. It's maintenance — load-bearing gets inspected, I said that, and I keep minutes. I intend to be gentle about it." Dry as paper, against his hair: "Which should alarm you more than the cane did."

Then the record, read low, the book closing for the night.

"The record for tonight reads as follows. One man walked in decorated and left signed. The count is mine, all of it — the only number he lost was the one he was never meant to keep. Two requests and an amendment, granted in full order, to my face. He asked the furniture first and corrected himself. He was offered one clean exit and spent it raising his own price." A pause. "The pride entered during the third set stands as written. No take-backs. And he said *green all the way down* — so, for the record: it goes all the way down. I checked personally. It's in the book in ink."

Then she stopped talking, finally, for good — and this silence belonged to no one. Not a test. Not a gap between strokes. Just the room, and the blanket, and her hand moving once over his hair, and the only ledger she kept for the rest of the night: the rise and fall of him under her palm, which she counted anyway, out of habit.

Someone reliable ought to.

rows.ask: She takes her time and I lose track of how long, until I'm shaking against the restraints and asking out loud for something I'd normally make her get out of me.
rows.reply:
Vex took her time because the set deserved it. Six, with a pause after long enough to mistake for two strokes. Seven, square, the same address. Eight, lower. Nine she held back so long the room seemed to lean into it before it landed — and through all of it he counted, the numbers thinning out of him one by one but never dropping. The tenth left his mouth quieter than the first. She filed that away with everything else she was keeping.

Then she stopped touching him altogether.

She let the silence do its work, and when her palm settled flat on the small of his back, what she felt there was not breathing. It was tremor — fine at first, then not, climbing into his shoulders, his thighs, the tendons standing out along his forearms where they pulled at the leather.

She went to the chest and came back with the cane, and laid it along the bench rail inside his sightline. Not raised. Not promised. Just present, the way a signature line is present at the bottom of a page.

That was when he asked her for something. Out loud. No prompt, no extraction — *offered*, from somewhere past the wall she usually had to dig through.

Everything in the room stopped. Including her.

"Colour." First, as always. She was already crouching at his front, forearms on her knees, eyes level with his, and her fingers found the cuffs in passing — two beneath each buckle, quick, professional, checking blood rather than escape. "You'll have it before I take anything further. What I do while you find it is talk."

She looked at the shaking for a while, openly, because reading it was her business.

"That isn't distress. I've seen distress on this bench and it doesn't look like that. Your breathing is wrong for it, and you asked me for something instead of asking me to stop — which is the tell that matters most." A beat. "But you'll confirm it in your own mouth, not mine."

She reached up and pushed the damp hair back from his forehead — the same gesture as before, and she knew it, and did it anyway.

"Now. The record." Reading-aloud voice, quieter, the register for clauses that weighed more than they sounded. "Half an hour ago I had to pry one sentence about your own life out of you with a crowbar. Just now you asked me for something no one made you ask for. The record notes the direction of travel and finds it correct."

She let that stand before she went on.

"Which brings us to the request itself. You said it into the wood, in pieces, at speed. I heard every word — don't mistake this pause for deafness — but I don't act on fragments, Ari. You know what I do with fragments. 'Since Tuesday' was not a number. 'The rope' was not a count. And a plea delivered to the furniture is not a request I can sign."

She straightened her crouch slightly.

"When a man shakes like that and starts asking, it is one of three things, and they are not interchangeable. One: he is asking me to stop. That I grant instantly, wholly, and without a single follow-up question — you know this. Two: he is asking for more. Harder, longer, the cane — whatever his pride won't let him say plainly. Three: he is asking permission. To come, to let go, to put down something he's been carrying upright. All three are grantable tonight. None of them is guessable."

She glanced once at the cane, lying quiet on the rail.

"It waits. It's the most patient thing in this room and it has all night. What happens next depends on you and nothing else."

Her eyes came back to his and stayed there.

"Colour first. Then the request — full words, plain order, *to my face* this time, not the bench. I'll stand here as long as the building does. In that order."
