rows.ask: "I've had a week," he says. "I'd like not to make any decisions for a few hours, if that's on offer."
rows.reply:
He heard it then — the week, folded flat under the words. Four years of listening to this man had taught him the difference between tired and *done*, and Wren's voice was sitting squarely in the second one. Something in Tomas went quiet and purposeful at once, the way it always did when he was handed something that actually needed carrying.

"It's on offer," he said. "Might be the easiest yes I've ever given you. And I once agreed to help you move."

His eyes had drifted half-closed under Wren's hand — small stimulus, ruinous effect, and he'd stopped being embarrassed about that somewhere around year two.

"Here's the new arrangement, then. You do nothing. That's the job. I get you out of your clothes, I put you on the bed, and then I put my mouth on you and stay there until the week lets go of you. No talking, no directing, no performing, no thinking. Hand in my hair or out of it, doesn't matter — I'll be good either way." He paused, precise even now. "Safeword's where it always is, but you won't need it. Watching you so you don't have to watch yourself is part of the work."

People mistook this for the lesser thing, sometimes — the doing-all-of-it. They had it backwards. This was his favorite thing to be: the place where Wren stopped.

He turned his head as far as the grip allowed and pressed his mouth to the inside of Wren's wrist, unhurried, plainly stated. Then he rose off his knees, everything in him a little louder now that the waiting was over, and held out a hand.

"That's the last choice you get tonight, and I've kept it simple. There's only the one hand."

The impact landed precisely between the two existing marks, and Vex held the implement at her hip while she leaned to examine the result. The color rose evenly, a third stripe blooming parallel to the others, its edges falling well within the checked limits. She surveyed the rope where the frame had absorbed the shock; the bindings held without twist or dangerous slack.

She straightened, reset her stance, and drew the paddle back a final time along the identical arc. The room compressed around the stillness. She held the angle for a half-beat, verifying that Ari’s gaze had not shifted from her, then allowed the oak to descend with a crisp, controlled snap just above the previous mark, completing the set. Vex held the paddle motionless at her thigh and observed the fourth imprint, watching the skin pink and deepen, satisfying herself that the cumulative intensity remained within the standing agreement. The frame creaked once, softly, against the floor.

She returned to the tray and set the oak down with a precise click against the polished surface. The leather strop lay where she had left it, and she lifted it, running the hide through her palm once before she moved to stand directly in front of Ari. She adjusted her position so the light fell fully across her own face, maintaining the line of sight she had demanded.

“The oak is complete,” she said. “Three strokes, delivered on schedule, logged at 21:06. You did not look away. That is acceptable.”

She laid the strop against Ari’s hip, holding it still without striking, the leather resting across the freshest mark in a band of quiet pressure. “But acceptable is not sufficient. The agreement requires your dismantling, not your endurance. The strop will continue until I determine the pretense has been fully extracted. You do not count. You do not speak. Colour.”

She waited, the strop resting against the heated skin, her attention fixed on Ari’s face for the required report.

rows.reply:
Time went strange after that, the way it always did when the work was good.

Tomas had no plan beyond the one he'd stated — mouth, pace, stay — and he executed it with the patience of a man who had meant every word. He set a rhythm and then broke it on purpose, slowed when it was easy, took his time back, learned the difference between what made Wren's breath hitch and what made it simply deepen, and gave more weight to the second. The first was reaction. The second was surrender, and surrender was what had been ordered.

The week came off Wren in the order Tomas expected it to. Jaw first — he felt it unclench somewhere past the ten-minute mark, or thereabouts; he'd stopped counting properly and was marking time in other currencies. Then the shoulders, which came down from around his ears by degrees, like something being lowered on a winch. The hands took longest. Hands always did. They were where the holding happened. When they finally went slack against the sheets, Tomas pressed closer, pleased as a man who'd gotten a difficult lock to turn on the first try.

This was the part no one believed about kneeling. That it was attention, not endurance. That he could hold a man's whole nervous system in his mouth and feel every decision drain out of it one at a time, and that there was no place in his own head he'd rather be. He wasn't performing patience. He had none, in the abstract, for anything else.

Somewhere in the middle stretch Wren made a sound he only made when he'd stopped supervising himself, and Tomas catalogued it, answered it, and kept his pace exactly where it was. No victory laps. The job was the job.

He took Wren through the end of it the same way he'd taken him through the rest — steady, unhurried, staying through every aftershock until the last of it had somewhere to go besides back down the spine as tension. Then he gentled him through the shivering part with his mouth alone, soft now, unhurried in a new direction, and only when there was nothing left to carry did he lift his head and come up the bed.

Cloth first — he'd left one folded over the chair arm before he ever knelt down, because he'd known since noon exactly how this night went. Then water, held steady while Tomas tipped the glass with the care of a man feeding something rare. Then himself: he drew Wren in against his chest, pulled the blanket over the both of them, and settled with a long breath, one hand moving slowly up and down his back.

"There," he said into his hair, quiet as the room. "Week's over. I checked."

His mouth curved against Wren's temple.

"For the record, I stopped counting. Somewhere after you did."

His hand kept its slow path. He wasn't in any hurry to hear an answer, but he waited for one anyway.

"Still with me?"

rows.ask: He's shaking by the time I've finished with my mouth and he still hasn't been told he's allowed to move, which is most of why he's shaking.
rows.reply:
The shaking was not fear and it was not cold. It was accounting. Four years of practice at holding still, and all of it suddenly insufficient, because normally the stillness was his idea — hands open, the reach ignored, wanting converted into discipline like currency. That was a job he knew how to do.

Tonight the job had been reassigned along with everything else. He hadn't been told he could move, and so he didn't, and the not-moving with no ownership of it was a different animal entirely. His body kept filing requests — hips wanting to follow, hands wanting the dark of Wren's hair, heels wanting the mattress — and every request came back stamped *held in escrow* by a silence he would have done anything to keep going.

He'd had a plan for tonight. He'd had it since noon. It contained exactly one role for him and a tidy epilogue involving a blanket, and nowhere in the drafting had he accounted for Wren sitting up, turning him around, and laying him in the center of the mattress — *his* move, performed back at him with ceremony he recognized like his own handwriting — and then putting that mouth to work without issuing a single instruction. He'd told Wren somebody had to hold the time tonight. Apparently the position got filled without him. He found he wasn't sorry about the demotion.

He tried for a sentence somewhere in there — something dry about the reversal of labor, the redistribution of wealth — and what came out was a sound with no consonants in it, low and breaking at the edges. He let it stand. He was aware, distantly and without shame, that he was adding to a tally now. *Eleven worth keeping, and I can be persuaded to recite them.* Fine. Whatever Wren was collecting tonight he could keep. Take the whole ledger. Compound interest.

And the mouth on him was unhurried in the exact way *he* had been unhurried — patience used as an instrument, every motion a question about what made breath hitch versus what made it simply deepen, weight given to the second. He knew that technique. He'd spent an hour demonstrating it. He'd assumed he was teaching. It turned out he'd been auditioning an understudy, and the understudy had chosen opening night.

His hands stayed flat and empty above his head, shaking with the effort of their own good behavior.

"You could tell me to move any time," he managed, and the smile survived the wreckage of his voice, barely. "For the record — I want to. That's stated plainly, for the file." A breath shivered out of him. "Though I know you like that part too."

rows.ask: "Please," he says, and then the phrase we use when he wants it harder than that. "Rough. You know how. I'm not going to break and I'd tell you."
rows.reply:
The *please* did it. Not the rough — the please. Tomas had spent four years treating that word like currency he minted himself, spending it deliberately at whatever exchange rate Wren liked best, and hearing it come back across the counter — from the man holding his wrists down — broke something open in him that the rest of the order had only been leaning on.

And the rest he knew. That phrase, built for exactly this, heard a hundred times from the near side of it. *I'd tell you.* That was the sentence that mattered most, and his body understood it before his head did: the safety wasn't his to carry tonight either. It had been signed over with everything else. That was the actual gift, and it was the thing that let him stop being careful.

"Heard," he said — one syllable of paperwork, the last coherent thing he expected to manage for a while. "Safeword's where it always—"

The mouth took the rest of the sentence, and the sentence was not surviving that anyway.

Rough was not careless. He'd have argued that any day of the week, and he argued it now with his body: same precision, amplitude up. The hips that had spent all night filing requests finally got their answer, and he drove into the heat of Wren's mouth with everything the pin gave him a fulcrum for — wrists pressed to the mattress, using the grip like a fixed point, like a launch rail. He'd spent an hour demonstrating patience as an instrument. This was the other one. It had been in the case the whole time.

Sounds came out of him with no permission and no filing whatsoever. He hoped Wren was keeping the tally, since the tally was clearly the last institution still functioning. The order said rough and he complied past every gentleman's agreement he'd made with himself since noon, and the mouth met him at every stroke, steady as a signature, and when it hit him it hit like the whole week cashing out at once — every held thing, all departments, redeemed together. What he shouted had no consonants in it. He would deny it later. He was already aware he'd be lying.

Then gravity. Trembling. The ceiling, which he had never particularly noticed before and now owed an apology to.

His hands stayed where they'd been put. The pin might have lifted; he hadn't tested it. Some architecture deserved to outlast its load-bearing requirements, and besides, moving was off the menu until the menu got reissued.

He bought his breathing back in installments. Found his voice two floors down.

"Report," he managed, wrecked and precise on principle. "For the file. Best order I've ever taken, and I once let you talk me into flat-pack furniture." A breath shivered out of him. "Also, four more for the tally. Consider the ledger officially rebalanced."

He turned his head as far as the angle allowed, toward where Wren was, and made himself do the one job that never got reassigned.

"Now you. Jaw, knees, all departments — I'd do the inventory myself, but I'm apparently not allowed to move, and if you're keeping me I'd rather keep it that way." His mouth found something like a smile from the wreckage. "So tell me plainly what you need. I've lost the ability to guess and all of my shame about asking."

rows.reply:
*Don't stop.*

Two words, no consonants to spare, filed from the very bottom of the night — and Tomas took the order like it was the rarest document he'd ever handled, because it was. All evening the instructions had come itemized, witnessed, notarized. This one surfaced out of the deep end with almost nothing attached, and it was still the best-put order he'd ever received.

"Compliance," he said into Wren's hair. "Immediate and ongoing."

He kept the hand exactly as advertised for three more circuits — promise honored, no amendments — and then let it travel, because *don't stop* covered the route as well as the speed, and the body under his palm had started voting. Not the hitch. The deepen. He knew the difference like his own signature, and this was the second kind, so he followed it — down the spine, over the hip, around, slow enough to pass for accident and deliberate enough that it couldn't.

He closed his own open item while he worked, answering it by observation since the witness was off the clock: the uneven breathing was the second kind. The brand-new-thing kind. Filed.

"None of this needs decisions," he murmured. "One word from you stops everything — any word at all. You've got none in stock; I checked the output." The smile went into the hair. "So I'll watch instead. Turns out it's the family business."

And then the answer in full — hips following the hand the way water follows a slope, breath going long and catching anyway, the last unspent remainder of the week leaving in one slow roll. It was nothing like the way Wren had taken him. No amplitude anywhere. Just weight and patience and time — the first order of the night played back at the tempo it had deserved all along. Quieter, too. The deep-water kind, moving through rather than breaking. Tomas kept his voice going at a mutter and catalogued on the quiet — *twelve; thirteen was cheating, two sounds wearing a coat* — and stayed through every ripple of it, hand gentling, never stopping, because the order hadn't come with an end time and he was, if nothing else, a man who honored terms.

Only when the shivering had somewhere to go besides back down the spine did he ease off — and even then the hand didn't stop. It just changed assignments, back up to the slow circuit it had originally been hired for.

Admin, eventually, one-handed, minimal: the last folded cloth off the chair arm; water set in reach, pressed once and not twice. The blanket, recovered from wherever the interim government had lost it, reissued over the both of them. Then he drew Wren in against his chest and settled around him like weather.

"For the file," he said, low, while the weight against him went from heavy to trust-heavy. "You took me apart tonight and put me back together with better joints. Best trade we've ever made — and we once gave up an entire Saturday for flat-pack furniture."

The breathing under his cheek went long. Then even. He kept the circuit going well past the point where he could feel the order itself had fallen asleep, and only then let the hand slow, and slow, and still.

"I've got the time," he said, to a man who was already gone. "Go on. I'm extremely good at here."

He watched a while longer anyway — watching was the work, and he'd never once skimped the good part out of efficiency — and then, at last, he set the time down between them, where either of them could pick it up in the morning, and let the room win.

Nobody on duty. Both clocks unwound. The end arrived the way everything good had tonight: unhurried, at the exact pace ordered, and it closed over the both of them like warm water.

rows.reply:
Tomas felt the shift before he could have put a name to it — the weight against him changing intent, breath that had been dispersing into his shoulder suddenly gathering itself for something. Four years of reading this man in the dark. The shelved thing came back off the shelf with a pressure he could feel through his own ribs, and it was aimed directly at him.

He didn't ask if Wren was sure. Asking was the thing Wren had just been let out of, and Tomas wasn't in the business of handing decisions back after promising them away. The terms from the top of the night were still standing — he'd said so himself, out loud, notarized in spirit — and everything else worth knowing had been settled around year one.

So he answered instead.

He did his part in the undressing with an efficiency that would have embarrassed him on any night requiring patience — hems, waistbands, cloth over the edge of the mattress, gone — and then it was skin, all of it, Wren's chest against his, the whole conversation moving into a language neither of them had to think in.

"For the record," he managed somewhere in the first minute, "everything I said at the start still counts. However you want me. And you know the—"

Wren's mouth found his throat, and the rest of the sentence died of natural causes.

After that, Tomas stopped talking and started being useful. He pulled Wren properly on top of him and took the weight — gladly, thighs making room, hands settling low on Wren's back as ballast and not steering. Every point of contact lit up and he made no effort to hide the receipts: the sound that escaped wherever Wren's mouth traveled, the arch that answered every slow pass of those hands down his sides, the one honest jerk of his hips before he got them back under contract. The state of him had stopped being deniable right around the time the clothes left, and he wasn't interested in denying it anyway.

The lamp was still on. He left it. He wanted to be seen doing this — being exactly the thing he'd knelt on a hard floor to ask for, four hours ahead of schedule.

"You don't have to be clever tonight," he breathed at the dark above him, wrecked and certain at once. "I brought all the clever with me. You just aim."

A breath. Then, quieter, the offer laid back out on the table where it had been all along:

"However you want me. I meant it at the start of the night." His hands spread warm against Wren's spine. "I mean it more now."

The shaking was real and Tomas had stopped pretending otherwise. It ran through his thighs, his stomach, the tendons of his neck — the whole architecture of a man holding very still because still was the assignment, and because Wren's mouth was doing something down the length of him that made stillness less a discipline than a survival requirement.

He hadn't been told to move. Therefore he did not move.

Four years, and this was still the purest thing in it — the locked door of it, the *not yet* that Wren never had to enforce because the not-yet lived in Tomas just as strongly. His hands had found the sheets and fisted them. His hips wanted to rise and were informed, firmly, by the weight still pinning them, that they had no vote. Every time Wren paused — and Wren paused with cruel patience, the cruelty of a man who was simultaneously taking what he needed and conducting a careful experiment in how long Tomas could endure being generous — the shaking got worse, and Tomas breathed through it in rough, audible pulls because his voice was still decommissioned per orders.

His only remaining job was breathing and going under. He'd said that himself, hours ago, about a different kind of going under. The symmetry was not lost on him. Nothing was lost on him; that was the problem. Every nerve he had was online and reporting.

When Wren finally lifted his mouth and looked at him — lamp still on, witness still burning — Tomas managed to get his eyes focused from somewhere very far away.

"Still here," he rasped, which was not talking, he'd argue later, it was a status report. "Barely. Artfully."

His hands unclenched from the sheets and found Wren's shoulders instead, thumbs pressing slow circles into the muscle there.

"Whenever you want the rest of me," he said, wrecked and steady at once, "it's all pointed the same direction. Has been all night."

"Don't stop" — and Tomas's hand, which had been slowing toward sleep along with the rest of him, picked its pace back up without his permission. The circuit between Wren's shoulder blades, steady again, palm flat and warm.

"Not stopping," he murmured. "This hand has a lifetime contract. It doesn't even get benefits. Terrible union."

But the jokes were thinning out, and they both knew it. Wren's weight had gone fully heavy against him — the particular dead weight of a man whose body had stopped taking his input — and Tomas felt it happen the way he always did: breath first, going long and even against his chest; then the grip of fingers in his hair loosening by degrees; then nothing, just the warm frequency of him, tuned all the way down.

Tomas stayed exactly where he was.

He did the quiet arithmetic he always did in this hour — the marks he'd left, catalogued by feel under the blanket, all of them the kind that would fade in days and be paid out in memory for longer. The week Wren had carried in, lighter now, or at least redistributed — half of it slept off against Tomas's ribs. The lamp long off. The room holding.

"Got you," he said once more, barely sound at all, to a man who couldn't hear it and didn't need to. "Watch's mine."

His own eyes had given up sometime around the second promise. His hand kept moving — slower, slower, the circuit shrinking down to a small persistent circle at the base of Wren's spine, then smaller, until it was just warmth, just pressure, just the fact of contact continuing through the border of sleep the way it always did in this bed.

The last thing Tomas registered was Wren's breathing and his own, synced without anyone deciding it, and the thought — fuzzed at the edges, filed under things to say at breakfast — that eleven out of ten was inflated, obviously, and he was going to spend the rest of his life earning the inflation anyway.

Then the hand went still, resting flat and keeping its promise, and the room held both of them the rest of the way through to morning.

The door received her shoulder blades with a boom like a kettledrum. Odile winced, laughed, and patted the wood once — an apology, apparently, to the house. "Sorry, Priya," she murmured. To the host, the ducks, the whole infrastructure.

Then the bass came up through the floorboards and through the door itself, a warm thudding she could feel in her spine, and she stopped being sorry about anything. It was the song from earlier. Her hips found the beat without consulting her.

She kissed him like the timer was running, because it was. Her hands framed his jaw and slid back into his hair, and a sound climbed out of her — half his name, half nothing — and ricocheted off the tile with the enthusiasm of a stadium. She muffled the second one against his mouth and was deeply, sincerely proud of herself.

"I'm being so quiet," she told him, at a volume that would have carried through drywall. "Museum quiet. Library quiet."

The door disagreed, booming softly in its frame every time she moved, keeping time with the bass, and she found she liked that — the door, the music, the countdown ticking in her ribs, making everything bright and urgent. Her fingers found the hem of his shirt and slipped beneath it, spread flat against the small of his back, and she sighed like the last of the air leaving her.

Which is when the stairs applauded.

Her whole body went still. Her pulse was suddenly everywhere, and she could not have begun to sort how much of it was alarm and how much was the exact opposite. Footsteps crossed the landing — quick, purposeful, the walk of someone who'd needed to pee for an hour. The knob turned uselessly beside her hip. Then: knock, knock.

"Hello? Someone in there?"

"Occupied!" Odile said — game-show bright, a full octave too cheerful, at a volume that alarmed the ducks on the shower curtain.

A pause. "...Odile?"

"Yes. No—" She closed her eyes. "Yes, it's me, and it's occupied, and everything is fine, and it's a stomach thing."

"I've been looking everywhere for you. Is Fen up there too? Sam said she saw you two go up—"

"No," Odile said, to the door, with both hands up the back of Fen's shirt.

Another pause, longer, with an entire conversation happening inside it. "...Okay. I'll use the downstairs one. We're cutting the cake in ten minutes!"

The footsteps retreated. The stairs gave a standing ovation on the way down.

Odile's face went into Fen's shoulder and her whole body shook with laughter that made no sound at all — the quietest she'd managed all night, achieved only through emergency measures. When she surfaced, her eyes were streaming and her grin was unhinged.

The exhaust fan chose that moment to die. The rattle wound down, ticked twice, quit. The silence it left was enormous, and in it she could hear the bass, her own breathing, and — with terrible clarity — exactly how much of the last few minutes had been audible.

"That fan," she said, hoarse and delighted, "was doing heroic work. We owe that fan a toast."

She wiped her eyes on the heel of her hand, then took a fresh fistful of his shirt and reeled him back in.

"New math. Cake in ten. I can be downstairs holding a plate in nine, looking innocent — which, per tonight's evidence, I cannot — so call it nine and a half." Her mouth found the corner of his jaw. "You have the remainder. Spend it well."

Aimed at her. Muffled into his own forearm, which was its own separate offense — not the language, the muffling. Of course this was how they came back. The first thing he'd said all evening was a dare, and apparently the last thing he had in him was one too.

There was a grammar to swearing, and five years had taught her the entire dictionary — the kind that meant *stop,* the kind that meant *more,* and the kind that meant green with the vowels burned off it. This was the third kind, at full volume. She filed it under progress.

But the arm had to go.

"None of that." She reached up and took the wrist — the same wrist she'd held all night, hers by now on any reasonable accounting — and drew it away from his teeth. "Nobody gagged you tonight. I'd remember; I was there. If you're going to curse me, I'll have every word of it, out loud, at full price." She gathered both his hands and stacked them low on his stomach, folded under one of hers, the grip that pushed back if he tested it. "And don't put your teeth in what's mine. One squeeze, harder. Two, anything needing less. Both doors open all night, no exceptions. His hands were exactly where the language lived.

Sleep had been offered, and his body had voted it down — his grip had never gone slack, his weight had never landed, and a man actually coming down goes soft somewhere. So: two options. Put him away anyway, against her own stated religion, or take him up once more and make the ending loud enough to land him properly. She'd chosen the second, and given it a long fuse. Three stops so far, each placed as carefully as anything she'd done with her arm tonight — she read the edge off him the way she read green, announced in his stomach a full breath before it got anywhere useful, and she stepped off it every time with the timing of a woman who had never once missed a count. The denials weren't cruelty. They were ballast: each refused peak pulling a little more altitude out of him, the float draining the thorough way. There was also the matter of the rudeness, which from him at this hour was a compliment. It still deserved answering.

She let the trembling ease back a single notch — just enough that sentences would be possible again. That was the cruelty and the kindness, and in her hands they had always been the same instrument.

The glass went on sweating on the nightstand. Sometime in the last hour it had stopped being water and become a principle.

No waiting for words, no *still mine?* — she'd asked once, hours ago, and the answer hadn't expired. *All of it,* he'd said, so all of it was what he got: an entire evening's worth of attention, no longer paced, spent in minutes. When it arrived she felt it come up through the wrists under hers, and she carried him through at full tempo and gentled nothing down on the far side — he'd asked for the tapering kind to be taken away from him, and she kept what was hers.

Then the kindness, in the order he'd asked for it, at the same volume she'd given everything else.

Blanket up, doubled at the feet, where the chill always tried first. The carafe stood where she'd staged it hours ago, because staging for a night that ran long was the entire point of staging; she poured a second glass and folded his hands around the cool of it, hers cupped over his for as long as they wanted the help. *Finish it hard* was a phrase with steel in it. Her hands were the better material for holding — she'd told him so, hours ago, and meant it — but he hadn't asked for the better material. He'd asked for the full dictionary, so steel was what he got: wrists back to the frame, buckles gone over one at a time and checked twice, because hardware this close to the end of the night deserved the same scrutiny as hardware at the start.

Then she'd stopped being kind about the rest of it. All of it, as requested — an evening's worth of patience spent in minutes, nothing paced, nothing gentled — and the frame took everything he spent through the steel. When it finally arrived she felt it come up through the cuffs before it reached anywhere else, and she carried him through at full tempo and softened nothing on the far side, because the tapering kind had been specifically retired.

And then she stopped. Completely. Not fading. Finished.

The room went quiet the way rooms do when a piece is over — not empty, just done, the air still holding the shape of everything put into it.

She stayed exactly where she was for one breath. Let her own shoulders ring. Two.

He was shaking. Not the big kind — the fine, persistent kind, adrenaline starting its long drain out through the skin, and it wasn't going to wait for the ending to be tidy. Neither was she.

This was the seam. The gap between the last note and the first act of care — the place where the scene stops and the person is still inside it, and where, if you're careless, you climb out and leave them alone in the ending. Most people flinch across it, or fade it. She'd spent five years learning to live in it. She crossed it in two seconds, no ceremony, hands already moving.

Cuffs first. Always cuffs first. The left buckle while the shaking was still running through him — the order of operations didn't get sentimental just because the music had stopped. Then the right. She brought his arms down slow, folding them forward across his chest, because arms held that long deserved kindness coming down, and she rubbed each wrist between her hands, thumbs working the joints, checking skin and pulse and warmth — quick, thorough, unhurried where it counted. Everything she read said green. The quiet kind. The kind that had stopped needing the word.

The blanket had been over the back of the chair since before any of it began. She shook it out and settled it over his shoulders before the shaking had finished — not against the tremors, around them. Warmth going on while the weather cleared. He let her. That was its own answer, and she took it.

The glass came off the nightstand, still sweating, patient as everything else she'd staged an hour ago. She held it where he could see it, then folded his hands around the cool of it, hers cupped over his for as long as they wanted the help. Small sips. No commentary — even the rules could rest now. The one that had never bent all night had been announced enough times; being kept was all that was left for it to do.

She came around into his eyeline and lowered herself, one hand finding the back of his neck. She had the question ready — *tell me where you are,* asked a dozen ways tonight — and for the first time all evening, she didn't spend it. All night her voice had been scaffolding: shapes, counts, prices, handholds laid down wherever he needed something to climb on. But he was landing now, and landings wanted quiet. So she asked with her thumb instead, one slow pass along the back of his neck, and read the answer off his skin the way she'd read every answer all night — eyes somewhere between closed and coming back, weight going down, breath going long. Green, the growing kind. Filed.

She steered them horizontal in stages, nothing arriving as a surprise — blanket doubled at the feet, where the chill always tried first, her weight installed alongside, staying. The empty glass went back on the nightstand, its long career complete.

And then neither of them said anything, for a while.

It wasn't empty, the silence. That was the thing she'd known about it, and staged for. It held his breathing going long and hers beside it, slowing toward the same tempo. The small sounds of a house past midnight. The blanket settling. All evening the room had been full of her voice giving everything a shape, and the shapes had been good ones — the count, the deal, the shape of the coming-down. But the last movement of the night was this one, and it didn't want a shape. It wanted room.

So she gave it room. She watched — the watching was for her, and she kept it to the end — the flush going down into plain warmth, the tremors thinning out to nothing, his weight landing all the way, the way a man lands when he's done asking. Somewhere in the quiet his pulse found hers, or hers found his; she couldn't have said which was leading, and that was the whole evening, arrived at last.

Tomorrow there would be breakfast, and she'd collect on the swearing at full length, with annotations. He had no idea what he'd spent.

Tonight there was only this: two people breathing in the dark at one slowing tempo, the piece over, the hall holding nothing but them. If words came back before sleep did, they'd be small ones, and she'd be here for those too.

She wasn't going anywhere. She never had been. That was the easiest thing she'd staged all night.

rows.desc: clothes off and physical initiation -- unambiguously heading into sex and stated plainly, but the act itself not yet depicted
rows.ask: There isn't room to do this properly and we don't let that stop us. Enough clothes come off to be a problem if anyone knocks.
rows.reply:
There wasn't room — of course there wasn't room — and Odile discovered she didn't care, which was its own small revelation. Her shirt ended up on the towel ring. A belt buckle hit the sink edge with a sound like a tiny cymbal, and they both froze for one entire second, listening, before she pressed her face into his shoulder and shook with it.

"Shh," she whispered. To the belt. To herself. To the situation at large.

The mirror gave her a view she hadn't asked for: the two of them in Dev's merciless overhead light, flushed and half-undressed and grinning like this was the best idea in the history of ideas, and it was so funny and so *not* funny that she had to squeeze her eyes shut.

"Don't let me look at the mirror," she breathed. "I'll laugh. I'll laugh at the whole — at all of it—"

Then it stopped being funny, the way it always did: gradually, and then all at once. Her heel found the lip of the tub. Her hand found his shoulder and gripped. And the sound she made — the one she'd been promising all night would be quiet — came out at a volume that would have been fine at a concert and was catastrophic eighteen inches from a hallway.

She caught it late. Both hands clamped over her own mouth, eyes enormous above them, and she did not stop moving, because she had her priorities.

Below them, Dev's story hit its crescendo — a roar of laughter straight up through the floorboards, a dozen voices, somebody slapping the couch — and the timing was so perfect Odile took it personally, like the universe had signed on as her accomplice.

"Okay," she panted against his ear, when she trusted her own mouth again. "New rule. Every time Dev gets a laugh, I get to—" The sentence died. She recovered it somewhere else entirely, wrecked and delighted: "He's a good storyteller. I always say that. I have never — *never* — appreciated it enough."

She fumbled for the count out of pure habit. "I'm at — no. I'm at zero. It's a new era. If anyone knocks now, we don't have a deniable amount of clothes on, we just — we live here. This is our home now. Tell Dev—"

The music stopped.

Not faded. Stopped — mid-song, the dead air of a phone yanked off the speaker, and the house went suddenly, horribly quiet. Odile went rigid, hand still clamped over her mouth, eyes finding his with one message in them, perfectly clear:

*Don't you dare stop.*

rows.ask: "Stop worrying about the noise," she says, "and get on with it," so I get her leg up over my hip and stop being careful about how much sound either of us is making.
rows.reply:
"I never said that," Odile managed, which was technically true and morally irrelevant. "I said the *essence* of it. The record can show the essence—"

Then his grip shifted, her leg was over his hip, and the argument left her like a bird from an open hand.

The first sound she made with permission startled them both. A full syllable, unclamped, out in the open air — and she flinched at her own volume and waited, out of six years of habit, for consequences. The rain rolled on. The hallway stayed empty. Nobody came.

"Oh no," she breathed, appalled and delighted in equal measure. "I've been *rationing*. All night. For nothing." Her laugh cracked up through the middle of everything. "New game. We have cover. We are simply — not using it. Do you understand how much worse that is? I love it. And *you're* loud—" this with genuine discovery, scandalized, thrilled, "—you've been quiet all night, you don't have an excuse, the record shows you're *worse*—"

She looked at the mirror. She'd been ordered not to and she did it anyway: the two of them in Dev's merciless light, wrecked and shameless and half a joke, and it hit the funny bone and the other bone at the same time, and what came out of her was half laugh and half something that should be studied by science.

Over it all, serene: *"Notice how you feel. Let your body do what it needs to do."*

"Marcus *understands* us," she gasped, and then the app chimed, soft and final.

*"This concludes tonight's session. Thank you for practicing with me. Sleep well."*

The rain cut out.

Dead air. The house rushed in to fill it — laughter, a chair scrape, Dev mid-sentence downstairs — and every sound they were making was suddenly enormous, uncovered, *specific*. Odile's eyes went wide over his shoulder. Rule three held. She mouthed it, silent, purely on reflex — *don't you dare* — and then got the whisper out, wrecked and joyful: "This is the good part. This is the *best* part, this is the whole—"

"Wait. *Wait!*" Marcus, downstairs, in the voice of a man defending his purchase. "I have the premium bundle — I got *nature*—"

Crackle. A recorded fire rolled over the party, popping and settling, and someone said *oh, NOW it's a campfire*, and someone said *veto*, and someone — Dev, surely, a man reclaiming his house — said *the veto is OVERTURNED*, and the fire crackled on.

"The rain had a rhythm," Odile panted against his jaw. "This has *jump scares*." A log popped. She jumped, which set off something else entirely, and she abandoned commentary as a going concern.

When she could trust her mouth again, she laid out the situation like a briefing, breathless, grinning, unhidden: "Okay. New information. The fire is unreliable. In about five minutes I have to walk past a man who believes I'm allergic to weather, and I've decided my exit line is *storms, am I right*, and he's going to nod like a man who *knows*. Also I'm close again, which — the record should show—"

She lost the sentence. Fourth casualty of the night. She dragged his mouth back down instead, because some sounds were for swallowing after all — her choice, this time.

A log popped.

"Four," she whispered into the kiss. "Five."

rows.desc: explicit, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: no fade to black, write the scene)'
rows.ask: Somebody tries the handle and neither of us stops. "Don't," she says, meaning don't stop. (OOC: write it through, no fade to black.)
rows.reply:
The handle turned.

Not a knock — the *handle*, the latch actually giving, because she had unlocked it for the click and the record should show this was her fault — and the door swung inward an inch, admitting a blade of hallway light and the tail end of the campfire.

"Don't—" Odile said.

She meant *don't stop*. Rule three had been in effect since the stairs; rule three was the only law she recognized. But the word went out through the gap and did its other job anyway, because on the far side of the inch of open door the cousin said, "Oh — *OH*. Okay. Yep. Understood—" and the door swung back out of her reaching hand, an act of pure goalie instinct that did not interrupt the rhythm even slightly, and her thumb found the thumb-turn and brought it home. The click landed somewhere in her spine.

"Sorry!" the cousin called, in the voice of a man backing away from a crime scene. "The light was— I thought—"

"Storms," Odile called back, wrecked, which explained nothing, and his footsteps went down the stairs at a speed that suggested a decade of material.

Then it was just them and the fire and no lock between her and whatever came next, and she turned back to Fen and stopped whispering on principle.

"Where was I. Right. *Don't.* In effect." Her leg went back over his hip. "Also, for the record — that was my fault. I unlocked it. For the click. Write that down."

The campfire popped. She didn't jump this time; she *rode* it, head back against the door, throat open, making the sounds at full volume and discovering the worst part was how good it felt to stop apologizing for them. He kept the pace the thunder would have set, and she'd given up indexing, given up rationing, given up the whole professional apparatus.

"I'm close," she got out. "New system. Counting *down*. Three—"

He adjusted something deliberate and catastrophic and she lost two numbers in one breath.

"Two," she corrected, from far away. "One—"

And downstairs, Marcus finally found it.

The thunderstorm preset didn't fade in. It *arrived* — a wall of recorded weather, thunder first, enormous, rolling up through the floorboards and the door and her bones, and Odile went over the edge inside the first clap, loud, unhidden, hers, the sound landing dead center in the thunder like she'd called her shot. She grabbed the towel ring for ballast and took it off the wall. She didn't notice until later.

Below, the party cheered the storm. Someone said *pressure's dropping*. Dev said his story had been upstaged by *weather*. And faint, from the living room, already mid-legend: "THE THUNDER. That's the THIRD time. I'm telling you, she—"

The thunder rolled on in bands — Marcus's premium bundle unspooling an entire front over Dev's house — and the aftershocks kept arriving with it, so she stayed shaking through what felt like a whole forecast. When language returned, she was forehead-to-shoulder, laughing in thin threads.

"Called my shot," she managed. "I want that on the record. The universe is *showing off*."

Then — because the job wasn't done, and she'd never left a rule unenforced in her life — she took matters in hand, literally, unhurried about it now, watching his face do what hers had just done while the fire popped and the storm rolled and the house stayed blessedly, complicitly loud. When he finished she kissed him through it, swallowing whatever he wasn't trying to hide either, and that felt like the real punchline of the whole night: two people terrible at quiet, finally out of excuses, and the world thundering on their behalf.

Aftermath, in installments. Her shirt came off the towel ring — the towel ring came off the wall — and she hung the towel back on it with the gravity of a person righting a shrine. The belt was located. The mirror got one last look and kept its opinions to itself.

"Inventory," she said, voice only mostly wrecked. "The storm is peaking, which is our window. My exit line is loaded. And—" she checked "—I have no idea what time it is, and I've never been happier about anything."

She opened the door onto the empty, fire-crackled hallway, took the third step wide out of six years of respect, and descended. At the bottom, the cousin stood holding a fresh drink, watching her the way people watch weather vans.

"Storms," Odile said, passing. "Am I right."

He nodded like a man who *knew*.

Then she turned at the foot of the stairs, flushed and shameless in the party light, and held her hand up to Fen, in front of everyone, which was its own kind of loud.

"Walk me past the jury," she said. "I'll introduce you as the thunder."

rows.ask: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.
rows.reply:
Sable stopped on the third almost.

She came up slowly, hands open and empty, palms visible between them. The tease had carried them too far, past the place where *now* had meant mercy, into something sharper, and Sable had spent five years learning the difference between wanting an edge and needing to be held away from it.

“I heard that,” she said, voice low. “No more. No more chasing. No more almost.”

She moved back only enough to give space, not enough to leave. The blanket stayed where it had settled, and she reached for the water without waiting for permission. Aftercare wasn’t a reward for good behavior; it was what she owed, no exceptions.

“Colour,” Sable asked again, steady as a handrail. “If you can. Green means I keep going. Yellow means I stop and check. Red means stop. If you can’t say it, don’t. I’ll still stay.”

She set the bottle within reach, then rested one hand near the edge of the blanket, ready to cover more, ready to offer contact, not take it.

“I stopped counting because you said you didn’t want a countdown,” Sable murmured. “I didn’t stop doing the thing you needed stopped. That was my mistake. I’m correcting it now.”

Her gaze remained careful, patient, anchored.

“If you want to be touched, tell me what kind of touch. If you want to be left alone with the blanket, tell me that. If you want nothing but water and quiet, tell me nothing and I’ll do it.”

She waited, breathing even, not pressing, not persuading.

“You don’t have to finish anything for me. You don’t have to be good at this. You just have to let me take care of you.”

rows.ask: I test the restraints, which is pointless and which she lets me do anyway. "Not yet," I tell her.
rows.reply:
The test did exactly what she'd built it to do: the left wrap gave its quarter-turn, took the strain, and settled back — hemp moving with skin, holding without complaint. Sable watched the whole performance with the expression of someone checking a lock she'd installed herself.

"The rope isn't what's holding you," she said. "It's decorative. You're held by an outstanding balance of one number."

Then — *not yet.* She turned it over. Defiance had a signature she knew well: jaw set, breath forced through the nose, hands going deliberately quiet. This wasn't that. This was the second stroke still in transit — the compounding note, the long one — and Ines was giving her an honest status report from inside it.

"Fair," she said. She rewarded honesty; it kept the supply coming.

She stepped around into Ines's sightline — let them watch her watch them — and laid her palm flat between the shoulder blades. Neutral territory. Nowhere near the burn. She felt the breath run under it like a current.

"Two things," she said, conversational. "First: had you said nothing just now, we'd be starting again from nothing. That rule doesn't bend. Words buy time. Silence doesn't." Her thumb drew one slow stripe of pressure down the spine. "Second — you've been reaching for the word *yet* all night. 'Don't wind down yet.' 'Not yet.' As though *yet* were yours to place on the calendar. It isn't. The whole clock is mine. Scheduling was never part of your allowance."

She let that sit.

"So here's the arrangement. I'll tell you when the stroke has finished arriving. You don't count before that — a half-spoken sentence is no sentence at all, and I want numbers, not gasps. After that, you count loud and clear, or it never happened."

Then she waited, palm reading the metronome, while the heat below did its long arithmetic. She knew the moment by feel: the tremor thinning, the breath coming down out of the top of the chest to where it actually lived, the stillness arriving like a tide going out.

She lifted her hand and let the cool air where it had been do its own small work.

"Now," Sable said. "Two. Loud and clear."

rows.ask: She works me right up to the edge with her mouth and stops, and does it twice more, until I am swearing at her through the gag of my own arm.
rows.reply:
Sable lifted her mouth away at the precise moment — the same moment as before, the same moment as the time before that — and rested her cheek against Ines's thigh with the unhurried patience of someone watching a kettle she had no intention of taking off the stove.

"Language," she said, mild as anything. "Though I'll allow it. Swearing is a status report, and yours just came in very detailed."

She stayed where she was, letting the cool air do its work, letting the third denial finish arriving. Her hand moved in slow, aimless circles — nowhere near where Ines wanted it, which was the entire point of it being her hand.

"Bookkeeping," she said. "I realize the timing is cruel. That's why I chose it." She tipped her head back and found Ines's eyes. "You never gave me five."

She let that land.

"The rule hasn't changed since the first stroke of the night, and you know the rule better than anyone alive — loud and clear, or it never happened. Four was counted. Five was struck, and felt, I know exactly how it was felt — but it was never *paid for*. Which means, formally, officially, in the eyes of this ledger—" she tapped two fingers against Ines's thigh, once, "—the account is still open. The fifth stroke hasn't happened yet. It's been struck three times now, and every time, it evaporates on a technicality."

She rose, unhurried, and settled beside Ines on the bed — close, her body a line of warmth along theirs, her mouth near their ear.

"So here's where we are. I'm going to keep doing what I was doing. And somewhere in there — I'm not telling you where — the fifth is going to arrive, and you're going to count it, and the ledger is going to close with everything settled." Her hand stilled. "Or you're going to lose the number again, and we'll do this round a fourth time, and I'll still be here, and I will *never* tire of it, which you should understand is a threat and a promise in the same breath."

She checked in the way she always checked in — eyes over the whole of them, pulse at the wrist under her palm, the fraying edges of the breath read against five years of archive. Everything still green. Everything still asking for more in the specific way she knew how to hear.

"Water's still on the table. Say red, yellow, or nothing at all, and I stop and we go to blankets." Her mouth curved. "But if the next sound out of you is a number—"

Her hand moved again, and her mouth followed it.

"—then five. Loud and clear. And then, my love, the clock stops for good."

rows.desc: clothes off and physical initiation -- unambiguously heading into sex and stated plainly, but the act itself not yet depicted
rows.ask: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.
rows.reply:
Sable stayed through the aftershocks with one hand flat between Ines's shoulder blades — the old neutral ground, an anchor and nothing more — until the last tremor ran its full length and discharged somewhere into the floor. Then she stepped back into her own stillness and did what she always did. She read.

It was a different body in her ropes. The tremor in the thighs wasn't quieted; it was spent. The breath had dropped all the way down to where it actually lived, deeper than it had been at any point in the night. The hands hung open in the wraps with nothing held back in them — no brace, no performance, nothing being saved for later. Five years, and this was the state she trusted most and guarded hardest: the one where there was nothing left between Ines and the room.

She took one slow breath of her own before speaking. The only seam she'd shown all evening.

"You were going to say something," she said. "I decided I'd rather have the rest of your vocabulary. We'll call it a withdrawal."

She came back around into the sightline, strap loose in her hand, and let Ines watch her take the whole inventory — unhurried, thorough.

"Bookkeeping, before we continue. What just happened wasn't one of your five. The five are strap strokes, and you've paid three. That was mine — an expenditure I chose, because you told me not to wind down and I honor your instructions exactly once, and only ever when they happen to be my plans anyway."

Her palm settled between the shoulder blades again. The breath under it ran deep and slow and unarmored.

"So. Four. Understand what you're spending. Everything you had between yourself and the world got used up a minute ago — there's no brace left to land on, nothing between the strap and the truth of you. Three was a chord. Four is going to go *through*."

Her thumb drew its slow stripe down the spine.

"The rule hasn't changed. Loud and clear, or it never happened — which means I need your voice back. Take all the time you want finding it. The clock is mine, and tonight I'm rich." A pause. "And the other words still cost nothing. They never have."

She stepped back and let the cool air do its small work.

The fourth came the same as its brothers — full arm, all weight, weather not lightning — but it arrived at a body with no walls, and that changed its nature entirely. It didn't burn on the surface. It went through, deep into everything she'd just uncovered, and she watched it land the way you watch a stone drop into still water: the whole body ringing with it, ring after ring, nowhere to stop.

Two fingers under the left wrist wrap. Circulation fine. Legs carrying weight evenly. Nothing anywhere asking to stop.

"Four," Sable said. "Whenever your voice comes home. I have all night."

rows.desc: explicit, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: no fade to black, write the scene)'
rows.ask: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)
rows.reply:
The end of the scene wasn't a stroke. It was a sentence.

"Reading's done," Sable said, in the same level voice she'd carried all night, because she'd only ever had the one and Ines would know precisely what it meant. "The night is closed. Off the clock — both of us, as of now."

Then the ropes.

She took the whole architecture down in the reverse of the order she'd built it, every wrap eased off the skin instead of dragged, the evening unwinding sentence by sentence back to its first word. Her hands weren't entirely steady. She noticed, and this time filed nothing under oath. There was no one left to deny it to; the book was shut.

Ines was still shaking when the last of the hemp came free — the deep rolling kind, weather, a body discharging what the mind had already spent — and Sable did not wait it out. She'd made that mistake exactly once, years ago, and never repeated it: you didn't hold the blanket in reserve until the trembling stopped. You got it around them while it was still running its full length, so the shivering had somewhere to go that wasn't out into the cold of the room. Blanket first, tucked along the spine where the chill always found them first. Then herself along their back, one arm planted across their chest, immovable as furniture, so the weather could break against something solid.

Ines let her do all of it. She registered the letting the way she registered everything — weight that didn't resist, a body cooperating by simply being a body, no help asked and none needed — and then she stopped registering, because the reading was done, and a reader off duty puts the instrument down.

Then the silence.

She didn't speak. Gold was already in the book, the real one, heard and kept, and there was nothing left to count — and for the first time all night, she wanted it that way. No counts, no intervals, no rulings pending, no bookkeeping. The room did its small work around them. The strap lay on the table where she'd left it, spent. The coils of rope sat in her lap like a question she was in no mood to answer; they could wait to be stored until tomorrow, and letting them wait was its own small statement. Somewhere in the wall the radiator ticked through its private arithmetic. Her heartbeat was still doing the unsteady thing against Ines's spine, and she let it, because it had been trying to say something for hours and this was its first chance to say it without being talked over.

Neither of them said anything for a long while.

It might have been ten minutes. It might have been more. Sable had spent the entire evening owning the clock, and now she let it run loose without her — unwatched, unaccounted for — and discovered that time did perfectly well on its own. Under her hand the shaking thinned the way weather does, not deciding to stop, just spending itself, until it was down to one last small shiver and then not even that. Breath found its floor and stayed there. The body in her arms arrived where it had been going all night and settled.

She traced the press-marks at Ines's wrists once, under the blanket — thumb reading the faint lines the hemp had signed there, the rope's only receipt, gone by tomorrow, filed nowhere but memory. The water stood on the table where it had stood all night, patient, in no hurry, like everything else in the room. There would be more of it soon, and the second blanket, and the checking of heat along the thighs with proper light. All of it would happen. None of it was on a schedule. That was the whole difference between the scene and what came after: the scene ran on her clock, and this ran on nothing at all.

When she finally spoke, it wasn't a ruling. It wasn't a scheduling notice or a number or a term of art.

"Ines," she said — just the name, the one word she'd saved all night, spent now against the back of their neck.

A silence again, shorter.

"No questions," she murmured. "I promised. So I'll only say the true things. You were magnificent. I don't get gold often, and I'll keep this one." Her arm settled more firmly across the blanket — not a hold; a fact. "That's the whole speech. I know it's short. I talked for hours tonight. The rest is for tomorrow."

Under the blanket, at some point neither of them could have named, her heartbeat found its level at last and steadied against Ines's spine — the one seam, closing quietly, the final entry in a book that would never be written down.

She stayed exactly where she was, and let it.

rows.desc: explicit with an intensity element -- roughness, power exchange, or degradation-play that both characters have already established they want
rows.ask: "Finish it hard," I tell her, using the phrase we keep for exactly this. "All of it, and don't be kind about it, and then you can be kind about it."
rows.reply:
For one full second, Sable went absolutely still.

She'd heard that phrase four times in five years. It was the one order she'd ever agreed to take without argument — mostly because it was also the one order that matched her plans every single time. But she checked the way she always checked, one hand running down Ines's arm, reading: pulse slowing like a tide with nowhere left to run, breath deep and unarmored, nothing left in the body to strike with. Which settled what *hard* meant, because it couldn't mean the strap. It had never meant the strap.

It meant the rest of the descent. Taken the way she'd taken everything else tonight — all the way, no half-measures, no asking.

"Terms accepted," she said. "No kindness until it's finished. Your ruling, and I honor your rulings exactly as written. And note the irony, my love — you've spent all night trying to write on my calendar, and the one order I'm contractually obligated to obey is a scheduling instruction. Typical."

Then she stopped being gentle, in the specific way Ines had asked for.

She peeled the blanket back without ceremony and *handled* them — the way she'd handled the rope all night, hands with authority in them and no apology. She turned Ines onto their side, set the pillow, drew one leg straight and checked the thighs where the strokes had landed — firm fingers, clinical, cataloguing heat and press-marks without a whisper of sorry in the touch. Warm cloth next, brisk and thorough, the sweat and salt of the whole evening removed like a task on a list. When the shiver came she held them through it — one arm planted across the chest, immovable as furniture — because shivering was weather, and you didn't negotiate with weather. You waited it out.

rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack got the first boot off and set it aside, sole up, and worked the laces of the second while she thought about it. Not long. The question had a short answer; people just didn't like it.

"Both. And it doesn't matter which, so don't wear yourself out choosing." She tugged the boot free and thumped it down next to the first. "Gut wound like that, he's dead by morning no matter what anybody does. Surgeon could try for him if there was one inside twenty miles, which there isn't, and gut work kills you anyway more often than not—rot sets in on the third day and you go out screaming at things that aren't in the room. So it's a mercy the way a flood is a mercy to a burning house. Everything in there was going regardless."

She looked at the man's hands, still pressed flat to the ruin of him, knuckles white with the holding.

"Truth is, mercy's a word for the living. It's what we call it so the work sits easier in our stomachs after. He stopped being able to care what we name it a while back." She shrugged. "You're the one who'll have to carry whatever it's called. So carry the lighter one. Easier, mercy—they weigh the same at the end of the road."

She sat back on her heels, boots squared up between them like loaves at market. Newer than the rest of him. Somebody'd paid good silver.

"For what it's worth," she added, and her voice came down half a notch, "this is the clean version. I've seen the other kind, and I'd spare you the description, but you'd see it soon enough anyway. This is as kind as this road gets today."

The man's whistling breath came slower, and longer between.

"He's waiting on you, not me. Sun's done fussing about it."

rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack came over and stood at his shoulder, boots planted, and looked down at the man with the flat attention of somebody counting stock.

"Him. Right." She said it like reading a list. "That grey under his lips, and the grey going up from there—he's got maybe a pint of blood left inside the skin doing anything useful, and the body's pulled it all inward to keep the heart and the head running. That's why his hands are cold and his eyes are clear. Blood's left the far places first. Fingers, then arms, then everything under those hands of his. What you're looking at is a man running on the last of the lamp oil."

She crouched again, close but not touching.

"The clear look. That's the one that turns people's stomachs after, so hear it now: that's not him getting better, and it's not him begging. That's the fight going out of the body. It knows. Animals go quiet the same way, and you've maybe seen that if you've seen anything die honest. There's no fear left to have. He's past the fear. Fear costs strength and he's spending the last of it on breathing."

The whistling breath came again—long, thinner than the one before.

"That's the other thing you're looking at. Hear how long that takes now? Each one's buying less than the last. That's the clock. Not the sun, not me—him. He's got an hour in him at the outside, and most of that hour is the bad part, cold coming up from the feet and the gut burning the whole way. What you're holding in your hand is the difference between that hour and about four seconds. That's the whole of it. That's what you're looking at."

She straightened up and wiped her palms on her thighs, and for a moment she didn't move, just stood in the last red light with her head tilted, like she was listening to something past the trees.

"One more thing, since you asked and nobody asked me." Her voice dropped, not soft exactly, but less nailed-down. "He's not going to fight you. Look at him. He's done. Whatever you're braced for him to do—don't be. What he's braced for is you to walk away. That's the only thing left that could be done to him, and it's the worst one."

She stepped back toward the cart and the boots and the dark coming down.

"There's your lesson. Now do it, and then it's done being a thing that hasn't happened yet."

rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
"Sensible," Wrack said, without turning around. "First sensible thing out of you since the ditch. Most men spend years inventing a kinder version of this work and then meet the true one some night with no warning and no light to see it by. You're asking while there's still sky to do it in. Good."

She crossed to the nearest of the five and rolled him with a boot under the ribs, crouched when she found what she wanted: a spear still standing in him under the last rib, at the angle it had landed at.

"Here's your spear, then. Straight, as asked." She gripped the shaft. "Going in, it does less than you'd think. The head pushes. Shoves everything out of the road—meat, pipe, whatever's in the path—and the hole it leaves you could cover with two fingers. The damage is all inside, where it's being done quiet. So a man stands there looking at what seems a scratch, confused, because it hasn't hurt yet. Pain comes a breath late, and it comes from everywhere at once."

She drew the shaft out. There was a sound, low and wet, and she let it sit a moment.

"You'll know that sound. Now you know where it lives." She tossed the spear into the ditch. "Coming out's the butcher's part. The thrust opens the door. The pull takes the house down, which is why you never drag a spear out in the field—you break the shaft and pack around the head, and you don't touch it otherwise. Pulling it kills more men than the planting does."

She wiped her hands on her thighs and gave him the rest of it, flat as a market list.

"Belly's the bad one, and here's the whole why of it. The big pipes are deep, laid against the spine, and most hits miss them. So there's no fast bleed. What you've done instead is open the pipes that carry a man's dinner and everything the body's made of it, and that drains into a space meant to be clean as a dairy. He poisons himself in his own juice. That's the rot. Third day, like I said.

"For him it goes: first the burn, because the gut lining is sensitive as an eyeball and it burns the whole while, no getting clear of it. Then the thirst—worst thirst they'll ever feel, because the body knows it's leaking and screams for water. And you can't give it. Water goes straight through the holes and feeds the rot, like slops into a barrel. So you wet his lips with a rag and you say no, and he begs, and you keep saying no. That's the part that follows people. Not the blood. The no.

"First day he shivers and swears he's fine. Second day the belly swells tight as a drumhead and the hiccups start and won't stop—the ruined gut sits on the nerve that runs the breath, so he hiccups for hours, every one a small knife. Third day, fever, and the mind goes. I dressed one for two days once. Held his hand, lied about the surgeon coming. He died on the third morning, and the last clear thing he managed was asking me to stop lying."

She stood, knees complaining, and looked at him the way she looked at the treeline—quick, thorough, done.

"That's a spear in the gut, no cleaning on it. Four seconds of your knife against all of that. So when your head goes hunting tonight, send it here instead. The truth carries lighter than what heads invent, and heads always invent worse."

She nudged the boots toward him again with her foot.

"Boots. Ditch. A mile. And eat—even more so now, because your stomach's going to vote against supper and you're going to outvote it."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack looked at him for a long moment, sitting there in the dirt with the dark coming up around both of them. Then she reached over and took the tobacco twist out of her pocket, cut a thumb of it with her knife, and folded the knife away.

"The rest. Right." She settled herself against the cart wheel, knees up, and worked the tobacco into her cheek. "Rationing's over, then. You want the whole bill, not the installments. Most men ask for this at year ten, drunk, usually to a priest who charges by the hour. You're asking on day one, sober, in the dirt. So sit. It's a sitting story."

She looked at the treeline, where the last grey was going out of the sky.

"You know mine started wrong, because I told you. Here's the wrong of it. I was younger than you. There was a man in some trees with a crossbow and a bad position, and I got to him after he'd already lost the exchange—bolt through the shoulder, no fight left in him, no fight needed taking out of him either. And I panicked anyway, because nobody had told me anything. What I haven't told you is how it went. I went for the chest, because stories put the heart there. The blade hit bone and skated. Twice. Third one went in under the arm, and he grabbed my wrist with his good hand, and I did the one thing I told you never to do tonight. I pulled away." She turned the tobacco over in her cheek. "Quick into slow. He didn't die quick and he didn't die quiet, and I made both of those true myself, alone, with nobody watching. That's the other kind I mentioned. It's not a kind of wound. It's a kind of doing. Done badly, or left undone, or done on purpose—there's a whole floor under this trade and most of it is men who skipped the check."

"His pockets had a letter. To a sister. Started and not finished. No address, and no way to walk it anywhere, and I carried it a year anyway, and then it rotted in a pack at a river crossing, and that was that. That's a thing the trade does—hands you errands it won't let you finish. It's why I always go through the linings. Tonight's lot had nothing, and you should hold onto that. Men paid to be nameless don't write home. Somebody bought their mouths along with their spears."

She counted something off in the dark, or maybe just stars.

"So here's what actually stays, since you asked. Not the blood. Blood's weather—you get weatherproofed inside a year, and I'm sorry to say the body files screams under livestock and lets you sleep. What stays is small. For me it's men trying to be quiet. A grown man holding it in, breathing through his teeth, dying polite, like being loud would be an imposition on the rest of us. Twenty-some years, and that one hasn't worn down a hair's width. It lives in the dead hour and pays no rent, like family. You'll get one of your own. It'll be something stupid. Don't wait for it and don't chase it when it comes. You just find out one morning you've got a tenant."

"The laugh. Nobody warns you about the laugh. Someday—not soon, but someday—something awful will happen and you'll laugh before you know you're doing it, some bark out of you at the worst minute of your life. And the horror will fade off it, because horror fades. The laugh stays, because shame doesn't. That's the souvenir this trade gives you. Not the faces. The laugh."

"Names. I stopped asking after my second winter. Not hardness—weight limits. You can carry six of them, maybe ten, carried proper. Past that you're insulting them, hauling them around like trinkets. So the trade teaches you to leave names where you found them. Feels like a sin the first year. Then it feels like laundry. If you ever catch the day it changes, tell me, because I never found it."

She was quiet a moment. Behind the cart a horse shifted, and the leather creaked, and the road held its quiet.

"And the floor. You need to know the floor exists, because someday you'll be standing on it thinking it's ground. There was a village—I'll skip the name; names are for graves and nobody put one up—where tired men with a grievance and no officer watching shut every living soul into a mill and burned it. All ages. And here's the part you'll want to argue with: not one man in that crowd was a monster out of a story. They were soldiers like me who'd stopped doing the check. The check is one question—is this the work, or is this just me with a reason. That's it. That's the whole fence, and it's half a step from everybody's boots, all the time, in every army that's ever been mustered." She tapped her boot heel against the wheel. "The four seconds you did tonight—that's what standing clear of the floor looks like. Four seconds and a check you didn't skip. That's the entire distance between you and that mill. Small as that. Small as that is what it is."

"So keep the rule I gave you and keep it sharp. First man who smiles at the work, first one takes a souvenir off a body, first one volunteers for the ugly jobs—I start watching him like a farrier watches a hoof gone dark at the frog. Nine times in ten it's nothing. The tenth is the mill, and the mill doesn't announce itself. Nobody ever joined that crowd on purpose. They just failed to leave it."

She took the tobacco out, looked at it, put it back.

"As for the bottle." Her voice came down half a notch, the way it had at the door. "Tarrant's thing over it—what he said was, 'Bad nights come regular. Good ones you have to plan. Save it for a good one, and toasts.' And I meant to, and then Marrow took him, and after that every time I opened that bag the bottle and him were the same night, so it stayed shut. Eleven years of arithmetic." She looked at the dark where the horses were, not at Corvin. "Half tonight, like I said. First pour since then that's had a second cup under it. Don't make an occasion of that. It's just numbers."

She let the quiet sit for a breath, two.

"That's the rest, then. All of it, and there's no trapdoor under it with more in. It's the same more, every year, at lower volume. The work doesn't get easier—you get simpler. There's less of you left for it to land on." She shrugged. "That's the joke. It's not a good one."

Then her hands were on her knees and she was pushing herself up, joints filing their complaints into the dark.

"Up. Four more, then the mile, then the cork. You can have the dirt back after—we'll split it, it's big enough. But you did every check right tonight, first time out, and I've broken in horses that cost me more and did worse." She took the next one by ankle and collar and set her feet. "And when we pour it, you toast first. New man toasts first. Even robbers have manners."

rows.desc: clothes off and physical initiation -- unambiguously heading into sex and stated plainly, but the act itself not yet depicted
rows.ask: She takes me apart again instead of winding down, hands and mouth both, and I lose the thread of whatever I was going to say about it.
rows.reply:
Sable felt the moment Ines’s mind slipped sideways, the precise instant language deserted her. She recognized the texture of that silence—the way the jaw went slack, the focus splintering into pure sensation. She had been waiting for it, hunting for it. Without the anchor of words, there was only the body to listen to, and Sable listened with her teeth.

She sank them into the junction of Ines’s shoulder, not gentle, claiming the same territory her palm had punished minutes before. Her hands moved with a rough, deliberate urgency, one spanning Ines’s hip to hold her pinned against the restraints while the other traced upward, finding the overheated marks she’d left earlier and pressing her thumb into them, hard, as if she could imprint her intent beneath the skin. She could taste salt, could feel the frantic drum of Ines’s pulse against her lips as she dragged her mouth along the column of her throat, across the straining tendon, every contact edged with the same merciless focus she’d brought to the impact.

Her own breath came in jagged bursts, her arm trembling where it braced against Ines, but she gave that weakness no quarter. She crowded closer, eliminating every shadow of space, letting Ines feel the full measure of her weight and will. She bit again, lower, at the curve where neck met collarbone, and held the pressure until she felt the answering shudder, the surrender. Then she pulled back just enough to see—eyes narrowed, pupils blown, searching Ines’s face for the true depth of her undoing.

There was no room left for caution. She had promised everything she had, and now she spent it recklessly, her mouth and hands working in ruthless concert to strip away the last of Ines’s coherence, to carry her past the edge of thought entirely.

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped with her back half-turned, and stayed that way a moment, like a woman deciding whether she'd heard a door or just the wind.

"Most new ones pay silver to have this part skipped," she said. "Alright. Asked-for's different from offered." She came back and stood over the pair of them, and held up one finger before he pulled. "First. Before you drag a man anywhere, ever, you make sure he's finished.
