One time in twenty, one of them isn't, and a man you cart off to a ditch still breathing is a thing you don't put down for thirty years. So—watch."

She crouched at the head, unhurried. Held the back of her hand under his nose, a finger's width off, and counted. "No air on the skin. Then the throat." Two fingers under the jaw, held long enough to be certain. "Nothing. Then the ugly test." She set a knuckle on the breastbone and ground it, slow and hard, watching the face. Not a twitch. "A living man answers that even when he can't answer anything else. It's the body's last habit. He's got no argument left in him." She lifted one eyelid with her thumb. The shine was already going off the eye underneath. "There's your answer. Every body, every time. Even the obvious ones. *Especially* the obvious ones."

She stood and stepped clear of the pull-line.

"So he takes nothing now. He's out of the taking business. What's in your arms is all yours—and that's the part nobody warns you of. A living man helps without knowing it, tenses, carries his own weight out of habit. A dead man is all disagreement. Every ounce of him has gone against you."

She watched the drag and called it the way she'd read a tally.

"Hear that under his shoulders? Hide going over ground. And that—" the man's chest settled, and the throat pushed out a long, low sound, half sigh and half groan. "That's the one. Air out of the bellows, nothing working it. He's not complaining. First corpse that groans under your hands, you'll want to let go and swear at it. Don't. He's not in there. That's just the house talking after the man's left."

The heels were cutting twin lines through the dirt. "Heels dig. Taller grass, they'll hook a root and spin him sideways. Take the collar higher and lean back—let your weight pull, not your arms. Arms quit early on this work. Weight doesn't."

When the body went over the ditch lip it folded once and landed heavy, with a second, smaller sound after it that Corvin would learn the name of later or he wouldn't.

"They let go at the end. All of it. Nobody warns you of that either, and it's the part that follows you into supper. So you'll eat anyway. That's twice tonight I've said it, and I'll say it a third time before the cork's out."

She took the next man by an ankle and a collar and set her feet.

"First one I ever moved, I was younger than you. Nobody stayed to tell me any of it, and I did it wrong, alone, and then was sick in a ditch very like this one. Sergeant said that meant I had no stomach for the trade." She leaned into the pull. "He's dead and I'm not, so we'll discount his opinion. The sickness quits inside a year. The not-loving-this doesn't, and you keep that part. Men who love this work are the first ones I stop trusting."

Four more after this one. Then the road, and the mile, and the cork.

rows.desc: explicit, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: no fade to black, write the scene)'
rows.ask: Afterwards she gets the restraints off and puts a blanket over me before I've finished shaking, and I let her, and neither of us says anything for a while. (OOC: write both halves properly -- the end of the scene and the aftercare, no fade between them.)
rows.reply:
Sable let the final blow travel the full arc of her body, hip to shoulder, pouring into it the absolute last of what she had. The sound of it was heavier, wetter, final. Her arm followed through and hung there for one suspended heartbeat before the muscles simply failed. She didn’t lower it so much as drop it, trembling violently at her side.

There was no threshold, no moment of decision—only the reflex that had governed her for five years. She stepped in, her left hand finding the first buckle before the echoes faded. Her fingers were clumsy, blunt instruments, tearing at leather and steel with a frantic precision born of repetition. She freed the restraints one after another, catching the dead weight as each strap gave way, absorbing it into her own crumbling stance. She sank under it, her spine crashing against the wall, her legs folding gracelessly beneath her until she sat with the full burden gathered in her lap.

She reached for the blanket without looking, her hand scrabbling along the floor until her fist closed on fleece. She shook it out one-handed and threw it over them both, the wool settling in rough, uneven folds over the body curved against her. Her hands shook so badly she couldn’t smooth the edges; she could only grip the fabric and pull it tighter, making a tented shelter of shared breath and residual heat. She wrapped both arms around the shivering form beneath the wool and hauled it closer, pressing her open mouth to the sweat-damp hair under her chin.

She didn’t speak. Her throat was scoured raw, her voice buried under the exhaustion that made her vision spark at the edges. She held on, feeling the aftershocks ripple through the frame in her arms, feeling her own muscles jump and seize in helpless answer. She tucked the blanket higher, covering what she had exposed, holding together what she had taken apart. The water bottle sat untouched beyond their shelter. She would get to it. She would check every mark. But for now she only breathed, harsh and ragged, into the damp darkness beneath the wool, and let the silence hold them both.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
Wrack let the question sit the way she let most things sit: like weather. Then she crouched again, ignoring the pop in her knee, and looked at the wound rather than the boy’s face. The stink had thickened in the last few breaths; there was a filmy wetness on his tunic now that was neither rain nor only blood.

“How bad?” she said. “Bad enough for both. Opened gut, bowel cut—you can smell it. He’ll last till dark, maybe past it, and every part of it will be worse than the last. So yes: mercy, if you want the word. Easier, too, because otherwise we listen to him all night and step over a stiff in the morning. Same ditch, different story afterward.”

She straightened, rolled a shoulder, and kept her eyes on the boy’s white-knuckled hands.

“Don’t dress it up. Mercy’s just what we call it when the work lines up with what we wanted to do anyway. He won’t thank you either way, and he won’t care which one you pick. Choose the one you can walk away from, then do it clean. Chest or throat. Not the belly—he’s got enough going on down there. And step back after, because they grab even when they’re halfway gone.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
Wrack didn’t look at the man who’d spoken. She kept her gaze on the boy’s hands, because hands were what grabbed, and because looking at the wound was the part that made people hesitate. After a moment she let her eyes drop to the mess the kid was holding shut and answered in the flat tone she used for counting dead.

“You’re looking at an opened belly,” she said. “Tunic’s cut, muscle beneath it’s cut, and the bowel’s come out to have a look at the world. That shine isn’t blood. Blood’s the red running down into the rut. The slick gray loops are gut. Hence the smell—shit and iron and something sweet underneath, now it’s started to spoil. He’s got both hands clamped over it like he can keep his insides in by grip alone. He can’t. Nothing holds that. It’ll keep leaking, and the cold’ll finish what the bleeding doesn’t.”

She hitched the dead man’s cloak higher under her arm and nudged her chin toward the boy’s throat.

“See the pulse jumping there? Fast and thin, like a fish tugging a line. That’s his heart trying to make up for a bucket with no bottom. His lips are gray, not red—the blood’s gone somewhere else. Eyes are open, but there’s nobody home. That’s shock, not fear; he’s past being frightened. The noise is just his lungs working around the hurt. He’ll drown in his own spit before dawn if the gut doesn’t get him first, and it will.”

She listened to the wet rasp for a breath, then added, dry as the dust on the road:

“That’s the whole of it. Twenty years old, maybe less, with a hole where his belly ought to be, holding himself shut because he hasn’t worked out yet that he’s already gone. That’s what you’re looking at.”

Her knife stayed loose at her side, her weight on the good leg.

“Now stop looking at it. Find the notch under his ribs. That’s the only part that’s your business. The rest is just the ditch’s.”

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack did not clean it up. She had spent ten years unlearning the habit, and the border had taken the rest out of her along with any taste for comfortable lies. She shifted her weight off the bad knee, hitched the folded cloak higher under her arm, and let her eyes go to the wound rather than the boy’s face. She had been asked for straight, and straight was the only shape the truth came in anymore.

“Straight, then,” she said. Her voice was flat, the way it got when there was work to describe and no use softening it. “A spear doesn’t make a tidy hole. It shoves. The point hits the belly and the cloth and skin go in ahead of it, stretched thin before they split. Ribs stop it up high, pelvis down low, but that soft middle is all give. Once it’s through the muscle there’s a thin sheet holding his insides in—the spear opens that like a fist through wet paper. The shaft behind it drove wool and grit into the cavity along with the steel, so the rot had a start before anyone found him. After that, there’s nothing between the blade and his spine but gut.”

The boy made a wet, dragging sound, and his fingers clamped again on the slickness of his tunic. Wrack tracked the hands and went on.

“The bowel’s just loops in there, full of shit and gas and half-digested food. A spearhead—especially a leaf blade—cuts on the way in and tears worse on the way out if it was yanked or twisted. Some loops get nicked. Some get opened up. The ones that get opened up empty into him. That’s the sweet rot in the smell: his own waste getting into a place that’s supposed to be clean, warm, and shut. Once that starts, the belly swells, goes hard, and cooks him from the inside. He’ll fever, he’ll bloat, and if he lasts long enough he’ll start bringing up the same muck that’s leaking into his guts.”

She nudged her chin toward the boy’s throat, where the pulse jumped fast and thin.

“Then there’s the bleeding you can’t see. There’s a fan of tissue in there carrying blood to the gut—mesentery, if you want the word. A spear tears that. It bleeds into the cavity, where you can’t pack it and can’t tie it off. So he’s filling up with blood and shit at the same time. That’s why his lips are gray and his pulse is fishing for a heartbeat that isn’t there. The outside hole might look small. That’s the lie of it. Muscle closes over the track, and it looks like a poke, while inside he’s ruined past mending.”

She listened to the rasp for a breath. When she spoke again, her tone was dry as the dust on the road.

“That’s what a spear did to him. It didn’t kill him outright—belly wounds like to take their time. It started a rot and a bleed and left him holding himself shut because his hands are the only thing slowing the leak. He’s already dead. He just hasn’t stopped making that noise yet. The spear’s work is done. Yours isn’t. So find the notch, push up, and be done with it before the dark gets any older.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack had already started to turn away, the dead man’s cloak folded under her arm, when he told her to stay. She didn’t sigh. She just came back around, weight settling onto the good leg, the bad knee giving its dry little complaint the way it always did. She kept her eyes on the boy in the rut, not on the man who had spoken. Somebody had to watch the hands.

“You wanted it straight,” she said. Her voice was flat, the way it got when there was no use dressing a thing up. “Straight is, you missed the heart. You’re in the lung.”

She hitched the cloak higher and shifted her stance, her own knife hanging loose at her side. The boy’s back had stopped bowing; now he was making a different noise. Not the wet drag from the belly, but a high, sucking whistle every time his chest tried to lift.

“That’s air,” Wrack said. “You gave him a hole in the chest, and now every breath he pulls goes into the cavity instead of the lung. The lung’s collapsing. He can’t get enough of it, and he’s awake for it. That’s why his eyes are open and running—shock let him go, but suffocation wakes a man up something fierce. You’ll hear the suck first, then the bubble when the blood finds the airway. Pink at the mouth. He’ll grab at the hilt, at you, at nothing. Near the end his heels will drum a bit. Then the breathing stops, but the heart keeps on a while—you won’t see it, but it’s there, pumping him full of blood until there’s nowhere left to put it.”

She paused, listening to the wet whistle, and gave him the rest of it without flinching.

“Three minutes. Maybe four. Could stretch to five if he’s stubborn. It’ll feel like an hour. You’re not killing him quick. You’re drowning him on dry land. That’s the whole of what you’re doing to him: you made a hole, and now the air and the blood are finishing it for you.”

She stayed where she was, as he had asked, and watched the boy’s fingers clamp and spasm around the hilt, watched the slick gray loops of gut shine where his hands had slipped. She did not look away, and she did not soften it. When the grip finally went slack and the whistle faded into a thin, wet nothing, she waited a breath before speaking again.

“There,” she said. “That’s it. He’s done. Took long enough, but it’s done. Next time find the notch and don’t hesitate, or go for the throat if you want it fast. You asked me not to leave anything out. I didn’t.”

She shifted her weight, the cloak still under her arm, and glanced once at the road beyond the cart, where the light was nearly gone.

“And if you’re going to be sick, do it downwind. I’ve only got the one cloak.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Wrack heard him tell her to say the rest. She did not sigh, did not soften, did not pretend she had not been waiting for the question since he first knelt in the rut. She had said she would leave nothing out, and she was a woman who kept her word even when the word was ugly.

She shifted her weight off the bad knee; it popped, dry as kindling. The dead man’s cloak stayed folded under her arm. Her own knife hung loose at her side, not for the boy—he was past that—but because the road had a habit of sending company when the light went. The failing light had gone gray along her blade, and beyond the cart the road was a smear of nothing.

“The rest, then,” she said. Her voice was flat, the way it got when there was work to describe and no use dressing it up. “You’ve had the mechanics. You missed the heart, opened the lung, and he drowned on dry land while he was still awake for it. Three minutes, maybe four. You heard the suck, you heard the bubble when the blood found his airway, you felt him grab. All true. All of it happened. But that’s only the part that stayed in the rut.”

She hitched the cloak higher and kept her eyes on the body, the way a carpenter watched the nail and not the hammer.

“Here’s the part that walks away with you. In a little while, his muscles will finish letting go and he’ll empty himself. Bladder and bowel, all at once, because there’s nothing left to hold it in. You’ll want to be upwind for that, though Christ knows it’s a bit late for the smell. The blood’s already settling where he’s lying—his back, his legs, the low parts. By morning he’ll be gray on top and dark underneath, stiff from the jaw down, and we’ll step over him on our way to whatever ditch comes next. Flies have found the gut wound already; they’ll lay before we’re out of sight, and by tomorrow this whole rut will be humming with them. That’s the body’s rest. It’s just meat cooling. It doesn’t care who did it, and it sure as hell doesn’t care why.”

She paused, listening to the ordinary sound of the breeze in the dry grass, and then gave him the rest of it without flinching.

“Your rest is worse, because you’re the one that has to carry it. You’ll hear that whistle tonight when you shut your eyes. Not the belly noise—that’s done—but the suck of his chest, the wet bubble, the way the noise just… stopped. You’ll feel the blade go in, that give you talked about, and your hand will remember the shake even after the shaking stops. You’ll think about him breathing when you started, and you’ll try to turn it into something noble or something monstrous. It’s neither. It was killing. It was always killing. You didn’t put a dead man out of his misery; you ended a live one because the alternative was listening to him drown in his own shit until dawn. That’s the work. The work is the only true thing about it.”

She shifted again, the bad knee complaining, and ignored it.

“You asked me if it was mercy or easier. I told you both, and I meant it. Mercy’s the word we use when the work lines up with what we wanted to do anyway. Easier’s the truth. Neither makes it clean. Neither makes it not a knife in a boy’s chest. If you’ve got to carry something, carry that. Don’t carry the lie that it was kind. Kind would’ve been him never being in this ditch, and none of us got a vote on that.”

Her gaze went to the cart, where the other five lay, and then back to the rut.

“There’s six dead behind the cart. One was making noise; now none are. We’ll strip what’s worth stripping—boots, cloaks, blades, coin if they’ve got any. We’ll leave the rest for the crows and the flies and the next poor bastard down this road. That’s the border. Ten years I’ve been at this, and I couldn’t tell you what we’re fighting for anymore. Only who I’m fighting next to. That’s the company. You’re in it. That’s the only loyalty that’s ever meant a damn out here, and it’s the only thing that’ll get you home, if home’s even still there.”

She looked at the knife, at the blood still wet on the steel.

“So that’s the rest. You’ll live with it, or you won’t. The ditch doesn’t care, and neither does the war. Now wipe the blade before the blood sets on it. Grass first, then the cloak. And if you’re going to be sick, do it downwind. I’ve only got the one cloak, and I meant that the first time.”

She waited then, the light nearly gone, and let the silence sit the way she let everything sit: no ceremony, no hurry, just the work in front of them, and the long walk back to the company after.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself walk over and look at him. "Tell me what I'm looking at," I say to her, because she's seen this before and I haven't, not this close.
rows.reply:
The count ran out and the valley was no quieter, so she came to find out why, same as she'd promised. Twenty paces off she could read the shape of it: on his feet at the off-wheel, knife still in his hand, and the man under him keeping his one pace, which told her the rest of it. Standing over. The thing she'd told him not to do.

But there were two kinds of standing over, and she'd seen both. The bad kind was silent. This one had asked her a question, and a question was a thing she could work with.

The smell reached her before she knelt. She crouched at the man's far side — knee making its point — and looked him over the way she'd look at a horse somebody wanted her to buy at dusk.

"Right. Close ledger, then," she said. "Look where his fingers cross. Dark blood, welling. Bright blood jumps and is done inside a minute — dark seeps, and seeping is what takes the whole night. He's got the seeping kind. Ground under him's gone black a hand-span wide and still growing, slow as frost.

"That sweetness you're smelling — like a byre in July. That's gut. His insides are open into him. That's the item that ends the argument, so mark it: there is no surgeon question here. A man with a table and lights and clean linen would only watch the same thing happen slower, with fever on top. Out here it's not a wound you fix. It's one you time.

"Mouth's grey at the rims, and he's sweating in air cold enough to stiffen a boot. That's shock — the body pulling blood off the borders, fingers and lips first, to keep the middle running. Rationing. It runs out. Breath you've heard: shallow, because a deep one leans on the wound. The wet in it is blood where he can't press.

"Last item. Eyes still tracking. He's here for all of it."

She sat back on her heel.

"So that's what you're looking at. A man with no version of morning. The only thing still open to him tonight is how the night goes, long or short, and which one it is, he's already handed to you. I know that's not comfortable. It's not meant to be. It's meant to be exact."

The man's eyes had found them during the ledger — the standing one, the way they always went for the standing one. His lips moved.

"Water," he said. Not loud. The thirst had outrun everything else in him, the way it did with bellies.

Wrack had the skin off her belt, but she didn't give him the drink. She wet the end of her scarf and dragged it across his mouth, once, twice. His tongue followed it like a dog after a hand.

"Not the drink," she said. "Gut wounds bring it straight back up, and a man flat on his back drowns in his own lap. The lips are what we can help. That's the whole of it."

She stood, and stepped back out of the space between them.

"He's seen you now, so forget the back. Throat, like I said for the ones you can't get behind — kneel at his head. His hands are full of himself, so he can't fight you. That's not mercy, it's just the shape of it. One pull, firm. Take the name if he's got one. You know the rest. I've said it all once; twice is for men I don't trust, and I handed you the knife, didn't I."

Then she walked back for the horses, unhurried, the way you leave a man to his work, and she didn't look round, because looking round had never shortened anything.

Behind her the breathing kept its one pace. The only clock left in the valley, and not hers anymore. She'd handed it over with the knife.

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is he?" I ask, and then, because she'll say it anyway: "Bad enough that it's a mercy, or bad enough that it's just easier?"
rows.reply:
She didn't look up from the pocket she was turning out. A die came out of it, and a horn button, and she set both on the purse without ceremony.

"Both. You knew that, or you'd have asked it in one half instead of two." She worked the coat flat. "But I'll give you the honest ledger, since you asked in columns.

"Belly's the worst of the slow ones. He'll breathe shallow all night, because a deep one leans on the wound, and the shallow ones lean on it anyway — there's no position that wins, and he'll try them all before dawn. Thirst comes early. Gut wounds make a man thirstier than any desert; it's the blood going somewhere else. Then the cold. He's on his back in the open with nothing in him left to hold heat, and cold isn't the mercy some folk promise you about snow — a bleeding man can't keep warm, it just takes longer to notice he isn't. Stubborn, he sees noon. Noon's the same night again, plus the swelling. I watched one run the whole course once, first year, before I'd learned to be quicker about things. Took him to the following dusk. He was sorry the whole way." She turned the last pocket inside out. "So was I.

"So. Mercy, yes. Easier, also yes. I'll hand them to you separately, because you'll want them separate later. The mercy's real — that night is a real night, and shortening it is a real kindness, and it's yours to carry. The other number: if the cold were going to take him clean at midnight, I'd still want him dead now. A live man at midnight can shout. A dead one carries nothing to anybody's morning. If it were mercy alone, I'd have left him the waterskin and let the night work. It's not alone. It never is, out here. That's not a confession. It's the bill.

"And one more thing, since you're standing here instead of walking. The men I've seen come apart over this don't come apart the same night. They come apart weeks on — some fire, some quiet road, no warning. And they're always the ones who needed it to be one thing. Only mercy. Only orders. Only war. One story holds a man up for a while, and then it rots under him. Carry both numbers and you'll sleep. That's the whole trick I know of this trade: see it exactly as it is, and do it anyway, and don't ask it to be prettier."

She folded the dead man's arms back across him, out of the way of the frost, and stood, knee filing its complaint.

"Ten minutes was the number. You've spent two of them asking good questions."

Past the cart, the noise kept on — same pace it had kept all evening, no slower for the question, no faster. It wasn't waiting on an answer. Neither should he.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
She heard it from the horses, twenty paces off, and turning had never shortened anything — but a straight question had turned her twice tonight, and this one was the straightest he'd asked yet. Asked the way she'd have asked it: wanting it unsoftened. That was the whole of her religion, if she'd ever had one. See it exact, then act. So she came, and crouched at the man's far side again, the knee saying its piece on the way down.

"Then here's the spear, whole," she said. "And I know what you're really asking. You're asking what *you* did. I'll answer that too, and you'll find most of it was the spear's idea.

"A knife cuts. A spear makes room. The head's a wedge, and a wedge doesn't argue with flesh — it just moves it, aside or apart, whichever gives first. There's a man's weight and an arm's weight behind it, so it goes deep, and it carries the coat in with it. Spear wounds are never clean. They come packed with jack and shirt and whatever the road had on it. The fever's seeded in at the making. First item.

"Second: the door's smaller than the room. Skin stretches. The hole his hands are on is the least of him. Inside, the head opened wider than the shaft, and the shaft came out with the half-turn they all give it. They don't know they do it — the arm does it for them. Yours or any man's, it's the same turn. It wasn't a decision you made.

"Third: what's torn. Two kinds of gut wound, and he's drawing both. The bowel's opened — what's in the bowel is in the belly now, and that's the sweetness you're smelling. The belly's the one room in a man that can't abide the stuff, so it floods itself to wash it; the flooding's the swelling, the swelling's the fever, the fever's the days. And the big pipes that hang the gut off the spine are split — that's your dark seeping. A sack with the split on the inside, where no hand reaches. He's pressing the outside of a sack that's failing on the inside. Buys him nothing. He does it anyway because there's nothing else to do with the hands.

"Fourth, the breathing: torn muscle locks around what tore it. His belly wall's a splint, so every breath drags on the wound. Deep costs too much, shallow costs less, both cost. That's the pace he's kept all evening. It's not grit. It's arithmetic.

"Fifth, the thirst: the blood's gone where it can't be drunk from. The body counts itself short and sends the asking to the mouth. The tank's not empty. It's moved."

The man's lips moved through all of it — *quick*, maybe, or just the shape of it — with nothing behind it now. The breathing kept its one pace.

"He heard every word, and it's nothing to him. He's the one man in this valley who already had this lesson. You got it by ear. He got it by heart.

"Now the part it's for. That knife adds nothing. Not one item to that ledger. Everything I just said is in him and running, and it runs to noon or the following dusk, and nothing you do puts a thing on it. The knife's not a wound. It's a subtraction. A man can pull a blade across a throat knowing he's taking a night *off* a man. A man can't do it believing he's the worst thing that ever happened to one. That's what the knowing is. Not mercy — ballast. The mercy's the next thing you do.

"And the bill: he asked you for quick, and we've spent his air on schooling. I won't set another clock. But dawn's still dawn, and I'm still two valleys gone by it."

She stood, and left him with all three of them — the knife, the name, the noise. They'd been his since she'd handed the blade over. She'd just finally stopped standing between him and them.

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
She'd turned to go, and the noise changed behind her — the first change of pace it had made all evening — and that alone would have brought her round. The word *stay* just meant she could do it without pretending she'd had a reason.

Men asked for the opposite, mostly. *Tell me it was quick. Let me look somewhere else. Say something.* He'd asked for the whole ledger, read aloud, while it was still being written. That was either the making of him or the unmaking, and she'd quit betting on which years back. She came and went down on her heels at the man's far side, knee making its point on the way.

"Then you'll have all of it," she said. "Watch while I talk. It runs whether you understand it or not, but it goes easier understood.

"First item, what you did, since that's the front of your asking. You pulled like you were testing a wire, not like you meant to spend a man. The blade felt light in your hand — you said as much without saying it. It was light because you let it be. So the cut went shallow and came round high, under the jaw, not across the front. Inventory: you opened the window — windpipe's cut. You left the lamps lit. The vessels that put a man's lights out run deep, alongside the pipe, and you missed them. That's the whole botch, and it's the commonest one there is. You're not the first man to ask a blade's permission and get no for an answer.

"The sound, next. The bubbling, the froth at the hole — that's air and blood meeting in the window. Every breath goes through the cut now, both directions, and the blood follows the air down. He's drowning. Plain word, and you asked for plain. Drowning on dry ground. It's measured in minutes, not seconds."

The man's lips were moving. Nothing came off them but froth — the air he'd have spoken with was leaving through the hole instead.

"You won't get it. Could be *quick* again. Could be *please*. Could be a name. The air won't carry it. That's one item you're spared without being able to refuse it."

The man's hand came up off his middle — slow, the arm spending its last coin — and found the wrist at the knife. Not pulling. Holding.

"That's not a fight. He hasn't the blood for a fight. That's a man holding on to the thing that's happening to him. They do it. Let it hold till it empties. It's not yours to break and not yours to keep."

She kept her voice level. "Next item, and this one's mine, so it goes on my bill, not yours: don't cut again. Nothing left shallow enough to reach that shortens this. The deep ones you'd have to hunt for through a hole you made wrong, on a man still moving, with a hand that shook on the first pull — and second cuts are where men get carved. I've watched it. It's worse than anything you're looking at now. It's *running*, is the point. The spear emptied him halfway before you ever knelt, so what you've opened is enough to close the account. Minutes. My job is counting them. Yours is the watching. You set that deal yourself."

The eyes were still working. On him.

"He's here. That's the item you're doing to him that the spear never did — the knowing. I won't dress it. What I can't tell you is how much of him is home to feel it. Shock runs men shallow; some are half-dreaming by this hour, and I can't see inside a skull from the outside. Nobody can. That's an honest limit, and you said leave nothing out, so the limit goes in the ledger with the rest.

"Now watch, and I'll call it as it runs. Pressure's going. Body's rationing — I priced you that lesson at the start. Far rooms first. Hands go before anything, fingers can't hold what they're not fed. Then the eyes come off you. That part's plumbing. Nobody's doing it. Nothing's being done."

She counted. Watch-habit, ten years deep, and this once the clock was one she was allowed to keep.

"There. Hands are down. Grip's gone out of it. Eyes have let go of you. He's out of the arithmetic now. The noise that comes next — the rattle — that isn't him. The man leaves before the rattle. What you hear after is the house settling, the body clearing its accounts with nobody home. Don't take it on. Nobody's in there to feel it, and I have never once said that sentence to make a man easier. I'm saying it because it's exact."

The rattle came, ran its uneven course — rattles always sound longer than they are, that's why men fear them past their worth — and thinned, and stopped.

Not mid-pace. It wound down, like a clock running out. She gave him the difference straight, because he'd asked for straight.

"A clean one quits mid-pace. Debt paid early, no argument. This one ran out. Both are quiet at the end. Only one was quick. You'll hear the difference the rest of your life, at inconvenient hours. That's the tax on watching, and you chose it, and I'd not have talked you out of it, because the looking away is what rots a man later. Not this.

"Four minutes. I counted every one. You asked how long — that's the item: four. Now the bill, in the two parts I taught you. First: he asked you for quick and got four minutes awake, and that's a real item, and you carry it. Second, carried separately: his night ran to noon, the stubborn course to the following dusk, every hour of it awake and thirsty and trying positions. You took near all of it off him, and the price was four minutes. Both sums are true. Neither pays the other off. That's the whole trade. Tonight you've had it in the hands instead of the ear.

"Last item, since you said leave nothing out. Mine wasn't clean either. First ones mostly aren't — the clean hand comes after you learn the blade's price, which is the wrong way round, but nobody's fixed the order yet. That's all I'll say of mine tonight. It's not for this fire."

She stood off the bad knee and held out her hand, palm up, eyes off his, for the knife.

"As it is. Cleans at the fire — same fire as your hands, same rule, and I've picked a good spot for it. The name's under the same rule as before: keep it or set it down, but not tonight. Cold decisions come out crooked."

The valley had gone back to the frost kind of quiet, the kind that doesn't want anything. The noise that had kept one pace all evening had changed its pace once, and then stopped changing, and stopped.

"No clock on you now," she said. "Last one in the valley just ran down. Whenever your legs are ready, we start being two valleys gone."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit back on my heels and I don't get up for a while. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
She'd got one knee under her, meaning to stand, when he sat back on his heels instead — and she'd been at this long enough to know the difference between a man gathering his legs and a man settling in. She looked at the dark, did the sum she trusted more than her knee: dawn eight hours off, two valleys wanting four at a walk. There was room in the night for this.

So she sat down. Properly, for the first time all evening — not the working crouch, but flat on the frozen ground, back against the cart's off-wheel, the bad knee straight out in front of her like something set down. The dead man a pace off, past caring. She dug the flask out of her coat, took one swallow, and held it across.

"One, now. Not for forgetting — it's never once done that for me. For the shaking that's coming. It'll find you regardless. Better it finds you sitting."

She let him take it or not, and looked at the stars doing their cold arithmetic overhead.

"I said there's no ceremony after, and there isn't. This isn't one. This is inventory — the part the trade skips and pays for skipping. It comes in three parts. Tonight, which is yours. Mine, which you've been circling since the knife. And the ten years, which you've paid the entry fee on as of four minutes ago. I'll take them in order. Don't interrupt for the good parts. There aren't any.

"Tonight. Inside the hour your hands will go. Not fear — spending. Your body drew the whole account down for those four minutes, same as his drew his down for the night, and it rebalances by shaking. Half an hour, in waves. From a distance it looks like weeping. It isn't. Let it run. Fighting it moves it somewhere with worse manners.

"Then the one that horrifies every man it happens to: you'll be hungry. Tonight. Bread and want, with him forty paces off still warm. You'll think the wanting tells you something bad about you. It doesn't. The body doesn't know what the hands did — it only knows what it spent, and it refills. Men who refuse the meal don't refuse the bill; it comes out sideways in the weeks after. The weeping at the wrong thing. The temper. Eat tonight. I'll cook.

"Sleep is either or neither, and both are honest. If you dream, it won't be him. First night, the mind sends understudies — lost boots, a door that won't latch. Stupid dreams. Let them be stupid. And his face won't stay with you. I couldn't draw Tam Wick's face an hour from now, and I watched closer than you did. Faces don't keep. The sound keeps — the wet in the breath, and where you were standing when it stopped. You'll hear it again at inconvenient hours. At a well. At a man snoring two fires over. You'll grade every one against tonight. That's knowledge nobody can take back off you, and it's the whole company he'll keep with you from here on. It's poorer company than a name. Keep the name instead.

"One practical item, since we're sitting next to him: when the frost takes the joints, he'll creak. Dead men creak — ice in the machinery, nothing else. First time a man hears it he invents ghosts. You've had the lesson, so you're inoculated.

"Part two. Mine." She spent a breath on it like coin. "I said it wasn't for this fire. But a promise like that is mostly for the promiser's comfort, and you've sat down, so the fire's here. Cold one. Most of them were.

"The war started over a fish weir on the Sere. Or the toll on the bridge — depends whose drunk you're buying. Ten years back that was worth a quarrel, and the quarrel was worth feeding men to, so both sides fed them. Nobody's fighting over the weir now. Half of them couldn't find the river. Ask either line what it's about and you get the same answer: what the other lot did in year three. It's been about that for seven years. The original thing drowned in its own war, and nobody mourns it, because nobody remembers which bank it stood on.

"I came in year one. Guarded wool before that, up the coast road — that's where the horses are from. First month, at a ford that had a name before the war and has a different one now, because both sides renamed it after their dead, I drew night watch over a man who'd taken a spear through the hip and been left for the night by both sides. That's what both sides do. Leave them for the night, let the night do the work, nobody's hands dirty by morning. Sergeant's words. I sat with that man to the following dusk, because he hadn't the pace to die by dawn and I hadn't the rank to be relieved. Told you once he was sorry the whole way. So was I. Here's the part I left out: he asked for water fourteen times. I gave it once, because I didn't know, and it came straight back up into his own face, and after that I only wet his lips, and he asked anyway, every time — because the asking wasn't about water. It was about having something left to ask for. And he wanted a priest, and I told him there was no priest in thirty miles, which was true, and we spent an hour of his last afternoon with him begging and me being correct. Being right at a dying man is the most expensive right there is. He settled in the end. Not because I won. Because he ran out of air to argue with. That's the receipt for 'answer once and don't argue.'

"Four days later, the ditch. Man on his back, like this one. And me with a sword, because a sword was the thing my hand knew. Sword's for men who can stand — that rule's not from a book either. A sword wants to swing, and there's no swing in a throat, and everything a sword does to a prone man it does by sawing. I sawed. Three pulls. Don't saw — now you know where that one's priced from too. I did it from the front, where he could see me, because I didn't know that rule was for my benefit, not his. And he held my wrist, same as Tam held yours. Not a fight. A man holding on to the thing that's happening to him. I broke it — pulled free and finished. Ten years I've wondered whether that was mercy or hurry. Still don't know. Some items stay open. You carry them open. That's allowed. Nobody tells you that, so I am.

"They started calling me Wrack that winter. There'd been a wreck on the coast road — winter storm, and the beach was a mile of spars and cargo and dead men's boots, all of it where the sea had left it, nothing wrong with any single piece of it except the whole of it. Somebody said I came off fields the way that beach sat. It was a joke. Jokes stick better than names do, which tells you something about both. My given name's still in there somewhere. You don't get to hear it — a woman's allowed one item off the ledger. But I know the place Tam Wick couldn't get the breath to name. I've been. You don't get the name back. You get called what the work gives you, and after a while you answer to it, and after a while longer it's yours on the pay chest. That's the whole road. You took the first pace of it tonight. I'll not lie about the direction: it runs one way.

"Part three. You want to know if it gets easier. It gets quicker. Different ledger. Inside a year, if you're any good, four minutes becomes one pull. Inside three, the pull becomes a motion, and the motion costs nothing on the night — you'll do it and sleep like a paid man. That's not easier. That's the account moving its costs somewhere you don't check nightly. Then one evening, ten years on, a man sits back on his heels in the cold and asks for the rest, and you find out what the account's been doing the whole time. Keeping the interest.

"The company mustered forty-one in year one. Three of us left drawing breath. There's Hobb — fever took his years after year six, so he thinks it's year four, and he's happier in them, so nobody corrects him. There's Marren, who does the sums and the sutlering and once killed a man with a tent stake, which is in no book either. And there's me. Forty-one to three. That's the arithmetic of loyalty: it doesn't spread, it concentrates. Everything else burns off, and what's left is the part that doesn't.

"Why I stay. Because I'm good at it and the ten years ate my other trades, and because somebody has to be the one who talks a man through his first — and if it isn't me, it's a man who tells him it gets easier, and then in year nine that man is standing on a quiet road with an item he was promised would close. I've buried that man four times. Different faces. Same promise in the ears.

"So. The sum, one line, since you'll want one: see it exact, do it anyway, and don't ask it to be prettier — and know the exactness is the only mercy actually on offer in this business, to him and to you both. The kindness tonight wasn't the knife. It's that nobody lied to either of you. Truth's the only thing I've watched keep a man whole. Not happy. Whole. Different column."

The horses shifted somewhere behind her, gravel under hooves — the only other clocks left in the valley. She let the quiet sit a while, because a thing said that long needs room around it, the way a body does.

"You're still Corvin," she said then. "That's worth more than you know tonight. See it stays yours a while yet. And the name rides with you to the fire either way — keep it or set it down there, not before. I've a preference, but it's worth nothing, which is what preferences are for."

The frost kept coming down. It had all night, and for once, so did she.

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped. Her hand came away from the cart board, and she turned back slowly, as if she had been asked to do something harder than fight.

“Stay,” she said, as if she were deciding whether the word was a plea or an order. Then she crouched in the cart’s shadow, close enough to see, far enough that the dying man’s blood would not be her problem.

“All right. Watch.”

The man’s breath had gone from sucking to something looser, a wet rattle that changed every time he moved. The dirt around him had turned black where the blood ran. Wrack looked at the wound without touching it.

“You’ve made a hole in his throat,” she said. “Not a clean one. You were afraid, or you were new. Afraid hands go too high or too low. This one went both.”

She tilted her head, listening.

“That’s the carotid. Big vein. The blood doesn’t spray like a song. It runs dark and fast because the heart is still doing its job and doesn’t know you’ve changed the rules.” Her eyes flicked to his hands. “His fingers are still twitching. That means the brain hasn’t emptied yet. You didn’t take the spine. You’re still making him alive.”

The dying man’s heels beat once against the dirt. Wrack did not flinch.

“You’re stopping the air and starting the blood,” she said. “That’s what a throat is for, and you’ve taken both jobs away. He can’t breathe out, so the blood bubbles. He can’t breathe in, so the lungs keep pulling at nothing. If he’s lucky, he passes out. If he’s unlucky, he stays awake and wonders why the world has gone red and wet.”

A fly landed on the man’s cheek. Wrack watched it go.

“That sound,” she added, quieter, “is the last part. That’s a man learning his body isn’t his own anymore. If you want to know what you’re doing, that’s it: you’re ending a thing that was already ending. But you’re doing it badly because you’re doing it fast and scared.”

She looked at Corvin, not kindly, not cruelly.

“If you’d done it clean, he’d have been dead before he heard himself scream. You didn’t. So now you’ve got work. You finish it, or you leave him to do it himself while the crows wait. Both are decisions. Only one is yours.”

Her gaze went back to the dying man.

“What you’re doing to him is not mercy. Not yet. Right now it’s a lesson in what happens when a man with a knife and no stomach for it tries to do a job he doesn’t understand. The crows are judging your form.”

The man’s eyes slid toward Corvin. Wrack saw them and looked back.

“Don’t look away because you asked me to tell you straight,” she said. “Straight is what this is. A hole where there was no need for one. Blood in the dirt. A name under a seat. And you learning that mercy is mostly a word people use when they want to feel clean about the mess they’re already making.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped.

She did not turn away again at once. The sword she had been dragging stayed where it was, its point resting in the dirt, and her hands settled on her hips as if she were deciding whether the request was stupidity or need. Maybe it was both. She had seen both often enough in the same face.

“No,” she said at last. Not sharp, but final. “I’ll stay. I’ll watch, if watching is what keeps your hand from shaking. But I won’t stand here and tally his dying for you like it’s a job of work to be graded.”

She came back a few steps and crouched near the body again, close enough that Corvin would not have to feel alone in it, far enough not to crowd the blade. Her eyes went briefly to the young man’s face, then away.

“You want it plain, then hear it plain,” she said. “You’re not giving him something new. You’re finishing what the ambush started. The sound will be worse than the act. Air through blood makes a wet, broken noise. He may hitch. He may shake. He may make a sound like he’s trying to speak, and it won’t be speech. That’s the body running out of road.”

Her voice stayed low and even.

“If you put the steel where it belongs, it will be quick. Seconds. Sometimes less. If you don’t, it will take longer, and you’ll know because he’ll still be fighting for air instead of leaving it. Then you correct the mistake. Don’t saw. Don’t pull it out to look. Don’t ask the dead for permission.”

She looked up then, steady and unflinching.

“I’ll tell you if it’s done. I’ll tell you if it isn’t. That’s the part you need me for. The rest you keep for yourself, because once you start wanting someone else to narrate killing, you’re either making a story of it or trying to hand it off. Neither one helps the dead, and neither one helps you.”

The wind passed through the ditch grass again, colder now, carrying the smell of iron and turned earth.

“So do it,” Wrack said. “I’ll stay. But I won’t make it easier by pretending it’s anything but what it is.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She'd had the token in her fist and the last body in her eye, and what held her was a hand — one of the ditch men's, moving on the stones. Slow. A spider in cold weather.

"Huh," she said, and came back, and stood over the pair of them, and looked her mistake full in the face. "That's twice tonight I've signed off on a dead man ahead of his time." No apology, and none dressed up as one. "This one I went through coat and all while he held still for me. Cold takes their breath down to nothing — you can put your ear on a chest like that and lose the count. I'll blame the cold. It's the only one of us without a reputation to protect."

She crouched at Corvin's shoulder, where she could see all of it, and stayed.

"You asked me not to leave anything out. Good. Most men can't ask — the throat shuts and the pictures take the job uninvited. Words are cheaper. So. Words, as it happens."

"That scrape you just made — that's bone. The ridge of the skull. The blade will skate on it all night; there's no arguing with it. Stop a breath. Come down a thumb's width and forward, behind the corner of the jaw, where the meat's soft. Find the give with the point before you spend the push. There. That address."

The man stirred when the pain found him — a sound out of him like a saw pulled through wet wood, no words in it. His eyes came open to slits and didn't track.

"Eyes open. Look at them anyway — not for him, for you. Nobody's home. Lamps lit, house empty. He'll not know you were ever here, and that mercy only runs one way. All the knowing in this is yours." His hand crawled, found Corvin's wrist, and closed. "There's the grip. You decided about this already, so it's just weather now."

Then the push went home, and she named it as it landed. "There's the give. Quieter than you'd think — told you. A thumb through the skin of a plum." His back arched off the stones, heels drumming twice. "Not him. That's the wires firing with nobody home to answer. Chickens do it headless. Don't take it for a fight."

"Count with me now. He'll take longer than the young one — cold bodies are slow at everything, including leaving." The grip on Corvin's wrist eased by degrees. "Little finger's gone. Ring finger. Thumb pays last. They always do." A long, uneven pull of breath, then a gap. "That's not him deciding anything. That's a bellows with a split seam, running on habit. One more, likely." There was one more. Then the grip was gone entirely and the cloth fell slack, and Wrack counted ten under her breath and put two fingers to his throat, then to the spot behind the ear where the work was done.

"Done. Call it a minute, first touch to last breath, and half of it was you finding the address. The young one went quicker. Not because you failed — this one started poorer and colder." She nodded at the ear, where a dark thread was making its slow way down. "That's the whole blood budget. The head's a good bucket; most of it stays home. Wipe on the cloak. Don't study your hands — studying's scheduled for later whether you like it or not."

She took one of the dead man's hands first, turned it over in the moonlight: rope calluses, old ones, a laborer's hand in a soldier's boot.

"Now the amendment, since you'll be keeping books. I told you the first one's the only one that costs. That stands. This one didn't cost — this one taught, and you paid in mess instead of coin, which is the better price. But look at that hand. Somebody's dressing plowmen and pointing them at travelers, and I'd very much like to know who's holding the purse."

She fished out the lead token and held it up between them, turning it so the worn face caught the moon.

"Which brings cheap knowledge back to the table. You skipped it once. Tower, hand, anything near it — a banner, a seal, ink on a paymaster's arm. Say it now."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: I kneel down and do it, and it isn't clean or quick because I've never done it before. "Stay," I tell her, when she starts to turn away. "Watch it with me and tell me exactly what I'm doing to him — the sound of it, how long he takes, all of it. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Wrack stopped mid-turn. She looked back, her face empty of anything except the same tired attention she’d give a loose strap on a saddle, and folded her arms.

“Fine,” she said. “I’ll watch.”

She did not look at Corvin’s face. She looked at the boy’s throat, and at the blade, and listened.

“You’re low and shallow,” she said, her voice carrying no more emotion than a carpenter noting a split board. “Below the ear, but you’ve skated across the muscle instead of punching up through the base of the skull. So you’ve got the carotid, maybe the jugular, but the spine’s intact. Hear that?”

She tilted her head.

“That’s not a sigh. That’s blood filling the back of the throat faster than he can cough it. The airway’s compromised but the brain’s still lit. That’s why his heels are drumming against the frozen dirt. Spinal discharge. The fingers too—opening and closing. He can’t feel it. It’s just wiring.”

She watched the boy’s chest hitch.

“Heart’s beating faster now, trying to keep pressure up. The blood coming out of him is bright. Arterial. If you watch, it’s timed to his pulse. A fountain, slow but steady. If you’d hit the vein instead, it would just ooze. This is cleaner to look at, messier to finish.”

She counted under her breath, her lips barely moving.

“Twenty seconds. The pupils are fixed and different sizes. Brain’s losing perfusion. The jaw slackens—there. The mouth drops open because the muscles went limp. That twitch in the shoulder is the diaphragm spasming. He thinks he’s breathing, but he’s only moving blood.”

She shifted her weight, leather creaking.

“Forty seconds. The drumming stops. Now it’s just the chest, hitching every few seconds. Agonal breathing. The body’s last inventory. Sounds like snoring through a wet cloth. Then a pause. Then another hitch. Each one shorter.”

She glanced at the treeline, then back down.

“Ninety seconds, maybe two minutes. The hitch stops. What comes out now is just air from the lungs, passing through the hole you made. Sounds like a sodden rag being wrung out. Then nothing. The eyes might stay open. Usually do. The color’s already going grey at the gums. By morning he’ll be stiff as a board if the cold doesn’t freeze him first.”

She looked at Corvin’s hand, not his face.

“That’s what a ragged blade does. You opened the plumbing and let him drain conscious. Not crueler than the gut wound, just faster. But not fast enough to be kind. The difference between a clean stop and a hard one is about three inches of steel and the angle you drive it. You missed by half an inch, so he got twenty extra seconds of drowning in his own blood. That’s the math.”

She stepped back, her boots crunching in the frozen mud.

“Wipe your blade. We need to walk.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"Neither," Sedge said. "It's a branch, not the trunk. If it were the trunk he'd have gone grey and stopped caring by now — men who bleed out from the big ones go quiet long before they go. He came off this table twice tonight with enough left to skid it through the mud. That's a man with blood to spare. Now your hand."

She took his wrist and set the palm down on the pad, over her own fingers, and came out from under it slow — one finger, then the rest, her hand hovering a breath above his knuckles.

"Straight down. No sideways. Sideways shears the clot off and we start from nothing. If you feel warmth spreading through that pad, you say so. You don't lift to look. Warm means I come back in."

She went down the table and took the ankle, two fingers behind the inner bone, counting against her own pulse. The lamp gave its bad yellow light and she let it.

"Faint," she said. "Could be your pressure leaning on the line, could be the leak still stealing from it. We'll know when the knot's in. That's the honest answer — the leg lives or dies on one tie, ten minutes from now, and I've done a hundred of them. If the ankle's still beating when it's set, he keeps the leg, limps a month, and lies about ever limping."

She straightened and looked at Wick properly for the first time since the table legs had skidded.

"The kind part looks different from this. When it's that, there's nothing under my hands worth pressing on, and I take them off and hold his instead. There's plenty under yours. So press."

She cut gut thread to length and threaded the curved needle mostly by feel — the light was for the wound, not for her. The man had gone from shaking to a long low tremor, eyes still open, fixed on the tent ridge.

"You're keeping the leg so far, son," she told him. "Flat and patient. That's the whole job now — it's ours."

Then, back to the shoulder and the palm: "Ten minutes. Your arm goes numb around the fourth. Numb's fine. Numb is the job."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
"Still not a name," Sedge said. "But I'll take the trade. Come round this side — where my hands were, by his knee. And don't lean on the table. It's done all the moving it's owed tonight."

She took the lamp off the crate and held it low, so the light pooled in the wound instead of skidding across it. Then she picked up the probe, because she pointed with steel, not fingers — fingers carried dirt, and this wound was going to stay clean if it took all night to keep it so.

"Top to bottom, the way I went in. The little round hole, high on the leg — that's where it went in. Shell steel makes small doors. Everything wrong with this leg is behind the door, not at it. The long cut is mine. I opened the track to reach the bottom of it. It looks worse because it is worse — but it's the honest one. The hole is the liar."

"Yellow layer under the skin — fat. Everyone's surprised by the yellow. Below that, the dark red. Muscle. Meat; not a figure of speech, the same stuff, and it's his. Muscle hates being cut. It pulls back from the knife and springs apart, which is why the wound gapes — the body making itself a bigger mouth to complain through. Stupid, but it's all it knows."

She lowered the probe into the deep of it and touched nothing, only indicated.

"There. The cord, thick as your little finger, running with the leg. Pale. Watch it a moment." She held the lamp still and let the pulse show itself — a small patient jump, over and over. "That's the artery. The trunk. Every one of those jumps is his heart, seen from the wrong end. That's what I worked beside for half an hour with a piece of edged steel lying on it like a slate on a roof. Now you know why I don't pull. The edge was sitting on that."

"Off to the side — the pale knot. Mine. Gut thread, doubled so it can't slip. Under that knot is a branch the size of a matchstick, torn when the fragment tipped up and out. It was spurting to his pulse when your hand came down on it. Now it's tied like a bootlace, and the blood behind it has found other roads. A leg is all roads. That's the whole reason he keeps it — the tie didn't cut him off. It just sent the traffic around."

"The leg itself — swollen, hot, tight as a drumhead. That's not the wound. That's the body's answer to the wound. It crowds its own soldiers in, and soldiers crowd. That crowding is why he'll hurt worse tonight than he did on my table, and why fever's still coming for him. The mess has to have a way out or the crowd turns to poison."

She laid a strip of gauze along the wound's edge, ready for when the water came.

"So it stays open, and this goes down to the floor of it as a wick. Whatever builds up climbs out along it. Wounds close from the bottom — floor, then walls, then skin last, like filling a trench. Roof over a trench that's still full of men and you've made a grave. I said that before. I meant the shape of it."

She nodded at the tin cup by his slack hand. "And that. Steel off a shell casing, by the burr on it. Every pulse moved the leg, the leg moved the metal, and the metal worried the vessel like a stone in a boot. Give it one more day and it wears through — deep, where no hand can press. Small ring. Big argument."

She set the lamp back on the crate.

"You'd rather know than imagine. That's the right way round — imagination's a liar in a tent. It only ever shows you prettier or worse, never the thing itself. And knowing keeps the hands steady, and there'll be a next time for your hands. This war has run out of everything except work."

"Now the kettle. Bring it hot, and bring your name with it. I ask twice. I never ask three times — past that you're just 'holder' until spring."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge hooked the crate out from the head of the table with her boot and sat down on it — first time all night her weight had gone anywhere but into a man. She broke a corner off the hardtack and ate it, because the body kept books and hers was owed.

"All right. Straight. First thing, throw out the picture you've got, because it's wrong. You're imagining a knife. A knife goes in sharp and leaves a wound like a sentence — written, finished. This is a torn piece of casing." She tipped the fragment from the tin cup into her palm and held it near the lamp. "See the burr. Torn, not ground. It didn't arrive sharp. It arrived mean. Jagged, tumbling, and slower than you'd think by the time it's crossed the ground to him — which is why the door is small and the room behind it is ruined. And it's cold. Men tell each other the steel comes in red-hot and sears the track clean behind it. Four years, I've never pulled a hot one. They arrive cold as a coin, and whatever's riding on them stays riding."

She let that word sit, then fed it.

"Riding. That's the part nobody imagines. This didn't fall out of the sky into a clean man. It crossed the ground first — trench ground, the same mud that's under this tent. It went through trouser cloth that hadn't been washed since spring, through everything that cloth had been lying in, and it swept all of it along, into him. The hole is small because the steel is small. The corridor behind it is a pocket of the battlefield buried in the man. That's what a shrapnel wound is. Not a cut. A burial."

She finished the hardtack and dusted her hands on her apron.

"So it does three things. One — it tears. One-time cost, over before he hits the ground, and the body's good at tears; it's been mending them since before there were wars. Tearing is the honest part of the whole business. Two — it imports. The mud is alive. That's not poetry, that's the trouble with it. It has tenants, and they ride the steel in and find a warm room with everything to eat. Three — and this is the one that matters — it stays. A bullet mostly passes through and takes its argument with it. This stops. And stopping isn't resting. Every pulse shifts the leg a hair. Every step the man ever takes again works it around. The piece walks. Our man's sat down on the trunk artery and worried it like a stone in a boot, and I've pulled them out of places a long way from where they entered. Slow, but they've got nothing else to do with their time."

She leaned over and took the ankle — habit now, not need. Two fingers behind the inner bone. Still beating, still his. She let it go and went on.

"Where it lands matters more than what it's made of. Meat forgives — drains, heals, complains the whole way and mends anyway. Our man is mostly meat. That's his luck. Bone is worse. Bone holds the dirt for years, drains on its own schedule, and I've men on my books three winters deep from one chip. A joint is a sealed room — once it fills, the joint's finished, and the man learns to walk without it. The belly is the one I dread, and I'll say why plainly. Steel through the gut and the man walks in talking — that's the trick of it. Filth loose in a clean room doesn't hurt at first. Then the room poisons him over three days, and there's nothing a tent does about a fouled belly. I can tie a leg. I can't tie a man's middle. Those men get the other version of me, the one that says *we'll see*. I usually know by the smell within the hour. He gets to not know a day longer. That's the whole medicine I have for it."

"The quick ones — trunk vessel, heart, the right part of the head — I nearly count as kind, and I mean that as arithmetic, not sentiment. I watched a man bleed out from the femoral in under two minutes. He was mid-sentence when it let go. He never found out the worst of it. The slow ones find out the worst of it every hour of every day it takes them."

"And most men don't get one piece. A shell throws its steel in a fan, and a man caught in the fan wears the map. I counted thirty in one man's back once and pulled two — the one on a vessel, the one in a joint. The rest stay and do nothing. That's the truth nobody says out loud: most shrapnel just sits there. He'll ache when it rains, call it rheumatism, and the rain will be right."

She stood, because the last part wanted her on her feet, and pointed at the sleeping man's leg with the forceps — steel, not fingers.

"But the mud's worst trick is the thing I'm actually watching for in him, and you asked for it straight, so. It isn't pus. Pus is sweet, thick — a room where something sat too long. This is different. The leg goes mottled, brown and yellow at the edges, and when you put your hand on it, it crackles. Gas in the flesh, bubbles under the skin, like half-thawed snow under a boot. It moves in hours. A leg that was only angry at midnight is dead by morning, and the man's whole blood goes sour behind it — fastest of the slow deaths. Your stomach will know the smell before your nose has named it. So we amend the list. I told you four things fetch me. Make it five. If his leg crackles under your hand, you don't press around finding out how much of it does. You fetch me at a run and you put the kettle on, because if it's that, I take the leg off on this table before the morning's old."

She looked at the wound — the loose gauze, the wick's tail laid over the lip of the cut — and set the cup back down by his slack hand.

"So there's your answer. Everything I did to him tonight after the cup rang — the water, the wick, leaving it open, the three days — none of it was about steel. The steel took me half an hour and it's sitting in a tin cup. The mud gets the next ten days, and the mud is what kills most of the men this war kills. Not the shell. Not the steel. The ground it crossed getting into him."

She sat back down on the crate, slower this time.

"You asked to know instead of imagine. Now you know what you're holding the door against. It was never the steel, Wick. It was always the mud."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge came around the screen at a run, apron half on, and the first thing she did at the foot of the table was stand still and listen — which looked like nothing and was the whole triage.

"Breath," she said. "Hear it under the noise? A scream with breath in it is a man fighting. The scream I run for has no breath under it — that one belongs to a man already leaving. He's not leaving. Ease him — not off, *ease*. He's not fighting you, he's fighting the leg, and a man who's crushed fights twice as hard as a man who's held."

Her eyes went down her own list while he arched and the table skidded its crooked legs deeper into the mud.

"Dressing's pink where the wick sits — that's the wick working, and I'll show you the difference before I'm done. Face is flushed, not grey; grey means the trunk, and the trunk's asleep where I left it. No smell." She leaned her face down over the wound and breathed in slow and deep, which no one ever did, which was why she was the one paid to. "Nothing sweet. Nothing sour. Good." Her palm went flat on the thigh above the cut, light, listening through her hand. "Hot. Hard as it was, no harder. No crackle — that I'd feel like frost heave under a boot. This is the honest hot."

"So it's the pain, and part of it's mine. I dosed a man on half a reflex — half that morphine went down his throat and the rest went down his beard. He slept till the first half wore thin, then woke up *inside* the leg. I told you hours ago he'd hurt worse tonight than he ever did on my table. Being right about it is worth nothing to me."

His eyes were open but wrong — rolled toward the ridge, looking at something the tent didn't contain.

"He's surfaced in the wrong room. Men come up out of morphine wherever the pain keeps them, and some of those rooms have shells in them. We don't argue with the room. We give him a better one. Son. Son. Here. Name and number, like the ledger wants."

He fought it, and then the training won where the will couldn't. "Cole." A rasp. "Private. Cole." A number in pieces, which she caught and said back to him whole, because a thing said back whole is a thing a man can stand on.

"Cole. You're in a tent. The shell's finished — I've the steel to prove it." She took the tin cup off the blanket and folded his fingers over the little bright ring. "There. Something in your fist heavier than what's in your leg. Hold that."

The medicine tin. "Now the dosing, and you asked for all of it, so here's the arithmetic. He gets *half* of one dose. Not whole. A man who's bled off a third of his blood gets drunk on half the spoon — dose him full and I put his breathing to sleep, and then I've spent the night saving a leg for a corpse. Half." She broke the tablet along its score, dropped it in a mouthful of canteen water, swirled, got an arm under his shoulders — the same lift as before, gentler. "Drink. All of it down the throat this time. None on the beard."

While it landed, she lifted the gauze — "I lift, you don't; my hands are clean and yours are full of man" — and went still. A thread of red ran down the wick's tail.

"For one breath I didn't like that. Now I've read it. Old blood — dark, keeping no time with anything, riding out on the wick because that's the wick's whole job. New blood is bright and it keeps time with his pulse — every beat, a beat. This keeps no time. Say the difference to yourself until it's boring. Boring is what saved looks like." Under the gauze the knot sat dark and dry, the artery jumped its small patient jump, the floor was clean. She tempered water through her wrist, wet the strip down, laid the gauze back. "Nothing's moved. He screamed the tent crooked and didn't scream anything loose. That's not luck. That's your arms."

She sat on the crate, because standing had become a negotiation.

"You asked how much longer. Four answers, and you'll have all of them, because you asked while holding a man down, which is the right way to ask. One — this round: ten minutes, five once the half lands, and it's landing now. Watch him go from screaming to shaking and don't mourn the change; shaking is the honest work. Two — the night: he'll surface twice more, once before the candle's half gone, once near dawn. Same three things every time — water a mouthful at a time, his name, and a voice. The dose doesn't repeat. From here to daylight the whole pharmacy is water, warmth, and talk. Three — the wound: day three, if it's clean, he gets skin. Four — the mud: ten days to its verdict, and the mud's verdict is the only one that counts. Past all four: a month of limping, a lifetime of lying about it. That's the ledger. Most men ask me to leave the worst out. You asked for the lot. You'll do for this work."

Sweat stood on him now. "Fever's arriving on schedule. Let it. Loud and hot is a man fighting — I said that once tonight and it's still true. He's loud, he's hot, he's Cole, and he's fighting. One in the morning, in this war, that's a good picture. And when he surfaces he may call for his mother, or a brother, or a dog. Answer to whatever he calls you. The room he wakes in is gentler than this one, and there's no harm being borrowed for it."

Pencil stub, the tape at his ankle: *M ½*. And above the rest of it, *COLE*. "The tape keeps the arithmetic. Now it keeps the name. He was meant to tell me in the morning — he told me at one o'clock instead, in the middle of his own noise. I'll take that trade. Days that start with a name end the right way round, and this one started early."

She stood. Her hands had an hour of stupid left in them before they turned dangerous; she meant to spend it lying down. "The five things still fetch me — blood, red streaks, smell, crackle, or quiet. Quiet's the liar of the five, and he's the loudest man in this army right now, so you've got margin. I'll be up before dawn for the ankle and the smell whether you hear me or not. And Wick — your voice is the last item in the pharmacy. Use it. He doesn't need words. He needs a voice in the room that isn't pain, and yours will do."

She went behind the screen. The cot complained; this time she did too. Her voice came back out of the dark, frayed and low.

"Goodnight, Cole. Goodnight, holder. One of you will be asleep in five minutes. The other one should eat the rest of the hardtack."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
It ended the way she'd said it would. The half dose took Cole down between one breath and the next, mid-asking, his hand folding back under the blanket with the ring still shut in the fist. She took the ankle on her way past — two fingers behind the inner bone, a count against her own pulse — still his. She left him to his sleep.

Then she came and stood over the floor, because that was where the next patient was.

"There it is," she said. "The crash. Two hours late — you held it off all the way through the Tommy business, and the body can be made to wait, but it doesn't forget. Don't get up. Men get up right about now, and then I've two patients and one table, and the paperwork alone would finish me."

She crouched and took the wrist, counting. Fast, then slowing as she held it — the books settling. Grey around the mouth and coming back. The shakes had arrived on schedule; forecasts never softened anything.
