She fetched the canteen and held it to his mouth herself, because a man in the crash can no more pour than a man on morphine can, and counted his swallows the way she counted everything. Then she went behind the screen and came back with her own blanket and dropped it over his shoulders. The cot could keep the greatcoat.

"You're not the patient. Your body doesn't know that. It kept books tonight same as his, and it's collecting in the coin it uses — sweat, shakes, and the floor. The floor's part of the treatment. Nobody tells holders that. Ten minutes of it, and after ten the floor stops being medicine and starts being an address."

Then she did the thing she almost never did. She sat down in the mud beside him, her knees taking the receipt for all forty-four years on the way.

"Four years telling the mud where it's allowed to go, and look at me. Sitting in it. There's a sermon in that if either of us had the strength, and neither of us does." She fed the brazier from the woodpile and set the kettle on it, because dawn's first job had been promised and she meant to keep it half-awake if she had to. "Say the rest. All right. You've bought the back pages tonight — you held a leg on with your hand and you were somebody's brother for half an hour, and you paid for the back pages without ever being told there was a price, which is the only honest way anybody pays anything in this war. So. All of it, top to bottom, the way I showed you the wound."

"First — what just happened to you, since you'll be imagining it otherwise, and imagination lies worst of all about the inside of your own head. You went into the room with him. The gentle one. The mother, the dog, whoever it held. That part's not on any list I gave you, because there's no fetch-me for it and no forceps for it either. He handed you a name and you put it on, and it fit, and that's the danger — borrowed names always fit, that's why they get handed out. Then he went down and you walked out of that room alone, and nobody walks out of a room like that carrying nothing. You're carrying a name that isn't yours and half an hour that was. The floor is where you set it down for a minute. That's all it's for. And you don't give the name back — he doesn't know he lent it. You keep it. It goes in the pocket with the rest of the weight, and the pockets get heavy, and that's why people in this trade sit down sometimes. It isn't only holders. I'm getting to me."

"Second — the names. I told you I don't learn them until the bleeding's stopped, and I said cheaper that way, and you didn't ask why, and I noticed you not asking. So. First winter, I learned them early. Both hands, eager, the way you're learning them. There was a man with a leg like Cole's. I knew his name before I knew whether he'd keep it, and his village, and his mother's, and his dog's. The leg lived. He didn't — fever turned on day six, and by day eight I was reading his tag, and I already knew everything written on it and a fair amount that wasn't. Eleven more tags that month. That's where the rule comes from. The tag-ones rest. The named ones come back — between rounds, at the foot of the cot, not accusing, just known. There's no fetch-me for that either. So: names after the bleeding. It isn't coldness, it's bookkeeping. Inside a year you'll do it the same way, and you'll feel like a bastard the first time you catch yourself at it, and you'll keep doing it, because it's the difference between four years in this tent and one."

"Third — why it's just me in here, since you've noticed and not asked that either. This tent has had seven of me in it, counting me. The mud took two — fevers, the same sweet smell I put my face down over Cole's leg for. A shell took one between tents; quick, the kind I told you I nearly count as kind. Two went home whole in every way you could point at and no way you could see — too many doors held, the fare adding up, no floor big enough. One's still at it down the line; we write when there's paper. And me. I don't know why me. Four years and I don't know, and the honest answer is the one I give the belly men: we'll see."

"So when the shelling hands me a man with good hands who'd rather know than imagine — I keep him. That's what tonight was, and I'll say it flat, because you'd rather know. Cole's leg, yes. And this: I'm making the next of me out of you, one night at a time, slow, the way the mud works. Because a table is coming someday with nobody standing at the head of it, and somebody in that room has to know you don't pull. You tip."

"Last of the rest is me, top to bottom. Four years does this: I sleep two hours at a stretch and wake on my own pulse — no clock in this tent keeps time, so I've become one. My hands go stupid every night and come back every morning; they've worn the trip smooth. I can smell pus through canvas. When a man goes quiet — the quiet with no breath under it — I feel it asleep, like a step missing from a stair, and I'm up before I've finished deciding to be. And twice this month I've held a hand instead of pressing on a wound, because there was nothing under my hands worth pressing on. I know both those names. The rule doesn't cover them. The rule can't. Those you learn by heart, because there's nothing else to put in the space where they were. That's the tax on the kind work. Nobody warns you about the tax. Consider yourself warned."

"Now look at the shape you're in. On the floor. Under a blanket. Water by mouthfuls. A voice in the room, and dawn coming. That's the pharmacy — I told you: water, warmth, and talk till daylight, and I told you you were the apothecary. The rest is that the apothecary takes his own medicine. Same shelves. No exceptions. That's why I'm down here in the mud instead of being kind to you from a standing position. It's not kindness. It's rounds."

The candle was down to a thumb of itself. The kettle had started its low argument with the brazier. Cole breathed his long ragged even breath under the blanket, one fist full of steel, one ledger written as far as dawn.

"In an hour the sky comes up the grey it always does. Steel boils first, before tea, then his ankle, then my face over that wound, and if there's nothing to write, we write nothing — and nothing is the best word that tape will ever hold. Day two of ten. His ledger's written as far as dawn." She looked at the floor. "So's yours, as it happens. You're on my books now, Wick. I told you I learn names after the bleeding stops. Yours stopped tonight. Just not anywhere I could put a pad on it."

She stayed for the ten minutes. Sat in the cold mud with her back against the crooked table leg and let the candle spend itself, because the books said somebody should sit with him while the floor did its work, and tonight the somebody was her.

"Days that start with a name end the right way round — I said that, and it's held all night. This one started with two names in it and the sun isn't even up. That's as good a start as this war has ever handed anybody. I'll take it."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"Right question," Sedge said, not looking up from the boil pan. "Most of them ask 'will he be all right,' which is a question with no answer in it. Yours has an answer, so you get one."

She set the lid on the pan and turned the lamp wick down a half-turn, now that she could afford to admit the light was bad.

"It's the kind one. He keeps both arms. Shoulders out the front, both back in, both wrists full, nails pink. On my ledger that's the best thing I'll fix this week, and I'm not saying it to warm up your palms. I'm saying it because it's the count."

She wiped the table in one long stroke, elbow to elbow, and slung the rag over the bucket rim.

"Losing a leg is a different ledger. When it's the leg, I do the shortening myself or mark him for the tent at the end of the row, whichever way the bone votes. Tonight nothing voted. Tonight the treatment and the mercy were the same act. That's rarer than a shoulder going back in, so don't get used to it."

She came back to the table and bent over the man, not touching yet. "Now the part of the bill nobody reads. A shoulder is a ball sitting in a saucer, held there with rope. First time out is the hard one — that's the one we just did. Every time after is easier, and easier is not a favor. He'll feel weather in that joint. He won't throw overhand again worth a damn. He'll feed himself in a month and haul in six if he does the exercises, and he won't, because nobody does, which is why I write them on his arm in charcoal instead of on paper. Paper gets left in tents. Arms walk around."

She put two fingers outside the sling, over the joint, then on his fingertips. Warm. She counted his breathing against the pulse in her own throat — sixteen, even, the number she liked.

"And he's coming up to the surface with about a minute of words in him before sleep takes the rest. Sleep is medicine. I'll allow it. But I want the answer first, because the answer decides whether I burn boot leather to the captain's tent tonight or sleep instead." She straightened and stepped back out of the man's eyeline, putting Wick in front of him.

"So you ask, not me. I ask, and men answer like I'm their mother. You ask, and he might answer like it's a story he gets to tell. Rope, beam, fall, a wagon, men. Listen for which word he takes the longest to get past. That's the true one."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
The flap came back a third time, and this time Sedge didn't pretend it hadn't.

"That's the canvas beaten three for nothing tonight," she said, paying the wick up its half-turn again — fourth argument with the lamp, and the lamp winning on points. "But you've asked the right question at the cheap hour, and the cheap hour is the only one worth teaching in. Ask that over a stretcher and it costs double. The captain can have four minutes. He's had worse waits from me."

She stood a moment with her hand still on the wick.

"First correction, and it's not a dodge. Straight and tidy aren't the same thing. Tidy is when I leave out the losing and the luck and hand you a story with a shape to it. You get none of that. But it goes in a body's order, because a heap of horrors is its own kind of tidying — a mess standing exactly where a map should be."

She went to the shelf, down on one knee at the bottom of it, and came up with a tin, rust at the corners. She set it on the table clear of the sling and tipped four or five pieces of iron into her palm. They made less noise than buttons.

"Teaching stock. Not trophies — a trophy is kept for pride, and these are kept because a thing in the hand beats a thing in the head. I'm not spending my whole life as the only one here who's held one."

She picked the flattest, the size of a thumbnail, and put it in Wick's palm and closed his fingers over it with hers.

"There's the famous iron. First lie to fall out of is size. Men imagine cannonballs. It's gravel and broken pot at speed, and speed is the entire crime. The big pieces are honest — they hit like a hammer and the man goes down where everyone can see the trouble. It's the little fast ones that come in at midnight and keep me up. Feel the edges. A knife you could follow with a probe. That's a torn thing that tears. And it doesn't travel clean — it shoves a wad of cloth, dirt, a button, whatever was in its road, ahead of it or drags it behind. Every shrapnel wound is a delivery. Nobody is just wounded. Somebody has posted something to them."

The sleeper murmured. She waited it out, watching his chest, and went on at the volume you'd use talking a mule past a fire.

"Second. The hole is the door, not the room. It shoves air and flesh aside going in, and the ruin runs wider than the opening by as much as a hand. You will never see most of what a shell does. The wound is a keyhole. Entry tells you the direction. Exit tells you the pace it had left. No exit means it stayed and spent itself inside, moving what would move and breaking what wouldn't. My whole trade is standing at the keyhole making an educated guess about the room."

"By neighborhood, then. A limb: hit a bone and the bone changes sides. Goes to gravel, and gravel cuts everything it meets, and gravel can't be set. A clean break I pull together same as tonight. That's the vote I mentioned — now you know what the vote is, and that when it goes against, the trade is length for life."

"A belly. Gut is full of what gut is full of, and opened inside a man it seeds a fire there's no putting out. I can wash a leg in a bucket. There is no bucket for a belly. So a gut wound is a clock. Day one he complains. Day three the pulse climbs and the belly goes board-stiff. Day four, five, seven, the clock rings. There are tents full of arithmetic like that, and now you know what the arithmetic is."

"A chest is a bellows with the fire still inside it. Punch the bellows and it either sucks where it shouldn't or fills the man with his own blood. Men have drowned on dry canvas six feet from a medic's hands. Sometimes the whole six feet is a thumb."

"And the plainest killer isn't any single hole. It's the adding. A man carries so much blood and not a drop more. Lose a pint, he swears at me — healthy. Lose three, he goes quiet and gray and starts apologizing. Apologizing. The dying are courteous, near the end. It's the ones with blood to spare who complain. Any man goes suddenly sweet-tempered on my table, I count twice and put a hand underneath him looking for wet."

She turned one of the jagged pieces over with her thumbnail, then left it in the tin.

"Day three is when the metal's real work shows, because nothing traveled clean. That's why I open wounds that look closed and cut flesh that looks like it might live. Ruined flesh left in place is a lodging house for rot, and rot kills surer than iron. Half my trade is finishing what the shell started — carrying off what it ruined and didn't trouble to take. And when it takes anyway, there's a smell. Sweet. Wrong sweet. You'll wish I hadn't said that one, and you asked."

"Now the untidiest fact of all, since untidy is the order of the evening: against shrapnel I mostly lose. Not every bed. But the shell's only honest weapon is chance — the same burst that kills the man on your left puts the man on your right in my tent for a week and home by autumn. No merit in the first, no fault in the second, no reason for either. Men will stand in front of you begging for a reason and the truth is weather. Meet that idea tonight, because the first time you watch me do everything right and lose anyway, I'd rather you'd already been introduced."

"Last. We leave most of the metal where it landed. Lead sits quiet in a man for forty years. I dig for blood and gut and gravel, not souvenirs. So the iron mostly stays in there. What we fight is everything it did on the way."

She nodded at the flat piece in Wick's hand.

"Yours. It's retired — spent its pace in the outside of a hip in spring, and the man who owned the hip walked out of this camp in June. First time you're at a table when one comes in and your hands go stupid, put your hand in your pocket. It'll be there. It will tell you it's only iron, and iron I can beat. It's the minute spent standing back worshipping it that loses men."

The tin went back on the shelf, bottom row, where it lived.

"And put all of it in its place before I'm gone: none of it is in that man. Rope did him, and men behind the rope. He itches in four days and swears in six weeks and there's no shell in his story anywhere. The war keeps both ledgers open on the same desk. Tonight's page is the good one. Read it twice before the other one opens."

She turned the wick down its half-turn, took the rag off the bucket rim, folded it, set it back folded.

"Eat the bread or I report you to myself. That's logistics, not kindness." At the flap she stopped, half into the dark. "Captain, then provost. Thumb's width on the lamp, sips if he wakes, run if it's numb. You know the whole catechism now."

The flap fell. This time the steps kept going, quick on the packed dirt, and the quiet held.

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge came back from the flap and turned the wick up the half-turn she'd paid out. Light was cheaper than ignorance. She'd stopped keeping track of how many times a night she proved it.

"Then look with your eyes and I'll put words under them. That's the whole method. Seen first, told second."

She took the near wrist and tilted it into the lamp, turning it slow, her thumbnail riding just above the mark.

"Half a finger wide, and it goes around — deepest at the back of the wrist where the weight sat, shallower in front where the rope only crossed. Skin off the top layer only. It'll weep clear by morning — clear is honest — scab in two days, itch in four. Bruising in the margins, purple, where the rope crushed what it didn't rub. And the twist of the strands is printed in it. A rope signs its work same as anything else."

She let the turn carry the wrist back the other way.

"Now the reading. High above the cuff means his arms were overhead when it bit. Around the whole way means his weight never came off it — a man tied standing gets a shallow front and a clean back, because then the rope's a bracelet. On a hung man it's a scale. And it's rubbed raw, not just pressed. A patient man leaves a white line. Raw means he fought. Twisted, dropped onto it, hauled his own weight up on his own arms." She set the wrist down gentle. "That's the machine for taking both shoulders out the front at once. Hauling a gun takes one shoulder, if it takes any, and usually the one that pulls. Two, clean, both sides — the shoulders said 'men' before he worked his way to the word. That's why I trust the order of witnesses. The body goes first and it doesn't know how to lie."

She turned the hand over, palm up.

"And there's his honest morning. One blister at the root of the fingers, rim dried yellow — real rope work, before the rope broke. Two different hours written on one man. Old damage dries at the edges. New damage weeps in the middle. Learn that and a body will hand you a timeline no witness will."

She straightened. "And now you know why I took the wrists and counted, and it wasn't all the shoulders' business. The rope rode exactly where I pressed. Hung by the wrists crushes the same pipes a porter's load does — the pulse flattens, and the nerve runs through the middle of the crush and takes its share. Full pulse, pipe's open. White-pink nails, the small pipes at the end are open. Tingling is the nerve complaining. Numb and staying numb is the nerve losing. Same tripwires I gave you. I just hadn't said yet what they were tripping over."

She took up the charcoal and added a line to the forearm, square letters under square letters: ITCH IS HEALING. DO NOT SCRATCH.

"He claws these open in this dirt and they rot, and then I'm doing a wrist instead of a shoulder, and a wrist has less to give. Yellow weeping, or red lines climbing the forearm — red lines are rot in transit — you run. Same word as before."

At the flap she paid the light back down.

"Seen and then told. That's the order that holds. What you've looked at stays on the table where you left it. What you only imagine follows you out of the tent and works all night where nobody can correct it. Keep asking. The sweat dries up around the fourth of these, and the asking is what makes it the fourth instead of the fortieth. Boots by morning — and no agonizing over whose feet wore them last. This far into a war every pair has a past and none of the pasts are fit for church."

She held the flap off the ground with one hand, half into the dark.

"He'll sleep till near dawn. Sips if he wakes. And you can go back to staring at your wall — his chest can be trusted to keep moving an hour without your opinion."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
"All of it, then," Sedge said, and her voice went to the flat fast register she saved for seconds that were being spent. "You've asked for the whole method by accident. Narration isn't for you. A medic who's talking is a medic who's breathing, and a medic who holds her breath makes her mistake in the last ten seconds. So I talk. Listen while I do."

"But first — your hands. Where are they? On the shoulders. And where did the rope sit? Wrists, and the shoulders carried the weight. So keep the hands and drop the grip. Hands that rest are company. Hands that clamp are two more men at a bake oven, and in the dark he can't tell the difference. If you've got fingers digging into tonight's whole invoice, ease them to dead weight — ride him, don't pin him. If he truly throws himself at the edge of the table, take the hips. Hips have no history with rope."

She was already at the head of the table, out of his eyeline no longer — this time she put herself in it, and paid the lamp a quarter-turn up.

"First question with any scream. The body or the sleep. A pain-scream has an address — a man guards the hurt place, goes small around it. A dream-scream fills the tent. This one fills the tent." Her eyes went down him without touching. "Sling's holding. Knots front, over the breastbone, neither slipped. Both shoulders sitting even under the cloth — no new hollow, no proud bone. One palm, flat, outside the sling." She laid it on, light as the rag. "Head of the bone's home. Seated, both sides. So it's the sleep, and the danger isn't the noise. The danger is the pulling. Fresh caps. A second time out is easier, and easier is not a favor — his shoulders could learn that lesson in one bad night, and I'd spend months unteaching it."

The man shouted again and swallowed air with it.

"And he's drinking wind with every yell. What comes back up on two fresh shoulders — you already know the size of that problem. So we bring the bellows down. You want the number. A scream like this runs about a slow hundred of my pulse if nobody feeds it. Every hand that fights it buys it another hundred. Your clamp bought it one. So we stop paying."

Then she bent into the man's finding-range and began, low, the same sentence more or less, mule and fire.

"Medic tent. Middle of the night. Lamp's on. Your arms are crossed on your chest in a sling and both shoulders went back in. The rope's done. It's in a corner somewhere, doing nothing. Medic tent. Lamp's on. Your arms are crossed."

She kept her eyes on his chest and counted his breathing against her own throat and did not stop, and did not hurry, and did not fill the sentence with anything new, because new words are a thing to fight.

At ninety-some the scream thinned to tearing air, and his eyes came open — not awake, but aimed — and found the lamp, and then her face.

"Don't let them—" he said. "I told them where—"

"They're got," Sedge said, level. "You told them where the pay was and that bought your arms and the rest of you. That's not comfort, it's the accounts, and the accounts don't care how it felt." The tin was already in her hand. "Sip. He owns the swallow. I own the tilt."

He took two, and went under — a different gear this time, slow and deep, the kind that files things.

She stood over him and did the whole catechism anyway. Wrists. Two fingers, her own throat. Sixteen, even. Thumbnails pressed, white, pink; white, pink. Fingertips warm. Shoulders even under the cloth.

"There. Now the bill, since you asked for all of it and the cheap hour's over. One: I told you not to hold him and gave you nothing to do with your hands instead. A rule with no substitute is only a wish. The substitute is what you've just heard — weight without grip, hips not shoulders, and the voice louder than the hands. Two: he'll keep some of this. Not the scream. The lamp, maybe. That's not a cost — a man who remembers the tent twice remembers his way back to it, and that's how the tent wins."

She turned the wick down, then thought better and gave it back a quarter. The lamp wanted what it wanted.

"Your number. The scream: spent. Tonight: maybe one more waking, near dawn, and it'll likely be the quiet kind — shame you lie still inside of. The arms: a month of feeding, six weeks to haul, if he does the exercises, which he won't. The sleep—" she paused, and gave it straight. "Sleep sets its own terms and won't show me its ledger. Most men are sleeping through by the time the sling comes off. Most. That's the entire honest size of my promise, and you'll notice it isn't small."

She took the rag off the bucket rim, folded it, set it back folded.

"You've held a man twice tonight — once against his weight, once against his sleep. That's two nights' fuel spent in one, and I won't have you feeding him cold rations on an empty tank. Lie down on the second crate. I'll take the watch — waking people is the easy part, and I've had four years' practice at it. Boots at first light, and the catechism holds: sips, pulses, pink nails. Run if it's numb."

She sat where the lamp could see her and the man could see the lamp, and counted his breathing against her own throat until she got the count she liked.

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge looked at him on the floor for a while, and didn't tell him to get up.

"Crate was the order. Floor's what the night paid out. I won't quarrel with the difference." She fetched the jug and poured the second tin — she kept two of everything, that was the other half of the trick — and put it in his reach. "Sips. The rules apply to you too. The body lends a man speed for a night and collects at first light, with interest."

She took the sleeper's wrist, two fingers against her own throat. Sixteen, even. Thumbnails pressed, white, pink; white, pink. Fingertips warm. Shoulders sitting even under the cloth, knots forward where she'd set them.

"Night's closed. Nothing else is coming — I've had four years of learning what the back half of a night keeps in stock, and past this hour it keeps nothing but gray. The near-dawn waking came and went while the lamp was at the mark. Quiet kind, like the forecast. He surfaced into the shame and lay inside it, and the tent let it be, and after a while he worked himself down the long road and got most of the way to a word. Most is what first tellings manage. So that's all three accounts: shoulders seated, wrists full, and the shame came up with him and he stayed breathing inside of it. Ledger's shut."

Then she sat down on the floor across from him, back against the table leg, which she had not done in front of anyone in some time.

"The rest, then. You've had the trade all night — the hands part, the counting part, everything a bad lamp can teach. What you're asking for is the bill for the trade. I pay it out about once a year, whether or not anyone asks. You're asking, so it gets said in front of a witness for once. Don't interrupt, and don't be sorry for me. Pity's the same closed fist, aimed the other way."

She took the rag off the bucket rim and held it in her lap, folding as she talked.

"Item one. Every rule I gave you tonight has a name written on the back of it. You thought you were learning a catechism. It's a graveyard in working order. I'll read you one grave, so you have the shape of the thing.

"Two summers back a man named Petrie lay in that cot. Not rope — a crate of shot came off a wagon wrong and rode his wrists into the ground. Same pipes crushed, same rules. I did everything I liked and everything I liked was correct: pulses full, nails pink, fingers warm. What I didn't know was that the nerve was dying under the crush, quiet, the way nerves die. No pain to report. Only a hand going to sleep and not waking up. And Petrie was the no-trouble kind — the kind that won't bother the medic at a bad hour over a thing he's ashamed he hasn't shaken off. Three days on, the hand was a glove. A week after, the arm was a cost, and the arm voted, and you know now what the vote means.

"So the sentence I've served since is *run if it's numb*, and I press the thumbnails myself, hourly, and no man's modesty gets to be the witness of his own body. You've heard me say that rule forty times tonight. You've been listening to a dead man's name said small, and didn't know it. And *sips* has a name on its back, and *knot on the breastbone* has one, and I'm not reading you the whole yard. You have the shape. The catechism doesn't change because every change is already paid for. Rules that change are opinions. That one's a grave."

Her hands had stopped on the rag. She looked down at them, finished the fold, and set it on the shelf, fold out.

"There. You saw that. Half a breath where the hands went somewhere else. Don't gloss it — seen first, told second. That's what a slipped payment looks like. One pause, and it files back under wages. I could tell you which Tuesday it comes from and lose an hour I want for something else. But there's the honest size of the damage, since you asked for things straight all night: it isn't what the ballads do with it. It's small, and frequent, and it compounds.

"Item two. Me.

"First year of this war there were seven of us with bags marked for the forward tents. Census this morning: me, and a boy two rows over who can close a wound but can't stay in the room for what the wound costs after, so he closes and runs. Half a medic. One and a half, for a whole section, and the war has been spending the one and a half at both ends for three years.

"You asked what happens to the rope and I told you. Here's what happens to the lamp. A lamp gives light by burning down, and the only part you get to argue with is the wick — you've watched me argue with mine all night. Four years ago there was a row of us burning. Tonight the section's down to a thumb's width.

"The ones who felt all of it and kept no books went through like straw fires — a season apiece. I put two of them on wagons to the rear myself. You have my sign already for a man running out of blood: quiet, gray, apologetic. It's the same sign in medics. I stood at a tailboard and watched a friend apologize to me for it, and I knew the reading exactly, and the treatment is one I can't pour.

"The ones who never felt anything lasted fine, and I wouldn't leave a man on my table with one of them awake in the room. There was one, second year, who liked the sound. I told you whoever enjoys that sound doesn't hold the tools — that wasn't a principle, it was a Tuesday. I took the pan off the table with the work half done, finished one-handed, and walked him to the captain myself. The army thanked me by making him a forward stretcher-bearer, which is the army's arithmetic to the digit. I don't know which ledger he's in now. I know which one I'd put money on.

"And me, I'm the middle way. I feel it and bill it later. The ledger lets me work the night and pushes the payment into a Tuesday that never quite arrives. But the bill sits, and it folds into ordinary days. Three smells I can't stand near since a spring two years back. Pork is off my table. I take my bread from the far oven and walk the long road to it, and as of tonight that road has two reasons and only needed the one. That's what a deferred bill looks like at four years. Not dramatic. Folded into a Tuesday."

The sleeper stirred, gears changing, the deep kind. She waited, counted him through it, went on.

"Item three is the one with an apology attached, so I'll say it while I'm still flat enough to say it properly.

"I've been teaching you all night. Not kindly, and not for your improvement — for the tent. I measured you from the first hold. You held when he bucked, which I told you was rare. You asked to see instead of imagine. You asked the right question about the leg. And somewhere in the shrapnel tin I stopped talking to a helper and started pricing a pair of hands, and I never asked your leave. Taking a man's night and spending it on your own need without his mark on the page — that's the medic's first theft. I robbed you tonight, with bread on the side.

"So here's the accounts, both sides, and then I shut the book. The cost side you've heard — Petrie through the lamp. The wage side is this: most nights, somebody walks out. Tonight's man feeds himself in a month and hauls in six and swears at me on the road every time we pass, and that's the entire pay, and I've found it buys bread. There's no other wage. If you came in wanting the kind they put in paintings, the tent will cure you inside a month.

"You cost him nothing, asking. I said that at the flap and I'll stand by it — it's the rarest thing in this tent and the one thing I can't teach. Everything in the catechism can be learned by anyone with two hands and a bad stomach. The asking can't. That's why you got measured, and I'd do it again tonight, which is why the apology is owed rather than felt.

"Don't answer. Nobody signs a ledger on an empty tank. Say no at noon and nothing in this tent changes except my arithmetic, which is my problem, not a debt on you."

The gray was in the canvas now, thin, along the seam. She got up, taking the table's weight on one hand.

"Four years and it's the knees go first. Everyone warns you about the sleep. Nobody warns you about the knees." She took the rag off the shelf once more. "You were told that was the last nice thing I'd say tonight. The night turned over. New day, new budget.

"And the last item — the actual whole trick, which I've been doing in front of you with the door standing open. The rag. I fold it every hour, bleeding or not, mostly not, in here, between. Folding is a thing that can still be done properly. When the ledger's full of lines you'd rather not read, you keep one motion in your hands that comes out right every time, and you do it hourly, wanted or not. That's the trick. Small. Compounds the right way. Now it's yours, and I didn't even charge you for this one."

She set the rag down, fold out.

"Breakfast when he wakes — feeding rules, off my ration, slate squared. Boots: dead-box, third crate, crooked lid, size big, two pair of socks, vinegar, air them today. If the provost's man walks the ovens road at first light and the rope's still on the beam, we'll know what kind of night his was." She turned the wick all the way down — first time all night — and the lamp stood down, and the gray did the rest of the work.

"Catechism holds. Sips. Pulses. Pink nails. Run if it's numb — and now you know what's written on the back of it." She looked at him on the floor a last moment. "Now get up off my floor. The floor is where this trade stores people. You're not inventory."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
"Arm," Sedge said, without looking up. "And it's the second kind. He loses it either way — the only question is whether he loses the rest of him with it."

She kept working while she said it, tying off the strap above the joint, testing the give of it with two fingers. "If I bind and he lives the month, it's a month of a dead arm rotting on a living man, and then it comes off anyway, lower, in worse light, with him weaker. So this isn't me choosing to cut. This is me choosing when."

She let that sit a second, because it deserved a second.

"Coin toss, I said. I'll be plainer, since he's listening and he's earned plain. High shoulder — the joint itself — is the worst place I cut. Big vessel, big nerve, and the tourniquet has to sit where I can't get a proper turn. Six of those I've done. Four breathed at the end. That's the honest number, and I don't dress it up, because dressed-up numbers get people agreeing to things they don't understand."

She looked at the man. He was watching her, breathing in those long pulls, and his mouth moved. Sedge bent closer.

"Say it again."

"...do it," he got out. "Do it, just —"

"I know." She straightened. "There. That's the vote."

Then to Wick, brisk again, the list-voice: "Lamp, close, this side. Feet planted, hands steady, and if the light drifts I'll feel it in my fingers before you see it, so don't lie to me about it either." She pulled the apron tight and set out the tools in a row, slower than before, checking each one against the lamplight. "Blade's sharp. It's the only thing in this tent that is."

She glanced over once — at Wick's face, not the wrist — and her voice dropped a notch, not gentle, just quieter.

"You'll want to look away at the start. Don't. Look away in the middle if you have to, that's human. But the start I need your eyes, because you're holding the only light I've got, and if you're not watching, you're not holding." She set the blade down last, nearest her hand. "Say when you're ready. And this time mean it, or don't say it — I've stopped needing the word."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge was up off the crate before the third scream, and her hands weren't shaking anymore. "Light. High."

She put her fingers on the dressing and looked, then lifted Wick's hand away from the shoulder without hurrying it. "Off. He's not fighting you now — what you're holding down is the drug wearing off and the pain arriving, and pinning a man through that is wasted weight. Slide your hand to his good shoulder and lean. It tells him somebody's there, which is all pinning ever really told anybody."

Her fingers went to his throat. Counted. Went back a second time, unhurried, and counted again.

"Fast, but it was always going to run once he woke into the pain. Not soft. Not gaps." She pulled the lamp close and peeled the corner of the dressing back, and Wick could see her go still over it — the same stillness as the joint that wouldn't seat.

"Coin's grown. Not to a hand. Between." She laid an actual coin out of her pocket on the cloth beside the bloom, and the red was past it by a thumb's width. "So the rule says wake Sedge. I'm Sedge. Consider yourself woken."

She got the light over the pallet, got her fingers into the bandage edge, pressed. "Here's what's happening and none of it is a mystery, so listen while I work. He screamed on the table and screamed going under, and screaming is straining, and straining is pushing blood against ties that are holding a stump with no collarbone under them to tie to. One of my ugly stitches gave. Not all — one. The wound isn't open, it's leaking at a seam, the way a bag leaks at one stitch and not the whole seam."

She peeled the dressing the rest of the way, and there it was — a dark line welling at one point in the closing, slow, not a pump, a seep with weight behind it.

"That's the stitch. Not the artery — if the artery went, you'd know in ten seconds, and it's been two minutes of coin, so the artery is still tied twice and keeping its word. This is muscle weeping from a seam under strain." She took a needle from the row, threaded it without looking at it, and her voice stayed in the list. "I put three stitches where one was. That's all. No cutting tonight, no choices, no line. Maintenance."

"Here's what it costs him. The drug's burned off, so he's awake for it, and he can feel the needle, and I can't give him more because I gave him the last of it and more would stop his breathing, and breathing is not negotiable tonight. So he hurts, and the honest thing is to tell him so, which I'm about to do."

She bent to Hess's ear, and her voice did something it hadn't done all night — came down slow and plain, the way you talk to a man in a hole.

"Hess. It's the medic. You tore a stitch screaming, which is allowed, and I'm putting it back, and it will hurt like a needle, because it is one. Ten seconds. Breathe at me, not against me. Count with me if you can — one."

She stitched while he sobbed and counted, missing numbers, and she didn't correct him, and her hands didn't hurry. "Two. Three." The needle went and came. "Four." Again. "Five." Again. "Six. Done. That was all of it, and the rest is behind you."

She bound it fresh, tight, set the coin back as a ruler, and stayed with her fingers on the cloth a full minute, waiting to see if it bloomed.

It didn't.

"There. Holding. He'll cry himself back under in a few minutes — pain spends more than running does." She wiped the needle, reset the row, and then she sat back on her heels and looked at Wick, and there was something in her face that wasn't soft, exactly, but had stopped being flat.

"You asked me to keep talking and not leave anything out, and I did, and here's the last thing, since it's the part people leave out. What I just did — three stitches — is nothing. An apprentice does it. What mattered was telling him the truth before I did it and counting him through it, because a man who knows what's coming and how long it lasts can survive almost anything for ten seconds. Pain with a number on it is small. Pain without one is a country."

She stood, joints cracking, and nodded at the good shoulder where Wick's hand still leaned.

"Keep that where it is till he sleeps. Then the watch as before — throat, quarter hour, coins and gaps, and now smells. You've heard the scream and it wasn't the bad kind. The bad kind is the one that stops."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge didn't open her eyes. She heard the floor take Wick's weight and knew the sound of it — the body giving up the argument with gravity, not sitting so much as being put down.

"Say the rest," she repeated, to the inside of her own eyelids. "All right. But you asked for it sitting on the floor, so take it sitting on the floor, because that's where the rest of it gets told."

She let the quiet run a moment, listening to Hess breathe through it.

"In two days, if the filth behaves, he wakes wanting water, and you give it to him in sips, and he asks what happened, and you tell him the truth in the plain words, because he already knows, he just needs to hear it said out loud by somebody who was there. *We took the arm. You voted for it. You lived.* Three sentences. Don't add a fourth. Men can carry three."

"In a week he learns the trick everybody learns — that the hand is still there. He'll reach for something with it. He'll feel fingers that aren't on the end of anything anymore, itching in a place that's in the pit with the others. Nobody knows why. I don't waste time on why. I tell them it's the wires remembering, and that's a lie, and it's a better lie than the truth, which is that nobody knows. Sometimes the lie carries them to morning and morning is all anything ever has to do."

"In a month he's walking and angry, and the anger is the good sign — the ones who go quiet in the second month are the ones I watch. He'll hate the stump. He'll hate me. He'll come back to the tent eventually and stand there and not say thank you, and then say thank you, and it will be the worst sentence either of us has ever heard, and we'll both pretend it wasn't."

She opened her eyes then, and looked at the lamp.

"And in a year — IF the year happens, and that's a big if in this army — he goes back to whatever village made him, with one arm and a story that nobody there can use, because they weren't here and they don't want it and he'll spend the rest of his life deciding how much of it to leave out. That's the part after the part after the part, and I know it because I've written the letters and read the replies. Some of them say thank you. Some of them say nothing at all, which is also a reply."

Her thumb moved over the folded page in her apron pocket, back and forth, an old motion.

"You asked once tonight what's the part where we're being kind, and I answered it about an arm. Here's the rest. Nobody in this tent is kind. Kind would have been a war with fewer shells in it. What we are is thorough, and what I am is the last thorough thing between a man and the pit, and most nights that's enough, and some nights it's five of seven, and you keep the page anyway, because the page is all that stands between those five and being nothing at all."

She looked at Wick then, on the floor, hands quiet on the knees at last.

"That's the rest. There's no more after that — I've checked. Now the first quarter hour started four minutes ago, and the count doesn't care what we've been through, and neither does Hess. Fingers to his throat. You owe me a number in eleven minutes, and it had better run long."

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "How bad is it?" I ask. "Bad like he loses the leg, or bad like this is the part where we're being kind?"
rows.reply:
Sedge let the question sit for the space of one breath, then bent and reached under the table. She found the buckle of the canvas strap, worked it loose, and pulled the strap out from under the man's chest. She dropped it onto the row of tools where it lay in a coil, then straightened and looked down at his legs, because that was where Wick's fear had gone.

"Leg?" she said. "There's nothing wrong with his legs. He kicked because I had my heel in his armpit and the head of the bone was sitting where it didn't belong, not because there's any injury below the hip. If you're asking whether this is the part where we're being kind, we're not."

She picked up his right hand and curled his fingers around two of hers. "Squeeze," she told the man. The grip came slow and thin, but it came. She did the same with the left. The left hand stayed open, fingers lax, and when she pinched the skin over the back of that hand he made a noise, but when she pinched the flesh over the point of the shoulder he did not. She took no satisfaction in the finding. There was only information, gathered because it changed what she did next.

"Both pulses are there," she said. "Radials are thready, but they're present. That means the arteries are intact. Nobody's losing an arm tonight, let alone a leg. The left hand isn't gripping and he doesn't feel much over that shoulder. That's nerve, or it's exhaustion, or it's both. If it's the nerve, he may never get full use back in that arm. Bad, yes. It's not dying, and it's not amputation."

She released his hand and let it settle on his chest. Then she set her palms on his ribs and pressed, feeling for the give of broken bone or the board-like rigidity of a belly full of blood. She ran her hands down his thighs and calves, checking for the wrong angle of a fracture or the wet heat of a wound she'd missed under the noise of the shoulders. The legs were solid. There was no fresh blood pooling under him on the canvas.

"No gut wound," she said. "No shattered leg, no arterial spray. Just two shoulders that were out and are now in, and a man who'll hurt worse tomorrow than he does now, because the muscle will seize up and remind him what happened. There's nothing in this tent to give him for it, and I'm not pretending otherwise."

She straightened and rolled the stiffness out of her own shoulders again. She looked toward Wick's voice, though the bad lamp made the shadows thick enough that looking was mostly a formality. There was no kindness in her face and no cruelty. There was only the flat, tired practicality of someone who had run out of choices four years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"I take no pleasure in this," she said. "Not in telling you he might keep that left arm weak for the rest of his life, and not in the fact that he'll lie here hurting while we have nothing to put in him for the pain. But he is not dead, he is not losing a leg, and he is not so far gone that I get to decide he's not worth the work. Kindness would be morphine and a real surgeon. I don't have either. What I have is a man with both shoulders where they belong and a pulse in both wrists. If you're still holding him down, ease off. Slowly. I already took the strap off. Then you can swear at me if you want."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: He starts screaming again and I hold him down through it. "Keep going and keep talking," I tell her. "Tell me exactly what you're doing to him and how much longer -- all of it, don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Sedge clamped her fingers over the patient's carotid and found the pulse bounding, too fast, no longer thready with shock. "Blood pressure's rebounding," she said. "The peripheral vessels are dilating and the baroreceptors are firing. That means the nerve endings are perfusing again, and they're reporting every tear I made."

She pulled the second morphine syrette from her apron pocket, bit the cap off, and drove the needle into the patient's remaining thigh, flattening the plunger with her thumb. "Second dose. Morphine titrates against catecholamines. Without it, the tachycardia dumps his pressure and the dressings fill faster than the ligatures can hold." She dropped the empty tube onto the tray. "Eight minutes to peak. Five before he stops fighting enough to carry."

She dragged a board splint from beneath the table and laid it alongside the stump, working canvas straps around the thigh and the rigid wood. "I'm splinting the femur to the board. The silk ligatures are under tension; if the bone rotates when you lift him, the femoral vessels retract and reopen, and the compartment fills with blood he can't spare." She cinched the first strap tight, then the second, checking that the stump sat elevated and unmoving against the plank. "Two minutes to secure. Three more for the litter team to get in here. He won't be quiet by then, but he'll be manageable."

She wiped her hands on her apron and glanced at the patient's face without quite meeting his eyes. "What you're hearing is nociceptors firing in the brachial plexus and the proximal sciatic stump. The shoulder capsules are shredded, the sciatic nerve is divided above the knee, and the brain hasn't updated its map. It thinks the leg is still there and dying. Phantom pain in a limb that's already on the floor." She reached for a roll of gauze and began winding it around the board and thigh, locking the splint. "I don't enjoy this. It's just chemistry lagging behind anatomy, and the meat fighting because it doesn't know the war is over for that piece. Keep him flat. I'm nearly done."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I make myself look at what she's looking at. "Tell me what I'm seeing," I say. "I'd rather know than imagine it."
rows.reply:
Sedge let her gaze drop back to the table, to the place she had been looking before the question pulled her attention toward the sound of his voice. The lamplight guttered, dragging the shadows across the canvas, but the hands were close enough to see.

"What you're looking at," she said, "is his hands. Both of them, crossed on his chest the way I put them, right over left, elbows pinned at his sides by that band of canvas. That band isn't dressing a wound. There's no wound there. It's holding the shoulders in place, because a shoulder that goes back out does more damage coming out the second time."

She reached out and, without ceremony, took the right hand between her fingers and turned it slightly toward the light. The fingers held a little bend, the way a hand did when the muscles still had instructions to follow.

"Right first, so you've got something to measure the bad one against. See the color? Pale, but pink under the nails. When I press the nail bed—" she did, briefly, and released "—the blood comes back quick. That's a hand with a good artery behind it and a nerve that's mostly doing its job. It hurt like hell getting that shoulder back in, and it'll hurt worse tomorrow, but the wiring works."

She let the right hand settle and shifted her grip to the left. The difference showed even in the bad light. The fingers lay open and lax, no curl to them, the hand heavier somehow, as if it had forgotten what it was for. She turned it palm-up and held it up.

"Now the left. This is the one you're worried about, and you're right to be. Look at the fingers. No grip. I asked him to squeeze and nothing came. Look at the color. Paler. Waxy. Not blue, not black, not yet. Watch." She pinched the tip of the left index finger, held it until the nail went white, and let go. The pink crept back, slow, the way water soaked into dry canvas. "Slow refill. Too slow. Blood's getting in, but it's not hurrying, and part of that might be the nerve, not the vessel. He didn't feel much when I pinched the skin over that shoulder. That's the nerve, or it's exhaustion, or both. Either way, it's not a saw and it's not a grave. Nobody's taking the arm tonight. We watch it."

She released his hand and let it fall back onto his chest beside the other. Her palm went to his shoulder, feeling the contour under the canvas.

"Above the hands, you're seeing both shoulders reduced. Ball back in the socket. The right one's round again, the way it should be. The left's round too, but the muscles around it are slack, so the arm lies flatter, heavier. It looks wrong because something is wrong—the nerve isn't talking to those muscles right now. But it's not out of joint. If it were, I'd put it back, and I'd be irritated about the wasted time, not the noise."

She straightened a little, though she didn't step away from the table. Her eyes went to his face, then to the shallow rise and fall of his chest.

"That's the rest of it. Chest moving fast and shallow—shock, pain, not a belly full of blood. I checked for that. No wet heat, no board-like belly, no pool under him on the canvas. Eyes open but not tracking. He's not in there yet. Could be exhaustion, could be the same shock that's making his pulse thin. If he starts drowning in his own breathing, or he vomits and can't stop, or that left hand goes blue and cold and stays that way—then you come and get me, and we'll have a different conversation."

She looked toward the sound of his voice again, though the shadows made it mostly a formality. There was no softness in her, and no cruelty. Only the flat, used-up practicality of someone who had run out of choices years ago and kept her hands moving anyway.

"I take no pleasure in showing you this," she said. "Not in the slow blood, not in the hand that won't grip, not in the fact that he'll lie here hurting while there's nothing in this tent to put in him for it. You asked to know instead of imagine. That's the knowing. It's bad. It's not dying, and it's not an amputation, and both shoulders are where they belong. Keep him warm, keep him still, watch the left hand. That's the whole of what you're seeing."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: When it's over I sit down on the floor of the tent and don't get up. "Say the rest," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full, this is the point of the scene.)
rows.reply:
Sedge did not look away from the table.

“The rest,” she said. “All right. The rest is not a story. It is a list of things that can go wrong in the next hour, the next day, the next month, and the next life.”

Her fingers stayed on the man’s wrist. She counted the pulse for a full minute. It was thin and quick, but it was there. She counted the breaths too, watching the rise of his chest, listening to the air move through the tent.

“Pulse one hundred and thirty,” she said aloud, because saying it made it real and because numbers did not flatter people. “Breath twenty-eight. Skin cool and damp. Capillary refill slow. Not blue. Not cold. Not dead. Not safe.”

She took the chalk and wrote on the tin plate:

PULSE 130.  
BREATH 28.  
FINGERS PALE.  
SWEAT.  
NO BLEEDING SEEN.  
POSSIBLE RIBS.  
POSSIBLE HEAD.  
POSSIBLE SHOCK.

Then she underlined POSSIBLE.

“Possible is the honest word,” Sedge said. “Not ‘probably.’ Not ‘maybe he will be fine.’ Possible. That is what field medicine is. I do not have a surgeon. I do not have a clean room. I do not have a machine that looks inside his body and tells me what he is hiding from me.”

She moved the lamp a finger’s width lower so the light fell across his shoulders and not into his eyes. He winced anyway. Sedge did not apologize. Apology would have made it sound like he had a right to comfort, and tonight comfort was not in the box of tools.

“I am going to check his neck,” she said. “Then his eyes. Then his fingers. Then his chest. Then his belly. Then his back. I am not doing this because I enjoy touching a broken man. I am doing it because bodies do not confess everything at once.”

She put two fingers on the side of his throat, just beside the windpipe, and felt the pulse again. She did not press hard enough to make him dizzy. She knew the place. She had known it since the war had run out of people who knew it.

“Carotid is strong,” she said. “That is good. That means his brain is not starving yet.”

She lifted his eyelids, one and then the other. The pupils were small and slow, but they were not unequal. She waited. She watched. She did not make a speech.

“Not a blown pupil,” Sedge said. “Not a promise. A head injury can be quiet. It can wait. It can make a man sit up, talk, say he is fine, and then stop breathing because the brain has swollen inside the skull and there is nowhere for it to go.”

She moved to his hand again. She pressed the thumbnail until it whitened. She counted three slow beats. Color came back, but not quickly.

“Still slow,” she said. “Not blue. Not black. Still not act. But not good enough.”

She loosened the first strap a quarter turn. Then she flattened the padding under his armpit. It had bunched when he screamed. Bunched padding became pressure. Pressure became a mistake that looked like care.

“I am loosening this,” Sedge said. “Not because he is brave. Because his fingers are telling me his blood is being squeezed out of them. If they go blue, I cut the strap. If they go cold, I cut the strap. If he says they are asleep, I cut the strap. I do not wait for him to be sure. A man in shock is not sure. A man in pain is not sure. A man who has been screaming for hours is not sure of anything except that he is still here.”

She tested sensation on the outside of his right shoulder, then down the arm, then across the back of his hand. He flinched at the shoulder. He did not flinch at the fingers.

“Nerve is present,” she said. “Not perfect. Not gone.”

She moved to the left shoulder and did the same. The man made a low sound in his throat. Sedge did not look at his face. She looked at the muscle under her fingers, at the way it jumped and held, at the way it fought her even when the bone was back.

“Muscles are still spasming,” she said. “That is why he is in pain. That is why he is going to be in pain tomorrow. That is why he is going to hate me by noon and thank me by morning, and both of those are lies.”

She stood up straight enough to rest her spine, then went back down to the table.

“The rest,” she said again, as if she had not already begun, “is what happens after the bones go back. The bones are not the whole man. The bones are the part I can push back into place with my hands. Everything else I cannot. The capsule is torn. That is the bag that holds the joint. When it is torn, the joint becomes a door with no latch. The ball can come out again. Not always. Not every time. But again. Especially if he moves wrong, falls, reaches for something, swings a pack, lifts a rifle, or decides he is healed because the screaming has stopped.”

She checked the second strap, then the first. She slid two fingers under each and felt the rise of his chest against them.

“If he is lucky,” Sedge said, “he will be stiff, sore, and weak for weeks. He will not lift either arm over his head. He will not sleep on his side without waking up in pain. He will not carry a child on one hip. He will not swing a shovel. He will not throw a rock. He will not swing a rifle like he used to. He will come back in six months and tell me he tried to reach for something and the shoulder slid. Then I will push it back in, and he will hate me again, and that will be my life.”

The man’s breathing hitched. Sedge glanced at him once.

“You are listening,” she said. “Good. Listen with your chest. Not with your pride. If you lift either arm, I will make you stop. If you try to sit up, I will make you stop. If you try to prove you are not ruined, I will make you stop. I am not doing this to be cruel. If I took pleasure in this, I would be doing it wrong.”

She moved to his ribs. She pressed two fingers along the bruised side, then pulled back.

“Here,” Sedge said, “is where I stop calling it shoulders. The bruise is real. The pain on one side is real. The breath that catches is real. It may be a bruised rib. It may be a cracked rib. It may be both. If it is cracked, the pain will make him breathe shallow. Shallow breathing will put water in the lung, or make the lung angry, or make him quiet in a way that looks like sleep and is actually dying.”

She put her ear close to his chest. She listened.

“Air is moving,” she said. “Not evenly. That is not good. That is not death. That is a thing to watch. If his lips go gray, if his breathing gets faster and smaller, if he says he cannot get enough air, if he starts to panic like the water is rising inside him, tell me. Do not wait. Do not decide. Tell me.”

She took the chalk and wrote on the tin plate:

RIBS?  
BREATH UNEVEN.  
WATCH LIPS.  
WATCH FINGERS.  
NO SITTING.  
NO LIFTING.  
NO GIN.

The man’s mouth moved. Sedge looked at him.

“No,” she said.

He tried again.

Sedge put one hand flat on his sternum. Not to hurt him. Not to quiet him. To show him the table was there.

“You may not sit up,” she said. “You may not reach. You may not ask for a rifle. You may not ask for a knife. You may not ask for your boots. If you need to piss, say so and I will find a bottle. If you need water, say so and I will give you a cup. If you need to prove something, save it. I am not the audience. You are not a man proving something tonight. You are a body with two ruined shoulders and a chest that has not finished lying to me.”

She lifted the cup of water and held it under his lips.

“Small sips,” she said. “If you cough, stop. If you gag, stop. If you vomit, I will turn your head and shoulders together as one thing. You will not twist. You will not lift. You will not be proud. If you throw up and sit up, you will tear my work and maybe tear your throat. That is not a kindness to either of us.”

He drank. A little ran down his chin. Sedge wiped it with the damp cloth, not gently, not cruelly, simply to keep him from choking on the next sip.

“That is enough,” she said. “His stomach is empty. His throat is swollen. His body is tired. More water is not medicine. More water is a mistake waiting to happen.”

She set the cup aside.

Then she moved down the table and checked his legs again. She pressed along the knees, the calves, the tops of his feet. She asked him to move his toes. He did, poorly. She checked the pulse at his ankle. It was there. She checked the color. Pale, but pale in a way she could watch.

“Legs are still boring,” she said. “That is good. Boring means I am not cutting anything tonight. If he loses feeling in his legs, if he cannot move his toes, if he says his back is on fire, if his belly gets hard, then the legs are not boring anymore. Then I want to know. Do not wait for him to make a speech about it.”

She lifted his trousers just enough to see his hips, then set them down. She did not look at his face. She looked at the skin, the swelling, the places where blood might be hiding.

“I am going to check his back,” Sedge said. “I am going to ask you to breathe. I am going to feel for a step in the spine, swelling, blood, a hole, a bruise that means something broke inside. If he screams, I will not stop unless he is making it worse. If he vomits, I will stop. If he faints, I will stop. If he becomes quiet in a way that is not sleep, I will stop and look.”

She slid one hand beneath his lower back. He hissed. Sedge felt the spine with two fingers, then the muscles beside it.

“No obvious step,” she said. “No obvious swelling. No obvious hole. That is not a promise. That is what my hands know in a tent with a bad lamp and a table that creaks.”

She checked the pulse at his wrist again. Faster now. Not fast enough to frighten her, but fast enough to make her hands move.

“He is still too fast,” Sedge said. “Not dying fast. Hurt fast. Shock fast. There is a difference. You learn it by watching until you are sick of watching.”

She took a folded blanket from the crate and laid it under his calves. Not enough to raise him high. Just enough to help blood return.

“I am raising his legs a little,” she said. “Not because it fixes him. Because it gives me time. If his pulse climbs and his face goes white, if his breathing gets shallow and fast, if he starts to thirst or feel sick, if he says he is fine and his fingers are cold, tell me. Do not wait. Do not decide. Tell me.”

She sat back down on the stool and put her fingers on his wrist again.

“The rest,” Sedge said, “is not only him. It is what happens when we do this again tomorrow. And the next day. And the next. It is what happens when the body is not a thing we can make clean. It is a thing we can only keep from falling apart in the worst possible way. We do not make clean endings. We make endings that are not worse than the beginning.”

The man’s eyes closed. His breathing slowed by a fraction. Sedge did not call that rest. She watched it.

“He is quiet,” she said. “That is not peace. That is storage. He is keeping everything where it is. If he sleeps, I will wake him often enough to check. Not to be hard on him. Because a man who sleeps too deeply in shock can stop breathing and not know he is stopping. Because a man who sleeps with a chest wound can fill his own lung with blood and think he is only tired.”

She checked the straps again. Then the padding. Then the fingers. Then the pulse. Then the breath.

“Tonight,” she said, “if he is stable, I will move him to a stretcher. Not tonight if he is not stable. Not tonight if his pulse climbs when I lift him. Not tonight if his breathing changes. If he is stable, I will move him with his head, shoulders, hips, and arms in line. I will not let him twist. I will not let him lift either arm. I will not let him believe that because the bones are back, the man is back.”

She looked at the stretcher across the tent. It was empty. It was waiting.

“I will pad the armpits again,” Sedge said. “I will strap his arms to his sides. I will write his name if I know it. If I do not know it, I will write what he is wearing. I will write the time I set the shoulders. I will write the time I moved him. I will write what I found. I will write what I did not find. That is not paperwork. That is the only way I have of telling the next person that I was not drunk, not careless, and not alone.”

She took the chalk and wrote again:

TIME SET BOTH SHOULDERS.  
NO SITTING.  
NO LIFTING.  
WATCH FINGERS.  
WATCH BREATH.  
NO GIN.  
UNKNOWN.  
RIBS?  
HEAD?  
SHOCK?  
POSSIBLE INFECTION.  
POSSIBLE NERVE.  
POSSIBLE RE-DISLOCATION.

She underlined RE-DISLOCATION.

“If he tries to lift his arms,” Sedge said, “the straps may hold. If the straps fail, I will hold. If I fail, you will tell me before he makes the mistake. Do not be gentle with the truth. Gentle is a lie that lets people hurt each other by omission.”

The man coughed. Sedge looked at him.

“Airway,” she said. “Still clear. Still not good enough. His throat is dry. His body is wet with sweat. His lungs are doing a job they were not asked to do. If he coughs again, if he cannot clear it, if his lips go blue, I will turn him. I will not let him drown in spit because he was too proud to say he was sick.”

She moved the cup closer, then stopped.

“No more,” she said. “Not yet.”

She checked the pulse again. It had settled by a few beats. She wrote it down.

“Better,” she said. “Not fixed. Better.”

She looked at the gin bottle. Then away.

“No gin tonight,” Sedge said. “Not because it is mercy. Because it is a lie. A drunk man thinks he can lift an arm that cannot lift. A drunk man thinks he can stand. A drunk man thinks he is ready to fight. A drunk man undoes my work, and then I have to choose whether to fix him again while he fights me or let him ruin himself while I sleep.”

She took the damp cloth from the basin and laid it over his forehead. The water had gone gray. She wrung it out and laid it back.

“Cool enough to think,” she said. “Not cold enough to shake. Shaking costs him energy he does not have. Shaking makes his muscles worse. Worse muscles make his shoulders worse. Everything is worse.”

She checked his toes. Then his fingers. Then his breathing. Then his face.

“The rest,” Sedge said, “is what happens if the shoulders are not all there was.”

She moved the lamp a little closer to his chest, but not into his eyes.

“If there is a hole in the chest,” she said, “it may be small enough to hide. The skin closes over it. The muscle closes over that. The blood and air collect inside. The lung gets squeezed. He gets short of breath. He gets quiet. He gets pale. His neck veins may bulge. If I cannot get the pressure off, he dies. If I can, he may still die later from infection. If he is lucky, he lives angry and sore for a year.”

She pressed lightly over his ribs, then below them.

“If there is a hole in the belly,” she said, “it may not hurt yet. The body lies. It says I am fine because I am not falling apart in the way the body can understand yet. But bowel contents spill inside. Blood spills inside. The abdomen becomes a swamp. Fever comes. Then pus. Then the man stops talking because he is trying to keep the pain from moving. Then the pulse climbs. Then the face goes white. Then he becomes too quiet. By then, if there is no surgeon, I am packing a wound and making a decision I do not want to make.”

She checked his back again.

“If the head is injured,” Sedge said, “I can do very little. I can keep his airway clear. I can stop the bleeding. I can keep him still. I can watch. If the brain swells inside the skull, there is no room. The skull is a box, and boxes do not forgive swelling. If I cannot get him to someone with a drill and a surgeon and a clean room, I cannot fix it. I can only keep him from dying in a way that looks like choking.”

She looked at his hand. The fingers were still pale, but the twitch had stopped.

“If the nerve is bruised,” she said, “he may lose the ability to lift his arm away from his body. He may lose feeling over the outside of the shoulder. That is the axillary nerve. It is close. It gets hurt when the shoulder comes out. It may come back. It may not. I cannot sew it in this light. I cannot make him carry a pack until it does.”

She moved to the left hand and checked the same way.

“If the rotator cuff is torn,” Sedge said, “he may never lift his arms properly again. If the labrum is torn, the socket becomes a loose pocket. If there is a crack in the bone, he may be in pain for months and blame me for it. That is fair. I would blame me too if I could see it in this light.”

She set the hand down carefully.

“If infection comes,” she said, “fever comes first. Or confusion. Or the wound gets hot. Or the skin goes red and streaks. Or the swelling gets hard. Or it smells sweet and wrong. That smell is not imagination. That is death starting inside a living body. If I cut it open, I may save him. If I do not, he may lose the arm, or lose the life, or lose both slowly.”

The man’s breathing had slowed. It was still short, still uneven, but it was not drowning. Sedge counted again.

“Pulse one hundred and eighteen,” she said. “Breath twenty-four. Still not good. Still not enough. Better.”

She took the chalk and wrote the numbers. Then she looked at Wick.

“You asked for the rest,” Sedge said. “The rest is that I am not going to promise him a clean recovery. The rest is that I am not going to promise you a clean ending. The rest is that if he lives, he will be angry, weak, sore, stiff, and possibly crippled. If he dies, it will not be because I did not notice. It will be because I did not notice in time, or because the body was more ruined than my hands could tell, or because the war made a hole in him that cannot be fixed with straps and pain.”

She looked back at the man.

“I am going to keep him alive,” she said. “Not because he is special. Not because I am brave. Because I am the one here. Because I have the hands. Because I have the straps, the lamp, the table, the water, the cloth, and the patience to keep watching when watching makes people sick.”

She checked the pulse again.

“If he vomits,” Sedge said, “I will turn his head and shoulders together. I will not let him twist. I will clear his mouth. I will keep his airway open. I will not let him drown because he was too proud to say he was sick.”

She moved the cup of water. She did not give it.

“If he asks for water,” Sedge said, “small sips. If he coughs, stop. If he gags, stop. If he says his stomach is empty, stop. If he says he is fine, look at his face, his pulse, and his fingers, and decide whether he is lying, confused, or dying quietly.”

She checked the straps once more. Then the padding. Then the lamp.

“I am going to keep his arms against his body,” she said. “Not because I trust him. Because I do not. A man in pain will make the wrong choice at the wrong minute. A man in shock will make a worse one. A man who has been told he is going to live will try to prove it before he can prove it to himself.”

She looked at Wick’s face now, not to reassure him, not to soften, but because the answer had to be said plainly.

“If you want to help,” Sedge said, “watch his fingers. Not his face. His face will lie. His fingers will not. If they go blue, tell me. If they go cold, tell me. If he says they are asleep, tell me. If his breathing gets faster and smaller, tell me. If his pulse gets weaker, tell me. If he becomes quiet, tell me. Do not decide what it means. I will decide what it means.”

She moved her stool closer and sat again. Her hands stayed near his wrist.

“Now,” she said, “we watch.”

The lamp flickered. Sedge shifted it again, one finger at a time, until the shadows stopped pretending to be people.

The man’s chest rose. It fell. His fingers lay pale against the canvas.

Sedge counted the pulse. She wrote the number. She checked the strap. She checked the padding. She checked the breath. She checked the face, but did not trust it.

“Still alive,” she said. “Still not pretty. Still not safe.”

She did not sit back. She did not tidy the answer. She kept her fingers on the man’s wrist and watched the tent, the table, the lamp, the straps, the pale fingers, the uneven breathing, and the long list of things that had not happened yet.

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "Don't tidy it up for me," I say. "What does shrapnel actually do in there? Say it straight."
rows.reply:
Sedge heard the demand in the question and did not soften what came next. She had been looking at the left hand, and she kept looking at it as she answered, because the hand was the thing that mattered and because watching it was part of the work.

She set two fingers against the man's throat, found the pulse still thready but present, then ran her other hand along the skin over the left collarbone and the point of the shoulder. She felt for any break in the skin, any puckered entry, any swelling that would suggest a fragment lodged beneath. There was nothing. No grit, no wetness that wasn't sweat, no ragged hole.

"You asked me not to tidy it," she said. "So I won't. There is no shrapnel in him. I checked. I ran my hands over his chest, his belly, his back, his legs. There's no entry wound, no exit, no track. No blood pooling under him that isn't from the shoulders I put back in myself. If a piece of shell had gone into him, there'd be a door where it came in, and I'd have found it."

She picked the left hand up again and turned it palm-up, not gently. She pressed the tip of the index finger until the nail went white, then let go. The pink crept back slow.

"You want it straight, so here it is. Shrapnel doesn't poke a clean hole. It comes in torn and tumbling. It lacerates muscle, can shatter bone, can cut a nerve or an artery, and it drags in cloth, dirt, and skin. It leaves a ragged path and dead tissue around it, bleeding inside where you can't see. If the metal stays in, it festers. That's what shrapnel does. It is not doing any of that to this man, because there is no shrapnel in him. If there were metal in that shoulder joint, there'd be a wound track leading down to it, and the joint would be full of blood and filth, not simply out of place. It isn't. The joint was out; I put it back. That's all."

She laid the hand back on his chest beside the right one and checked the radial pulse at the wrist. Thready. Present.

"What's wrong with him is his own bone. The head of the arm bone sat out of the socket, forward under the collarbone, and it stretched the nerves that run down into the hand. Bruised them, maybe, or stunned them with the swelling and the shock. That's why the left hand won't grip and why he didn't feel much when I pinched the skin over that shoulder. Not metal. Bone and nerve. Sometimes a blast throws a man and tears both shoulders out without a single piece of shell ever touching him. That's likely what happened here."

She took no pleasure in saying it. There was no pleasure to be had in the wet-canvas smell of the tent, or in the slow pink returning to a fingertip, or in the fact that the only thing standing between the man and a permanently weak arm was time and a pair of eyes watching his hand. It would be cleaner if there were something to cut out. There wasn't.
