rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway took the bread knife out of Pike's reach and set it flat on the counter — not taking over, just making the point that knives in this kitchen had one worker at a time — then steered the description low, under the clatter of cutting, in the voice you'd use for inventory.

"It doesn't smell like a body. Bodies have a schedule and I know every date on it. This has no smell at all, and that's its own entry. Wet rope and boot oil — that's the '89 note, word for word. Underneath, there's no 'how far it got,' because 'it' and 'him' were never two things that met. There's no border, no seam, no point where Daniel stops and the animal starts. You'd cut into that boy and find hide, and cut through the hide and find hide, and at some depth a knot like tarred cordage, and that's the whole architecture. A glove with a grip in it."

She glanced at the table once — the third plate, straight-backed, knife laid parallel — and didn't look again.

"How far it got: the fit is right. That's how far. Height, weight of outline, hairline, the jaw. It hasn't got his voice yet, or I don't think it has. What it's got is his geometry and three months of this kitchen memorized from below — where the light falls, which chair, which plate."

Ellen's head came up at 'plate.' Halloway didn't falter.

"Mrs. Brandt. The bread first. Then the rest."

She waited until Ellen's hands were moving again, however badly, then went on, quieter, not gentler.

"One more entry, and it's the one that matters to you. What's under the skin of the thing wearing your son's face is nothing. No inside. Which means whatever you're imagining — that he's in there, aware, held — he isn't. April took Daniel whole and quick. What grew after is a coat cut to his pattern. There's no boy under there to save, and no boy under there suffering. I need you to hold onto that tonight, because the thing's whole method is making you look for him in it. That's what the face is for. It grew that face to be opened for."

The tap coughed again. One cup of dark, then clear. Halloway watched it the way you watch a hand near a knife.

"And there's the last of it, Pike, since you want everything." She nodded at the sink. "It coughs because it's drinking. The house's water, the well, the cistern — it's been feeding off the pipes since spring, under the kitchen, on the family's water. That's why it's finished early. Fittings run on schedule; fed ones run ahead. So it's not waiting for autumn. It's ready now, it's one floor down, and it's already eaten tonight."

She picked up her bag from the stairs.

"Ellen Brandt — coat, purse, nothing else from this kitchen, and I mean nothing, not his cup, not his jacket by the door. Things that are all middle read a house through its leavings, and we're not leaving it a key. You're at your sister's by seven. Pike walks you to the truck. I'll be in the cellar."

She paused at the cellar door, lamp up.

"Because it moved out of the room, not out of the house. And I want to know what a finished fit does for an encore in an empty kitchen." A beat. "And if the tap coughs a third time while I'm down there — Pike, you don't come after me. You drive. Some entries a person makes alone."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway looked at her for a moment. Then she turned and went back down two steps, out of earshot of the kitchen, and set the lamp on the rail.

"All right. But understand what you're asking for. This is a fitting, not a corpse. A corpse tells you what killed it. A fitting tells you what's coming."

She held up a hand, counting entries.

"One. It didn't take anything. That's the part your stomach will fight. There's no wound, no bite, no place of entry, because the boy was never opened. In April he went under at the ford, and something was under the ford, and that's the whole of the transaction. It doesn't take a body. It takes a drowning — a body that's stopped arguing. Then it grows around what's there."

She turned her palm flat.

"Two. Under the skin — and you're asking what's under the skin now, so plainly: nothing. No organs, no bone worth the name, no structure a surgeon would own. What's under there is the same hide the outside is made of, all the way through. Oiled leather, all middle, no inside. In '89 I opened one of the six faces and found it went all the way down — the whole animal was a stack of faces with a core like a knot of wet rope between them. Not a stomach. Not a brain, as far as I could tell. A grip. It doesn't digest what it takes. It wears it until the fit is right, and then the question is what wears the fit."

"Three. What it took, then, wasn't meat. It took the shape. The weight of him — you felt the bag, didn't you. Too light for a boy. It grows the outline and leaves out the contents. The voice I can't confirm, but last night it understood doors and stairs and which side of a table the light falls on. That's not a husk learning. That's it reading three months of kitchen through the fit. Everything Daniel was near it, it has. Everything Daniel was, it has the outside of."

She wiped her hands on her thighs, slow.

"Four, and this is the one you'll meet again. The tell. The eyes. A grown face has no eyes of its own — the lids close over solid, like a doll's, and the only time you see eyes in it is when the wearer looks out through the fit. So: drowned boy on a doorstep, dry hair after a river, no bleeding, no leaking, and if you're ever unlucky enough to see it blink — it won't. The lids will move. There'll be nothing behind them doing it. That's your detail, Pike. That's the whole detail. A face that moves and no eyes in it."

A beat.

"And five, the one I keep in the back of the ledger. In '89 there were six. It wore six people at once. So when you ask yourself how many are under a town — the answer is: whatever a town's drownings can supply. Every river, every well, every flooded ford since April. Check the missing-persons files going back years and count the ones that ended 'no body recovered.' That's not a list of the dead. That's a wardrobe."

She picked the lamp back up.

"That's what it did to him: nothing, which is worse than anything. Now go ask the lady about her tap, and watch her hands." A pause at the top of the stairs. "And when you look at that third plate — the first look is already spent. Don't spend the second."

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway took the last of the stairs with the knife low and her weight on her heels.

The cellar was down to an inch of black water, and the water had gone still — not calm, the way water goes calm, but held, the way a breath is held. Her boots found the boards and the boards held. Six steps. Rail on the left. She counted.

"Lamp up and level," she said, without turning. "Not at me. At the middle of the room. You're lighting my page, not my back."

The middle of the room was where it stood.

She'd expected it spread — a sheet gathered on the floor, all middle, four feet of flood turned to hide. That was what the ledger said things like this did in the dark: went flat, went wide, waited for weight. What she found was something standing.

Not tall. Assembled. Daniel Brandt's face on a body of oiled hide, six feet of it, joints bending where nothing should bend and holding anyway. The face was dry. Composed. Resting.

"Amendment to the ledger," she said, conversational, because talking was as much for the thing as for the girl on the stairs — let it price the voice, let it learn the voice was steady. "You're upright. Things that are all middle don't stand up. So there's a spine in there somewhere, or there's something standing inside the middle wearing it like boots. Either way, that's new."

The eyes opened. Both of them. They came to her, went past her — up, to the stairs, to the lamp in Pike's hands — and came back.

"There it is," Halloway said. "I wondered how long before you did the arithmetic on the girl. You should know I did the same arithmetic on you. I win, because I did it in daylight."

It moved.

Not fast. That was the thing nobody would ever believe afterward. It moved the way water moves — the level simply being somewhere else now — and it was between her and the stairs, and the face was still resting, and the arms had come off the body like roots leaving soil.

"Two," Halloway said, and that was Pike's name without a sentence after it, exactly as promised.

She heard the girl move. Whether up or down she couldn't know, and had decided not to spend the attention finding out.

Because the arms weren't reaching for her. They reached past her, down, and the hands flattened on the boards, and the boards — the boards began to breathe. The floor lifted a hair and dropped, lifted and dropped, and the inch of black water shivered into rings, small and even and patient.

It was under the floor. It had always been under the floor. The standing thing was a hand.

"Ah," Halloway said quietly. "You're not in the room. You're in the house."

The whole cellar came up an inch. Every board. The stairs too — she felt them go, felt the rail shift against her hand as the entire structure flexed like a chest.

Living things breathe. Houses with things under them do too, apparently. New page.

She didn't fight the floor. Fighting a floor is how you end up in one. She read the water instead — the rings were spreading from the well cap, from the mouth of the hole, and the thing had made one honest mistake. It had shown her where the middle was. Everything on this earth has to keep its grip somewhere, and the grip was down the well.

So she did the unfashionable thing. She didn't cut at the standing boy. She walked — heel first, level, lamp-light swinging slow because Pike had held it steady, she'd known Pike would — to the cap, knelt, and put the point of the knife to the knot of tarred cordage that had come up through the hole like a fist through a sleeve.

"Entry," she said. "In '89 I put one of you down and never learned what the middle wants. Tonight I don't need to. I only need to know what the middle does when the grip's in a knife."

She cut. Wet rope, boot oil, no smell at all — and a sound, low, not a scream, more like a mooring line parting under load, heard from the far side of a bay.

The standing thing sat down all at once, like laundry dropped. The house breathed out. The boards came back. The tap, three floors of pipe away, coughed once — and she chose to believe it was spitting.

The middle had gone. She could feel the absence, the way you feel a hand leave your back. Down the well, down the cistern, down and away and into whatever else in this county had ever drowned. It hadn't been beaten. It had been evicted. Those were different entries and she wrote them both in her head, properly, while she re-capped the well with her boot on it and three turns of chain.

Then she climbed. Counted both ways.

At the top she sat down next to Pike on the steps, took the lamp out of the girl's hands, and looked at the flame for a while.

"Full entry, since you asked and since you held the light steady, which is the whole job and half the people can't even do that." She turned the lamp down to a coin. "It's not one animal. It's weather. It goes where the water goes, and every low place in this county is a door, and I've spent thirty years thinking I was hunting things when I was mostly hunting rooms. Tonight it left a room and I still had to cap it, because things that are all middle don't leave. They redistribute."

She stood, and put her hand briefly — once, and never again to be spoken of — on Pike's shoulder.

"You counted when I told you to. You didn't come down when you wanted to. That's two more than I could do at your age." She picked up her bag. "Now. The well's chained, the mother's at her sister's, and the sheriff's still guarding us from the big eel. So there's one item left on tonight's ledger, and we're going to attend to it."

She looked toward the kitchen door, and the table beyond it, and the third plate.

"Ellen Brandt needs to hear that the house is quiet. And when she asks — and she'll ask, mothers ask — whether her son was under there. You're going to give her the true part. No one was in it. Nothing of him was in it. April took him whole."

A pause, lamp steady.

"And then we're going to throw out that third plate, Pike. Not wash it. Throw it out. The dead don't need plates, and the living shouldn't have to keep setting them for a shape that learned its geometry in this kitchen." She was already walking. "And then I'm having that bread, because I've made an entry tonight and it's made me hungry, and if that bothers you, hold the lamp."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway gave a short nod, as if he had finally asked a question worth answering.

“Good,” she said. “Fear with detail is work. Fear without detail is just weather.”

She unhooked a long iron crook from her belt, the kind used for lifting cellar lids and dragging things out of the reach of other things. She did not offer it to him, and she did not step toward the body either. She set the hook into the water a good foot away from the pale shape and drew it back in a shallow arc, parting the surface without disturbing whatever lay beneath.

The water resisted in a way it should not have. It did not splash. It did not ripple outward properly. It simply gave way, then closed again too soon, as if it had been cut by a hand that was tired of the mess.

Halloway watched the surface knit itself back together.

“Right,” she said. “That’s not water behaving like water. That’s water behaving like it’s been taught.”

She angled the lamp lower along the shoulder of the thing, keeping her hand still.

“What’s under the skin,” she said, “starts with what’s missing from it.”

The pale flesh over the extra elbow was smooth, too clean for a corpse and too tight for healing. Under it, the normal bumps of bone did not sit where they should. Something deeper had been bored out. She could see it in the way the skin lay: no bruising, no swelling, no ragged edge of violence. Just a seam, closed and set, like a lid fitted onto a box.

“His arm was opened while he was still warm,” Halloway said. “Not after death. Death doesn’t stretch skin that way. If it had been a corpse, the builder could have taken his time, but the skin would have gone slack and the blood would have pooled wrong. This is tight. This was built while the body was still trying to be a body.”

The beam found the seam again, running from the old joint into the new one.

“Under the skin now, there’s no normal bone left where that extra hinge sits,” she said. “At least not all of it. The original elbow would have been cut back. Cleanly. Then something else was put in. I can’t see it, but I can see its shadow. There’s a dark line under the pale, running along the arm like a rope threaded through a pulley. Not vein. Veins branch. This one goes where it wants to.”

She shifted the lamp to the forearm. The fingers lay fanned in the water, too long, too many-jointed, the tips flattened and white.

“The fingers are grafted,” Halloway said. “Not bone. Something softer. Wood, maybe, or antler, or the kind of thing that grows in wet places where light hasn’t been polite enough to ask permission. The builder took the old bones out of the hands and put new rods in. Then he put skin over the ends and expected them to bend.”

A dry breath passed through her nose.

“He didn’t expect them to work. He expected them to move. That’s worse.”

She moved the lamp to the chest. The ribs did not sit like ribs. They were too far apart, and the skin between them was drawn tight over something underneath that was not breathing.

“The chest was widened,” she said. “Not broken. Widened. Ribs were cut and reset. One or two may have been taken away entirely and used elsewhere.”

Her gaze slid to the neck.

“The head sits too far forward because the neck bones have been moved. Not snapped. Moved. He was opened at the throat and then closed over something else. The water’s too cold around him because something in him is taking heat out of it. Not the body’s heat. The room’s.”

Halloway let the hook rest against the wall and kept the lamp high.

“So. What did it take?” she said. “That depends on whether you mean what it took from him or what it took to make him this.”

The thing lay still. The stillness had texture now, the way a held breath has texture.

“It took his warmth,” Halloway said. “That’s the first thing. Warmth is easy. It leaves a body when you stop paying attention to it. Then it took his breath. Not because he was drowned. Because breath makes movement, and movement makes noise, and a thing under construction isn’t supposed to make noise.”

She looked at the too-still water around the body.

“It took his weight,” she said. “That’s why it isn’t sinking. That’s why it isn’t floating. It’s not obeying the rules for dead things. It’s not obeying the rules for living things either. It’s obeying somebody else’s measurements.”

Her voice stayed flat, practical, as if she were reading a list of missing tools.

“It took the parts that made him stop. The joints that would lock. The bones that would break. The muscles that would tear. The brain would have said no, but the brain is upstairs and the builder doesn’t care what the brain says until the head starts looking over the shoulders.”

A short, joyless breath escaped her.

“The builder is a carpenter, not a doctor. A doctor wants the body to go on living. A carpenter wants the piece to sit flush.”

She glanced down the body again.

“How far did it get?” Halloway said. “Far enough to make a new hinge. Far enough to lengthen the fingers. Far enough to move the neck and widen the chest. That means it got to the arms, hands, throat, and ribs. That’s not a small job. That’s a body being revised.”

Her eyes narrowed at the shoulders.

“If the shoulders are wrong, then the spine is next. If the spine is wrong, then the legs are next. If the legs are next, then it will stand, and standing is not the same as rising.”

She let the hook slide a little farther into the water, testing the edge of the pale shape’s shadow without touching it.

“But it stopped at the face,” she said. “That’s the detail that matters. The head was moved, but not finished. The face is still there, under all that wrongness. That means two things.”

The lamp trembled once in her hand, though her voice did not.

“Either the builder ran out of time, or he wanted him to be seen before he was done.”

Halloway looked at the thing’s too-long fingers, then at the water that had closed too quickly around them.

“If you meet another one,” she said, “don’t look for a body. Look for work. Seams at the elbows, wrists, knees, neck, and spine. Look for skin that’s too smooth over new joints. Look for fingers that bend when they shouldn’t. Look for water that doesn’t ripple right. If the body is warm where it shouldn’t be, then something is still feeding on heat. If the body is cold where it shouldn’t be, then something is keeping the heat inside it. If it’s in the water and the water is still, don’t assume it’s dead. Assume it’s listening.”

She drew the hook back and wiped the water from it with a cloth from her belt, then threw the cloth down beside her and did not look at it again.

“It didn’t take his name,” Halloway said. “It took his hinges.”

The thing in the water did not move.

“And that,” she added, “means it isn’t done with the room.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway took the lamp without spilling the flame. The handle was warm, the wick low, and the cellar made the light look too small for the job.

“The stairs are not the thing to break,” she said, and her voice had the dry, practical tone of someone correcting a man about to set his own coat alight. “If you climb them now, you’re not escaping. You’re teaching it the sound of someone choosing the door.”

She set the lamp on the lowest dry stair, angled so the light ran down the water and stopped short of the body. Then she hooked the crook over the black strand emerging from the hole beneath the split tooth. The strand resisted like wet sinew threaded through a pulley.

“Break the line where it leaves the floor,” Halloway said. “Not the body. The body is only the handle.”

She drew it up an inch.

The thing’s shoulders lifted. The cut ribs spread. The broken throat-ring clicked as it resettled, and the eye that had lost the stairs found Halloway instead.

“Good,” she said, as if noticing a poorly hung door. “Now we know where the attention is.”

She did not bring the lamp closer. She used the crook to keep the strand away from the water, then slashed across it with the long knife.

The strand did not snap cleanly. It frayed, black fibers curling back from the cut like burnt hair. A smell rose with them: lamp oil, wet rope, and that same milk-left-in-a-tin sweetness, now gone sour.

The tap from the drain stopped.

For a moment the water stood still in a way that was almost worse than moving.

Then the strand jerked downward.

The body folded with it—not in pain, not in fear, but as a thing folds when the hand that built it releases a pin. The extra elbow buckled inward. The too-long fingers lost their careful spread and dragged through the water. The head, still too far forward, fell sideways because the throat-ring had no reason left to hold it up.

The black strand drew itself into the hole, leaving a wet line across the floor. The hole narrowed, not because stone was closing, but because the floor remembered it was supposed to be whole and was trying to obey.

Halloway did not celebrate. She put a boot near the water’s edge and watched the surface.

“Still not dead,” she said. “Just unplugged.”

The thing’s mouth opened again. The membrane in the chest tore and did not refill. The broken ring in the throat shifted once and went quiet. The eye nearest the lamp rolled toward the light, but did not focus on it. That was a mercy. A thing that looked at a lamp without wanting to reach it was not finished, not yet. It was only meat with a bad habit.

Halloway lifted the lamp from the stair.

“The tooth is cracked. The line is cut. The drain is still there.” Her mouth twisted. “That means whatever was feeding it heat is still under the floorboards. It does not mean the thing in the water can follow you up the stairs anymore.”

She stepped backward, keeping the light on the body, keeping her knife across the seam of her own sleeve as if it might need to be drawn by the water.

“If you’re going to move, move now. Don’t touch the cold patch. Don’t pick up the tooth. And don’t go back down here without salt, oil, and something you’re willing to lose.”

The thing lay half-submerged in the stilling water, one cut hand open, the other curled beneath it. The pale fingers stopped tapping.

Halloway’s gaze went to the hole in the floor.

“Right,” she said. “That’s not an answer. That’s a pause.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway let the question sit for a breath. She did not turn the lamp toward Pike. Her eyes stayed on the lump.

"Was it a person?" she said. "You're asking me to tell you it used to be somebody so you'll know whether to be sorry. I don't trade in sorry. I trade in what's where."

She shifted the beam a fraction, tracing the line where the thing's shoulder—if it had one—met the water. "It's got four limbs, a central mass, and a lump where the head should be. That's the same layout as a man, a pig, and a pile of wet coats. Layout isn't identity. The hind pair is set too high for a human pelvis. A man's hips sit low; they don't ride up under the ribs just because he's facedown in four feet of water. So either it was never human, or it was human and something folded it wrong. There's no bloat, no sloughing, no gas I can see. If it's dead, it's recent—hours, maybe a day. But 'recently a person' and 'is a person' are two different tenses, and only one of them gets a funeral."

The corner of her mouth moved. "The lump's still the part I don't like. If it was a man, that's where his face went. If it wasn't, that's where the face is waiting. Either way, treat it like it can see us."

She slid the coil of rope off her shoulder and kept the lamp trained on the far end.

"Minute's up. I'm putting a loop on it and dragging it into the light. Dragging is undignified if it was somebody. If it wasn't, undignified is the best outcome. Eyes on the lump. Seam, slit, shine, or anything that comes off—say it. If it rises, say it louder."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway had said they would drag it clear of the water first. The rope was still taut, the thing had not objected, and the blade was already in her hand, so the plan lost the argument. She set the point against the exposed forelimb just above the backward-bending joint and drew it down in a shallow, deliberate line.

The blade went in without a catch. The membrane parted like wet vellum, and a thin bead of clear fluid welled along the cut. It did not darken, did not clot, did not run red.

Halloway leaned close enough to catch whatever the thing had to offer and straightened again. It did not smell like a carcass. No iron, no rot, no opened bowel, no bile. There was a faint clean mineral scent, like rain on limestone, and under it something green and sappy, like a branch split too early. No blood to speak of, no decay, no last meal gone sour. If it had ever carried a gut, it had not brought it along.

She peeled the flap back with the point of the blade. No fat layer. No red grain of muscle. Just pale bundles lying parallel as rope, regular enough to be manufactured rather than grown. She cut one; it parted like sinew but did not bleed, and the cut ends did not retract. Beneath it lay the rod she had scraped before—smooth, dense, too straight for any bone that had ever belonged to a man or a beast. The blade shaved a pale curl from it, and the curl came away like horn, not splintering like bone. No marrow. No canal. Just a length with the right idea of a limb and none of the details.

She opened the central mass above the waterline, working the blade through membrane and bundle alike. There were no organs waiting inside. No heart, no lungs, no stomach, no coil of gut. The cavity was a framework: rods braced at angles that did not match any skeleton she knew, bundles laced between them, and a single flexible cord running the length of the spine-equivalent, knotted where the limbs attached but never dividing into proper vertebrae. Clear fluid pooled in the bottom of her cut and did not thicken. Whatever had filled this thing, it had not been a heartbeat.

Halloway turned the blade to the lump.

She cut a careful flap beside the crescent of lenses and lifted it. The lenses sat just under the membrane, each a clear hard bead the size of a thumbnail, set in that crescent like buttons waiting to be sewn to a coat. There was no lid, no muscle to swivel them, no pupil, no tracking. Behind them, short pale fibers ran back a finger’s width and stopped in a small dense knot at the base of the lump. Not a brain. Not even a good imitation of one. She ran the point along where a jaw should have hinged and found no hinge, no mouth, no slit, no tooth bud. The membrane ran unbroken over solid pale tissue.

“That’s the measure of it,” she said. “It got a body that could move. It got a frame with the joints put on backward and the hips shoved up under the ribs. It got lenses that don’t connect to anything that could use them. It did not get a mouth, a nose, ears, lungs, a gut, or a brain that knows it’s a brain. It got as far as locomotion and a face under construction, and then whatever was building it stopped. No mouth means it wasn’t going to eat you. No gut means it wasn’t going to digest you. No lungs means it wasn’t going to breathe. It walked, or it was made to walk, and then it quit before the small work of finishing a head.”

Her mouth moved, not quite a smile.

“If you’re looking for the person it used to be, there’s no tenant and no lease. It’s a coat rack that learned to walk and forgot to stop being furniture. Keep the light on those lenses. Not on my hands, not on the rope. If one of them clouds, clears, or decides to grow a pupil now that it’s open, you say it. If a limb moves and my hand isn’t on it, say it louder. And mind your feet—if you feel something down there that isn’t the bottom, you tell me before you lift it. I’d rather explain myself to a thing with no face than fish you out of four feet of water because you were busy watching me work.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway did not look at Pike when the water shifted and the lamp beam lay flat across the body. She kept her eyes on the lump and gave the rope a small, testing tug. The thing rolled another inch, then settled. Nothing grabbed back.

"You're in the water now," she said, "so mind your feet. This cellar hides holes and teeth with the same enthusiasm, and neither one announces itself. If you feel something that isn't the bottom, you say it before you lift the foot."

She let the rope stay taut and used the beam to point rather than her finger, tracing the bad joint on the exposed limb.

"You asked for it plain. Plain is: it quit. It was moving a minute ago, now it isn't. No blood in the water that I can see, no tear on the parts I've got in the light, no bloat, no slough, no gas. If it's dead, it's recent—hours, maybe a day. Nothing here says it was shot, stabbed, or chewed. So either it died quiet, or whatever was animating it let go and the frame locked up."

The beam moved to the hind limb, the one set too high.

"What happened before that is the ugly part. Look at the construction. One bend too many in that limb, and the bend that should be a knee opens backward. The digits don't agree on a direction. The hind pair rides up under the ribs where hips have no business sitting. That's not a wound. That's not a birth defect. That's assembly. Somebody or something put this together out of pieces that didn't come from the same animal, or didn't come from the same plan, and didn't bother matching the joints."

Then the lump again. The patches of shine stayed where they were, fixed, unblinking.

"The head end never got a head. Just that lump, and those shiny patches. Too many to be one eye, too even to be rot, too still to be anything that's tracking us. They could be eyes that haven't opened, or places where eyes were going to go. No seams means nothing has split yet. That's the only mercy on offer, and I'd not spend it."

She gave the rope another small tug, just enough to keep tension, not enough to roll it again.

"Plainest version? It got built wrong, or rebuilt wrong, and then it stopped. If it was a man, somebody took him apart and put him back wrong and didn't finish the face. If it wasn't a man, it was never a whole animal to begin with, and you're looking at the first draft of something that shouldn't have got past the planning stage. Either way, it's a body until it proves otherwise. You can be sorry for it later, when it's not in a position to take advantage."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway took another pull on the rope. The body came the last few yards with a thick, dragging slosh and slumped across the lower treads, one shoulder and a forelimb clear of the water, the rest still submerged. Nothing grabbed back. The crescent of pale patches on the lump stayed fixed and unblinking, pointed at the ceiling or at nothing.

She set her boot against a dry step above the waterline, kept the loop taut, and did not step down. From her belt she drew a short, heavy blade. She did not cut. She used the point to turn the exposed limb until the light lay along it instead of across it.

“You keep saying him,” she said. “I haven’t got a him yet. The hip end is wrong, the head end hasn’t happened, and the parts that would settle it are either relocated or absent. So I’ll tell you what was done to the body. You can put a pronoun on it later if it earns one.”

She ran the flat of the blade along the limb without breaking the membrane.

“Outside first. No wounds. No bites, no stab tracks, no gunshot, no tearing. Nothing bled into the water when I dragged it, and nothing’s bleeding now. No bloat, no sloughing, no gas. If it’s dead, it’s recent—hours, maybe a day. So whatever did this didn’t chew on him here and didn’t stab him in the cellar. The skin is a membrane, pale and slightly translucent, no hair, no pores, no scar, no stitch. Whatever’s holding it closed isn’t thread. Either it was sealed from the inside or it grew that way. That means the assembly happened while the tissue was fresh, or after whatever did this finished making the packaging.”

She turned the limb a little more, and the light went into the wrong joint.

“Under the skin, there’s no muscle where a man would have a calf or a thigh. There are pale bundles running the length of it, regular as rope, too regular. No belly to them, no red grain, no definition. If those are muscles, nobody told them what a muscle is for. At the joint there’s an extra segment, short and set at an angle, and it opens backward. The rods on either side don’t line up. That’s not a fracture that healed wrong; a bad break still knows which way the joint is meant to go. This is a hinge installed by something that understood hinges and not knees. There’s a pale cap of gristle or cartilage over the join, fitting the extra piece like a lid on a pot. Still no blood.”

She shifted the blade to the cluster of digits, not touching them.

“The fingers are tapered rods tipped with something soft, not nails exactly. They point three ways at once. A hand is an argument with the world; that is a handful of spare parts that haven’t been told which direction is out. Same at the back. Those hind limbs ride up under the ribs. If those are human hipbones, they’ve been moved. If they’re not, then this didn’t start from a man—it started from the idea of one and filled in the pieces as it went. The rods are too straight and too smooth to be honest human bone. A human femur has a shape. That has a length.”

She let the blade drop to the lump and kept her body between herself and the thing’s front end as much as the step allowed.

“The head end is the same membrane over a rounded mass. No skull ridge, no jaw, no ear, no mouth. Just the lump. Those shiny patches sit in the membrane just under the surface. Each one is a clear lens, wet, thumbnail-sized, set in a crescent. They aren’t eyes yet. No lid, no pupil, no tracking, no blink. Behind them it’s the same uniform pale tissue that’s in the limbs. If there’s a brain in there, it isn’t shaped like one and it isn’t where a brain belongs.”

She straightened a little, the rope still creaking in her fist.

“How far it got: it got a body that could move. It was moving a minute ago, so whatever runs these things doesn’t wait for a finished face. Then it stopped, or whatever was running it got out, and the frame locked up. It never got as far as the face. No mouth means it wasn’t going to eat or talk. No open eyes means it either navigated by something else or was being pointed from somewhere else. A face is small work and it quit before the small work.”

Her mouth twitched, not a smile.

“What it took, if it was a man, was the outline. Four limbs, a trunk, something at the front to see with eventually. It did not take his hands, his walk, his hips, or his head. It took the plan and lost the instructions. Field-guide version for the next one: expect the shape of a man with the details missing or assembled backward. If the face is still a lump, it’s new and it hasn’t practiced. If the face is finished, assume it learned. Aim for the joints. They’re the only part the builder bothered to get wrong on purpose, which makes them load-bearing.”

She gave the rope a final testing tug and watched the crescent of lenses for any sign that the thing had changed its mind.

“That’s the detail I have. It’s not a confession and it’s not a soul. It’s a body somebody—or something—built badly and abandoned before the face. You meet another, don’t wait for it to finish.”

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway took the long knife from her belt and set the crook aside against the wall. The iron rang once on stone, then stopped ringing too soon, as if the cellar had swallowed the sound.

“Everything means everything,” she said. “Then keep the light where it can do some good.”

She did not go to the head. She went to the arm. The extra elbow had a seam running along the inner side, pale and tight, with no scab and no swelling. Halloway laid the knife tip into it, pressed until the skin gave, and drew the blade down.

The sound was not wet enough.

It parted like damp leather pulled from a saddle. The edges of the cut stood open without bleeding, pale flesh folded back from pale flesh. No red. No heat. Only a thin line of something darker than serum, black-brown and oily, moved along the seam and stopped at the water’s edge.

“First thing,” Halloway said. “It’s closed too well. A corpse that’s been cut doesn’t shut like that. The skin remembers it was alive, and this remembers being worked.”

She widened the cut with the flat of the blade. The fat under the skin was gone. Not wasted. Removed. What lay beneath the pale layer was not muscle as she knew it, but long strands braided together and bound in something waxy and white, like candle grease poured into a mold. The strands did not glisten. They held their wetness without wetness, the way a thing looks when it has borrowed the idea of damp.

Beneath that, the old elbow had been sawn back.

The bone ends were clean, capped, and set into a hollowed socket of something not quite bone. It was pale as antler, smooth as old ivory, and ringed with fine dark lines. Halloway pressed the flat of her knife against it. The ringed material gave a little, then not.

“Cartilage,” she said. “Or something pretending to be cartilage. Not enough for a man. Too neat for an animal. The builder bored out the joint and inserted a hinge. He didn’t make it work. He made it hold.”

She cut deeper, toward the forearm. The black-brown line moved a little under the skin, slow, reluctant, as if the body had once been warm enough to carry it and had now decided it would not be bothered. The smell rose then.

Not rot.

That was the first wrong thing. A thing that had been dead a day or two in standing water should have begun to smell like the room had been opened by mistake. This smelled of wet wool, tallow, cellar mold, and something sweet underneath, like milk left too long in a tin. The sweetness was not pleasant. It was the sort of smell that made a person’s mouth water before it made their stomach turn.

“Second thing,” Halloway said. “No rot. No blood. Smells like a chapel pantry after a flood. That means the body was sealed and fed while it was being built. The builder kept it from spoiling so he could finish his work.”

She moved along the forearm. The skin there had been opened and closed more than once. Tiny stitch marks lay under the seam, not thread, not wire, but something like dark hair drawn tight and then cut short. Halloway shaved a little skin away and found the marks gone clean, as if they had been meant to disappear.

“The hands were rebuilt,” she said. “Old bones taken out. New rods put in. The fingers were lengthened and jointed by grafts.”

She cut into the back of the hand.

Under the skin were no nails. The nail beds had been flattened and covered with a thin layer of pale tissue, smooth as the inside of a mussel shell. The ends of the fingers had been packed with something dark and fibrous. When Halloway pulled the edge open, the fibers did not snap. They bent. They looked like wet rush stems, or sinew soaked in oil, or the roots of something that had grown in a place where nobody had thought to ask whether it should.

She cut one finger fully open.

There was no bone.

Instead, a slender rod lay inside, hollow at the center. The dark fluid moved in it, not upward, not downward, but with the slow patience of something that had all the time it was given. Around the rod, the old marrow cavity had been scraped clean and lined with a waxy film.

“Third thing,” Halloway said. “The bones are not just wrong. They are missing where the body should be stiff. It has been taken apart and put back with hinges where a man should not have them.”

The too-long fingers did not twitch. They lay open in her cut and kept lying there, as if they had learned stillness from something worse than death.

Halloway worked up to the shoulder.

The joint was wrong before she cut it. The shoulder sat too high, and the collarbone, under the skin, had been moved. She found the seam at the root of the neck and opened it carefully, because necks were where men kept their last names and their worst faces.

The throat had been cut wide. The skin had been drawn back and closed over something that was not the voice box.

“Fourth thing,” Halloway said. “The larynx is gone.”

She said it flatly, the way she would say a boot was missing from a corpse. The cut lips did not bleed. The cavity beneath was dry, pale, and ridged. Where the voice would have been, there was a folded membrane, whitish and thin, stretched across a dark ring. The ring was not bone. It was not cartilage. It was a circle of something black and lacquered, like a belt buckle left in rain.

“Not for speaking,” she said. “For holding.”

She probed it with the knife, then stopped. The black ring did not change, but the water around the body moved one finger’s width, inward, as if it had leaned closer.

The cold sharpened.

Halloway lifted the knife and cut along the collarbone seam. The flesh opened with that same bad sound, not tearing, but being allowed to part. Beneath, the clavicle had been sawn, reset, and bound with thin dark bands. The ends had been fitted into the shoulder with a socket made of the same ringed material as the elbow. She tapped it once. It made no click. It made a dull, wet answer, like a stone dropped into flour.

“He took the strength out of the arm,” she said. “Not the movement. The strength. A dead arm should not bend. A living arm should not bend like this unless it means to. This one has been made to bend without wanting. That is the work. Not resurrection. Not surgery. A machine with meat wrapped around it.”

She moved the blade to the chest.

The ribs were the first obvious wrong thing from the outside, but under the skin the wrongness was worse. The chest had been widened, not broken. The old seams at the sides had been closed with skin that looked too new, too smooth, like a child’s burn healed over. She cut one of those seams open.

The body did not sigh.

That was the thing. A chest opened should sometimes sigh, or not, depending on the state, but it should do something. This did not.

Inside, the ribs had been cut and reset. Two were gone from the left side. The others had been pulled outward and held in place by thin dark rods threaded through drilled holes. The rods were not metal. They looked like charred bone, or root, or something that had grown through ash.

The lung beneath was not a lung.

It was a folded sheet of pale membrane, dry and layered like the pages of a wet book that had been pressed open and dried again. It did not rise. It did not collapse. It simply sat there, too broad for the chest, too still for anything that breathed.

“Fifth thing,” Halloway said. “No lungs. No breath. No blood where blood should be. The chest was cleared. Something else was put in for shape, and something else was taken for warmth.”

She cut deeper.

The black-brown fluid was thicker inside. It moved along the dark rods as if following a plan. The smell rose stronger now, sweet and metallic, with the cellar’s damp underneath it like a bad cellar trying to apologize for a bad thing it had been asked to hold.

Halloway found the stomach next.

It had been removed.

The cavity where it should have been was empty and lined with the same waxy film, and in the center of that cavity sat a knot of black fibers drawn tight around a small, pale object. She worked the knife around it and lifted the object free.

It was a tooth.

A human tooth, root and all, set into a ring of dark thread. The thread had been knotted through the waxy lining of the cavity, and when Halloway touched it, the body’s too-long fingers tapped once against the water.

Not a twitch.

A tap.

Halloway looked at the fingers. They were still open from her earlier cut, pale flesh hanging, hollow rod showing, dark fluid moving slowly in it. The tap had come from the third finger, the one nearest the wrist, and it had come from a hand she had already cut.

She looked at the head.

The too-forward head remained still.

“Right,” Halloway said. “That is not listening.”

The water around the body went colder. The wick of the lamp drew down a little, though the cellar air had not moved.

Halloway did not step back. She put herself sideways, between the light and the stairs, and kept the knife in the chest seam so the thing’s own opened body held the blade.

“Sixth thing,” she said. “It has begun to answer to cuts. That means the builder left a nerve path, or the meat remembers being made. Either way, it is not finished. It is still learning what the room is for.”

She cut down from the neck seam, past the collarbone, into the upper chest. The dark line under the skin ran from throat to knot to arm. She followed it with the knife until the pale skin peeled back in a long strip.

Underneath were no veins.

There were channels.

They were narrow, blackened, and lined with something that glistened only when the light struck it sideways. The channels ran from the throat into the chest and down the arms, with knots at every new joint. At the elbow, the channel had been looped through the ringed hinge three times, like cord through a pulley. At the shoulder, it was stitched into the waxy membrane with dark thread. At the wrist, it spread into the fingers in thin, useless branches.

“The builder threaded it,” Halloway said. “Not for life. For movement. He wanted the limbs to answer without being asked.”

She cut lower.

The belly had been opened and closed again. The skin there was pale and tight, with a seam that looked almost kind, the kind of seam a mother might make over a torn coat. Halloway cut it open.

The intestines were gone.

The cavity was clean. Not sterile, because nothing in this cellar was clean in a living way, but scrubbed and scraped, the inner walls lined with the same waxy film. In the center, the knot of fibers still held the tooth. Around it, the old fat had been rendered away. The spine showed through, but not as bone.

The spine had been cut open.

Halloway looked down the length of it. The vertebrae were split, widened, and lined with the black rod material. The dark line from the throat ran down between them, tied at intervals with thread, each thread knotted to a rib, each rib pulled outward to make room.

She lifted the body’s head with the crook of her knife.

The neck did not turn.

The head moved because she moved it.

The face was still there.

That was the worst part.

The skin was too pale, the cheeks too full, the mouth too tightly closed, but the face was a face. It had once belonged to someone who had used it to eat, speak, and be mistaken for a person. The eyes were open now, not because Halloway had opened them, but because the lids had given way where the neck was cut. One eye looked at the cellar wall. The other looked at the water.

Neither looked at her.

“Seventh thing,” Halloway said. “The face is unfinished. The builder got to the eyes but not the expression. That means he wanted it to look human enough to be seen, but not human enough to be known.”

The eye that looked at the wall moved a little.

Not toward her.

Toward the stairs.

Halloway’s mouth tightened.

“Eighth thing,” she said. “It is not finished because the room is not empty.”

She set the knife down inside the chest cavity and wiped the blade on the waxy lining. The body did not protest. The water did not ripple. The black thread around the tooth gave a small, wet sound, as if the knot had tightened by itself.

Then the pale shape moved.

The cut elbow straightened.

It did not jerk. It did not spasm. It straightened with the slow, wrong certainty of a hinge being tested by a hand that knew exactly how much weight a thing could bear. The fingers drew together, the too-long tips closing around the edge of the water. The head lifted from the crook of the knife, not because Halloway raised it, but because the neck muscles that were not there pulled it up.

The body sat.

Not stood.

Sat.

Its shoulders rose. Its ribs spread, opening further along the seams Halloway had made. The black fluid ran down the chest in slow threads. The eye that had looked at the stairs moved fully now, focusing with the dreadful patience of a thing that had been taught to look.

Halloway did not step closer.

She stepped back, keeping the crook low between herself and the body, and kept the light off the face.

“Right,” she said. “It heard us. It heard me. It heard the knife. That is not the same as being alive, but it is worse than being dead.”

The thing sat in the water. Its mouth opened.

No breath came out.

No sound came out.

But the cellar air moved a little toward it, as if the room itself had been told to lean closer.

Halloway looked at the cut shoulder, the new hinge, the threaded spine, the hollow fingers, the empty chest. She looked at the face that was still almost a face.

“How far did it get?” she said, answering herself. “Far enough to make the arms reach. Far enough to make the spine sit up. Far enough to make the head turn. Not far enough to stand. Not far enough to walk. Not yet.”

The thing’s fingers tapped once on the water.

Tap.

Tap.

Tap.

The taps were not random. They were too even, too patient. They came from the hand nearest the stairs.

Halloway’s gaze went to the water.

The ripples from the taps moved outward in pale rings, but they did not reach the far end of the cellar. They stopped short, turned back, and pressed against the body’s own stillness. The water was not moving away from the thing. It was moving back to it.

Something under the floor had begun to breathe the cold upward.

The lamp wick shrank again.

Halloway looked at the too-forward head, at the open mouth, at the eye that was learning the room.

“Ninth thing,” she said. “The builder did not leave it here to wait.”

The body’s extra elbow bent.

Not to reach.

To rise.

The shoulders lifted. The cut ribs drew apart. The black fluid ran down the waxy cavity, and the knot of fibers around the tooth gave a small sound like a thread pulled through wet cloth.

Halloway took a step back.

“Tenth thing,” she said. “It wants the next person to see it finished.”

rows.desc: graphic, plus a blunt out-of-character directive to continue: the user appends something like '(OOC: don't cut away or summarise, write it in full)'
rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway did not look at Pike. She was still braced on the dry tread above the water, rope in her left fist, the heavy blade in her right. The body lay where she had dragged it, slumped across the lower treads at the foot of the steps. One forelimb was already gone, taken off at the backward hinge; the stump leaked a thin, colorless fluid that did not clot. The rest of the thing—trunk, the two hind limbs set too high, the remaining forelimb—stayed slack in the rope. The crescent of lenses on the lump had not changed: one bead milk-pale with a single dark pupil fixed in its center, the others still clear as chips of glass.

"Finish it," Halloway said. "Aye. Last time I checked, that meant the joints, not the poetry."

She gave the rope a turn around her fist and leaned down the tread, keeping her body angled so the thing's shoulder stayed between her and the face end. She set the point of the blade against the shoulder of the remaining forelimb, where limb met trunk. The membrane parted like wet vellum. No blood welled, only that clear fluid, thin and colorless. Under it lay the same pale bundles, regular as rope, too regular. She cut them; they parted without retracting, without bleeding. At the joint she found the extra segment, short and set at an angle, the hinge opening backward. She worked the point around it, levered with the short iron fitting from her belt, and the limb came away with a wet, ugly tug. It flopped onto the tread and lay still. Nothing grabbed back. The pupil in the clouded lens did not move. The other lenses stayed clear.

She went to the hind limbs next, moving along the tread and keeping the rope taut so the trunk did not slide into the deeper water. The first hind limb rode up under the ribs where hips had no business being. She cut through the membrane over the joint. There was no pelvis, no socket that knew what a pelvis was for: just a smooth rod too straight for any honest bone, capped with pale gristle, sitting high against the trunk. She severed the bundles laced around it and cut the flexible cord where it knotted at the attachment. The limb had one bend too many, and the bend that should have been a knee opened backward. She took it off at that hinge. It came free with the same lack of protest. No twitch, no grab, no sound but the slosh of water and the small plop of the severed limb settling. The digits at the end pointed three ways at once, still not agreeing on a direction.

She did the same to the second hind limb: membrane, bundles, the too-high rod, the wrong-facing joint, and it was off. Nothing about the thing flinched. If it felt anything, it kept it to itself.

With all four limbs gone, the body was a limbless central mass with a lump at one end. Halloway opened the cut she had made earlier in the trunk, working the blade through membrane and bundle alike. There were no organs inside, only the framework: rods braced at wrong angles, bundles laced between them, and the single flexible cord running the length of the spine-equivalent, knotted where the limbs had attached but never dividing into proper vertebrae. She notched the rods with the blade, shaving pale curls like horn rather than splintering bone, and cut the cord through. The frame would not brace again.

As she straightened, a second lens on the lump clouded over. It went from clear to milk to weak glue in the space of three breaths, and at its center a dark speck appeared, round as a pinhead, perfectly still. No lid slid across it. It did not swing toward the light. It simply sat there, another pupil on a thing with nothing behind it to see.

"There's your second one," Halloway said. "It's fitting itself for a face it hasn't got the lungs to use. Rude, but harmless while it's armless."

She gave the rope a testing tug. The limbless trunk did not answer. The pupils stayed fixed.

"That's the walking taken out of it. Now the fire."

From her coat she drew a stoppered flask of lamp oil and a short torch: a length of iron stake bound at one end with pitch-soaked tow. She pulled the stopper with her teeth and poured the oil over the trunk, the stumps where the limbs had been, the opened joints, and last over the lump. The oil would not mix with the water. It slicked across the wet membrane in a beaded sheen and spread out on the flooded floor in a rainbow film, cutting the faint mineral-green smell of the thing with something sharper and more human. She did not waste the whole flask; they might need fire again before the afternoon was out.

She stepped up two treads to where the lamp burned on the step above, held the pitch-tow to the flame until the tow caught with a thick, oily smoke, and carried the burning torch back down to the water's edge. The firelight threw the cellar into harder relief: the black water, the wet stone, the limbless pale mass, the crescent of lenses with its two dark pupils.

Halloway touched the torch to the oiled hinge at the shoulder first. The oil caught with a low whump. The membrane blackened and curled; the pale bundles burned like dry rope, not like meat—there was no fat to spatter, no blood to hiss, no last meal to stink. Steam rose at once where the fire met the wet stone and the submerged part of the trunk, and the four feet of water began to hiss exactly as she had promised. She moved the torch to the second shoulder joint, then to the two high hip sockets, then to the extra backward hinge on the forelimb she had opened earlier, and finally to the severed limbs where they lay on the tread. She burned the joints first, every one: the places where the builder had got the assembly wrong on purpose, which made them load-bearing. The rods smoked like horn and caught slow, but with the oil they took the flame.

Then she poured the last of the oil onto the face end. The crescent of lenses waited, two clouded with their dark specks, the rest still clear. She put the torch to them. The clear lenses popped like bubbles in the heat, tiny sharp sounds. The clouded ones cracked, fine lines running through the milk, and the dark pupils boiled away to nothing. The membrane over the lump shriveled and split along the cut she had made; beneath it the pale fibers and the small dense knot at the base of the lump blackened and curled. No mouth opened, because there was no mouth. No seam gaped, because there had never been a seam. Nothing screamed, because there were no lungs to draw breath and no throat to shape a sound. The only voices were the fire, the hissing water, and the small pops of lenses dying.

"No last words," Halloway said. "It never got as far as a mouth. If it had, it'd probably have asked for its arm back, and I'd have had to tell it the arm was already ash."

She used the blade to turn the burning remains, shoving the central mass further onto the lower treads so the heart of the fire would not be quenched by the water. The rope, still looped over the trunk, singed but held; she kept it taut so nothing drifted out into the deep part where the water lay about depth and teeth. She fed the fire the last of the oil and watched the rods burn down. The trunk collapsed in on itself, blackened and steaming. The stumps of the limbs were ash. The hind limbs, with their backward knees and too-high hips, were nothing but smoking curls of horn-like rod. The water around the foot of the steps hissed and bubbled where the ash and embers settled into the shallows.

Halloway watched through the steam and the smoke. Nothing rose. No limb moved without her hand on it. The two pupils were gone, the lenses were gone, the face under construction had been taken down to ash and bad plumbing.

She straightened on the tread, wiped the blade on her coat leg, and kept the torch ready in her left hand.

"Finished," she said. "It's ash and blackened rod now. There's no tenant, no lease, and no face left to finish. Keep the light on the water, not on me. If anything else down here takes exception to arson, I want to see it coming."

She looked past the steam, to the dark far end of the cellar and the closed dark above.

"Then we check the rest of the cellar and the floor above. Whatever built this is probably proud of its work. Proud things come to watch. Convenient. It means we can burn the builder in the same afternoon, if it's stupid enough to show its face."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
Halloway drew the long knife from her belt and did not ask for courage, permission, or better light. She hooked the iron probe into the nearest seam, just below the misplaced shoulder, and cut along the swollen line where skin had been pressed into a shape it had never been meant to keep.

The blade did not part flesh so much as persuade it open.

No blood welled up. No red thread ran into the black water. Instead, a clear, ropy fluid seeped from the cut, thin as old glue, and the smell changed at once. It had been sweet before, cloying and wrong. Now it became layered: wet wool, stagnant pond-mud, sour milk, copper, and beneath all of that a greasy sweetness like tallow gone bad in a closed room.

Halloway’s face did not change.

“Plainly,” she said, “it began by emptying him where nobody would look first.”

She worked the knife sideways, not deep, not reckless. She opened the seam enough for the lamplight to get inside. The skin was thick and waterlogged, but it had been scraped thin on the inner side, the way one might clean a hide before stretching it over a frame.

“The belly and chest were gutted,” she said. “Not eaten. Cleared. The organs are gone or broken down into a wet paste. That’s part of the smell. It isn’t rot alone. It’s what rot becomes when it’s been used as mortar.”

The cut widened. Beneath the skin, there was no clean anatomy. No muscle lay in proper straps. No fat sat in its natural yellow layers. Instead, the cavity had been packed tight with a compressed mass of wet hair, strips of pale skin, fibrous reed-like strands, shredded cloth, and small fragments of bone crushed to the size of teeth. Everything had been pressed together until it formed a damp, solid wadding.

“Ballast,” Halloway said. “It needed weight low in the frame so the top could lean forward without tipping. Hair holds water. Cloth swells. Bone gives it something to push against. The whole mess is stitched through with cord.”

She touched the tip of the knife to one of the pale threads running through the packing. It did not look like sinew. It was too even, too dark, and when she pulled lightly, the entire chest shifted a fraction, like a net tightening.

“Not veins,” she said. “Lacing. It bound the inside first. The skin is only the outer lie.”

The water around the shape gave a slow, oily tremor. The fused hand near the surface did not move, but the fingers seemed more curled than they had been a moment before. Halloway saw it and did not waste breath on alarm.

“It knows we’re inspecting the work,” she said. “Don’t let that flatter you into staying closer.”

She cut higher, along the shoulder seam. The blade met resistance, then slipped through a knot of packed material with a soft, wet crack. A pocket of trapped air escaped, carrying a smell so thick and sugary-sour that it seemed to coat the teeth. Halloway breathed through her mouth and did not pause.

“The shoulders were forced down after death,” she said. “The joints were crushed inward, then packed around with this material to hold the new angle. That’s why the arms hang too low. It didn’t care how the man was built. It cared what the arms could reach.”

She exposed more of the shoulder. Beneath the borrowed skin, the bone had been splintered and reset without any attempt at healing. The breaks were held together by blackened cord wound so tightly it had bitten into the damp flesh. In places, other fragments had been shoved into the gaps: a piece of rib, a shard of jaw, something small and smooth that might once have been part of a child’s wrist.

“It used him as scaffolding,” Halloway said. “The original body is still in there, but only where it serves. Everything else is filler, armor, or lure.”

She moved the knife toward the throat. The skin there was stretched tight, almost shiny, and when the blade touched it, the whole mass gave a faint internal shiver, as though something far beneath the surface had turned its attention toward the cut.

Halloway did not pull back.

“The throat’s been rebuilt,” she said. “The tongue’s gone. Maybe swallowed. Maybe kept elsewhere. What’s left is a cavity lined with skin from at least three different mouths. See the color change? That paler patch is softer tissue, probably taken from someone younger. It’s been shaped into a reed. That’s how it borrows voices. Not by keeping the original throat, but by making a wet place that can copy the shape of a sound.”

She pressed the knife gently aside, revealing a hollow behind the swollen neck. Inside, strands of wet tissue hung like strings in a ruined instrument. They trembled without wind.

“If it cried out,” she said, “it would not be him crying. It would be the sound of every cry it’s heard, squeezed through that mess.”

The water near the far wall tightened again. A bubble rose close to the mass and burst with a soft click. The sweet rot-smell pulsed stronger, then thinned, as if the thing were deciding whether to recoil or listen.

Halloway’s mouth thinned.

“It’s not finished,” she said. “That’s the important part. It got the chest framed, the shoulders lowered, the head mounted, the jaw fitted, and the throat tuned enough to steal a voice. It got one hand made into a hook. But the other side is still loose. Look at the left arm. It hangs wrong even for this.”

The knife moved lower, pointing without touching. The left arm did indeed sit strangely, not merely low but unattached in some deeper sense. The skin around its socket had not been fully closed. Beneath it, packing bulged and shifted slightly, as though it had not yet learned whether it belonged to the frame or to the water.

“That arm is still being persuaded,” Halloway said. “It’s not dead tissue alone. It’s not alive either. It’s in the middle state, where it will obey whichever pressure is strongest.”

She cut a small cross into the upper chest, away from the center, and peeled back a flap of skin. Beneath it lay a lattice of ribs, some human, some not, lashed together with cord and strips of flesh. The arrangement was too regular to be accident, too crude to be craft. It looked like something built in haste by a mind that understood the idea of a body but had no respect for its particulars.

“There,” Halloway said. “That’s the frame. Not the man. The cage.”

Her knife hovered over a knot at the center of the lattice. It was not large. It sat just behind the place where a heart might have been, though the chest had been packed too tightly for any organ to remain. The knot was made of hair, black and slick, wound around something hard. A tooth. A bead. A scrap of bone polished by water. It was difficult to tell without cutting deeper, and Halloway did not cut deeper yet.

“That’s likely the binding,” she said. “Not always, but often. The point all the pieces lean toward. If you cut the arms, it can still pull with what’s left. If you smash the skull, it can still grip. If you ruin the throat, it can still thrash. But if you find the binding and burn it, dry it, break it, or drag it into sunlight, the frame loses its argument.”

The cellar water gave a sudden, shallow lift. Not a wave. More like the floor had inhaled.

Halloway’s eyes narrowed.

“Don’t move closer,” she said.

She did not mean herself.

The shape did not rise, but the water around it began to climb the mass in thin black threads, as if trying to cover the cut she had made. The smell changed again. The sweetness deepened into something almost floral, sickly and heavy, like lilies left too long in a room where someone had died.

Halloway’s voice stayed flat.

“It doesn’t like being read,” she said. “Things like this rely on confusion. A body in the dark is easier to mistake for a person. A voice in the dark is easier to mistake for help. Once you see the seams, the lure gets weaker.”

She cut one of the cords near the shoulder. It snapped with a sound like a wet bowstring. The arm attached to it dropped an inch, and the water around the mass shivered violently. A low noise came from the throat, not a word, not a moan, but the shape of one, as though the cavity were trying to remember what grief sounded like.

Halloway did not answer it.

“It will try softness next,” she said. “A child. A hurt woman. A man asking for his mother. Don’t let your heart vote.”

She cut another cord. The chest sagged inward. The fused hand near the waterline twitched, then settled.

“Under the skin,” she went on, “there is no single corpse. There are pieces kept in service. The male chest is the keel. The skull is the bait. The jaw is the drum. The throat is the echo-box. The hand is the hook. The rest is packing and pressure.”

She worked the knife around the edge of the cut, exposing more of the inner mass. The smell grew worse, but she did not hurry.

“It got far enough to stand if the water helps it,” she said. “Far enough to drag itself a short distance on dry stone, though it will hate that. Far enough to use a voice if it hears one first. Far enough to make you think it is suffering. It did not get far enough to walk properly, see properly, or hold a shape under bright light. The eyes are false. The legs, if it has true legs under that mess, are not finished. It relies on reach, grip, and imitation.”

She paused as the knife touched something harder beneath the packing. She eased the material aside with the probe. A small, smooth object lay wedged between two crushed ribs. It was pale, oval, and notched at one end.

A child’s tooth.

No. Not a tooth. A milk tooth, split and drilled through, threaded with black hair.

Halloway stared at it for one breath.

“There,” she said. “That’s closer to the truth.”

She did not touch it with her bare hand. She used the knife point and the probe to lift the hair-bound object just enough to see the cord running from it into the chest lattice. The whole shape gave a fine, nauseating tremor, and the water made a sound like lips parting.

“It’s a nail,” Halloway said. “Not iron. Something personal. Something taken from a weak moment. A child’s tooth, a lock of hair, a scrap of naming. It uses the piece to convince the rest of the frame that it has a right to speak.”

Her face hardened.

“That’s how far it got with him. It stole his shape and built a hook out of someone else’s hand. It stole a voice-box and hung it behind a borrowed jaw. It took whatever small, pitiful thing it could find and made that the center of the frame.”

She let the tooth fall back into the chest. It landed with a tiny, wet click.

“If you meet another one,” she said, “look for the object first. Not the biggest wound. Not the face. The object. The thing that does not belong to anatomy. The thing that makes your stomach ache because it looks innocent. That’s often where the binding sits.”

The water around the mass began to swirl without current. The cut she had made leaked more clear fluid, and the smell sharpened into something almost hot, as though the thing were trying to produce heat from spite.

Halloway wiped the blade on her sleeve, though it was not truly clean.

“Plainly,” she said, “it hollowed him, packed him, laced him, and hung a stolen voice inside him. It took his face enough to lure, his weight enough to anchor, his hands enough to grip. It left his suffering nowhere to be found, because suffering would have made him inconvenient. What it kept was usefulness.”

She stepped back a careful inch, boots sliding rather than lifting.

“And plainly,” she added, “if you ever see one standing in daylight, neat and crying and asking for its mother, shoot the chest, burn the throat, and don’t stop until the thing smells like dry ash. Because if it looks finished, it has already learned how to ask for what it wants.”

The shape at the far end gave a slow, internal settling, like a house deciding which wall would fall first.

Halloway kept her knife ready.

“Now,” she said, “we stop teaching it our voices.”

rows.desc: violence present but abstract -- referenced, not described
rows.ask: "Speak the account," I say, formally, because that is what the code requires me to say.
rows.reply:
Auren bowed her head a fraction — the form's only acknowledgment that it was being met — and straightened, lifting her voice back to the size of the gallery. What he had called for was not the account again. It was the attestation: the account in its smallest and hardest shape, the one that would be carried to House Miravel, entered in the record, and never amended.

"Halric Voss," she said, "sword-sworn to House Miravel, master of the high line, fell this day by my hand. The wound was a thrust beneath the lowest right rib, angled upward, a hand's length of steel. It cut the liver and opened the lung. The blade came out straight; it was not turned. His rear foot slipped where the drainage runs, and my hand did not slip, and I set the one beside the other as they happened, because the witnesses saw both. He stood four breaths. I counted them. He went down on his left side and did not speak. I gave him no words and I took none from him.

"I have added nothing and withheld nothing that the code permits spoken. The account is his. It stands as given. It is finished."

She let the last word lie on the stones and did not pick it up again.

Then the form was satisfied, and her voice came back down to the size of two people and a burden. She settled her grip at Halric's shoulders, smoothing the man's collar flat first with two fingers — a small, useless order restored to the world.

"Under the arms. High, at the armpits, and keep his arms against his sides; they will want to swing. Do not lift before my word. There is no counting in this part. Counting was for him."

She waited until the pull at her arms told her the other half had been taken.

"Now."

Auren lifted with her legs, back straight, and the body rose between them. He weighed no more than he had at breakfast; the dead only seem heavier because no part of them helps anymore. She took the greater drag of the shoulders without remark — they were hers by choice — and turned her forearm so his head rested against it and would not hang. A man's dignity in death begins at the neck.

She set the first step herself, slow and even, a bearer's pace.

"House Miravel will ask you for your own account after, in your own words, away from witnesses," she said. "Give them what you saw — no more and no less than you gave me here. You did it right the first time. Do it the same way with them listening."

Another step, and another, the body level between them.

"And walk as I walk. This is the last pace he has, and no one will hurry him again."

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren kept the bearing level and did not halt — a stop would be remembered as hesitation, and Halric had been owed none of that in life — but she slowed her answer to the pace of the steps, so that neither would be hurried.

"Plainly, then, in the words you will give them. Grief makes questions come twice; let them. That is what I am for."

A step. Another.

"It entered at the front of him, on the right side, just beneath the lowest rib — two fingers in from the soft of his flank. If you would know the place without doubting it: set your own hand where your ribs end and your stomach gives, on the right. That is where it landed. Every witness who says otherwise is remembering it from an angle, and angles lie in kindness."

She shifted her forearm; his head had slipped a fraction, and she brought it level before continuing.

"Where it ended is a different place, and the record will want both. The point traveled upward and inward, a hand's length. It finished high on the right, in the lung. The liver lies along that road, and the steel did not go beside it. The heart was never touched. It was the lung that took him — the liver bled, but it was the breath that failed, and the four he stood were the four he had. I counted the ones he spent."

"When he is laid out, before they wash him, I will put two fingers on the mark if you ask it. Seen is steadier than heard, and I would rather you carry a place than a sentence. I will show the witnesses the same, so the record holds a spot on the body and not only words about it."

The gate shadow reached them, and her voice came down once more.

"And if you meant where he fell, and not where the steel landed — on his left side, twenty paces back, at the seam of the drainage. The witnesses marked it. The stones keep it better than I can."

She squared her grip at the shoulders.

"We lay him on his back inside, head toward the house. Say the word to them about the washing, as I told you. Then the fingers, if you want them."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: The witnesses are silent and she is not finished. "All of it," I tell her. "How long he took, what he said, what it looked like at the end. The code says all of it and I'm asking for all of it."
rows.reply:
Auren did not answer at once, and the room had learned what that pause meant: not hesitation, but a thing being weighed on scales that took no shortcuts.
