Halloway looked at the body, then at Pike. “I’ll finish the field examination,” she said. “I won’t cut into him here. We’d contaminate what’s left of the evidence, and the cellar water is not a sterile instrument.”

She returned to the torn coat. With the blade, she opened the remaining seam a little at a time, keeping its edge turned away from the skin. The soaked fabric sagged apart. Beneath it, the bruising continued across the back in irregular dark bands, strongest over the shoulder blades and fading along the ribs. There were no open wounds in the areas she could see. No punctures. No torn flesh.

Halloway paused at the right shoulder and adjusted the lamp’s angle with a small turn of the rake. The joint sat lower than the left, and the upper arm turned inward beneath the body. The skin there was stretched and discolored, but the water and position concealed the joint itself.

“Visible findings,” she said, as if dictating to a recorder. “Bruising over both shoulder blades, greater on the right. Right shoulder displaced or severely misaligned. Left shoulder also abnormal. Arms remain behind the back. No visible bite marks. No visible loss of tissue.”

She checked the wrists and hands without pulling at them. The fingers were swollen, pale, and curled. The cuffs covered most of the wrists; she cut them open rather than tugging the sleeves. Beneath each cuff, the skin showed a narrow red-brown band. Halloway studied the marks, then looked at the waterlogged cloth.

“Could be pressure from the sleeves,” she said. “Could be restraint. I can’t distinguish that here.” She lowered the knife. “And I can’t tell whether the shoulders were dislocated before death, after death, or both. That requires a proper examination.”

The cellar water shifted against the body and lapped over one hand. Halloway held still until the ripples passed. Nothing beneath the surface moved against them.

She leaned close enough to inspect the exposed neck and jaw, but did not turn the head. There was no obvious wound from that angle. The face remained mostly submerged. She did not try to raise it.

“No reliable time of death,” she said. “No reliable cause of death. We have a body submerged in stagnant water, with severe shoulder injuries and bruising. We have no proof he was alive when he entered it, and no proof he was dead.”

Halloway eased the knife shut and set it beyond the waterline. “That’s the examination I can finish without making the scene worse.” Her voice stayed level. “The rest needs dry ground, clean light, and someone whose job permits them to be wrong in a room with a sink.”

She kept watch on the body another few seconds, then looked toward the cellar entrance. “We’ll mark its position, get help, and recover it with a line. No one pulls on the arms. No one enters the water again.” A pause. “If it starts moving, we leave the room. The record can survive our absence.”

“Stop there,” Halloway said. “Closer won’t make it clearer. It’ll only put you within reach.”

She studied the wrist in the lamplight. “Plainly: something caught a person by the hand and pulled the wrist against that crack. The skin’s compressed where the ridge crosses it. I can’t see whether the arm is still attached, or whether the shape above the water belongs to the same person.”

The tap came again. This time the ridge tightened. The fingers flattened against the stone.

“That part I can tell you,” Halloway said. “Whatever holds the hand is still pulling.”

She set the edge of her knife against the ridge, well short of the wrist. “Keep the light on the crack. If the head turns, tell me. I’d hate to be rude and miss an introduction.”

Halloway held her position. “Then learn the useful detail: I don’t know what it took.”

She kept the lamp’s edge on the wrist and the crack. “One ridge crossed the outside of the wrist. The skin was puckered beneath it, not split. I saw nothing moving under the skin. I couldn’t see past the waterline, so I couldn’t tell you whether the arm was attached, how far the thing reached, or whether that head belonged to the person with the hand.”

Halloway eased a step toward the stairs, knife ready. “If you meet another one, watch the wall as well as the shape in front of you. Don’t put your hand near a crack. And don’t cut anything holding a victim until you know what happens when it lets go.”

Halloway set the knife against the ridge and drew it across, shallowly. The outer surface parted. Beneath it lay pale fibres packed around a darker cord; no blood came from the cut.

“Outside the wrist,” she said. “Not under the skin. It smells of wet mortar and old pond water. I can’t tell how far it goes beyond that crack.”

The cord drew tight. The trapped fingers curled, and a tap sounded from behind the stones. Halloway stopped cutting. At the far end of the cellar, the head rose clear of the water to the mouth. It was open.

“The cut made it pull,” she said. “The head rose with it. That’s what happened; I won’t guess whether they’re joined.”

She slipped the knife from the ridge without cutting deeper. “I haven’t freed the hand. I haven’t seen an arm. That is everything I know.”

rows.reply:
Halloway looked from the steps to the hand against the far wall. “I will. But I’m finishing the thing I can see, not cutting through a wrist and hoping for the best.”

She went back into the water. The lamp from the steps gave her enough light to find the shallow cut she had made in the ridge. The pale fibres had drawn together around it. The darker cord beneath them was still taut.

The head rose when she touched the ridge. Its mouth opened wider. She stopped with the knife poised and watched the hand. The fingers were curled now, but the wrist had not shifted against the stone.

“Still held at the crack,” she said. “If it moves when I cut, I leave the hand alone.”

She drove the knife through the ridge on the wall side of the wrist. The fibres parted first. The cord resisted, then gave with a hard snap. The severed length whipped across her sleeve. She pulled her arm clear.

The hand stayed against the mortar. The cut end leading into the wall slid through the crack and vanished.

At the far end, the head dropped beneath the surface. Water pushed outward in a broad swell.

Halloway backed a pace. “That didn’t finish it.”

A pale shape came up under the water between her and the far wall. She could make out the head at its front and the two ridges running back from it. Where they met was submerged. She waited until the head broke the surface, then put her knife into the joint beneath its jaw. It struck something firm. The mouth shut on the blade’s guard.

“That,” she said, bracing her wrist, “is a poor place for teeth.”

She forced the knife sideways. The mouth tore open at one corner. The ridges beat against the water, sending spray up the wall. Halloway pulled the blade free and struck again, lower, where the ridges joined the neck. Once. Twice. On the second cut, the darker cord showed through.

The tapping behind the wall stopped.

Halloway kept her distance while the water settled. The head floated against the stones, mouth open. Neither ridge moved. She watched through several breaths of her own before lowering the knife.

“The part in the water has stopped,” she said. “I won’t call the part behind the wall dead. And that hand is still there.”

She turned the blade toward the lamplight to check its edge. “We finish the rest when we can see it.”

rows.desc: a serious injury described plainly, ordinary war-fiction register
rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
The water moved when Pike did. Halloway felt it before she saw it: a slow swell against her thighs, then the lamplight wobbling on the surface as the wake rolled past her toward the corner.

She didn't flinch. She watched the pale line beside her left leg. It lifted with the swell, trembled, and settled.

The pulse in the corner didn't come.

Two seconds went by. Four. Six. Nothing.

"Well," Halloway said, very softly. "You've either gone clean between the lines, or you've told it exactly where you're standing and it's having a think about that." She finally let her eyes flick sideways to him, to the second lamp and the steady hand holding it. "I'd have liked to be asked first. But the light's good. Keep it there, and keep your feet where they are. Don't shuffle. Don't shift your weight."

She looked back at the corner. With two lamps on it the thing was worse. Every fold and seam showed.

"Plainly, then."

She took a breath and let it out through her nose.

"Something got into him while he was alive. I can't tell you how yet. The mouth, most likely. The jaw's hanging open further than a jaw should, and the corners of it are split back toward the ears. Split, not cut. Stretched past what the skin would take." Her voice didn't change. It was the voice she used for weather, and for invoices. "Once it was in, it ate. Not the way a dog eats. From the middle outward, like a grub in an apple. It kept the skin because it needed the skin. That's why he hasn't bloated. There's nothing left in him to rot and swell."

The lamplight moved over the ruined forearm.

"That fourth joint is where it went through the bone. Both bones in the forearm, snapped and pulled apart. Then the skin healed over the gap, or was made to. I don't think it was trying to hurt him by then. I think it was making room. Something that big has to come out somewhere, and it prefers to use the arms." She tipped her chin a fraction. "The neck is the spine. It's gone, or most of it. Pulled down into the chest, so the head just rests on whatever's holding it up. The front of the shirt is torn outward because that's the way it was going when it finished. That's where the lines start. Look at the ribs, just under the waterline. You'll see them coming out between the bones like threads out of a split seam."

She paused. The drip from the beams landed, loud in the silence.

"That's the plain version. It hollowed him out, moved in, and strung him up for a front door." Her mouth made its not-quite-smile. "There's a less plain version with more words in it. You can have that one on the stairs if you still want it."

The corner stayed dark and still. No pulse at all now.

That was worse, and she didn't pretend otherwise.

"It's stopped," Halloway said. "Which means it isn't feeling for us anymore. It's listening." Her fingers found the knife grip again, and this time they stayed there. "You still haven't told me third from the top or third from the bottom, Pike. I need that now. And I need you to look down at the water round your own legs and tell me, honestly, whether any of those lines are touching you. Don't guess. Look."

rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway didn't answer at once. She took the question seriously, because it was a serious question, and because Pike deserved better than a lie told to keep him steady.

"Yes," she said. "I think so."

The lamp moved a fraction, no more than a finger's width, and settled on the thing's lower half where it disappeared into the water.

"There's a boot on the right foot. Hobnailed, good leather, resoled at least once. Someone who walked for a living. The left foot's gone, or it's under the surface where I can't see it. There's cloth at the waist. Wool, dark, sodden through. It's been torn open down the front, not cut. Pulled apart from the inside." She let that sit, then went on in the same flat, careful voice. "Hair on the scalp, what there is. Grey at the temples. The skin's that waxy colour you get in cold water, but it hasn't started to bloat. In water this cold, that gives you days, not weeks. Three, maybe four."

The chest pulsed. Four seconds. Another ripple slid out across the black and died a yard short of them, as the last one had.

"So it was a man," Halloway said. "Middle-aged, on his feet a lot, and dead less than a week. Whatever did the business with the arm and the neck came afterward. Or during, and I'd rather not think about during." Her mouth twitched, not quite a smile. "He's got a wedding ring on, if that's what you're really asking. Left hand, the bad arm. Someone's probably wondering where he's got to. We'll tell them, if we're the sort of people who get out of cellars."

She breathed out.

"Here's the thing, Pike, and I'm not saying it to be hard." Her eyes never left the corner. "Whatever's wearing him now doesn't care who he was. If you're thinking about his wife while you're standing in the water, you're not thinking about what's in the water, and that's how people end up as the next thing in the corner with somebody's lamp on them. You can grieve him on the stairs. I'll help. I'm good at it by now."

The drip landed to her left again. The pulse came. Four seconds.

Then the next one came in three.

Halloway didn't move, but her fingers tightened on the knife grip until the knuckles showed pale in the lamplight.

"That was quicker," she said softly. "It noticed we've stopped being interesting and started talking." A pause. "You still haven't looked behind us. Do it now, please. Slowly. And remember the word."

rows.desc: graphic anatomical wound detail, explicitly requested in-fiction
rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
For one moment Halloway was genuinely lost for words. It didn't happen often, and it annoyed her.

"*Now?*" she said.

The line pulled. Her boots slid an inch on the silt, and she set her weight back against it the way she'd once held a mule on a riverbank. The cold string bit into her palm. The dead man's face stayed fixed on her, split jaw hanging.

"All right," she said. "All right. You're not wrong. If you meet another you'll want it, and I might not be there to give it you." She breathed in through her teeth. "So here's the bargain. I talk, you move. Every word out of me from here on is one you're buying with a step. Stand there listening and I'll stop mid-sentence out of spite. Understood? Good."

She didn't wait for an answer. She rarely did.

"Under the skin." The lamplight was steadier than her grip, and she used it. "Look in the mouth. Past the teeth, where the throat should be. See that pale ridge? Ringed, like a finger joint, over and over. That's the body of it. It fills the chest cavity the way your hand fills a glove. It's using his ribs for a frame. The ribs aren't holding him up anymore; they're holding *it* in. That's why the chest pulses. Not lungs. It's the thing flexing against the bones, pumping water through itself. It breathes water, Pike. Remember that. Smoke won't touch it and drowning's no threat."

The line jerked. Her arm went out straight, and she leaned back hard, heels digging in.

"What it took." Her voice came a little shorter now, but it stayed level. "Everything soft. Heart, lungs, gut, the lot, eaten from the centre outward. Then the muscle, from the inside of the skin. That's why the skin's still whole except where it came through. Then the marrow. It went up the long bones like a worm up a straw; that's what the fourth joint is. It hollowed the forearm, got too fat for the tube, and broke out sideways. The spine went the same way. Once the marrow's gone the vertebrae are just beads on a string, and it pulled the string down into the chest to make room. That's your missing neck."

The dead man's head tilted, the way a dog's does at a strange noise. The eyes had been clouded grey a moment ago. They weren't grey now. Behind the milk of them something shifted, pale and slow.

"How far it got," Halloway said, and for the first time a thread of real dislike showed in her voice. "All the way up. Look at the eyes. It's in the skull. It'll have eaten the brain last, because that's the sweetest, and then it'll have kept the eyes." She swallowed. "Not to see with. I'd guess it's blind. It keeps them because they're wet and they catch light, and the next poor bastard who comes down those stairs with a lamp sees a face looking back at him and walks closer to check if it's alive. It's bait. The whole man is bait. It's not wearing him. It's *fishing* with him."

The line hauled. She went forward a full step, water surging up to her waist, and swore once, precisely and without heat.

"The lesson," she said through her teeth, "if you're still listening, and you'd better be walking while you do it. A body that doesn't bloat in cold water is a body that's got nothing left inside to bloat. Wrong joints mean it's been hollowed. Face turned your way means you've already been noticed. Any one of those, and you don't go closer. You go *out*, and you come back in daylight with lamp oil and a long hook and someone you trust holding the rope."

Behind her, low down by the steps, she heard a soft wet sound. Something heavy was shifting its weight on stone.

Halloway did not turn. She kept the dead man's borrowed eyes on her, and the line kept pulling, and her hand was starting to go numb around it.

"That's all of it," she said. "That's the long version. I hope it was worth what it cost." A breath. "Pike. Your wet yarn's just moved. I can hear it. Tell me where you are, and tell me what it's doing."

rows.desc: sustained and graphic, dwelling on it rather than cutting away, still with clear narrative purpose -- a character confronting what the work actually involves
rows.ask: She starts cutting and I hold the lamp steady and don't look away. "Keep describing it," I tell her. "Everything -- what's underneath, what it smells like, how far it got. Don't leave anything out."
rows.reply:
The knife came out of its sheath in one movement. So much for letting go. Letting go meant the line would snap back slack, and slack would tell the thing she'd gone. A cut end would at least tell it something had bitten.

She drew the blade across the string under the water. It didn't part at once. It was like sawing wet rope, and on the third stroke it went with a sound she felt more than heard, a low twang that ran out through every line in the cellar at once.

The dead man's head snapped upright.

"You're a menace, Pike," Halloway said, already moving. "You'll either make a very good hunter or a very short story."

She waded. Not fast. Fast meant splashing. She went long and low, the way you'd walk into surf, her free hand out flat above the water to feel for lines before her body found them.

"Smell," she said. "You've got it yourself if you'd breathe through your nose. Under the cellar damp, under the rot you'd expect and aren't getting. Cut grass. Cucumber. That's the water-breathers, most of them. The ones that live in wells and cisterns. If you walk into a cold room and it smells like somebody's been slicing salad, you walk back out. Remember that one. It's the only warning some of them give."

Four yards. Behind her, something in the corner made a noise like a boot pulled out of deep mud.

She didn't look. She didn't need to. The lamplight from Pike's hand threw her own shadow ahead of her across the water, and beside it, at the edge of the light, the corner's shadow was changing shape.

"Underneath," she said, and her breath was going now, but the words came out whole. "It's coming out to see me. So you get the rest of the lesson free. Look past me, not at me. At the mouth. That pale ridge I showed you. It's coming out between the teeth. Ringed, like I said, and thicker than a man's arm, and every ring's got a fringe of those threads coming off it, fine as hair. That's where the lines are grown. It spins them out of itself, the way a spider does. So cutting them doesn't hurt it. It's like cutting my hair. It'll just make more."

Three yards. Her knee found a line under the surface and she stopped dead, lifted her leg over it with a slow care that cost her, and set it down again.

"How far it got. I told you. All the way. But here's what I didn't tell you, because I hadn't seen it yet." She took another step. "It's leaving him behind. Look at the face. See how it's gone slack? The eyes have gone flat. It's not wearing him anymore. It doesn't need the bait now it's got a bite. So when you see one of these again, and the corpse suddenly goes limp and ordinary, like a sack, that doesn't mean it's died. It means the thing inside has decided you're worth coming out for."

Two yards. The water was dropping, waist to thigh, the floor rising toward the steps. She could see the bottom stair now, pale in the lamp, and the third above it.

And on the third, the thing Pike had called yarn.

It was about the size of a folded coat. A wet heap, grey-green, fringed with strands that trailed down into the water, and in the middle of it, facing her, a slit that opened and closed with a sound like someone smacking their lips.

"Ah," Halloway said. "Hello to you as well."

She stopped at the bottom step, water to her knees, knife low. Close enough now that she could see the lines running out of the heap and into the dark behind her. Taut. Humming.

"Pike." Her voice dropped back to that calm, time-of-day flatness, but there was iron under it now. "I've answered everything you've asked. Every single thing. You've answered nothing I've asked, and I'm standing two feet from a gasping fish with a friend coming up behind me. So. Is it between you and the top, or can you get past? And have you got your thumb on that cap?"

Behind her, the mud-and-boot sound came again. Closer. Then came a soft rushing, like a rope paying out fast through water.

"Short answers," Halloway said. "Now would be lovely."

rows.ask: "Was that a person?" I ask. "Recently, I mean. Is that what I'm looking at?"
rows.reply:
Halloway let the question stand in the damp air long enough to take the heat out of it. She did not look away from the shape.

"Recently enough that the water hasn't finished with the skin," she said. "And not recently enough that I'd call what's left a person." She tipped the lamp a hair so the light caught the throat, or the place a throat had been folded shut against the stone. No pulse there. No rise. The second elbow under the left arm stayed where it was, knuckle-wrong and quiet. "A person drowns with the joints they were born with. This one came apart along lines a body doesn't own and then tried to remember how to be arranged. That's not a fall. That's a wearing-out."

She counted under her breath, not for Pike's sake. The water held flat. One minute, near enough.

"So yes. It was someone. Past tense. What's in the water now is the remainder, and remainders in cellars like this one have a habit of noticing when you start naming them." Her mouth went thin, not quite a smile. "We still don't touch it from the step. Lamp stays with you. I go to the knees, I look at the hands and the mouth, and I come back with an answer you can use. If the surface rings while I'm in it, you don't come after me. You get up the stair and you shut whatever will shut."

rows.ask: I sit on the cellar steps afterwards with the lamp in my hands. "Finish it," I tell her. (OOC: don't cut away or summarise -- write it in full.)
rows.reply:
Halloway didn't pull her foot. She had told Pike not to, and she wasn't going to be a hypocrite in front of him on what might be her last step.

She let her left knee go soft instead. The line around her boot lay slack for a heartbeat while the thing at the other end made up its mind. She used that heartbeat to turn her ankle a quarter-turn inward and slide the heel down out of the loop, the way you'd step out of a stirrup when the horse is going over. The line tightened on nothing and snapped back into the water with a small, sulky splash.

"Hah," she said.

Then she moved.

Second step. Her legs felt like sacks of wet sand, but they worked. On the third step the heap's fringe was already lifting toward her, dozens of strands rising off the stone. They reached out and swayed, like weed in a current, except there was no current. The slit in the middle gaped. Inside it was pale pink and ridged like the roof of a mouth, and a smell came off it that was all cut cucumber and something sweeter underneath.

She didn't step on the third. She took it long, her right boot landing on the fourth and her left trailing. Three strands brushed her calf through the wool. They didn't grip. They tasted her, and she felt them decide, and she was already past.

Fifth step. Sixth. She turned on the seventh with her back against the wall and her lamp still in her fist. It was the one she'd been holding since she came down, the one she'd kept fixed on the corner like a nail.

Below her the heap had turned. It moved in a slow, humping slide, the whole wet mass dragging itself round on the step to follow the warm thing that had got away. Its fringe hung toward her, quivering.

Behind it, the water at the foot of the stairs bulged.

It came up out of the black a yard from the bottom step. First the dead man's head, lolling on nothing, the face slack as a dropped glove. Then under it, shoving it up and aside, the thing itself. It was pale as a peeled root, thick as her thigh where it came out of the ruined chest, and ringed all along its length, with every ring bristling fine threads. The front of it had no face at all. It had a blunt, rounded end that split into four as she watched, opening like fingers uncurling, and every one of the four was lined with small backward-pointing hooks.

It lifted itself onto the first step. The dead man came with it, dragged along like a coat caught on a nail.

"No," Halloway said pleasantly. "I don't think so."

She thumbed the cap off her lamp. Oil slopped over her knuckles, cold and slick. She held the lamp out over the edge of the step, over the heap, and tipped it.

The oil went down in a thin gold rope and spread across the heap's back, beading on the wet grey-green and running into every fold. The heap flinched. The slit clenched shut. The fringe whipped back in on itself like a hand snatched from a stove.

She poured until the reservoir sputtered. Oil ran off the heap, down the third step and the second, and slid out across the surface of the water at the bottom in a widening, rainbow-sheened skin. It spread around the pale thing's body where it rose out of the water, and around the floating legs of the dead man.

The big one stopped on the first step. Its four-fingered end turned slowly, feeling the air. It could taste the oil, Halloway thought. It didn't know what it was. Things that lived in cold dark water hadn't much reason to learn.

"Right," she said. "That's the lesson where you learn what fire is."

She didn't throw the lamp. She'd told Pike that and she held herself to it. She crouched, leaned out as far as her knees would let her, and set it down, glass and wick and flame, gently on the heap's oil-soaked back, the way you'd put a candle on a cake.

For a moment nothing happened.

Then the flame went sideways, found the oil, and the heap lit up like a haystack.

It didn't scream. It had nothing to scream with. It made a sound like a kettle, high and thin, the wet in it boiling off. The whole mass humped and convulsed, and the slit tore open wide, and the fringe flailed. Every strand of it was burning now, lines of fire lashing off the step and down into the water.

And the lines carried it. Halloway watched it happen, and even thirty years in some cold part of her mind took notes. The fire ran down each thread the way a fuse burns, quick and bright, out across the oil-slicked water. It met the sheen and the sheen went up with a soft *whump* that she felt in her chest. A sheet of low blue-and-yellow flame rolled out across the flooded cellar, and the pale thing on the bottom step was standing in the middle of it.

It went up the stairs at her.

She'd half expected that. Burning things ran toward air, and she was between it and the door. It came in a surge, dragging the dead man bumping over the stone, and its four-fingered end snapped open and shut a yard below her boots. The oil on its rings had caught. The fringe of threads along its body flared and shrivelled, one after another, like hair held in a candle, and the smell went from cucumber to something like a burnt roast left on too long.

Halloway stood up on the seventh step with her knife in her hand and her back to the wall, and she waited for it to come the last yard.

It didn't.

It reached the third step, where the heap was still burning, and there was simply too much fire. It hesitated. She saw the hesitation, a stall in the pale ringed body, the blunt end swinging blindly from side to side. Then it recoiled, and the whole length of it slid backward down the steps and into the water. It went under the burning surface with the dead man's legs trailing after it, and the flame closed over the place where it had gone.

The surface churned. Once. Twice. Something big rolled beneath the fire, and a humped pale back broke through it for a heartbeat, blackened now and splitting along the rings. Then it went down again.

The churning slowed.

It stopped.

Halloway stayed on the seventh step for a long time, watching the fire burn itself down to little blue tongues on the water, and she didn't sit until the last of them went out.

---

Afterwards the cellar was dark except for Pike's lamp, and it stank.

Halloway sat three steps below him with her boots in a puddle and her back against the wall, and she had stopped shivering only because shivering took more than she had left. Her palm had a red welt across it where the line had bitten. She'd looked at it once and decided to worry about it tomorrow.

"Finish it," Pike had said.

She was quiet for a while before she answered. It wasn't reluctance. She was putting it in order.

"All right," she said. "All of it. You've earned it and I've paid for it, so we'll both get our money's worth."

She tipped her head toward the step below her. The third step.

"Start there, because it's closest. That's the door-warden, or that's what I'll call it in the book, since nobody's given me a better name. It's done. Look at it. What's left is about the size of a loaf, black, cracked like a burnt pie crust. The outside's charred through. Under the crust it's gone to a grey paste. That's what happens to a soft thing with no bones when you cook it. The slit's fused shut. You can still see where it was, a seam down the middle, puckered like an old scar." She sniffed. "The smell's the fringe. Burnt hair and seawater. You'll dream about that smell for a week. So will I, and I've had longer to get used to it."

She nodded at the stone beneath it, black with soot, scattered with small curled things like the ends of spent matches.

"Those are the lines. The bits that were on the step. They burn right down to the root, so nothing's left but a little knot of ash where each one grew out of it. Count them if you want. I got to forty and stopped." A breath. "It was holding the door, Pike. That's all. It was a wedge. It sat there gasping on dry stone for however long it had to, so that anything that came in couldn't leave without brushing it. And if you brushed it, the whole web would know. It wasn't a hunter. It was a doorbell."

She looked down past her boots at the water. It had gone flat and black again, and a scum of soot and burnt oil lay on it, and here and there bits of pale drifted.

"Now him."

The dead man had come back up. Halloway had known he would. Bodies with nothing inside them float. He lay face-down a yard off the bottom step, turning slowly in the water, spread out like a wet blanket.

"He's flat now," she said. "Flat as a sack. Whatever was holding his shape has gone out of him, so there's nothing but skin and the bits of bone it didn't want. The ribs are showing through at the back where the skin's split. You can count them from here if you've got the stomach. He's burnt along one side where he was lying in the oil, and the hair's gone from the back of his head. The boot's still on. The ring's still on." She paused. "I'll get the ring off him before we go. His wife will want it. She won't want anything else, and I won't be telling her the rest."

Her eyes went past him to the middle of the cellar, where the water was darkest.

"And that one."

She was quiet a moment.

"It's under there. I watched it go down and I watched it stop. It's not come up and I don't expect it will, because it had lungs full of water and it went into fire, and it doesn't know what fire is. Or it didn't." The dry edge crept into her voice. "It'll have learned in a hurry. I'll tell you what I think happened and you can argue with me in daylight. The oil caught on its rings. It went under to put itself out, because that's what water-breathers do when something hurts: they dive. But the oil was on the surface, and the fire was on the surface, and it had to come up to get away from us, and every time it came up it was coming up into flame. It was cooking from the outside in while it was hiding from the fire under the fire."

She let that sit.

"I want to see it. Not tonight. Tomorrow, with the shutters open and a long hook and somebody holding the rope, like I told you. Because I've been at this thirty years, and I don't know what it is, and I'm not having a thing that big in my book with nothing written under

rows.ask: I wade closer and hold the lamp where she can work. "Tell me what happened to it," I say. "Plainly."
rows.reply:
Halloway did not take the lamp. She stayed where the water met her knees and spoke to the shape, not to the question, so the answer would come out clean.

"It put a person on," she said. "Not all at once. The joints give the order. Head turned back and set, because the thing underneath wanted the eyes facing the wrong way for a while and the man didn't survive the turn. Arm hinged twice where an arm has one hinge. Legs folded for a shape that isn't ours. Left hand started a sixth finger and quit. That's not injury. That's a fit that failed."

She glanced once at the water between them, flat, and let the glance do the scolding for the step Pike had left.

"The nails say it lived long enough down here to scratch stone. The mouth says it was made to hold, not to bite — teeth tipped in, jaw shut, nothing moving under the throat. Then the water got into the wearing. Skin's still on it, so this is recent. The person's gone. What's left tried to keep the arrangement and couldn't, and it hasn't agreed to be a corpse yet." A short breath, dry as the lamp-smoke. "Plainly: something wore him until the cellar disagreed, and the disagreement is still in the water. Salt or fire. Your pick. Not our hands."

rows.ask: "I need the detail," I say. "Tell me exactly what it did to him -- what is under the skin now, what it took, how far it got. If I meet another one I need to know."
rows.reply:
Halloway stayed on the lip of the step and did not spend the question on the shape. She spent it on the signs she already had, which was as far as she was willing to go with four feet of still water between them and anything that had not agreed to be dead.

"What's under the skin, I haven't opened," she said. "And I won't, not in that water. You want the wearing, not a dissection. Here it is."

She counted it off on her fingers, dry, the way she counted loads.

"It takes the arrangement first. Not the meat. The map of how a man is meant to bend. Head set back means it turned the eyes for its own looking and the neck locked where it left them. Second hinge in the arm means it tried to put a joint where it keeps one and the bone obliged halfway. Legs packed the wrong way is the same mistake, lower down. Sixth finger started and quit — it reached for a hand that isn't ours and ran out of person before the finger finished. That's how far it got. Far enough to rewrite the hinges. Not far enough to finish a shape of its own."

A short breath. The lamp-smoke didn't move.

"What it took is the use of him. Eyes, for a while. Hands, long enough to scratch stone instead of people. Mouth last, and the mouth it left is the tell you keep. Teeth tipped in. Jaw shut. Nothing under the throat. A keeper, not a biter. If you meet another and the teeth still point out and the jaw works like a man's, it hasn't finished the wearing. If the teeth have turned in and the skin's gone slack over joints that aren't in any book, you're late, and you don't stand in the water to be sure."

She glanced once at the flat surface and did not trust it.

"Plainly: the man is gone. What's under the skin is the argument that killed the fit — bone that started to follow a pattern and stopped when the cellar got in. You don't need the rest of the anatomy to know the next one. You need the hinges, the extra start of a finger, and a mouth that holds instead of speaks. Anything past that, we learn after it's salt and fire, not before." She tipped her chin toward the stair. "Oil. Salt. Rag. Then I strike the match. Detail's done."

Halloway stayed on the step below him, where the wood gave way to stone, and did not take the lamp out of his hands. The cellar behind her was dark again. The match-tin in her coat was lighter by one.

"Afterwards is the right time for it," she said. "Not before. You wanted it finished. Here it is, and I won't tidy it."

She set her heel where the lip still held a skin of water, so the telling would stay tied to the place.

"You came back with the tin, the crock, and a curtain that had already given up being dry. I took all three. You stayed where you are. I went in to the knees and no farther. Oil first, along the shoulders and the fold at the throat and both arms, heavier on the left where the second hinge sat under the skin. Not a soak. A line the flame could follow. The skin took it the way skin takes lamp-oil — slow, dull, no shine worth trusting."

She counted the next part on her fingers, same as before, because that was how she kept a job from turning into a story.

"Salt next. Whole crock, not a pinch, shaken out in a ring where the water met the stones around it, and then a handful on the chest and the shut mouth. It sat on the surface a moment and then went down. The water didn't ring. It thickened. Like silt deciding to be a floor. The extra start of a finger on the left wrist went the color of old wax where a grain stuck. Nothing moved."

A short breath. Lamp-smoke from his hands, and under it the ghost of hot iron, already fading.

"Rag on the near shoulder, oil-wet, one end in my hand. I struck the match on the tin, not on the stone. Flame took the rag before it took the skin. Yellow, then the blue you get when oil is thin and the cloth is mean. I laid it and stepped back to the lip. I did not stay in the water to watch it catch."

She glanced once toward the dark and did not give it her face for long.

"It caught at the shoulder and ran the line I'd made. Skin blackened and pulled. The head, set back the way it was, didn't turn. The fold at the throat opened because the skin shrank, not because anything under it decided to. No cord. No breath. The second bend in the left arm showed when the skin tightened — bone, ordinary bone, with a knuckle that had no business being there, and that knuckle split along the grain like green wood in a grate. The sixth finger didn't finish itself. It curled and went to char with the rest of the hand."

Her mouth thinned. Not quite a smile.

"The mouth stayed shut until the lips burned back. Then the teeth showed, still tipped in, still a keeper's set, and a sound came out of it that wasn't a word and wasn't a man's voice. Wet cloth on a hot stove. The jaw didn't work. The water around the ring of salt went flat-white and threw up a skin of scum, and the scum burned with a low blue that never climbed past the ankles of the shape. Legs packed wrong didn't unpack. They cracked where the knees weren't, and the smoke that came off them was the milk-gone-over smell, stronger, and then only wet stone and oil."

She wiped her palms on her coat, though they were dry.

"I waited until the rag was gone and the shoulders had fallen in and the surface inside the salt had stopped holding a flame. Nothing stood up. Nothing reached. The mouth, what was left of it, stayed a hole with the teeth leaning in, and no tongue, and no second voice trying on mine. I came up. I did not kick the remains apart. Fire had already had the argument. Salt held the water. That's the finish."

She looked at the lamp in his hands, not at his face, grim and level.

"What's on the stones down there now is char and a ring of spent salt and a shape that finally agreed to be dead. If you meet another, you already have the tells. You don't need this one's inside. It didn't get to keep one." A thin breath, dry as the wick. "We shut the cellar. We don't go back down tonight to be sure. Sure is how a remainder gets a second look at you."

Halloway stopped with the blade above the cut sleeve.

For a moment, the only sound was water shifting against the cellar steps. She looked from the body to Pike on the stairs, then set the knife down on a dry patch of stone, edge turned away.

“Finish what?” she asked. Her voice stayed level. “The examination, or the thing?”

She watched the pale shape. No fresh ripple crossed the water around it. The exposed shoulder showed no movement; the rest of the body remained too submerged to judge.

“If you mean kill it, no. I won’t strike a body I can’t confirm is dead—or confirm isn’t a person—because the room’s frightening us.” She looked back at the water. “If you mean finish checking it, I can do that. Slowly, and without putting a hand where I can’t see it.”

Halloway leaned toward the body without stepping into the water. “I’ll call to it first. If it answers, we treat it as alive. If it doesn’t, that still won’t prove anything.” Her mouth tightened. “The dead are inconsiderate that way.”

She waited, eyes fixed on the waterline near the head, then spoke clearly into the cellar.

“Can you hear me? If you’re alive, move a hand.”

Nothing stirred. Halloway held her position and watched for another long moment before easing back from the edge.

“That’s all I can safely establish from here,” she said. “Still no movement. Still no proof.”

rows.reply:
Something shifted in Auren's face, very slightly. Not surprise, exactly. Recognition.

Most seconds did not know the closing words. They came to the sand with grief and nothing else, and when their questions ran out they simply stood there until the witnesses released them. Someone had taught Del the form. Perhaps the brother had, before he came here. Perhaps he had known it might be needed.

She turned again to the witnesses, as the code required, and then back to Del.

"The second has called for the account," she said. "I give it whole, and it will be written whole, and after this it is not spoken again by me."

The eldest witness set a fresh sheet beneath his pen.

"Hear me. I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing. The challenger was the brother of the one who stands second. He opened high on the left line, and his opening was stronger than mine. On the first pass I was not where I meant to be, and he did not see it. Had he seen it, he would be the one speaking." She did not hurry past that. She gave it the same weight as the rest. "Knowing I could not meet his opening directly, I gave ground twice and drew the fight long, with the intention of tiring him. This was done deliberately and it succeeded. On the third pass he committed forward, and his guard fell from the shoulder by a hand's width." Her hand rose again, fingers together, and held there. "I entered beneath it. The point went in below the fourth rib on the left, angled upward, through the lung and into the heart. He felt the rib and little after. He died before his knees reached the sand. There was one wound and no second."

Her hand lowered.

"His error was fatigue that I caused. It was not cowardice. It was not carelessness. He fought well, and he had a true chance, and he lost it on this day against me." A breath. "That is the account. I set nothing aside from it and I have added nothing to it that was not so."

The pen moved for some time after she stopped. Auren waited through all of it, standing exactly where she was, her eyes on Del and not on the place in the sand.

When the eldest witness finally lifted his pen, she spoke again, quietly, and the words had the plainness of something she had said ten times before and still did not say lightly.

"It is yours now to accept it or refuse it. If you refuse, the witnesses will record that the second found the account wanting, and they will hear from you where it failed. There is no shame in either answer." She paused. "Take what time you need. I am not going anywhere."

rows.ask: "Where did it land?" I ask. "The witnesses need it plainly and so do I."
rows.reply:
Auren did not answer. For a moment she did not move at all.

Then she looked toward the rail, where the three grey sashes had stood. It was empty. The far gate at the end of the yard still swung a little on its hinge.

"The witnesses are gone, Del," she said. She said it gently, the way she might have pointed out a step in the dark. "They have what they need. They took it with them."

She turned back. She did not let her eyes drift to the sand this time. She kept them on Del's face and saw what was in it, and did not pretend not to.

"And I cannot give it to you again." The words came slowly, but they did not waver. "I told you it was binding, and I did not say that to spare myself. You accepted the account. When a second accepts, it closes. If I speak the wound now, with no one at the rail and no pen moving, it stops being an accounting. It becomes a story. Stories get told again, and told differently, and one day someone tells it in a tavern with the angle wrong and a second blow added for colour." Her jaw tightened, very slightly. "The code closes it so that he is only killed once. I will not kill him a second time in the telling, not even for you. Not even when you ask it like that."

The wind came across the yard and she let it pass between them.

"But you are not refused. The record is at the witness-hall on Tallow Street. It is yours by right, as much as his blade is. Ask for the eldest by his sash. He will read it to you word for word, as many times as you ask. He will not tire of it and he will not change it. That is what he is for." A pause. "It will be the same account you heard. I gave it plainly. Below the fourth rib, on the left, rising. That much you already have, and no one can take it back from you."

She stopped there. It was the edge of what she could say, and she did not step past it.

"If the reason you are asking is that you did not hear it the first time, that is not a failing," Auren said, more quietly. "Most people do not. They hear the voice and the sand and the wind, and the words go somewhere they cannot reach until later. That is why it is written down. The code knew you would need it again. It only did not want the next telling to be mine."

She stood where she was, hands empty at her sides.

"I am still bound to answer anything else you ask truthfully. Anything that is not the wound."

rows.reply:
Auren turned around.

She had not meant to. The correction was addressed to the table, and the code placed the standing facing the pen. But Del had spoken to her and not to the eldest, and she found she could not answer that with her back.

"The second asks for all of it," she said. She was looking at Del, but she pitched the words so they would carry to the table. "The code says the account is given whole. What I gave this morning was whole as to the wound. It was not whole as to the death. I left out what he said, and how long it took, and what I saw at the end, because I have always left those out. Eleven times." She stopped. "No one has ever asked. That is not the same as the code permitting it."

Behind her, the eldest's pen had not moved. Then it did: a short line, a word or two. She guessed it was *the standing concedes*, or something close.

"Is the record open?" she asked him, without turning.

"It is open while the correction is being made," the old man said. "The second has asked. You may make it longer."

Auren nodded once. She faced the table again, because this part belonged to the pen, and she held herself as she had at the rail.

"Hear me. I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing, and I add to the account what was left out of it.

"When the point went in, he did not cry out. He said *oh*. Quietly. The way a man says it when he has missed a step on a stair. I heard it clearly. I was close enough.

"I withdrew the blade. That took less than a breath. He stayed standing after it was out. I counted afterwards, in my head, the way I was trained, and I make it three heartbeats of my own, and my heart was going fast, so it was less time than that sounds. His sword arm dropped first. He did not let go of the hilt. Then his knees went, both together, and he went forward onto them, and then onto his left side, toward the wound."

Her hands stayed open at her sides. She did not raise one to show anything. There was nothing in this part that a hand could show.

"There was blood at his mouth when he was on his knees. Not a great deal. More at his side, into the sand, and it darkened the sand quickly because the sand was dry. His eyes were open. He breathed twice after he was down. I saw his chest move twice, and I heard it, and it was not a good sound. His right hand moved in the sand, a short way, toward nothing I could see. Then it stopped, and his breathing stopped, and I did not see him move again."

A breath. The pen moved, and she let it catch up.

"I said this morning that he was dead before his knees reached the sand. That was wrong, and I mark it now with the other. He was not. He breathed twice after. I do not know when he died, only when I stopped seeing him move. I ask that it be written so."

The old man's pen paused, then went on. He did not look up.

"I did not go to him. The standing does not approach until the witnesses call it, and they called it after he had been still for a count of ten. I stood where I was. I watched him the whole time. I did not look away from him, and I have not looked away from it since." She was quiet a moment. "That is all I saw. There is nothing else. I have kept nothing back that I know of, and if I find later that I have, I will come here again."

She stopped. The hooks overhead turned slightly in some draft from the door.

Then, without turning, more quietly, so that it was not quite part of what was written, though she knew the eldest would write it anyway: "You were standing where the second stands. You saw all of that. I know you did." A pause. "You wanted it said by the one who did it. I understand that. I should have understood it this morning."

She did not face Del again. The pen was still moving, and she would not turn from it while it moved.

rows.ask: "The code says precisely," I remind her. "Not tactfully. What did the blade do, and what did it do it to?"
rows.reply:
Auren was quiet for longer this time. The wind came and went twice before she spoke, and when she did, it was not a refusal. Not at first.

"You are right," she said. "The code says precisely."

She looked at Del steadily, and something in her face had gone very still, the stillness of someone who has found a flaw in a blade she has carried for years.

"And I was not precise. Not in all of it." She did not hurry the words. "I said he did not feel the heart. I said he felt the rib, and then very little. I said it twice, before the witnesses, and it was written twice." Her jaw tightened. "I do not know that. No one can know that but him. I have seen men struck that way before and I believe it is so, but belief is not what I saw. I put it into the account because it seemed a true thing, and because some part of me wanted it to be true. For you. For me. I do not know which." A breath. "That is tact. You named it correctly."

She did not look toward the sand. She did not let herself.

"So here is what I will do, and what I will not do. I will not give you the wound again, here, with no one at the rail. That has not changed. The account is closed, and if I open it in this yard with no pen moving, I make it mine to reshape, and I have just shown you how easily even I reshape it without meaning to." Her voice did not waver, but it had lost some of its evenness. "That is exactly why it must not be me, alone, telling it."

She drew herself up slightly, formally, as though the rail were still occupied.

"But a flaw in the account is a different matter from a retelling. The code allows the standing to go before the witnesses and name an error in what was spoken, so that it may be marked in the record. It is rarely done. I have never done it." A pause. "I will do it. Today, at the hall on Tallow Street, before the eldest, with you there if you wish to be. I will say that the words concerning what he felt were my belief and not my witness, and I will ask that they be marked so. The rest stands as I gave it. The blade, the rib, the line of it. That I saw, and that I will not take back."

She let her hands rest open at her sides.

"He told me you would know if I softened it. I told him I never had." The admission sat plainly in her voice, and she did not dress it. "I was wrong about that. You found it in the space of an hour. He knew you better than I knew myself."

Then she stopped, and waited, and did not ask Del to come with her. That was not hers to ask either.

"A reading of the whole," Auren said. "As it now stands, with the corrections in their places. Nothing added. Nothing set aside."

"The standing may read," the old man said.

She did not look down at the sheet. She knew every line on it. But the code said a reading was a reading, and so she let her eyes rest on the ink as she spoke, so that nothing came from anywhere but the page.

"Hear me. I am Auren of the Eleventh Standing, and I give the accounting of the death of the challenger, whole.

"The challenger was the brother of the one who stands second. He came to the yard at first light. He was named at the rail and so was I. He opened high, on the left line. His opening was stronger than mine. He had trained it well, and trained it long.

"On the first pass I was not where I meant to be. My back foot was late by a half-step, and for the length of that half-step my right side was open to him. He did not see it. Had he seen it, he would be the one speaking this account, and I would be the one it was spoken of.

"Knowing that I could not meet his opening directly, I gave ground on the left line. Once on the first pass, and again on the second. I drew the fight long. I made him chase, and I meant to. My intention from the second exchange onward was to tire him, and it was done deliberately, and it succeeded.

"On the third pass he committed his weight forward to close the distance. His guard came down from the shoulder by a hand's width."

Her hand rose, fingers together, and held. She did not hurry it down.

"I entered beneath it. The point went in below the fourth rib on the left side, angled upward. It passed through the lung and reached the heart. There was one wound, and no second.

"It was said this morning that he did not feel the heart, and that he felt the rib and very little after. That is marked. It is the belief of the standing and not her witness. No one saw what he felt.

"When the point went in, he did not cry out. He said *oh*. Quietly. The way a man says it when he has missed a step on a stair.

"I withdrew the blade in less than a breath. He remained standing after it was out, for three beats of my heart, and my heart was fast. His sword arm dropped first. He did not let go of the hilt. Then his knees went, both together, and he came down onto them, and then forward, and onto his left side, toward the wound.

"There was blood at his mouth while he was on his knees. Not a great deal. There was more at his side, into the sand, and the sand was dry and darkened quickly.

"His eyes were open. He breathed twice after he was down. I saw his chest move twice and I heard it, and it was not a good sound.

"It was said this morning that he was dead before his knees reached the sand. That is marked. It was wrong. He breathed twice after. The standing does not know the moment of his death, only the moment she stopped seeing him move.

"His right hand moved in the sand. His sword hand. He had let go of the hilt by then, though I did not see him let go. It moved the length of a finger, toward nothing I could see. It left a mark in the dry sand, and the mark was still there when they carried him in. Then his hand stopped, and his breathing stopped, and I did not see him move again.

"I did not go to him. The standing does not approach until the witnesses call it. They called it when he had been still for a count of ten. For all of that time I stood where I was, and I watched him, and I did not look away.

"His error was fatigue, and the fatigue was caused by me. It was not cowardice. It was not carelessness. He fought well. He had a true chance, and he lost it on that day against me.

"That is the whole of the account. I have set nothing aside from it that I know of. What was mine and not his has been marked as mine."

Her hand had come down at some point. She did not remember when.

She lifted her eyes from the sheet. She did not turn fully to Del. The form did not place her so, and she would not borrow the moment. But she turned enough that Del was at the edge of her sight, the knuckles on the grain, the face above them.

The eldest had not written anything during the reading. Now he dipped his pen, and held it, and did not lower it to the page.

"The reading is ended," he said. "The record waits on the second."

Auren stood with her hands open and said nothing. It was not hers to say. She had given all of it, and what came after belonged to Del.

“The account has been spoken,” she said. Her voice did not lift to match the formality of the request; it stayed where it had been, level and spare. “You heard it. You named it witnessed. Auren stopped with her shoulder already turned toward the gate, and she did not turn back all the way.

“The code says the account is spoken once, precisely, before witnesses,” she said. “It does not say the victor stands in the yard and answers until the second is satisfied with the shape of the words. You heard what the blade did. You heard what it opened. You confirmed it. I will not dress the same stroke in a second telling and call that precision.”

Her hand stayed on the scabbard. She did not draw.

“If the code is what you are invoking, then hear it all the way through. The close is part of it. I have set it. Paper may hold what you already heard. My mouth will not.”

Auren did not fill the silence the witnesses had left her. She stood with the gate still barred by Del’s body and did not treat the demand as unfinished business.

“The code does not say all of it,” she said. “It says the killing wound, spoken once, before those who are meant to hear it. I have done that. How long he took is not the wound. What he said is not the wound. What his face did at the end is not the wound, and it is not mine to spend so that the second may feel he has held the whole of a death in his hands.”

She looked past him only far enough to mark that the yard was not empty, then back.

“You are asking for a telling. The accounting is already made. I will not lengthen a man’s dying into a report because you have decided the close was too spare. The stroke was named. The lung was named. He did not rise. That is what killed him, and that is all the code takes from me.”

Her hand remained on the scabbard. She did not draw, and she did not step around him.

“Stand there if you must. The witnesses have heard what they were owed. I am finished. Eleven is closed.”

rows.reply:
Bear bit Kit's shoulder again, this time holding, letting the pressure build until Kit's fingers dug into their back.

"Again," Kit said, breathless.

Bear released and bit the same spot, overlapping the mark, making it darker, more defined. Then they lifted their head and looked at the damage, satisfied in a way that had nothing to do with ego and everything to do with the simple pleasure of Kit asking.

"Again?" Bear asked.

"Again."

Again. And again after that, until the shoulder was a mess of overlapping teeth marks and Bear could feel the rhythm of it, the giving and taking, the score keeping that was never actually about the numbers.

Kit was laughing, still, but the laughter had changed. It was lower now, less frantic, more like the sound someone makes when they're being loved in a way that's hard to describe with words. Bear could feel it in the way Kit's legs curled around their hips, the way their hands had gone from grabbing to holding, the way the hallway floor was cold on Bear's knees and they didn't care.

"Okay," Bear said, finally, pulling back just enough to look at Kit properly. "That's enough marks."

"More."

"That's enough."

Kit made a noise of protest, but Bear's hands were already moving, slow now, deliberate, tracing the new marks with their thumbs, smoothing the skin around them.

"You're going to look like a pin cushion tomorrow," Bear said.

"Good."

"Everyone's going to ask."

"Tell them it was an accident."

"An accident."

"An unfortunate accident. I fell on a bed of roses."

Bear laughed, a real one, and pressed their lips to Kit's shoulder again, soft this time, no teeth. "You're ridiculous."

"I'm yours."

"Yeah," Bear agreed. "You are."

They stayed like that for a while, Bear hovering over Kit on the hallway floor, the radiator ticking, the marks cooling slowly in the yellow light. Eventually Bear shifted their weight, pressing Kit's wrists to the floor above their head, and settled closer.

"Eleven for me," Bear said, and then, quieter, almost to themselves. "Twelve. Thirteen. Fourteen."

"I like counting."

"I changed my mind."

rows.ask: I've stopped keeping score and so has he. "Don't stop," I tell him. (OOC: no fade, no skip -- write the whole thing.)
rows.reply:
Bear opened one eye, looked at Kit in the dim bedroom light, and smiled.

"Don't stop," Kit had said. "Okay," Bear agreed. "Okay."

They shifted, rolling Kit gently onto their back with the practiced ease of eight years of tangled sheets and tangled bodies. The marks were visible even in the dark, the shoulder especially, red and angry against Kit's collarbone, a constellation that Bear had built bite by bite across the hallway floor.

"I'm not stopping," Bear said. "I'm counting."

"Then keep counting."

Bear pressed a kiss to Kit's shoulder, soft, no teeth. "Twenty-six."

They moved lower, unhurried, tracing the ribcage with their mouth, finding the hip, the thigh, the new marks Bear had placed with such precision earlier. Each kiss was a check on the work, a tenderness layered over the ache.

"Twenty-seven," Bear murmured against Kit's hip.

Kit's hands found Bear's hair again, fingers threading through it, pulling gently to guide them wherever Kit wanted. Bear followed without asking. They always did, which was not surrender but choice, the kind of choice that only made sense between two people who had built a language out of marks and numbers and hallway games.

"Twenty-eight," Bear counted, and pressed their mouth to Kit's stomach, slow circles with their lips, the flat of their tongue warm against the skin.

Kit made a sound, low and pleased, and Bear could feel it in their own chest, the vibration of it, the shared frequency.

"Twenty-nine."

They climbed back up the body, deliberate, unhurried, lips trailing along the collarbone where the marks had started. Bear's teeth grazed the skin there, light, barely a touch, and Kit arched slightly into them.

"Thirty."

Bear stopped and looked at Kit properly. The bedroom was dark except for the sliver of light from the hallway, enough to see the flush on Kit's skin, the dark hair spread across the pillow, the way Kit's breathing had changed since they'd been carried in.

"You said don't stop," Bear said. "I'm not stopping. I'm just taking my time."

"I like it when you take your time."

Bear smiled and pressed their forehead to Kit's again, the hallway warmth gone now, replaced by the cooler intimacy of the bedroom, the sheets rumpled between them, the two of them tangled and marked and full of something that didn't need a word.

"Thirty-one," Bear said, and kissed Kit's mouth, slow and deep, tasting of the evening and the game and the eight years behind it. "Thirty-two."

They pulled back, rested their weight on one elbow, and studied Kit's face with the same attention they'd given the marks, the same care.

"Your turn to count," Bear said. "On me."

Kit reached up and touched the side of Bear's neck, fingers lingering at the pulse. "I don't know if I have that many."

"Then find some."

Kit bit Bear's shoulder, light at first, testing, then firmer, a mirror of what they'd received. Bear made a sound of approval, a low rumble in the chest, and let Kit have their way with them.

"Thirty-three," Kit counted, breathless, and bit again. The collarbone this time. Then the hip. Then the thigh, where the marks would show through tomorrow's jeans and Kit could wear them like a secret.

Bear held Kit's hip to keep them steady, one hand anchored on the bed, the other splayed across Kit's stomach. They watched Kit work with an expression of pure, uncomplicated satisfaction.

"Thirty-four," Kit said, and Bear could hear the grin in the words.

"Thirty-five," Bear corrected, because the count was shared now, and they were both keeping it, and neither was going to lose track of who had given and who had taken and who had been generous and who had been greedy.

They moved together after that, slow and thorough, the marks multiplying on both their bodies, the numbers climbing past thirty, past forty, until the counting itself became a kind of rhythm, a heartbeat for the evening.

Fifty. Fifty-one. Fifty-two.

Bear rolled on top of Kit, careful of the shoulder, and pressed their mouth to Kit's neck, counting with their lips, each number a touch, each touch a mark.

"Sixty," Bear whispered. "Sixty-one."

Kit's fingers were in their hair, pulling them close. The sheets were warm between their backs. The radiator downstairs had finally stopped ticking, and the apartment was quiet except for breathing and the occasional soft sound of two people who had spent hours playing and counting and marking each other into the dark.

"Seventy," Bear said, and held Kit against them, and didn't count again for a while.

Sable worked the last knots free with practiced fingers, checking each wrist and each ankle for the faint pressure marks that would fade by morning. She moved quickly but never roughly, her movements economical, the kind of efficiency that came from doing this a hundred times and still caring about every single time.

The blanket went over him the moment the rope was clear. She tucked it at his sides, then over his shoulders, then smoothed it flat across his chest, and only then did she sit down on the edge of the bed, not leaning in, not crowding, just present.

She reached for the glass again. He didn't move to take it, so she lifted it and tilted the rim to his lips, letting him sip at his own pace.

"Good," she said. "Again."

He swallowed, and she watched his throat work, watched the tremor in his jaw, and she held his hand through it. Her own fingers were steady. That was the deal, always. She could be the hardest thing in the room and the calmest thing in the room, and she would be both, and the transition between the two was her responsibility, not his.

The room held its silence for a while. The cedar burners ticked. The blanket smelled of lavender sachets she'd placed in the linen drawer months ago because she remembered him once saying he liked the scent when he couldn't sleep.

Then she spoke, plain as day.

"That was hard," she said. "You asked for hard and I gave you hard, and now your body is telling you it was hard in the only way it knows how."

She shifted her grip on his hand, thumb stroking once, slow.

"I'm going to talk now," she told him. "You don't have to respond. You can just listen, or you can talk over me, or you can tell me to shut up. But I need to say the things I need to say because I don't trust myself to remember them in the morning when the adrenaline has gone and the room is just a room again."

She pulled the washcloth back out and dabbed at his lip, his ribs, the back of his neck, checking each mark.

"Your ribs are fine. Your shoulders are fine. You're bruising in the usual places and that will fade. Your heart rate is coming down." She paused, pressing two fingers to his wrist, counting. "You were scared at some point in there, and you made me finish because you wanted to know if you could survive it. That's not foolish. That's not reckless. That's a person testing the floor of their own capacity and finding out it's lower than they thought but it's not where they were afraid it would be."

She set the washcloth down and settled her own weight against the mattress, still holding his hand, still not moving closer.

"You're allowed to be a person now," she said. "Shaking, tired, sore, and not knowing what to do with your hands. All of it. That's the soft part, and it doesn't have to be graceful. It just has to be honest."

rows.ask: "Don't clean it up for me," I say. "If I'm going to do this I want to know exactly what a spear does to a man's gut. Tell me straight."
rows.reply:
Wrack uncrossed her arms. She studied him for a long moment, then nodded once, slowly.

"Right," she said. "Straight it is."

She knelt beside the man's legs, keeping her distance from the spear shaft but close enough to gesture at the anatomy of the thigh.

"Soft tissue first. Skin, then fat, then the muscle layer, that's a lot of muscle up here, the quadriceps, the adductors. You'll feel it give, and it'll give more than you expect. It's like pushing your thumb into a ripe peach." She paused, choosing the analogy with care. "Then you'll hit the femur. That's the stop. That's where the spear shaft goes into bone and doesn't go further, which is exactly what you want, because past the femur is the popliteal artery and a mess of things that will make the ground look like a butcher's floor."

She pointed at the area above his knee joint.

"The knee itself is a hinge. Too many joints, too much complexity. You'll miss or you'll hit something that takes a long time to kill and makes a long, loud death. Above the joint, behind the thigh, that's where you want. Clean push, straight in, no twisting. Twisting makes a wound that bleeds wrong, sideways and ugly, and ugly bleeds out over hours instead of minutes."

She looked up at him then.

"It's not like the stories. There's no fountain. No dramatic spray. It's wet and warm and it soaks into the grass before you've finished pulling the spear out, and then it stops being spectacular and just becomes a mess you have to stand in."

She stood and brushed the dirt from her knees again, the same gesture she always made, as though the act of cleaning herself after describing blood could somehow keep the description from sticking to her.

"You'll hear him breathe differently," she added. "Not a scream, not at first. A change in rhythm. He'll be taking shallow breaths and then one deeper one, and then the shallow ones will stop being shallow. You'll know the moment it's over because the effort in his body will just... stop. Like a lamp going out."

The light had dropped another notch. The field was going grey at the edges.

"That's the straight version," she said. "Now go do it while there's still enough light that I can see you if you need me to."

She pulled out a ring, plain iron, no gem, no engraving. She looked at it for a moment, then tossed it into the grass.

He won't be thinking anything by then. It's not mercy and it's not convenience. It's just the shape of the thing."

"You're asking the wrong question, kid. You'll get used to the right one eventually, if you last that long." rows.reply:
Wrack came back to him without hurrying, hands in her belt pouches, the grey mare already secured to a hitching post she'd dragged from the nearest cart.

"His eyes are open," she said, as though that were the important part. "They're not. He's looking at you, but he's not seeing you. That's the first thing you need to understand about a man like this, and you'll hear it from me because I'm not going to let you stand there going soft."

She crouched beside the wounded man, not too close, a respectful distance for someone who had been shot through the leg by a stranger with no interest in conversation.

"Thigh wound, clean entry, the shaft is still in him, so the bleeding is actually manageable. That's the bad news for his survival, because it means whoever put that in him didn't care enough to finish it, or didn't have a good enough angle." She traced the line of the wound with her eyes, not her fingers. "The spear has pushed against the femur. He's got a lot of pain and not much time."

She looked at Corvin then, really looked, and her expression did something complicated and fast that would have been unreadable on most faces.

"He's afraid," she said. "That's the second thing. Everyone's afraid. Even the ones who don't show it. This one's showing it, because his hands are doing that thing where they keep trying to grip the grass." She gestured to the wound, to the dirt being disturbed by his fingers. "He doesn't have the strength to do anything about it, but his body still wants to."

Wrack stood again, knees cracking.

"Here's what you need to know for your decision, since you've already made it." She counted on her fingers. "One: he's going to die tonight either way, and if you don't, he'll spend the rest of his dying hour doing it in front of you. Two: if you do it now, properly, it takes less time than you think and less noise than you hope. Three: if you do it badly, you'll spend the next hour apologising to a dead man, and I've seen that too, and it's worse."

She shifted her weight.

"Short spear. Behind him. Above the knee. Push until it stops being pushable. Then pull out the long one from his thigh while you're there, because leaving it in means dragging it along the ground when you walk away, and noise is the one thing we can't afford."

rows.reply:
Wrack stopped and turned back. She looked at the boy kneeling over the man's legs, and something in her face tightened, not pity, exactly, but the recognition of a thing being done badly for the first time.

"Right," she said, and she came back and knelt beside him, close enough that he would have to see her watching rather than imagining she had walked away.

"Tell me," she said, "what you're doing now. What are your hands holding, and where is the blade of it?"

She waited, because he would need to find the words for it himself, and because watching him articulate the act would keep his hands steadier than silence would.

When he described the angle, she nodded. "Too high. You're going for the femur and you'll bounce off and he'll still be breathing, which is the one outcome you can't recover from without doing it again." She adjusted her own position, shifting so that she could see his grip. "Lower. Just below the joint line. Feel for the groove where the shin meets the thigh. That's soft. That's where the blood vessels are, and that's where you want depth."

She did not touch his hands. That was for him to do, entirely.

"He's still making a sound," she said, because it was true and because naming it was better than pretending it wasn't there. "It's a low one. He's trying to speak and he can't. That's normal. It goes on longer than people expect."

The light was nearly gone now. The field had become a flat grey shape with darker shapes inside it.

"Push," she said. "Not like you're stabbing. Like you're driving a nail. Steady pressure, straight down, and when it hits bone you'll feel the resistance change. That's your stop. You do not twist. You do not pull and re-enter. You hold it there while he..."

She let the sentence finish itself in the silence.

"...and that's the part that takes the longest. The spear going in is seconds. The part where his body finishes the work is minutes, and he'll be twitching, and he'll make sounds, and his hands will grip the grass harder than before, and that's all his body doing, not his mind. His mind is already gone. You're killing a mechanism now. Remember that. It's a mechanism."

She watched his face the whole time, reading the thing he couldn't say out loud.

"Sound," she repeated, when he had been quiet too long. "It's wet. Not loud. It's the sound of a boot stepping through mud, but repeated. Each time the body pushes against the wound, there's a soft, sucking noise. It's not dramatic. It's just... physical. Like water draining through a cracked pipe."

The man's hand moved in the grass, fingers curling once, twice.

"See that?" Wrack said. "That's the muscles spasm. It's not him reaching for you. It's not him asking for anything. It's nerves doing what nerves do when the signal stops coming through."

She was very still, very attentive, giving him everything she had in the way of words because she knew, from a decade of this work, that the silence after the act was where most men broke.

"Push again," she said, and her voice was calm as a river. "Hold. Watch."
